en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Master Rulin Tianru:
The World-Honored One entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Mahākāśyapa, commanding that it be widely transmitted and taught;
this constitutes the school of the "Special Transmission Outside the Teachings. After twenty-eight transmissions, it reached Bodhidharma, who sat facing a wall at Shaolin.
The Way of the Mind first spread in the eastern lands. It was transmitted five times to Lingnan, and another five times to Hebei.

Then, after six further transmissions, it reached Master Ciming Yuan of Hunan, where the lineage flourished even more, branching out and diversifying while remaining under the seal of a single Dharma.
This is just as shells, jade, gold, and pearls—though diverse and manifold—are each produced from within the imperial treasury. Ciming...
Directly descending through ten transmissions, it reached Master Xueyan Qin, who smashed the "broken sand bowl" with a single blow, reducing it to a hundred fragments;

his fierce blows and scorching shouts were applied without distinction between the intimate and the distant. Furthermore, after two more transmissions, it reached National Teacher Puying Ben, who sat firmly at Mount Tianmu, where the waves of Dharma-nature surged like thunder throughout the age.
The Master has passed away; his disciples shall inherit his style to propagate [the teaching].

As for his teaching, where could it not be found? Yet, when seeking the authentic lineage that has been transmitted with absolute precision—one that responds skillfully and appropriately to every shifting condition and individual capacity—it is none other than the Venerable Master Rintei of Shōrin-in.
I have often cross-examined what I have heard from Zen practitioners throughout the four quarters, and my longing for this true sound has long endured. It was just as Master Kotei arrived.
He came from beneath the forest trees and showed me the *yulu* (recorded sayings) he had brought with him. I read several sections in haste, before I realized the volume was finished.
Although my old eyes were blurred and dim, they suddenly regained a hundredfold clarity and vigor, like a *maṇi* jewel in a room where light shines through six windows.
It is as if the finest essence (amṛta) has been poured upon one’s head, bringing clarity and coolness to the five internal organs.

This is sufficient to illuminate this degenerate age, to exert the strength to stem the turbulent waves, and to powerfully revitalize the legacy of the National Teacher (Guo-shi), serving as a banner of light for a hundred generations—all of this is contained herein.
As for what is called being like the udumbara flower, like an iron caltrop, like a cauldron of boiling oil, or like a hair-cutting sword, these too are to be contemplated within this.

The compiler possesses his own discerning eye. I am already in my dotage; yet when I return south in the future, I shall still support myself with a staff to visit the forest retreats once more, to satisfy my longing and thirst for the Dharma.
Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianru, respectfully composed by Yang Zongrui of Changsha, Imperial Scholar and Grand Master for the Cultivation of Benevolence,
Director of the Bureau of Memorial Drafting, and Joint Compiler of the National History, on the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Jichou,
the ninth year of the Zhizheng era.
In the past, Master Zhongfeng propagated the Way at Mount Tiantai in Hangzhou. Students gathered there like clouds.
After he passed away thirty years ago, it was Chan Master Tianru Ze of our Luling who was able to shoulder the weight of his transmission and uphold the expectations placed upon him.
He buried his brilliance and polished away his splendor, yet over time his virtues became even more prominent; standing tall and solitary, he was indeed Master Tianru Ze. Chan.
Once the Master had received the secret seal, the great monasteries vied with one another to invite him.
He subsequently withdrew to Lion Grove (Shizi Lin) at Wumen, where he lived alone in a single room amidst the clouds, remaining detached and indifferent to the affairs of the age.

Nevertheless, those from all quarters who sought the Way took refuge solely with the Chan Master; thus, his words spread widely during his lifetime without waiting for formal compilation. His disciple Shanyu...
I have briefly recorded this in seven fascicles. The śramaṇa Master Ju of the Tiantai school, deeming it capable of awakening those who come to study, has carved it for circulation.
Alas! The Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma is attained only by those who receive the subtle smile; outside the teaching, there is nothing else to be transmitted separately.
Why labor to point directly at the human mind? As for the terms "separate," "transmission," and "direct pointing," they are intended merely to cause one to realize it for oneself.
I have attained it. When I observe the words of the Chan Master, they are like a bird flying through the sky or the moon reflected in water;
whether spreading or contracting, opening or closing, shallow or deep, they respond to all circumstances, yet they transcendently leave no trace to be sought.

If a student can rely on these words to forget the words themselves, not becoming stuck in the traces but attaining their ultimate intent, only then will they know that which stands forth majestic and solitary.

How could this have been obtained from any person? I once traveled through the region of Wu on business; though I admired the lofty character of Master Chan, I had not yet found the leisure to visit him.
Later, while Master Siju of Yichun was traveling to Mount Wutai, he placed his writings in a satchel at Jiqiu and presented them to me.
Thus, I was able to compose a preface for the opening fascicle, and I rejoice in this encounter with the joy of the Dharma.
Preface by Wei Su of Linchuan, Court Gentleman for Literary Service at the Hanlin Academy, Acting Director of the Bureau of Imperial Edicts,
and Compiler of the National History, on the *xinmao* day of the first month of the fifth lunar month in the summer of the ninth year of the Zhizheng era.
Preface to the Supplementary Record of Chan Master Tianru.
Chan Master Tianru was originally from Yongxin in Luling and belonged to a distinguished clan. My own family is from Chaling in Xiang.
The Master’s residence was only some twenty-odd *li* away, and we frequently visited one another for matrimonial alliances; thus, I had early on heard of the Master’s reputation.
Furthermore, I was honored to travel extensively with the Master’s younger brother, Xingyuan, and so I have previously read the poems and prose he composed.
At that time, I was merely in my early twenties; my knowledge of him was limited to this extent, and I did not know the Master.
As for the Way of the Master, what has it become? Since wandering between the Huai and Zhe regions, I have frequently heard that the Master’s reputation grows ever more prominent;
I know that the Master’s Way is increasingly full and his practice ever more extensive, and those who receive its benefits are ever more numerous.

Thus, I have begun to regret that I had not yet been able to see him once. Recently, while in the Wu region, before my seat was even warm, I went to visit the Master at Shizi Lin (Lion Grove). At that time—
At that time, the Master had already abandoned brush and ink, no longer discoursed on written characters, and ceased all social interaction;

thus, there was no way to witness the Master’s creative expressions and compositions firsthand. Consequently, I obtained from his disciples a single volume of a supplementary collection of the Master’s past poems, prose, and correspondence.
Having read it several times, I could not bear to let go of my hands; for this volume is truly the very essence of his legacy.

These are merely incidental remarks; the subtle phrasing and profound meanings certainly do not reside therein. Nevertheless, when teaching others, the Master invariably revealed them according to their individual capacities, manifesting them everywhere.
If one can seek [the truth] by means of these [remarks], one may still gain some slight insight into the Master’s way of practicing the Path.
Moreover, the Master’s *Lengyan jing huijie* (Collected Explanations of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) and his *Jingyao yulu* (Recorded Sayings of the Essential Points) have both already been published.
If readers gain realization according to what they perceive, then the Master’s Way is present right here;

how could there be any distinction between the refined and the coarse, or the fundamental and the derivative? Having heard the Master’s name early in my life, I was only able to meet him in my later years.
Now, having obtained this compilation and ventured to examine it, I have composed this preface for it.
On the first day of the twelfth month of the ninth year of Zhizheng, the year of Jichou, Li Qi, a former Assistant Director of Education for the Jiangzhe and other regions,
holding the rank of Chengwulang, respectfully writes this preface.
Preface to the Supplementary Record of Shizilin:
The school of Shaolin is one that does not rely on written words; it is called "Direct Pointing. For one who has grasped this pointing, even the texts of the Tripitaka are but dregs;
how much more so the so-called prose and poetry of the world! Yet, as for this school’s attainment... [the text continues].
The Patriarch [Bodhidharma] then composed the "Inscription on Faith," and in the Yongjia era, there was also the "Song of Realizing the Way.
Is this not to contradict his own fundamental principle? Those who understand say it is not so; rather, these works serve to assist in manifesting the Way of Direct Pointing.
From that time onward, the patriarchal masters, in their exhortations and invigorating teachings, could not help but speak; thus, one may trace back to the source.
As the distant branches spread, scholars of devious learning and peripheral knowledge arise one after another.
Those whose talents and insights are so preeminent that they produce prose and poetry—though their poetry may be poetry and their prose may be prose—is it truly what the connoisseurs would prize?
Now, the Venerable Tiantu of Shizilin received the Dharma from National Teacher Puying Zhongfeng Ben.
He then loudly proclaimed his Way to rectify the lineage of Shaolin; responding universally to circumstances as they arose, there was nothing he did not encompass.
His disciples compiled a separate record of his poetry and prose, in addition to his recorded sayings, totaling six volumes.
I have privately examined the principles and intentions expressed therein, and find that all are sufficient to elucidate the Way of Direct Pointing. How could this be merely what the world calls...
Of poetry and prose!

Now, at the beginning of His Majesty’s reign, there was an imperial decree granting the National Preceptor’s *yulu* (recorded sayings) along with his poetry and prose to be carved into printing blocks and included in the Tripitaka for circulation throughout the world. And so, upon examination—

There are those who harbor certain doubts regarding this matter. Therefore, by means of this preface to the separate record of Chan Master Tianru, I have been able to set forth my humble views, so that those who doubt may know there exists a teaching that aids in its clarification.
In the summer of the Jichou year of the Zhizheng era, the humble countryman Yuanzhe,
a Retired Scholar of the Hanlin Academy and Director of the Bureau of History,
respectfully presents this preface for the Table of Contents of the Recorded Sayings of Venerable Tianru of Shizi Forest.

Compiled by his junior disciple, Shōgo.
The Master did not reside permanently on the mountain; therefore, there are no records of his formal ascending of the hall (*shàngtáng*) or entering the room (*rùshì*).

Nevertheless, he would sometimes respond to the requests of monks for instruction, or engage in spirited exchanges with fellow practitioners, or offer seasonal greetings, or converse with visiting guests.
Regarding the circumstances for citing evidence: sometimes, based on a particular event, ancient precedents were cited to awaken beginners.
These were recorded according to when they were heard, without regard for chronological order; they are collectively titled "Instructions to the Assembly" (Shizhong).
The World-Honored One said: "I have the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvana;
I entrust them to Mahākāśyapa so that they may be widely transmitted. The Master said: "Today, this unworthy descendant wishes to question the Old Man with the Yellow Face:
from where did you obtain these two things?"
In various quarters there are the "sea-slug Chan," the "sea-shell Chan," and the "iron-spade Chan. This old monk’s, however, is the "water gourd Chan":
it moves as soon as it is touched and turns as soon as it is pressed down; it is so lively and slippery that you have no way to deal with it.
Yesterday, the return of the first yang began; I hear it has already taken root. Everyone, bring it up for me and look!
To practice while clinging to the dharma is like an ox pulling a millstone; the headless fellows of Guansi can exert their full strength, yet they achieve only half.
To practice without clinging to the dharma is like a millstone pulling an ox; this mountain monk, unable to restrain his impatience, can likewise speak only of half.
Rest, rest. By what dharma is it realized? By what dharma is it cultivated? Recognizing one's nature as it flows with the stream, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
Even where there is no elegance, one is elegant. [He suddenly brandishes his staff and says: "I cannot bear this Great Master Yunmen," he said. Furthermore, he said:
Guanyin uses money to buy sesame cakes; when he lets go of his hand, they turn out to be steamed buns. Strike the staff!
Were it not for the wild geese arriving last night, who would have seen the autumn at the sea gate?
Sometimes he extends the Buddha-hand; sometimes he lets out a donkey’s hoof—wrong. Sometimes he slaps the meditation seat; sometimes he strikes the incense table—wrong.
Sometimes his tongue grows hair and his lips grow mold; his staff has long leaned against the corner of the wall;
Linji and Deshan’s nostrils are all at once pierced through—wrong. O Zen practitioners, recognize these three points of error.
Yes. This old monk invites you to eat noodles made without flour.
Where the Buddhas and Patriarchs have not traveled, travel a single step; where the Buddhas and Patriarchs have not spoken, speak a single word.

This is a place where Buddhas and Patriarchs have not spoken; yet this old monk has spoken here. He gave a shout and said: "It is better to suffer with a person of wisdom."
Reproach: Do not converse with those who lack wisdom.

Mazu’s shout startled Baizhang; Huangbo was so shocked he spat out his tongue. This is an unforgivable enmity that cannot be shared under the same sky; its resentment has penetrated deep into the very bones.
Although he struck Linji three times and clearly knew that neither side was affected, it was only later when Linji said, "Not much," that he first realized the staff was like an iron stake.
From then on, whenever he encountered someone, he would shout at them; this was precisely because his pain had not yet been fully endured.
Yet toward others, he spoke of the "moss branch whisk" and said, "If one were to strike me once more after further reflection, no one would be able to bring their hand down. This—
Who has ever recognized this mind? Now, it fills the eyes; every one of these descendants knows how to shout "Horse! and shout "Ox!

There is only this beardless bearded man who, seeing injustice on the road, is burned by a fire-serpent to the face until his whole body is hot. O Zen adepts, what a pity! What a pity!
Zhaozhou spoke the word "wu" (no). Opening one's mouth reveals the heart and liver. Why then do you all create obstacles for yourselves?
At that time, a monk requested instruction, saying: "All sentient beings, down to the smallest insect, possess Buddha-nature. Why is it that this dog alone has none?"
The Master said, "Do not speak of the dog. Even if you were to ask him whether Śākyamuni and Maitreya possess Buddha-nature, he would also say 'no.
The monk said, "Zhaozhou’s Chan is on the tips of his lips; why is it that he only knows how to say the word 'no'?
The Master said, "Zhaozhou’s insight only reached this point. The monk said, "Does the Master not approve of Zhaozhou?"
The monk said, "Is it so? The Master said, "Yes. The monk said, "Zhaozhou was an ancient Buddha; why did you, Master, refuse to acknowledge him?
The Master said, "Where is Zhaozhou now? He then gave a shout.
Nanquan said, "At eighteen, I already knew how to manage my livelihood. Zhaozhou said, "At eighteen, I already knew how to break up the family and scatter the household.
The Master said, "Who would have known that Nanquan’s very livelihood was precisely the breaking up of the family and scattering of the household?"
This mountain monk dares to guarantee that Old Zhaozhou did not recognize Nanyuan’s thoroughgoing poverty;

he mistakenly suspected that his livelihood was private property, yet he spoke of "breaking up the family and dispersing the estate. Someone might say, "Zhaozhou did not mistakenly suspect; rather, it was you, the Master, who mistakenly suspected.
Thereupon, this mountain monk claps his hands, laughs "he-he," and says to him: "Excellent! It is well that this mountain monk mistakenly suspected as well."
Zhaozhou’s lack of doubt is even better.

Usage. At all times, tell me: is this the same as Linji’s, or is it different?

those who linger in phrases are deluded. To conceive a thought is already an error; to stir a single notion is already to go astray. Not so!
He is like one who stands rooted to the spot, dead on the ground. Therefore, when you encounter him suddenly under the gate of our Ancestors, there is no place for you to turn back;
he acts according to the mandate, leaving you with no opening to speak. To take even a single step is to face an iron wall and a silver mountain;

by the time you blink your eyes, it is already a flash of lightning or a spark from flint. Even if the Buddhas of the three periods of time were to appear before you, they would have no choice but to retreat, gazing at the precipice.

Thus, you, Venerable Sir, have no sinews in your eyes and no strength in your wrists. You are like one trying to control six horses with a rotten rope—though you know clearly the six horses cannot be controlled.

Knocking at the eastern fence and beating on the western wall, he divines by the wind’s direction and the flight of birds, speaking of yellow paths and black omens.

"To slander oneself is to slander all sentient beings of the great earth.

"Friends fill the world under heaven, but how many can truly know my heart? A monk asked, "Regarding Nanquan’s killing of the cat—what was his meaning?
He replied, "The living lives by itself. The monk asked, "And regarding Zhaozhou saving the cat—what was that? He replied, "The dead dies by itself.

The exchange continued. The monk said, "I do not understand. He replied, "If you do not understand, go ask the two head seats of the two halls.

Each of you must take care of your own wretched life.
The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally without mystery or marvel. It simply requires each of you to know that the eyes are horizontal and the nose is straight, and then rest there.
Now, in this assembly before me, those with noses all have them straight; those with eyes all have them horizontal. Facing one another face-to-face, what then?
One does not know this. Even to the point of seeing the sun by day and seeing the stars by night; eating rice when hungry and adding clothes when cold. The lantern and the pillar intersect;
the kitchen and the storehouse vie for prominence with the main gate.
This is a matter within your own eyes and nostrils—something everyone knows. When the fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, it strikes the nostrils of Śakra.

If you know it, I grant that you know; but have you ever attained immediate rest? Since you have not yet attained immediate rest—
Do not let this pass by in negligence; you must apply yourself with fierce energy in a state of cool clarity and search for it yourself.

On the forehead. The Master called to the assembly, saying, "This fellow was originally afraid of birth and death. How could he possibly understand this old monk’s Chan?

Suzhou’s fool! Suzhou’s fool! Outside the gate, the snow piles high. To the very bone, let him freeze once more."
While receiving inquiries from newly arrived monks in Hangzhou, he addressed the assembly: "The Buddha-dharma is in decline; the monastic groves are in autumnal twilight.

The worthy and sages are hidden away, while false teachings blaze ever more fiercely. *Tut!* What kind of talk is this? Four or five hundred lanes of flowering willows and poplars, two or three thousand towers of pipes and strings.
Who do you believe when they say Suzhou has them, or Changzhou has them?"
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? Yunmen said, "There is porridge and rice on the long benches.

The Master [Dongshan] said, "The lame-legged Great Master only knows how to enjoy what is already present; he does not know the hardships of plowing and sowing. If you were to ask me, I would say to him:
'From the First Day of the Year to the Human Day, there has never been one that was not cloudy. I suspect this year’s peach and plum blossoms will be the same.'"
How noble! It is not as good as planting crabapples at the bottom of a well.
A man comes from Jiangxi carrying a report from Hunan: it is announced that in Huaizhou the oxen are eating the grain, while in Yizhou the horses have bloated bellies.
Beneath the Lion Grove, hot water is being prepared for tea; one idly watches the tea-servant’s three horses and nine bundles of tea leaves in disarray.
When the Buddha arrived, he was invited to stay outside the gate. Where else could there be a spare room for White Cloud?
It is not that this old monk refuses to open his doors or reject things; rather, I simply do not wish to compete with others in their own market.
You now eat the food of various quarters and wear the roof of various quarters. (Holding up a whisk) There is only the nostrils and the eyes.
"It is, however, right here within this old monk. You practitioners of Zen, do not make false conjectures. If you attempt to grasp it, errors and disputes will arise;
to err by a hair’s breadth is to miss the mark by a thousand miles. He threw down his whisk and descended from the seat.
The monkey on the summit of Flying Eagle Peak does not submit to human fetters. I do not dare hope that you will extinguish your wind of joy or quench the fire of your anger;
I only hope that you will forget a hundred hungers with one full meal and, for a moment, transcend the distinction between self and other.
Only then will you recognize that the flavor within the bland is enduring—sour pears cannot be exchanged for *bimba* fruits.
When the former companion arrived, he addressed the assembly: "How much better it would have been not to have passed through the net!
Even if you suddenly attain a point of entry, it will be very difficult indeed even for a fellow traveler."

Sometimes the words reach [the meaning] while the intent does not; sometimes the intent reaches [the meaning] while the words do not. Sometimes there is difference within the same, and sameness within the different.
Sometimes it appears the same yet is not the same; it appears different yet is not different. Thus it is said: "To raise [the whisk] and fail to look back is a mistake.
Though the elder sister-in-law is the wife of my elder brother, the nun is nonetheless a woman.
Last night, the two Great Beings Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra debated the Buddha-dharma without ceasing. I gave them a shout and said, "Stop, stop!
Listen to my instructions: You, Master Hao of Yuyuan, are placed upon the waistband of your trousers inside Guoqing Temple."
"I am teaching you how to light fires and sweep the floors. Now, here in my presence, you do not pick up a blade of grass lying horizontally nor grasp one standing upright.
Having eaten ready-made gruel and rice, you still wish to contend over idle vexations. Why do you not reflect upon where this comes from?
Thereupon, the two great masters smiled and were resolved.
"How many people have been deceived by the claim that 'seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood'? Everyone says that attaining Buddhahood is urgent while seeing one's nature is not.

They make their thoughts regarding attaining Buddhahood frantic, yet their thoughts regarding seeing their nature remain lax. Alas, the more lax they become, the further away they drift; the more frantic they become, the slower they progress."
They only crave fine food to eat, yet they do not believe it is made of rice. Today, I, this mountain monk, respond to circumstances as they arise;
for their sake, I have shifted the pivot of the discourse, changing it to "seeing the Buddha and perfecting one's nature," or otherwise, changing it to "becoming a Buddha and seeing one's nature.
Is this not delightful? There was a man who, however, scolded me for being perverse and contrary to principle, so I spoke to him gently:
The Way. Do you not hear that the sagely nature has nothing it does not penetrate? Whether following or opposing, all are skillful means.
You may not revile me, nor may you revile you. Wait, then, for a person of clear eyes to pass judgment.
"I have already met you before your parents were even born. Do you recognize this old monk? Whether you recognize me or not, set that aside for a moment.
As his eyes flickered, [the Master] struck him a blow straight through the chest with his fist.
There is a man who, having seen through it, would not even wish to be a Buddha. For him, I, this old monk, prostrate three full bows as a witness.
As for the Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, and the elder monks of the world—they have mouths that can only hang upon the wall.
Zhou Shanzong of Jiangling rebuilt the Xiaofeihong Bridge and addressed the assembly: "The Xiaofeihong Bridge is within Lion Grove;
beneath the bridge, the breeze through the bamboo is as cool as water. The old dragon has flown away and the new dragon arrives; my crossing upon the dragon begins from this very moment.
Let everyone go back and forth as they please—there is neither this shore nor that. Treading firmly on the ground, one is like an elephant."
The King turned his body; with a single leap he was like a lion.
The venerable masters of the various quarters offered their hands in different ways: some extended their hands from outside the gate, while others extended them from within the gate.

Some say that outside the gate there is great extravagance, while inside the gate there is great frugality; others say that inside the gate there is great extravagance, while outside the gate there is great frugality.

In either case, one is merely entering the grass to seek a person; whether inside or out, they cannot avoid laughing at one another. Let us set aside this mutual derision for a moment: what, then, do you call the "gate"?
If you say that having no gate constitutes the Dharma-gate, then what do you call "inside" and "outside"?
Students exhaust their strength and energy while cherishing the goal of saving effort; yet to strive with effort to save effort is an error.
To not strive with effort while seeking to save effort is likewise an error. How, then, can one avoid falling into error? One is forbidden from traveling at night;
one must arrive by the break of dawn.
Do you all know where this mountain monk stands? Looking up is heaven; looking down is hell.
Do you all know where this mountain monk falls? It is best to sleep soundly in the water; it is best to bathe in the fire.
While at Guoqing Temple, as they were roasting eggplants, Shide struck the Rector with a bamboo skewer.
The Rector cried out, "Look at this madman! Shide said, "Heaven! Heaven! Hanshan asked, "Why did you hit him?
Shide replied, "How much salt and sauce have been wasted! The Master said, "A large tree is wrapped in large bark; a small tree in small."
The skin is wrapped around it. Once the rector has accepted the discarded items and inspected them, the discarder himself must also be subject to inspection by others.
Do you know where the discarder ought to be inspected? Try to say.
In the school of the patch-robed monks, there is gathering and releasing. When released: "The spring tide, with the rain, rushes on late.

When gathered: "At the wild crossing, no one is there; the boat drifts alone. What is it like when neither gathering nor releasing? "If you are not a man who plays in the tide, do not enter the surging waves."
The jade dragon stirs the sea and a thousand rivers swell; the ocean-patrolling yakṣa whips his iron staff.
Startled, the iron ox of Shanzhou rises up and swallows the great elephant of Jiazhou. You all must grip the head of this dead snake firmly and not let it move;
if you move it, there shall be thirty blows of the staff.
Those who rely on words lose their way; they die in fire and are buried in water. Those who cling to phrases remain deluded; they tread upon soil above and mire below.
Without relying on words and without clinging to phrases, the great river flows eastward and the setting sun goes west.

The Abbot of Jiangshan arrived; he addressed the assembly: "Full presentation and partial presentation; the complete treasury and the partial treasury. Ten inches make one foot; ten feet make one fathom.
A foot has the form of a foot; a pair of scissors has the pattern of scissors. Even a whisk is used to strike a circular mark."
Carrying his staff across his shoulder, he pays no heed to others. How could Master Zhi be a mere idle monk?
When he comes face-to-face, how can one entrust him to the steward? A leaking bamboo sieve; a stainless wooden ladle.
Small Vehicle coin-strands; Great Vehicle well-ropes. If one learns to answer in such a manner, one could provide a million answers in a single day.
How cleverly he turns and twists! Yet, when questioned about the true host, he remains ignorant of its whereabouts. This "spirit-tortoise" knows only how to deceive others;
before it has even died, people have already pried it out of its shell.
The donor has finished constructing a wooden shrine. He addresses the assembly: "Birth-and-death and nirvana—six times six is thirty-six. Impermanence and its like do not come;
I shall first close my eyes. O practitioners of Zen, tell me: as for Tianru right now, is he dead or alive?
To kill the living Tianru, yet to bring the dead Tianru back to life—for this very reason, Buddha after Buddha undergoes saṃsāra. It is solely because of these few matters.

My son, relying on the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra*, I have set a goal for one hundred and twenty days to enter a period of seclusion (*yan-shi*) for the summer retreat. I have written this verse upon the door to show the assembly:
"A firm barrier established upon level ground; Even if a Buddha comes, there is no path to meet him. It is clearly right here in the ordinary."
It is as if separated by a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks.
My fellow practitioner, Ceng Guanzhi, established the foundation for the pagoda at West Original Spring (Dingshui Xiyuan). He addressed the assembly, saying:

"I and all the Buddhas and patriarchs share the same joy and the same suffering; we die together and are buried at the same time. In the same pit, there is no different soil. Although it is thus, within this...
There are also some points of difference. I, this old monk, have given you prior notice today:
when the grave is being covered with earth in the lower realm, everyone must watch closely; he will submit to death but will not submit to burial. This fellow has always been thus.
He gave an instruction to the assembly on account of a specific matter. Striking the left side of the meditation seat with his whisk, he said:
"Do not mistake it! Do not mistake it! The whole body is the illness; the whole body is the medicine. Striking the right side, he said: "Do not mistake it! Do not mistake it!
The whole body is the medicine; the whole body is the illness. Holding up the whisk, he asked: "Now that both medicine and illness have been forgotten—do you all see? Three coins for sale."
He pushed aside the black ladle, beat the earthen drum, and sang a village song. Uttering "Svāhā" wherever he went, he tossed his whisk and descended from the seat.
On New Year’s Eve, he addressed the assembly: "If you wish to realize the meaning of Buddha-nature, you must contemplate the conditions of time and season.
The old official records are not worth a single coin; there is another way of speaking beneath the Lion Grove. Once the thirtieth day of the twelfth month has passed, tomorrow morning—"
It was decided that this would be the New Year’s assembly.

It was universally announced ten days prior to the commencement of the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Monks from near and far gathered together; the secretary Jizang was appointed to serve as the presiding official for the assembly.
[The Master] said: "Pressing stones to extract oil; striking ice to seek fire. There are many in all quarters who find this unbearably bitter.
Selling water at the riverhead; teaching a monkey to climb a tree. I too have laughed at people in the past. Now, having no choice in the matter, I adapt the high to the low.
Carrying my staff and wooden block with me, I perform as the occasion demands. If you are one who has long been in the ranks of battle..."

One should not stand by with hands in one’s sleeves and look on; come forth and see how you may spur one another on. A monk asked, “The Buddhas hand over to the Buddhas, and the Patriarchs transmit to the Patriarchs.
Ultimately, what is it that is transmitted? The Master said, “Before your feet have even crossed the threshold, I have already given you thirty blows.
Another asked, “If Bodhidharma had not come to this eastern land, and the Second Patriarch had not gone to the Western Heaven, would there still be a way to benefit others?”
[The student] said, "There is not. The Master said, "There is. The student asked, "Furthermore, what is the Master’s way of acting for the sake of others?
The Master said, "In the bathhouse, the lantern laughs with half its mouth wide open. The student asked, "Is this not the place where the student turns himself around?
The Master said, "There is no road to ascend to heaven; there is no gate to enter the earth. The student said, "Today I am most fortunate to have heard the lion's roar."

The Master then gave a shout. The monk bowed. The Master said, "As for bowing, you may bow as you wish; however, this one shout has never fallen to the ground. He then struck his whisk and called to the assembly, saying:
"A single path prior to sound is not transmitted by the thousand sages. Without leaving this very place, it is eternally serene.
*Shout!* Taken up at random from the hand, it undergoes ten thousand transformations and a thousand changes. Seek it and you know it cannot be seen. *Shout!* Furthermore—"
Regarding the "Two Shouts," are they the same or different? If you say they are the same, how can they be two shouts? If you say they are different, how can they be but one?
If you understand it here, even a flame does not hinder a mosquito from alighting;
if you do not understand it here, a lotus fiber will pull up Mount Kunlun. If you are a person of stubborn nature, it matters not whether you understand or not. It matters not—
"Same or different. These two phrases spoken by the ancients and these two shouts of this mountain monk are simultaneously cast away beyond the boundaries of other worlds.
Behold, however, as the homeless practitioner conjures up divine heads and demonic faces:
sometimes he swallows the void of the ten directions, leaving all sentient and insentient beings with no way to emerge; sometimes he lets them out.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—let the myriad phenomena of the universe extend freely throughout the realm.
Arriving at this point, you may not call it "ever-abiding and profoundly still right where one is," nor may you call it "if you seek it, you will know it is invisible.
You may not view it as divided into two parts, nor may you view it as unified into one. It cannot be grasped.
One cannot bear to let it go. Within that which is unobtainable, one simply attains it. Do you understand?

Only through personal realization can its unfathomable depth be known. O practitioners of Zen: the single point of the ancestral school lies in its subtle nature of self-realization and self-attainment.
This subtlety of self-realization and self-attainment is a principle that is lively, liberated, and independent; it cannot be transmitted, nor can it be taught, nor can it be learned.

It cannot be grasped; it cannot be grasped. Even with wisdom like that of Śāriputra, one cannot fathom it through deliberation; even with eloquence like that of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, one cannot analyze it through discrimination.
Since the time of our own School’s founding, everyone has said there is "investigation" (can) and "study" (xue).
Who knows that what is self-realized and self-attained has no connection whatsoever with investigation and study? What the world calls "learning" and "speaking"—
It is entirely based on emotional consciousness, relying on cognition and understanding; this is precisely the root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas.

Even if you have cultivated seeds of wisdom from past lives and are not swayed by emotional consciousness, and even if you possess the correct cause from birth and are not obstructed by intellectual understanding—such that you recognize it with distinct clarity—it is still a dead dharma. To hope for the living meaning within it is as far as ten thousand miles.

Li Yaizhou: To speak with complete clarity, even if you have studied until you accord with the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, and can explain until you accord with the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, if you have not yet reached the state of being lively and free from dependence, it cannot help but remain entirely within the realm of dead dharmas.
Therefore, the Great Master Linji said: "In my place here, this is the living meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. When you need to use it, you use it; everything..."

Temporarily. Those former masters of great attainment who had grasped a small portion of the lively and unimpeded principle would respond to circumstances with spontaneity, acting both contrary to and in accordance with the flow.
Their ways were perplexing and deceptive, manifesting a thousand wonders and ten thousand marvels; this was called "the Great Function appearing before one," existing without fixed rules.
It was truly a place where you could find no foothold. For instance, one day Master Guizong Chiyen was weeding...
While staying in the grass-thatched hut, a presiding abbot-monk came to pay his respects. He happened to see a snake, whereupon the Master immediately cut it with his hoe.
The monk said, "I have long admired Guizong; it turns out you are merely a monk of coarse conduct. Guizong replied, "You are coarse, and I am coarse.
This kōan is treated as a point of confusion within the monastic community, yet they fail to realize that the old man Guizong was sitting in a state of total liberation.
He has no fixed abode; thus he grasps things crosswise and employs them upside down with complete freedom.

If you have not yet seen where this old fellow lands, how can you know where he employs his means? Since you do not yet know where this old fellow employs his means, how can you blame him for calling it a paradox?
Furthermore, when Master Danxia arrived at a village monastery, encountering snow and cold, he took a wooden Buddha statue.
He burned a wooden Buddha and turned toward it. The head of the monastery questioned him with astonishment. Huixia said, "I am burning it to obtain the *śarīra* (relics).
The head of the monastery said, "A wooden Buddha—how could it have any *śarīra*? Huixia replied, "Since there are no *śarīra*, let us burn another statue.

The head of the monastery became enraged and reviled him. The next day, the head of the monastery's eyebrows and beard fell out. This public case is even more perplexing; judging by the principle, how could there truly be a self?
To establish a principle for another’s reception [of the Dharma] is impossible; since such a principle does not exist, how can one ever find a point of entry?

Later, when Master Zhenjing resided at Guizong, he cited the karmic occasion of Chijian (Red-Eyed) and said: “Venerable assembly, consider this: when Chijian cut the snake and told the monk, ‘You are coarse, and I am coarse,’ what was the ancient master’s insight?

He then raised his whisk and said: *(Note: This passage addresses the paradox of transmission—how a teacher can guide a student when no objective "principle" exists to serve as a bridge—and uses the story of Chijian to highlight the necessity of direct, non-conceptual realization.)*
Today Guizong raises his whisk; is this the same or different from when Guizong cut the snake? After a long silence, he said:
"Everyone possesses a natural, true reality, yet no one knows its wondrous function, which moves freely in all directions. Today I point it out clearly for all:
who else could it have been that raised the whisk after cutting the snake? This old Zhenjing, though acting with skillful means for the sake of Chijian, [has revealed the truth].
To analyze this: alas, it is like painting a snake and adding feet—only to make it all the more absurd.

Again, he cites the case where Master Danxia burned a wooden Buddha and the temple steward’s eyebrows and beard fell off. Suddenly picking up his staff, he says, "This is no wooden Buddha," and then throws it down, saying, "Who dares burn you?
He asks, "If one were about to do so, the eyebrows and beard would fall off; but if one does not intend to, what then? Thereupon, he calls out loudly to the attendant.
He raises his staff. This old fellow can truly be said to be unrelenting regarding his own eyebrows and whiskers; he wishes to provide full protection for the ancients with all his might.
Yet, alas, it is like wrapping a tiger in wet paper. Tell me, where does the confusion lie? All you Zen practitioners!
If you wish to see where Danxia Chiyen took up [the staff] crosswise and used it upside down to benefit others, you must personally reach his realm of living liberation and total non-reliance;

only then will you succeed. Let us set aside this story for now. You should know that even to speak of "living liberation and total non-reliance" is already a case of being driven to necessity, forcibly assigning a name to that which is beyond naming. As for what he realized and attained himself—
One does not even know what "vivid liberation" (huótuō) is; when responding spontaneously to circumstances, one does not even know it is the wondrous function of vivid liberation.

Nowadays, when people hear the name "vivid liberation," they immediately prepare to leap about like a sprite, pointing east and marking west, waving and flailing wildly, imagining this to be vivid liberation.
In truth, it is merely the deadest thing within the realm of the dead.
It is indeed the Dharma. For this liberated realm is fundamentally without fixed direction; therefore, it cannot be pointed out to others.
Those predecessors who attained it likewise possessed no fixed method; therefore, one cannot imitate or settle into it by mere calculation.
It is just like when Master Jueyi was dwelling in his hermitage: a nun wearing a bamboo hat came and circumambulated him three times, asking three questions.
The nun said, "If you can say it, then set down your rain hat. Kuti was unable to speak. The nun then departed.
Kuti called out, "Why do you not stay? The nun replied, "If you can say it, then stay. Kuti again had no words, and the nun left.
Kuti felt deep self-reproach and lamentation. Later, he recounted this to Master Tianlong, who said, "Ask me; I will give it to you."
"Way," said Jueyi. "If you can express the Way, then set down your straw hat. Tianlong then held up a single finger. Jueyi suddenly attained great enlightenment.
From that time on, whenever anyone questioned him, he would simply hold up one finger. He often said of himself, "I have obtained Tianlong’s 'finger-head Chan';
it will serve me for the rest of my life without being exhausted. Beside Jueyi was a young boy who served him.
Whenever anyone asked him about something, the boy would also learn to respond by raising his finger.
When Juzhi heard of this, he secretly tucked a knife in his sleeve, called the boy over, and asked him, "I hear you also understand the Buddha-dharma, is that so?"
"It is so," [said] Juezhong. He then asked, "What is the Buddha? The youth immediately held up his finger.
Juezhong then cut off the youth's finger with a blade. The youth cried out and ran away. Juezhong called to the youth again. The youth turned his head back.
Juezhong asked once more, "What is the Buddha? The youth raised his hand again, but the finger was no longer there. Suddenly—
He attained great enlightenment. All you virtuous practitioners of Chan: when Juzhi was initially unable to answer the nun’s question, it was not that he did not understand the Buddha-dharma;
he simply understood a "dead" dharma. Only upon seeing Tianlong raise his finger did he finally awaken to a "living" one.
When the boy learned to raise his finger, he too only learned a "dead" dharma; it was only when he saw [Tianlong] without a finger that he truly understood.
Only then do you realize that there is something truly alive and free. To state the essential point: Jueyi attained this state of being alive and free because he saw the finger;
the lad attained this state of being alive and free because he did not see the finger. Observe how the way these two men attained it was inherently different from one another.
How could there ever have been a fixed dharma? Since there is no fixed dharma, for whom, then, would you prepare yourself to settle or rely?
Furthermore, when Master Xiangyan was formerly in Baizhang’s assembly, he would answer ten questions for every one asked, and a hundred for every ten.
Later, upon arriving at Mount Gui, when Guishan pressed him with a single word regarding the time before one's parents were born, he was unable to respond.
Thereupon, he searched everywhere through all that he had previously understood and recorded, yet in the end not a single word could serve as a reply.

He then sought out Guishan to have him explain it for him, but Guishan refused to speak. Thereupon, filled with indignation, he cast aside everything he had learned and went directly to Nanyang to dwell in a hermitage.
One day, while throwing a tile that struck a bamboo and produced a sound, he attained awakening. He immediately spoke this verse: "A single blow extinguishes all that is known;
there is no longer any need for cultivation or maintenance. Moving one's countenance, one reveals the ancient path; one does not fall into the silent mechanism. And so forth.
O Zen practitioners, when Xiangyan was in the assemblies of Baizhang and Muzhou, it cannot be said that he did not understand the Buddha-dharma. It was simply...
To attain the ultimate through the convergence of conditions is itself a dead dharma. One must simply wait until one lets go of everything with total sincerity.

When letting go reaches the point where there is nothing known, suddenly one attains a state of liberation; then one can say: "Every movement reveals the ancient path, never falling into the silent mechanism."
Observe how Xiangyan’s realization differs from that of both Juizhi; how could there be any fixed dharma here to which one might attach oneself?

Later generations did not understand this and assumed that "losing what is known" meant being like withered wood or a dull stone, and they attempted to forget their form and extinguish their minds in order to attach themselves to it.
To attempt such an attachment is precisely to be able to know what is known.
One knows that they arise in a burning competition; one must reach the point where all objects of knowledge have perished. Even in a donkey’s lifetime, such a state has not been dreamed of.

Later, when the Great Master Dàhuì lamented that students were falsely imitating and attempting to settle into [the truth], all of which was merely generating emotion upon seeing objects and producing intellectual understanding following words, he sought to remedy this ailment and said:
"Jùzhī’s attainment did not lie on the tip of his finger. Xiangyan realized...
The locus does not lie at the edge where the bamboo was struck. Great Wisdom (Mahāmati), these words are like nudging a pearl rolling on a plate;
they become all the more impossible for it to settle there. Let this matter rest for now.

You should know that when one speaks of the word "attainment" or the word "awakening," it is likewise like suddenly waking from a great intoxication or suddenly awakening from a great dream—it is merely a forced designation established out of necessity.
Regarding the names used for these states: for instance, a person who does not drink wine is inherently sober; what need is there to speak of the word "awakening"?
If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord; why labor to speak of the word "enlightenment"?
For one who is neither deluded nor lost, what use could the words "attainment" or "realization" possibly serve? Have you not seen the Patriarch say:
When deluded, one is deluded only about awakening; when awakened, one awakens only to delusion. When both delusion and awakening are forgotten—what is it, right here?

Once you understand this teaching, you should know that the two characters "Buddha-dharma" are merely provisional designations established out of necessity as opposing names and phrases to manifest the truth;
they are medicine prescribed according to the illness. If you sit within the ground of non-reliance, [you will realize this].
Since one perceives neither ordinary sentient beings nor both nirvana and birth-and-death, then what use are the two characters "Buddha-dharma" within your own sphere?
Thus, National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang said: "Treading upon the crown of Vairocana—what need is there to speak of the 'Ten-Body Tamer'?
Once you understand that these are merely provisional designations established through relative opposition, you should then...
To know that what is called the Buddha, the Dharma, sentient beings, and the lands are all established from the standpoint of non-reliance—therefore, Master Linji said:
"The person of non-reliance is the mother of all Buddhas; the Buddha is born from non-reliance. If one awakens to non-reliance, even the Buddha cannot be attained.
This is what is meant by traversing the lands of the three eyes in a single kṣaṇa, entering into all...

Entering the Buddha-worlds, entering the worlds of sentient beings, entering the worlds of all Māras, and even pervading entry into all dharma-realms—whether ultimate or conventional, pure or defiled—to do so without attachment or obstruction is, in total, the self-reliant person of no-abode playing with spiritual transformations and sporting in samādhi;
it is the state of attaining great mastery in letting go and gathering back. Why is this so?
Lately, people have cast aside their own spiritual powers and wondrous functions; instead, they laboriously seek the Buddha and the Dharma outside the mind.
Seeking an externalized Buddha with form is not like you. Fundamentally, there is no dharma outside the mind;
those who seek it turn away from the truth. How much more so when one drags along a corpse of a person to enter the gate of the Buddhas, seeking only words and phrases?
To take intellectual understanding as the goal of study—how bitter, how tragic! The Patriarch, driven by no other choice, tells you:
"Study must be true study; awakening must be real awakening. King Yama does not fear much talk.
This is intended for you to cast off words, letters, knowledge, and conceptual understanding, to strike at yourself and study on your own to seek self-awakening. Since you do not...

If one is willing to strike at oneself and investigate inwardly to seek self-awakening, yet instead turns outward to carry in dung until one’s belly is full, being oneself unaware of its stench and filth while further exhaling it to infect others—is this not truly great suffering and great injustice?
Among those who call themselves students of the Chan school in recent times, five out of ten suffer from this very ailment; this is because:
From the outset, lacking the eye of wisdom, you mistakenly took the expedient teachings intended for manifestation as literal reality.
Unaware, you sat entirely within the conceptual knowledge and views of the Buddha-dharma, causing your mind to boil with agitation and your mouth to flow with empty words.
You spoke of the profound, the subtle, the marvelous, and the strange; not only does this constitute an obstruction, but it also leads to further hindrances.
This gate of awakening is also the very cause by which one may commit the karma of the Avīci hell; the Tathāgata says such a person is truly pitiable.

Among them, there is a certain class of practitioners who are able to reflect back upon this and realize their error, fortunately avoiding the hindrance of conceptualizing and understanding through the Buddha-dharma’s views and realizations;
yet they remain seated within a state devoid of the Buddha-dharma’s views and realizations. Opening—
The mouth moves and the tongue speaks only of "mountains are mountains, waters are waters. When the sky is clear and the earth dry, rain falls and the ground becomes wet.
What is it like inside the Buddha Hall? What is it like outside the Gate of the Way? A single flavor of ordinariness covers all; strike it back into the armor of non-action.
A dead man on level ground—once dead, he cannot live again. This is also called the Real.
How pitiable! Furthermore, there is another type of practitioner who is able to reflect back upon this point.

They realize that both of the aforementioned two approaches are incorrect and distance themselves from both. They maintain right mindfulness alone, and fortunately achieve a state where body and mind are extinguished and the past and future are severed—a "single thought for ten thousand years.
Yet, they remain seated upon a clean patch of ground, considering this to be the ultimate realization.
Thereupon, the Patriarch rebuked him, saying: "You have been obstructed and held back by a sublime state of realization; thus, true awakening cannot manifest before you.

You are indeed to be pitied. Furthermore, there is a certain kind of eminent and superior person who can penetrate through this very point, letting go completely at the precipice so as to revive after death; such a one truly possesses realization. Truly...
If one has something seen, the Patriarch likewise rebuked him, saying that he was sitting in a deep pit of liberation;

his realization of the ground was not yet liberated, his correct knowledge and vision were obstructed, and not even a hair’s breadth remained exhausted—still separated by the Iron Ring Mountains. Master Xueyan also said:
"At such a time, you must see a person. Sitting here, you become a mere dharma-dust; only when struck by blind shackles and blind clubs will you break free."
When you need to use it, use it; there is no distinction between the intimate and the distant. The Master’s repeated and intense pressing has no other purpose than this:

he fears that although your ordinary nature may have been exhausted, your saintly views have not yet been forgotten, and thus you fail to reach the state of being lively, liberated, and without dependence.
One can know, then, that this single point under the School of the Lineage is by no means easy; how much more so for those of the present day who are a kind of "empty-plundering" fellows?
They have never met a true teacher, nor have they ever performed genuine practice. Their feet remain unsteady and floating, while the path before them is shrouded in darkness;
thus, they speak with blind ignorance, babbling at random.

Among them, there are also those who have indeed met true teachers and performed genuine practice, yet who have withdrawn on their own due to narrow ambitions or an inability to endure the long journey.
Some, due to obstacles and hardships, are unable to maintain steadfast endurance and thus yield themselves;

some, because their worldly toil has momentarily ceased, mistake this for realization and thus deceive themselves; some, having found a point of entry, consider it sufficient and thus limit themselves;
some, following the errors of their teachers, fall into heterodox and inverted views and thus sink into ruin; or some, due to [the entanglements of] the thicket...
In the forest, there are those who, arrogant regarding their names and status and vying for power and profit, give rise to madness and lose their beginner’s mind.

Furthermore, there are those whose initial resolve is half-truth and half-false: one part of their mind seeks to understand birth and death, while the other part seeks to act as a spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Unable to realize awakening quickly, they falsely claim to have realized it. None of these are genuine.
This is the true breed of weeds: those whose illness lies in their desire to act as teachers for others; who urgently seek respect, honor, and offerings;
who follow along by learning to beat upon their mouths with drum-like chatter and falsely discourse on Prajñā; even employing staffs, shouts, waving hands, and brandishing fists;

fabricating mad words and strange speech; composing verses on *hwadu* and *gongan*; speaking of their "places of practice" and "reasons for awakening"; and using the "winter melon seal" to entice and provoke others.
A pack of heterodox deities and wild ghosts clamors at the gate and courtyard. Disciples and masters form factions with demons;
they even fabricate karmic conditions to insert them into recorded sayings (*yulu*), arranging titles and inserting names into the charts of patriarchs.
They claim they can deceive everyone, yet how can they avoid being seen through by that Faceless One? Leave behind this record of no interval.
The Iron Ring Mountains wait for you to come and offer them sustenance; those like this, blindly leading one another on, mistakenly cause future generations to fall into ruin.
How can they blame the Patriarch when he said, "To bury thousands and tens of thousands alive upon a heap of refuse—what crime is there in that?
This mountain monk has heard of the affairs of the Zen school since childhood and has practiced seated meditation. Alas!

Had one not encountered the harsh hammer and tongs of a true teacher, one would inevitably be hindered by a mere fragmentary understanding, further obstructed in the breast by a mind that seeks sudden enlightenment; thus, one remains unaware that this itself is the illness.
It was only upon reaching Tianmu and relying on the Old Monk Huanzhu that I frequently heard him say: "Throughout my life of Zen practice, Old Huan..."
I attained awakening. Within my mind, I privately harbored some doubts; it was only later that I realized the Old Monk possessed the marks of a great man.
He was neither eccentric nor strange, neither boastful nor self-aggrandizing. Throughout his life, he refused to speak of his own reasons for awakening or how he had attained it.
Furthermore, the reason for strictly binding the assembly and practicing in secret is intended to cause those of the present age—
who have not attained yet claim attainment, who have not realized yet claim realization, and who falsely style themselves as "men of knowledge" (jñānin) to deceive the common people—
to know shame and feel dread. This is precisely a vital remedy for the disease of falling into error in the present age, serving as a warning against the empty plundering of later students.
This is the place where the Master dwells for the sake of others; the situation changes anew from time to time.

Reaching this point, even an elder undergoes another shift in the strategic layout—how could it be fathomed by ordinary sentiments? Although I, this mountain monk, have relied upon him for many years, I have nonetheless attained not a single dharma.
Not only have I attained nothing of a single dharma, but furthermore, I have [attained] nothing of what I previously studied...
He resolved to cast everything away all at once. For this reason, he realized that his debt of gratitude was too great to repay;
thus, he simply let go. By the mountains and by the waters, he became one who was humble, compliant, and lacking in outward brilliance.
Whatever this old man had throughout his life forbidden or constrained him from, he did not dare to lightly violate. Thus it was for the second time.
It has been thirty years. Today, because others pressed me with their request for a general discourse, I could not help but see what was unjust on the road and vomited forth this mess.

It is much like a wind-stricken, vicious dog that barks wildly at everyone alike, regardless of whether they are good people. As for those who are buried alive amidst heaps of refuse, they cannot do without me by even a single fraction.
Now, as for this present assembly of Chan practitioners— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the partial nature of the source.)

Virtuous one, you who are pure, sincere, and stainless, untainted by any admixture of poison—regarding the depths of what I have thus explained, I do not permit you even to record a single word or character.
You should simply believe and take it for granted that within yourself there exists something lively, liberated, and independent.
Vibrant and agile, it is free from all obstruction; though it has no form and no location, it can penetrate the ten directions and universally enter into all phenomena.
All supernatural powers, samādhis, and transformations are exercised with sovereign ease, lacking not even a single hair’s breadth.
The divine light of the six realms has never ceased day or night; it requires no contrivance and admits no discrimination.
To realize it directly is it; to have a single thought of resonance is it.

If you wish to attain this resonance of a single thought, simply let go of all mundane and supramundane affairs, and rest the mundane and supramundane mind. Do not resent worldly matters for obstructing the mind.
One can thus use the mind to avoid entanglement in affairs. You need only, at all times and in all places, be without mind regarding the mind and without affairs regarding affairs;
then, naturally, you will encounter the source wherever you turn. Therefore it is said: "Right here and now, heaven is vast and earth is level.
When you wish to act, everything is already perfected; how effortless this is! How celebratory for one's entire life! But should it not be so—
There is no other expedient. For now, simply seek the long within the short; single-mindedly maintain the very phrase you have taken up for investigation.
You must not give rise to a second thought to engage in forced interpretation or commentary. You must not allow it to drift into a state of natural indifference, falling back into a bag of dullness.
You must not knit your brows, glare with your eyes, or exert strenuous effort. Do not set time limits or dates to seek a quick result.
To attain awakening: one must not deliberately relax one's efforts or prolong the process in expectation that awakening will occur spontaneously;
one must not be panicked and lose one's composure amidst the confusion of external circumstances; one must not be self-indulgent and complacent when circumstances are quiet;
nor should one rely entirely on the rigid methods of the ancients. One should know that each person’s practice is different; you ought to act for yourself.
Harmonize your own mental transformations; the essential point is for [the practice] to be constantly present with vivid clarity, never departing from you at every step.
Suddenly, you will reach a state that is flavorless, without reliance, and beyond helplessness—like having fallen into a pit or trench from which you can neither advance nor retreat.
That is precisely the good news. You must hold the rope tightly.
Press on until you reach the point where the water ends and the mountains exhaust themselves; there, naturally, will come a time for a turning.

If you cannot directly realize this, yet are unwilling to settle for a "tasteless" phrase, and instead urgently wish to speak of Chan or the Way, abandoning this true investigation to seek elsewhere for Buddhist views and intellectual understandings—then you will surely become a member of Mara’s retinue. This is so.
Furthermore, it is entirely up to you to follow your own inverted desires—to learn and transmit as you please, and to wield the brush with grand strokes as you wish.
I only fear that when the single breath ceases and you tumble headlong into the presence of Lord Yama, he will refuse to show any human sentiment and glare at you with his crosswise iron countenance;
even a Buddha could not save you then. If you are a true man of integrity, you ought to exert yourself fiercely right now.
Farewell. Take care.
On the winter solstice festival, the monk Jueyi gathered various Zen friends and invited Pujue.

A monk asked, "The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind. I wonder, Master, how do you guide people? The Master said, "A frog."
[Pei] leaps up into the sky; an earthworm crosses over the Eastern Sea. The monk advances and says, "If that is so, then one transcends both Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The Master says, "Where do you see this? The monk replies, "Throughout ancient and modern times, it has never fallen;
it is clearly right before one's eyes. The Master says, "You fabricated Chan practitioner! Step back. The monk says, "Linji asked Huangbo three times about Buddha-nature..."

The general meaning of the Dharma. [The student asked: "Regarding the three times he was struck with painful blows—what is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Do not speak of one's sorrows to another who is sorrowful.
[The student] further asked, "Later, having been enlightened by Dayu, he said, 'Originally, Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma was not much.
What does this mean? The Master said, "It is good to speak of one's sorrows to another who is sorrowful. [The student] further asked, "This was Dayu..."
[The monk] asked about Huangbo’s portion. The Master said, “You should speak for yourself first. The monk said, “When a dragon gains water, its spirit increases;
when a tiger encounters mountain scenery, its fierce majesty grows. The Master said, “This is Huangbo’s portion.
What about Dagu’s portion? The monk hesitated. The Master then gave a shout. The monk said, “A descendant of Linji naturally possesses [this quality],” and then returned to the assembly.
The Master then said: "When the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind.

Because they each attain understanding, universal understanding is revealed; because of that universal understanding, universal preaching is revealed. If the preaching were not universal, the understanding would likewise not be universal.
Therefore, in every single syllable the preaching is universal, in every single phrase the preaching is universal, and in every gradual progression the preaching is universal."

I speak of the suddenness within the sudden, the universality; I speak of the phenomena within the phenomena, the universality; I speak of the principle within the principle, the universality. I speak while remaining silent, the universality; I remain silent while speaking, the universality.

This morning, I, this mountain monk, accepted the request of all of you for a general discourse (*pǔshuō*). Therefore, borrowing from what the Zen guests have asked, I have briefly clarified the meaning of the general discourse.
Let us set aside this discourse for a moment and simply rely on that solitary, vivid clarity right before our eyes—this is that which can hear the general discourse.
Who is it that speaks? Who is it that can understand what is universally preached? Who is it that joins the palms in greeting?
Who is it that bows the head in prostration? Everyone, examine yourselves individually.
Do not stubbornly defend yourself by claiming that the one who can hear and understand is your "original master. Let me ask you: is this original master long or short?
Is this great or small? What kind of face do you have? What sort of appearance? Where do you establish yourself and find your livelihood?
Even if you know it clearly, see it clearly, and explain it clearly, I shall further ask you:
who is the master that knows and sees? Who is the master that says, "This is I"? You—
Who would have known that what is spoken, what is seen, and the very basis of these, along with the host himself, are all merely provisional names?
To say they "are" is not permissible; to say they "are not" is not permissible; to say they "both are and are not" is not permissible; to say they "neither are nor are not" is not permissible.
You must realize this for yourself before you can attain it. Have you not seen the Patriarch say: "This very mind is Buddha"?
Furthermore, it is said that the Way is neither mind nor Buddha. It is also said that the Way is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing.
Now tell me, if it is neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing, what exactly is it?
Unless you have attained realization here, how could you presume to claim, "This is my master"? Therefore, when I was at Jing [Mountain] many years ago...
During the summer retreat at Cisi Temple, while presiding over the whisk (bǐfú), a monk stepped forward and asked: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not an object—what is it?
I replied offhand: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not an object—what is it?
The monk said: "This is the very question I asked; why did you not offer a different phrase? I answered again:
[The Master] said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing—what is it? Having spoken thus, he fell silent. The monk was at a loss.
I then let out a shout and looked left and right, asking, "Is the staff here or not?
If the staff were here, the Senior Monk himself would deserve thirty blows. To have raised the matter in such a manner at that time may be called exceedingly direct. This monk...
To fail to see through this is to be a blind fellow. Examining it closely, it is all nothing but leftover soup and rancid rice, unfit for chewing.
Now, being here in the Lion’s Grove, I ought to provide a special offering for you all.
Since you recognize the Lion’s Grove, do you also recognize this old monk? This old monk is a dull-witted teacher who has neither fangs nor claws.
My son, I have never leaped about, nor have I ever roared. How many people have retreated at the mere sight of me?
How many have dared not enter my gate? Some harbor both doubt and faith; some hold both good and ill in equal measure; some offer both praise and censure in equal measure.
This old monk pays no heed to anything; he simply wanders and sits alone in leisure, smiling and rejoicing within himself.
It is fortunate that no one recognizes me; were everyone to know me, what use would I be?
Today, for no reason, you people have disregarded your own lives to crash into this place, crowding and pressing against me. What is to be done?
This means that when meeting on a narrow path, there is no room for avoidance.

If you do not provide the fodder of one's own fundamental nature as an offering, even after thirty years, people will still say, "I once met this old monk. Will you not thus be mutually obstructing each other? As the Zen guest said just now:
The descendants of Linji naturally possess their own place. This old monk also says: those of you who enter this gate are all descendants of Linji;
you must not allow yourselves to become discouraged. "Since he was a man of such stature, why should I not be so?
Linji’s eyes were askew and his nose straight; your noses are straight and your eyes are askew—search for even a hair’s breadth of difference, and it is utterly impossible to find.
It is attained. Yet, not even a single hair’s breadth of a common characteristic can be found. Since these are the weeds of our own school, who cares whether they are different or the same?
They extinguish the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and uphold the orthodox lineage of Linji. But how is the orthodox lineage of Linji upheld?
Is it by upholding the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials? Is it by upholding the Four Kinds of Discriminative Selection? Is it by upholding the Four...?
Is it the guest or the host? Is it the four shouts used when helping someone up? Furthermore, this shout is merely the breath of rice and gruel;
who does not know it? You see the farmer shouting when driving his oxen; the groom shouting when leading his horse; the woodcutter shouting when seeing a snake;
the beggar shouting when chasing a dog; the gambler shouting when throwing dice; and the master shouting at his servants—these are all [instances of this shout].
"First-class gruel and rice have a foul odor. How can you call this the true lineage of Linji?
Even if one says, 'A single shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function proceed simultaneously;

if you understand the meaning within this, it is like striking the third watch at noon,' such talk may deceive you all, but it cannot deceive this old monk. You all must test it for yourselves. After a long silence, he shouted.
A shout was given. Before this shout had taken form, were the guest and host, their illumination and function, existent or non-existent?
After this shout has dissolved, are the illumination, function, guest, and host non-existent or existent?

At the very moment of the shout, are the host and guest, their illumination and function, within the shout, without the shout, or neither within nor without? Furthermore, [the Master] gave another shout.
He gave a shout, saying: "This one shout has already revealed the meaning within it all at once.
It may deceive oneself, but it cannot deceive others; yet even others must wait until midday to strike the third watch before they can understand.
According to this old monk’s critique, does this still sustain the true lineage of Linji? Since it cannot be sustained, I dare say—
The true lineage of Linji is definitively not found in the realm of illumination and function; it is not found in the realm of host and guest; it is not found in the four shouts;
it is not found in the four methods of selection or the three mysteries and three essentials. It is not found in any place at all.
Since it is not found in any place, where exactly is it? It resides solely within the sphere of each person’s own self. You people should...
Know that this one stroke within your own portion is brilliant as heaven and earth;

the Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, and the old monks of the world dare not even look upon it with a direct eye. It is simply a matter of your own immediate and direct acceptance.
Because the venerable predecessors of old did not wish for you to accept it directly, they were driven by necessity to provide expedient teachings through indirect means.
I shall simply instruct you to investigate a "meaningless" koan. For instance, when a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature?
Zhaozhou replied, "No. This was already like placing the entire dish before you on its stand; yet since you were unable to grasp it, I had no choice but to act as a physician treating a dead horse.
Thus, I further instructed you to single-mindedly hold up the single character "No. First, take the four elements...

The five aggregates, the six sense organs, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses—even the mountains, rivers, and great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness, the myriad phenomena arrayed before one’s eyes, and all things sentient and insentient—take them all together and reduce them to a single character: "Mu.
Grasp it up once; grasp it up while walking, grasp it up while sitting, grasp it up even in dreams, and grasp it up in every movement.
Bring this up while eating and drinking; bring it up continuously and densely, without interval or interruption.
When you bring it up, let the teaching become a single, solid mass, impenetrable as if pierced by a needle, resembling a silver mountain or an iron wall.
Suddenly, without knowing or noticing, with one pressure, you will break through to yourself. This one point will be naturally clear without waiting for formal realization. This is it.
Once you have clearly understood this, the face of your parents before they were born is clear; the place where the four elements disperse after death is clear;
the affairs of daily life are clear; the point where this old monk’s tongue deceives you is clear;
and the points of confusion amidst the myriad differences of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past are clear. Since each and every one of these is clear—
It is clear. This is precisely the moment when the true lineage of Linji is upheld. At this time, worldly dharmas and Buddha-dharmas are entirely without seams or gaps.
One then perceives the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials, the Four Aids to Selection, the Four Guests and Hosts, and the Four Cries;

furthermore, the four elements, the five aggregates, the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses, as well as the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the myriad phenomena of the universe—all are revealed.
There is not a single dharma that is not the true lineage of Linji; it arises spontaneously without waiting for support.

Only then can one uproot things, can one establish them, can one walk hand-in-hand with the Buddhas of the three periods, and can one cause the Buddhas of the three periods to stand behind me with palms joined.
This is what is meant by: "I am the Dharma King, sovereign over all dharmas."
This is so. Today, this old monk’s affairs have reached a crisis at the family gate; my tongue drags upon the ground.
Is there anyone among you who can directly take this up? If there is, try to show your skill.

If not, do not blame the old monk for acting as if he were the only person in the world, opening his great mouth and speaking great falsehoods—thus extinguishing the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. A-ha!
"Hah! Do not misunderstand this. [He] suddenly took up his staff and said: "Poison is nectar; nectar is poison.
Whether one errs or does not err, it is better to spit it out than to swallow it. He struck the ground with the staff and descended from the seat."
