Compiled by his junior disciple, Shan Yu.
At the request of Huiqing Chan Temple for a general discourse, the Master said: "A single turn of the phrase beyond the category cannot be contained within the entire Great Canon;
the ultimate point above has not been reached by the seventeen hundred patriarchs. Under the gate of a true adept, capture and release are exercised with ease;

even if Buddhas and Patriarchs were to arrive, they would have no choice but to remain tongue-tied. Is there anyone among you who transcends the Buddhas and surpasses the Patriarchs? Come forth and reveal it!"
"Look at this message. After the question and answer were concluded, he said: "Just now, a Zen guest asked about the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvana.
I told him: 'It makes the cat and the white ox laugh to death; it leaves all the monks in the world in doubt. Do you know whether he ever understood it or not?
O Zen practitioners, as for the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvana, throughout the three periods of time..."
The Buddha does not know "there is. Yet the stray cat and the white ox do know "there is. Now tell me: is it the one who knows "there is," or is it the one who does not know "there is"?
For now, let us set aside the question of knowing or not knowing. Where can the single word "is" be placed?
Since there is no place for it to rest, what can be called the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana? And what can be called the Three [Bodies]?

The various Buddhas of the world, the *lirnu* (cats), and the *baigu* (white oxen)—how many heroic and sagacious men have looked here and failed to see them, groped for them and failed to find them, hesitated and failed to respond, or attempted to engage them and failed to penetrate? If one does not apply the "sesame twist," it is like swallowing a whole jujube.
Later, when Master Linji saw a monk enter the gate, he immediately shouted; when Master Deshan saw a monk enter...
He struck him with the staff at the gate. This one blow and one shout pointed out the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana on the spot, confronting him directly.
It was intended only for easy seeing and easy understanding;

yet, how can one ignore that within this staff and shout there is yielding and seizing, illuminating and functioning, giving life and taking death, and the host and the guest? Sometimes the host and guest stand apart. At other times...
At times guest and host intersect; at times host and guest alternate; at times both guest and host are forgotten.
It is simply because one seeks to simplify matters that they become more complex, adding yet another layer of mud upon the earth.
This brings trouble upon the Old Man Yunmen, whose eyes cannot bear to see it, so he comes forth and says: "Yunmen’s fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nose of Śakra."
"Kong! A carp from the East China Sea receives a blow, and the rain pours down like a basin being overturned.
Such words have already clearly annotated and torn asunder into pieces the wondrous mind of Nirvana and the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
Although the annotation is clear, alas, it remains difficult to comprehend as before. If one does not realize the true dharma, Yunmen’s transgressions fill the heavens. If...

They do not hold assemblies for the realization of true Dharma; Yunmen beats his breast and cries out in grievance. It is precisely because things are so extremely clear that what is attained is delayed.
Little do they realize that in every movement, every state, every word, and every phrase of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, there is fundamentally no confusion and no extraordinariness;
there is neither profundity nor concealment. It is entirely the matter of daily life and constant practice for all people.
What are called the Buddhas of the three periods and the "tawny cat and white ox" have, from the beginning, breathed through a single nostril.
This nostril is already fully present within each of you; though your eyes may not see it, when you reach out your hand, you have already touched it.
How could there ever be the slightest difference? If you possess your own mastery and are not led astray by others...
Mán! I guarantee that the Buddhas of the three periods will borrow your nostrils to breathe through them.
Whether they let go or gather in, whether they move left or right—all shall proceed according to you. If you yourself lack mastery, you cannot avoid having one of your nostrils pierced by another;
in every movement and stillness, you will have no freedom at all. Therefore, regarding the Buddha...
The ancestral opportunities for awakening become obstacles at every turn. As I, this mountain monk, proclaim them thus, is there anyone among the assembly who is not obstructed?
Try once more to present them from the beginning. [He displays the whisk and says: "Yunmen’s fan is right here. [He lets out a shout and says:
"Linji’s shout is present right here. [He plants his staff on the ground and says: "Virtue!"
The mountain staff is also right here. The fan, the staff, and the shout are all seen and heard in a single moment.
Yet, what is the sound of the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye? What is the countenance of the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa?
Ask Old Wang of the north bank and the south bank; one doubt after another doubt arises. It would be better to cut through this tangle and open up a different path.
He departs. Striking once with his staff, he says: "O Zen practitioners! When the Buddhas and Patriarchs appear in the world, they do not do so for any other purpose;
they act solely for you all, because each and every one of you has a great matter of birth and death beneath your own feet that remains unresolved.
They have skillfully manifested expedient means to cause you to settle this matter. What is meant by the 'matter of birth and death'?"
Great! Not knowing the place from which one comes when born is called the "greatness of birth. Not knowing the place to which one goes when dying is called the "greatness of death.
Such birth and death are not trivial or mere idle speculation. It is like a vast net covering the heavens, encompassing all people throughout the world.
Since ancient times, there has not been a single person who has not been swallowed up by birth and death. Do not—do not—[be complacent].
I speak from antiquity; I speak only of you since your birth. Reflect back upon ten or twenty years ago:
how many relatives, friends, companions, and acquaintances have died? Their bodies and their names have rotted away together with the grass and trees.
Knowing that the great night of death is vast and boundless, where will they find a place to settle their bodies and establish their lives? How truly lamentable this is! Do not—do not—[neglect this].
You speak of others, yet you are only speaking of yourself. You falsely conceive of this present body of the four great elements as "I.
From morning until evening, your eyes roll about, your mouth flaps open and shut, and your entire frame is restless and agile.
You provide for it with all manner of nourishment and protect it with all manner of care; yet it changes and passes away from moment to moment, never remaining new or still, like a fire.
Reduced to ashes, it gradually vanishes away. Unaware and unperceiving, the thirtieth day of the twelfth month suddenly confronts you.
At that moment, when you examine all that you have done and practiced throughout your life, not a single thing will be of any use.
It was all in vain—a mere rolling of worldly toil and a vast expanse of karmic consciousness; a tumultuous clamor, a frantic dragging along. What have you actually accomplished?
Matters at the periphery—how one merely delights in being so flustered that hands and feet are in disarray, resembling a crab falling into boiling water. One regrets it too late;
one cannot undo what has been done. Alas! How lamentable! Alas! How painful!

Even if you hold a rank of the highest grade, possess wealth of ten thousand *zhong*, your merit covers heaven and earth, and your fame resounds through the court and the common world—once the three-inch breath is severed, [all is lost].
The fire blazed brightly; I gathered a handful of cold ashes and buried them in a mound of yellow earth.
At dusk, the foxes sleep upon the tomb; deep in the night, children laugh before the lamp. Where, indeed, are those heroes and paragons of our lives?

Thus the ancients said: "Make your livelihood as best you can; life and death are like pushing a millstone. When that single breath does not return, it all— [Note: The source text appears to be truncated.]
"This is indeed another person. Truly well said! Furthermore, after one has died for three or five days, the physical form becomes disfigured and foul, its stench overwhelming.
Even those who are one's closest kin and flesh-and-blood relatives are unwilling to look upon it with a steady gaze."
Where, then, does the affection and righteousness of a lifetime now remain? Thus our Patriarch said: "When a single breath ceases, one is as good as ashes and soil.
The path ahead is vast and boundless; one knows not where one will go. To simply die and be cremated in this manner is already pitiable;
how much more so when there is still that vast and boundless path ahead, where one must undergo retribution according to one's karma? This is precisely the most urgent matter."
What is meant by "receiving retribution according to one's karma"? Throughout your life, there was nothing you did that was not karma.
As soon as there is karma, there is retribution; the retribution follows the karma just as a shadow follows a form.

Once this body has died, a single consciousness (vijñāna) may fall into various hells such as the Mountains of Knives and Swords, or the Cauldrons of Boiling Charcoal, where it undergoes immeasurable suffering. Or else, it may crash into the womb of a donkey...
In the realm of hungry ghosts, such as those with the bellies of pregnant mares, they transmigrate through the cycle of rebirth and undergo immeasurable suffering.
Therefore, a former master said: "The tea is poured three times, then poured again three times; yet one skull is never fully consumed by the fire.
The karmic consciousness drills back into the skin-sack once more—were even an iron man to hear this, his hair would stand on end. This is the state of experiencing retribution. Which, then, is...?
The root of karma is the cycle of birth and death. This root of karma resides within this very moment of your present thought.

Since beginningless time, due to greed, hatred, delusion, ignorance, afflictions, and the madness of deluded thoughts, you have encountered circumstances and conditions, chasing after sounds and pursuing forms.
This causes you to stumble and fall in every direction, committing every kind of karma; this is precisely the very root of the karma of birth and death.
When one contemplates the matter of birth and death, even an iron-hearted man would lose heart.

For this reason, the Buddhas and Patriarchs exercised great compassion and aroused profound pity, extensively establishing words and teachings to instruct you in Zen meditation and the study of the Way, or to have you hold a *huatou* (critical phrase).

Or perhaps you have been taught to recite the Buddha’s name and cultivate the Pure Land, so as to sweep away deluded thoughts and the wild mind, to recognize the true master, and to discern your original face.
Seizing this moment when your eyesight is clear and your feet are strong, become a free, unencumbered, and pure practitioner of liberation.
Then, at the time of death, you will attain the enjoyment of others, remaining unimpeded by birth and death as you come and go.
This is what is called a great man who has realized life and attained liberation from death.

Viewed from this perspective, the Buddhas and Patriarchs possess great benevolence and virtue toward humanity, and the Way of Chan and the Buddha-Dharma possess great spiritual efficacy for humanity. Alas!

Lately, the human mind has grown indolent and the ancestral path has fallen into desolation; yet, though there are those who engage in Zen meditation and inquire about the Way, [the true essence remains obscured].
As for those practitioners who, despite the passage of many years and long ages, have not obtained spiritual efficacy—what is the reason for this?

To discuss it briefly, there are three kinds of maladies. First, from the very beginning, they do not encounter a true and authentic *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend) to open their minds and provide instruction.
Consequently, their fundamental footing is not secure, their direction is not upright, their practice is uneven and deficient, and their vision...
There is a mistake here: it is called "striking the head but not meeting a master. In the end, it turns into mere antiquarian curiosity.
Second, one is unable to take the great matter of birth and death as a primary concern.

Lacking both the effort of courageous diligence and the resolve of long-term non-retrogression, one is like ten days of cold following a single day of heat—vague and drifting, unaware that one has struck upon the state of *amoha* (non-delusion).

Among these matters, for twenty or thirty years one may ply the oars like a stake driven into the ground, or remain like a stone submerged in water, with no time when awakening or movement will ever occur.
Thirdly, one may fail to penetrate or let go of worldly hollow fame and fleeting profit;
or one may remain stuck, unable to sever or cast off worldly false conditions and evil habits. At every moment...

Stirred by the winds of sensory objects and tossed about by the waves of the world, one remains unaware as the entire body rolls toward the sea of karma, drifting east and mooring west until it is gone.
How could there then be any spiritual efficacy? Therefore it is said: "There is no secret formula for practicing Chan; it simply requires that the matter of birth and death be urgent.
If one is a true practitioner of the Way who feels a piercing urgency regarding birth and death, how could they possibly remain complacent midway through the path?
Yet [the practice] has fallen into neglect. One must overturn old nests, shake off old spirits, take up old *huatou*, and rouse old aspirations.
Where one cannot gain entry, one must precisely gain entry; when one cannot plant one's feet, one must precisely plant them. One should trust in the Way of the Patriarchs:
"A hair’s breadth of lingering thought is a karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting stir of emotion gives rise to ten thousand..."
Bound by the shackles of the kalpas, one must practice true practice; one must realize true realization. King Yama does not fear much talk.
Furthermore, you must have faith in the Way of the Patriarchs. When miscellaneous thoughts fly about, how can you apply yourself? A single *huatou* (critical phrase) is like an iron broom:
sweep away the "is," sweep away the "is not. Sweep on and on; as they multiply, sweep on and on. If you cannot sweep them away, you must stake your very life.

Sweep! Suddenly, sweeping shatters the great void; ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences are traversed by a single path. All you practitioners of Zen: exert yourselves now, for you must bring this to completion in this very life.
Do not allow yourselves to suffer the remaining retribution for eons to come. This is a matter of vital importance.

Furthermore, there are sons of the Buddha—both monastics and laypeople—who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and cultivate the Pure Land. They harbor doubts regarding whether mindfulness of the Buddha is the same as investigating the [koan].

Zen and the recitation of the Buddha’s name are not the same. It is simply that people do not realize that while Zen meditation and the recitation of the Buddha’s name differ, they are ultimately the same.

Zen meditation is for the sake of resolving birth and death; the recitation of the Buddha’s name is likewise for the sake of resolving birth and death. Those who practice Zen directly point to the human mind to see one's nature and attain Buddhahood;

those who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name reach the Pure Land of Mind-Only to see Amitābha as their own original nature. Since it is said that Amitābha is one’s own original nature and the Pure Land is Mind-Only...
How could there be any difference regarding the Pure Land? A sutra states: "For example, a great city has four gates;
those who come from various directions do not follow but a single path. This is because although the gates through which they enter differ, once they reach the city, they are the same.

Those who practice Chan meditation and those who recite the Buddha’s name likewise each follow what is appropriate for their own faculties and capacities; how could there be any divergence? Nevertheless, as for the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name—
Among these, there are those that are efficacious and those that are not. Why is this? It is because if one recites with the mouth but does not contemplate with the mind, it will not be efficacious.
However, if the mouth and mind correspond in every sound, and the mind and the Buddha are never separated for even a single step, [then it is efficacious].

There is indeed spiritual efficacy in this. Nowadays, there is a certain class of people who clutch their prayer beads with their hands and recite the Buddha’s name with their mouths, yet their deluded and frantic minds wander aimlessly to the east and west.
This is to recite with the mouth while not reciting with the mind; it is a mere waste of energy—what benefit is there in such a thing?
It would be better to remember the Buddha with the mind and recite the Buddha’s name with the mind, even if the mouth does not.
The sound that issues forth is, in fact, true nianfo (Buddha-recollection). Have you not seen it stated in the sutras:

"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish and pity sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. When sentient beings fall into the sea of birth and death, they are like children who have wandered abroad to a foreign land.
The Buddhas, like compassionate mothers, constantly remember them. Although they do not open their mouths to speak of this remembrance to others, [their compassion is ever-present].
As one recollects, the mind of mindfulness naturally becomes earnest and uninterrupted.
If a child recollects its mother with a heart identical to the mother’s own, then there will surely come a day when mother and child meet. Therefore, it is further said:

"If sentient beings recollect the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha both in the present and in the future. "The present" refers to the current life; "the future" refers to lives to come.
This refers to future lives. If one is truly able to thus recollect the Buddha and mindfully chant his name, I venture to guarantee that one will certainly see the Buddha in this very life.
Since it is said that one sees the Buddha before one's eyes, how does this differ from investigating Zen (*chán*) to awaken to the Way?

Master Huànzhù once said: "Investigating Zen is solely for the purpose of clarifying birth and death; reciting the Buddha’s name is intended only to resolve birth and death. But if one simply turns toward this one...
Each must find its own entry point; these two paths do not compete with one another. Although the paths do not compete, they do not permit each other to be practiced concurrently.
One who studies Chan should exclusively study Chan; one who recites the Buddha’s name should exclusively recite the Buddha’s name.
If the discourse is divided between the two, neither will achieve success. An ancient master had this analogy: [The text continues with the analogy regarding the "two-headed snake."]
It is said: "For example, it is like a boat with feet on both sides; one does not cling to this side or that side.
While there is no harm in not clinging to either side, if you fail to guard your entire body, you will sink completely. Take note, take note! Exert yourselves, exert yourselves!
Bhikṣu Weize has failed in his studies and cannot save himself. Now, having received the favor of Chan Master Ruoyu, the Abbot of Huiping, and...

At the request of Master Juezhao and Abbot Keting and other gentlemen, I was asked to deliver a general discourse for the fourfold assembly. Having no choice but to decline, I have reluctantly accepted this command.
Now, you sons of the Buddha here present who are newly studying Prajñāpāramitā, you should believe all that has been said above;
it is all like striking the head of a stone man with a staff—exposing the bare facts. Yet, what has been spoken does not go beyond a matter of urgent necessity.
This is merely an analogy for the great importance of the matter of birth and death, and the two dharma gates of Chan meditation and Buddha-recitation.
As for those who recite the Buddha’s name, they simply rely upon the four-character phrase "Amitābha Buddha" as their *hwadu* (critical phrase); there is nothing else to say.

If one is a beginner in Chan meditation, it is feared that they may not yet have a point of entry or a direction toward which to incline. However, even in this case, there is nothing else to say; it is simply...
Each of you has an original face of your own. You have simply not recognized this original face, which is, in its very immediacy, of the same substance as all Buddhas.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day—whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—you do not fail to receive its sustaining power.
Simply recognize it intimately and secretly within yourself; this very recognition is itself the descent [into the Way].
The "place of the hand" is precisely this very point of orientation. You must directly accept it right now; be careful not to let it slip away through indifference.
Arouse great courage and exert great diligence; the essential point lies in the meeting of arrowheads and the fitting together of trigger-pins.
An ancient said: "If one does not do the first, one does not rest until the second. With a single punch, he topples the Yellow Crane Tower;
with a single kick, he overturns the Parrot Isle. When there is spirit, he adds to that spirit; where there is no elegance, he creates elegance.
If you truly possess such a strategy as the ancients, then Deshan, Linji, and you are fellow practitioners; Śākyamuni and Maitreya— [The text ends abruptly.]

Dahui once had two [collections]. He combined the seventeen hundred cases of the ancestral patriarchs' encounters with the *Zhengfayan zang* (The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) and the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, stringing them together as a single garland and setting it aside.
Thereafter, he walked alone upon the great earth and universally proclaimed to all people:
"A man of spirit has a path that reaches through the heavens; do not walk where the Tathāgata has trodden. At this time...

At such a time, it is only right that the Elder should prostrate himself upon seeing the wind of [the Master’s] presence. Should this not yet be so, do not be surprised if the noble is pressed down and treated as base;
let me add another footnote: The affairs of the world are vast and boundless, with no end in sight. One must urgently awaken to one's own livelihood.
Everyone sees the crab boiling in the soup; everyone knows the moth flying into the flame. Only when illness strikes does one finally pity the body.
This is suffering. When death arrives, only one's karma follows. Like floating light and illusory shadows, they pass in an instant;
to practice with urgency is already late. It is like people climbing a mountain: each must exert their own effort.

The Vice Commissioner Puda Shili, the Vice Commissioner Tuo Tie-muer, the Deputy Governor Mai Nu Haiya, the Imperial Commissioner Mang-ge-la, the General Manager Feng, and other officials and scholars came to the Lion Grove Monastery to offer a vegetarian feast and request a general discourse (*pūsè*).
The Master said: "Studying Chan is the most vital and supreme matter of all. Regarding this matter, whether one calls it a monk or..."
Ordinary people possess their share [of this reality], let alone those who have it fully present and manifest from the very beginning.
Yet, alas, worldly people often miss it right before their own eyes and never take the trouble to investigate it. Not to mention not investigating it—they have never even asked about it.
Viewed with a direct eye, they are truly to be pitied. Since you gentlemen have raised this question today, I shall conclude.
Ultimately, there is a great causal connection regarding this matter. Yet, as soon as one attempts to speak of it, it becomes a realm at the very brink of birth and death;
it becomes words that pierce the heart and sting the mouth. I hope you gentlemen will cleanse your hearts and purify your thoughts to listen to and reflect upon this.
Why is it said that "investigating Zen" (chán) is the most vital and urgent matter of the higher path? It is because one must clarify the mind and realize [Buddha-nature].

By nature, one understands how to transcend birth and death. When birth and death are not yet clarified, it is called the "Great Matter. The Patriarchs said: "Studying Chan is solely for the sake of resolving birth and death;
if birth and death are not resolved, all effort is in vain. Wang Xizhi also said: "Birth and death are indeed momentous."
How painful it is! It is precisely because the matter of birth and death is so great that taking up Zen meditation (*chán*) is regarded as the supreme, ultimate task.
What is meant by "birth and death"? You all possess bodies in this world;
yet these bodies are neither the indestructible diamond-bodies (*vajrakāya*) of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, nor are they solid, unyielding forms forged from pure steel or cast from raw iron.
This body of mine is but a temporary confluence of the four elements—a fragile, illusory, and ephemeral form. It is like a bubble upon the water, or dew upon a blade of grass. Behold it:
the hair turns white, the teeth waver, the skin withers, and the face wrinkles. Old age, sickness, and impermanence leave one unable to guarantee even tomorrow;
there is birth, and there must be death. Having died, one returns again to birth, yet we do not know when this present cycle of birth and death will end.
To fall into any of these paths is truly pitiable. The Buddha has taught that the three realms are like a burning house and the six destinies are like a wheel of suffering.
From immeasurable kalpas until now, you have wandered east and west within this burning house of the three realms, not knowing how to seek an exit;
you have rolled back and forth within the wheel of suffering of the six destinies, without end.
There is a momentary pause. If one wishes to cease the wheel of suffering and exit the burning house, it is necessary to understand birth and death.
If one wishes to understand birth and death, it is necessary to see the Buddha-nature. If one wishes to see the Buddha-nature, it is necessary to have a great awakening once.
If one wishes to have a great awakening, it is necessary to practice Chan. Thus, we know that among the immeasurable Dharma gates, the practice of Chan is the foremost and most essential.
What is meant by the "Infinite Dharma Gates"? To speak of them in detail, there are eighty-four thousand varieties; yet, when discussed in general, they comprise three schools:
the School of Teaching (Jiao-zong), the School of Meditation (Chan-zong), and the School of Vinaya (Lü-zong). Vinaya refers to the precepts and laws.
There are the precepts for laypeople in white robes, the precepts for ordained monks and others, the precepts of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), and the [precepts] of the Great [Vehicle].
The Dharma of the Vehicle and Precepts extends broadly to the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices;

all of these serve to restrain body and mind and to prevent wrongdoing and cease evil, and are thus called the Vinaya School. As for the Teachings, they extensively expound the Dharma-gates of cultivation and realization according to the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as the Sudden and Gradual approaches.
Some speak of the six pāramitās, such as generosity and the rest; some speak of extensively planting fields of merit;
and some speak of extensively cultivating the roots of virtue—these are the teachings of the [Exoteric] Schools. However, when discussing the Chan School, there are not so many matters.

It is said that it does not establish written words, but transmits outside the scriptures, pointing directly at the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha. Therefore, those who practice Chan first take...
Cast all that you have studied, memorized, seen, heard, known, and understood throughout your life onto one wall.
Furthermore, cast aside all matters of fame and profit, as well as the heart of attachment and craving, to one side.
Cut off all diversities and sweep away all anxieties; maintain single-mindedly the right mindfulness and advance with courage. It is, for example, like this:
To enter alone with a single blade into the midst of a hundred thousand troops, disregarding peril and death, gain and loss, self and others, right and wrong;

to fiercely stake one’s life and penetrate the adamantine barriers of Buddhas and patriarchs; to ascend directly to the inner sanctum of Buddhas and patriarchs without traversing the rungs of a ladder—this is called the Zen school.
Long ago, there was a King of Different Views in the Western Heavens who once asked the Venerable Pratibhāna: "How..."
"This is the Buddha. The Venerable said, "To see one's nature is to see the Buddha. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside? The Venerable replied, "Nature resides where it functions.
The King asked, "In how many places does it appear when functioning? The Venerable replied, "It appears in eight places. The King asked, "What are these eight places?
The Venerable replied, "In the womb, it is called the body; in the world, it is called a person; in the eye..."
"It is called seeing. In the ear it is called hearing. In the nose it smells fragrances; in the tongue it engages in discourse; in the hands it grasps; in the feet it moves and runs.
When fully manifested, it pervades the entirety of the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*; when withdrawn, it is concealed within a single speck of dust.

Those who awaken to this call it Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); those who are deluded call it the vital spirit (*jīva*). Upon hearing these words, the King attained immediate realization. Indeed, this is what those who awaken call...
As for this Buddha-nature, whatever one sees, hears, knows, perceives, acts, or does is none other than wondrous function.

Having attained this wondrous function, one immediately transcends birth and death. Those who are deluded call it the "spirit-soul" (jinghun); thus, whatever they see, hear, know, perceive, act, or do is none other than karmic consciousness.
Having formed karmic consciousness, they immediately fall into birth and death. What is meant by delusion? Delusion is not seeing the Buddha.
As for their nature: since they do not see the Buddha-nature, although these wondrous functions exist, they cannot be utilized.
Not only can they not be utilized, but they are also unaware of their own wonder. Take, for example, the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth, which are called the "seven apertures.
The nose has two apertures—why does it not hear sound? The ears have two openings—why do they not smell fragrance? These wondrous functions are already [present], yet...
One cannot fathom its depths; how much less so when the entire body lacks a sovereign master and there is confusion everywhere.
Hearing a sound, one runs after the sound; seeing a form, one runs after the form. Having thus run recklessly after forms and sounds, one is then entangled and bound by delusive objects.

From this point on, miscellaneous thoughts fly about and deluded imaginings become inverted. Such activities of the karmic consciousness and worldly toil are called defiled habits (*saṃkleśa*). As it is said:
This defiled habituation is the very root of the cycle of birth and death. Alas!

Though the Buddha-nature is one and the wondrous function is one, a difference as slight as a hair’s breadth results in a separation as vast as heaven and earth. Nevertheless, there is no root to delusion or enlightenment; the marvel lies in the point of transformation.
Therefore, in ancient times, the eminent and talented men turned their light back toward themselves here, tracing the current upstream to its source.
Among them were those who turned upon being struck and awakened upon hearing; there were also those who accumulated great effort over a long period before finally awakening.
Furthermore, there are those who, from youth until old age, spend their entire lives without attaining awakening.

This is due to nothing other than the varying degrees of the weight of their habitual defilements (*saṃkleśa*). Those with light habitual defilements awaken quickly; those with heavy habitual defilements awaken slowly.
Let me cite one or two examples as proof. For instance, in the past, the Vice Minister Fan Chong asked Chan Master Min: "I..."
Jiā was unfortunately immersed in the midst of worldly honors and purple robes, and thus remained somewhat distant from this matter. Míng called out the name of the Left Vice-Minister;
the Left Vice-Minister responded immediately. Míng said, "What distance is there? Lord Fàn leaped up in joy and requested further instruction once more. Míng struck his knee once.
As Lord Fàn pondered, Míng said, "This matter is seen the very moment it is seen; do not engage in deliberation."
He was cured immediately. Master Fan then attained sudden and thorough enlightenment. Is this not a case where, because one's habitual defilements were light, awakening occurred swiftly?
Furthermore, when Minister Yu Zhati of the Tang dynasty asked Chan Master Tong of Ziyu Mountain, "What is the Buddha?"
Tong immediately called out the name "Yuti. Master Yu responded at once. The teacher said, "This very thing is it; do not seek anything else.
Although Master Yu rejoiced in these words, he had not yet attained awakening. Consequently, he continued to consult and inquire from various masters, day and night without ceasing for a long time.
Later, when Master Yaoshan heard of this, he sighed and said, "What a pity for the Yu family!"
Han Huo was buried alive in Mount Ziyu. When Yu Ti heard of this, he went directly to Yaoshan to seek a resolution.
Following the previous inquiry, he asked, "What is the Buddha? Yaoshan also called out, "Yu Ti! Yu Ti responded accordingly. Yaoshan said, "What is this?
At these words, Master Yu attained great enlightenment. Comparing Yu Ti with Fan Chong, one can clearly see the difference between their respective speeds of realization.
Indeed, there are differences in the speed with which one attains realization, and there are also variations in the depth of that realization.

For instance, the lay practitioner Zhang Wujin traveled extensively to study under many great masters and further studied under Master Zhaojue of Donglin; he considered himself liberated and claimed that his understanding of the Chan school’s *jiyuan* (critical encounters) was thorough and penetrating.
At that time, while serving as the Regional Commissioner for Jiangxi, he was touring the administrative districts and arrived at Fenning in Hongzhou. The various mountain monasteries—
They went out to receive him. He invited them to sit and questioned each one in turn.
When it came to Chan Master Doushuai Yue, who sat at the end of the row, the abbots of the various mountains spoke on his behalf, saying, "This is Doushuai Yue, the High Priest.

Wujin then said with delight, "When I was in the capital, I heard that Doushuai was quite skilled in literary composition. Yue Gong replied with a stern expression and a firm voice, "I am a student of the Buddha-dharma."
"The Way of Single Transmission has little to do with literary composition. If I were to speak of literary composition to you, Excellency, it would be as if you were speaking of Chan to me.
Wu Jin was struck with wonder. When the various mountain monks had retired, he immediately ordered his carriage to visit Doushuai.
During a conversation at night, Yue asked, "I have heard that when you were at Donglin, there was no ancient or modern kōan through which you did not penetrate thoroughly;
is this true? The Master replied, "It is so. However, I have doubts regarding two instances: Deshan’s carrying of the almsbowl and Xiangyan’s climbing the tree.
Yue said angrily, "I took you for a man of substance, yet it turns out to be like this! If you have doubts about these two cases—"
"Then everything you have realized until now is not it at all. Now, please leave. He then closed the door to the abbot’s quarters.
Wujin could not sleep throughout the night in the guest pavilion; at the fifth watch, he suddenly attained realization. He immediately hurried to the abbot’s quarters and knocked on the door.
Xue asked, "What are you doing? Gong replied, "I have caught the thief. Xue said, "You have caught the thief; where is the stolen goods?"
"Where? The Master remained silent. Yuan said, "Not yet; you may go for now. The Master’s knot of doubt grew even hotter;
whether walking or sitting in the guest pavilion, he found no peace. Just as he turned to go up to his bed, it suddenly fell away from him.
He then ran back to the abbot’s quarters. At that time, Master Yuan had anticipated his arrival; he prepared incense and candles, opened the door, and received him, saying, "I am glad to see you."

When the Duke’s great affairs were concluded, they merely looked at one another and smiled; only then did I believe that when two eyes face two eyes of a Zen master, understanding occurs without waiting for a word to be spoken.
Only then did I believe that within the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), there are varying depths and heights in the realization of awakening.

Although the speed with which these several individuals mentioned above attained awakening and the depth of their realization depended upon the lightness or heaviness of their habitual conditioning, it was nevertheless...
It depends solely on whether one's faculties are sharp or dull; "faculties" refers to the seeds planted in past lives.
If one has cultivated and nurtured the seeds of goodness in past lives, one's faculties will be sharp and clear, and one will awaken quickly.
If one has not cultivated and nurtured the seeds of goodness in past lives, one's faculties will be clouded and dull, and one will awaken slowly. When I was in the mountains years ago...
While Master Zhongfeng of Tianmu Mountain was attending by his side, he saw five or six government officials sitting together at night discussing the Way.
Among them, one man suddenly sighed and said: "Those who have left the household life do not touch water with their ten fingers; they concern themselves with nothing.
Beneath the three-raftered roof and before the seven-foot mat, they hold up the staff and practice alone day and night, three times each. Yet even after ten years, two..."

"Ten years is not enough for awakening. We, who serve the state with our labor on the official path and act as shepherds and governors for the people, have not a single moment of stillness and concentration throughout the twelve hours of the day;
yet you wish to accomplish this matter—is that even possible? The Master said, "This argument is not so.
Whether one succeeds in office depends on the depth of one's roots; whether one awakens to the Way quickly or slowly depends on the capacity of one's faculties."

It is like a village child who wishes to become an official. From childhood he practices calligraphy and studies the arts of administration, beginning his career as a minor clerk in the district offices.
He plays at this until old age, yet he never manages to attain even the ninth or eighth rank.

By contrast, those who enter the service through the lineage of high-ranking officials (zhòng xiànggōng) obtain the fifth or fourth rank as a matter of course; there are even those who, despite being commoners (báisēn), attain the third rank. When these are compared—
"How far apart are minor officials? The study of the Way is likewise so. How can one distinguish between the difficulty and ease [of practice] based on the distinction between monk and layperson?
Those present at that time who heard this were all pleased and submissive, considering it a statement of ultimate truth.

Now, you Excellencies, my fellow Vice Commissioners, have personally experienced the Imperial Censorate; the handle of the law is in your hands, and your reputation shines brilliantly, shaking and illuminating the seas.
Within this assembly, there are those who occupy key positions and grasp the reins of governance; those who have entered military headquarters to hold the banners of command;
those who reside in the secretariat to manage official documents; and those who serve as instructors and act as masters of literature.
All of these were former disciples who once practiced within my school; therefore, their right mindfulness remains vividly clear. Not...
Obscured by wealth, status, fame, and achievement, they have instead come together to visit my Lion Grove to seek resolution regarding the supreme point of the Chan school.
How could this be a mere coincidence? Yet, here within my gates, I have no other method of instruction;
I simply ask that each of you take up the "Mu" (No) koan for investigation. This will not hinder you from proceeding to the various administrative offices as duty calls.
While governing the state and tending the people, whether engaged in military exercises or the cultivation of letters, one must constantly uplift and vigilantly scrutinize.
If one suddenly pierces through the pivot of the teaching, the eyes become empty of the world; who then would be willing to yield to those like Fan Chong or Yu Di as men of accomplished affairs?
An ancient said: "The governance of affairs does not depend on many words; it simply depends on how one puts them into practice.

Today, this mountain monk has already spoken far too much. To speak excessively is to distance oneself further from the Way. If you are those who can truly listen, you need only realize it at the point of the direct root.
But what is the point of the direct root? After a long silence, he let out a shout.
Descend from your seat.
At Mount Mace (Majiashan) on the road to the Prefecture, Qian Junxiang requests a general discourse. The mountains, rivers, and great earth fully reveal the body of the Dharma King;
the grasses, trees, and forests all perform the lion’s roar. If it is thus, then the marks and signs of the Buddhas of the ten directions are radiant.
The light fills the void, pervading the eyes and ears; the immeasurable Dharma gates of the Tripitaka are constantly and fervently proclaimed throughout the six periods of day and night.
Where there were once pleasure towers and wine pavilions, there are now nothing but pure lecture halls; where there were sword-trees and knife-mountains, all are now precious flower-throne kings.
Manifesting in one place, they simultaneously appear in a thousand places, ten thousand places, and in every single place at once.
Preaching the Dharma in one place, they simultaneously expound it in a thousand, ten thousand, and indeed all places.

They may manifest many bodies from a single body, or manifest a single body from many bodies. They may take a single dharma to be ten thousand dharmas, or take ten thousand dharmas to be a single dharma.
Like the pearls of Indra’s net, they mutually reflect and enter one another; like the images in a great round mirror, they interpenetrate and blend together. Its...
Bodhisattvas of the middle stages, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, all sentient beings, and even insentient things—each and every one of them simultaneously attains Buddhahood.
Although this is a plain and practical discussion of the manifest principle, it does not yet clarify the meaning beyond words;
it would leave the whole world in doubt. If one relies on the "nose-ring" of a monk to hold up what lies above, one cuts off the thousand [senses] at once.
He was sent to the head of the road. When the Buddha arrived, he was invited to stay outside the gate. Therefore it is said: "Do not be a companion to the myriad dharmas;

It can be eliminated. There is no enlightenment to be realized, no sentient beings to be saved, and no Buddhas to be accomplished.
To reach this point and yet still intend to preach the Dharma for others, or intend to teach people to practice Chan—how is this different from painting legs on a snake?

It will only invite the laughter of bystanders and bring shame upon the old Gautama, whose face is now three inches thick. If you have not yet attained this realization, then today the mountain monk...
I shall now go away, trailing mud and water, to deceive you all. O Great Assembly! Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally of one and the same substance;
it is only because of delusion and awakening that there is a distinction between the ordinary and the holy. That they share the same substance means they share this very mind.
To be an ordinary person through delusion is to be deluded regarding this mind; to be a holy one through awakening is to have awakened to this mind. Therefore it is said: "Delusion..."
To follow [delusion] is the beginning of birth and death; to awaken [to truth] is the cessation of saṃsāra. Alas! Sentient beings and Buddhas are originally of one essence;
yet, due to a single moment of awakening or a single moment of delusion, they are separated by a distance as vast as that between heaven and earth.

Therefore, our Great Master Bodhidharma traveled ten thousand miles from the West to establish a distinct school of teaching known as Chan (Zen). Its essential purpose lies in directly pointing to the [nature of mind].

It is simply that the mind of same essence is to be awakened. Since the transmission of our school’s fundamental tenets to the East, there have been countless disciples of the lineage—along with kings, ministers, elders, and lay practitioners—who have attained a vast and clear realization therein, secured the Great Dharani, and understood the liberation from birth and death.
Yet, among them, there are occasionally scholars and officials who harbor doubts and do not believe.
This is for no other reason than that your delusion is too deep and your faith has not yet been awakened.
You fail to reflect that the Buddha’s teaching on birth, old age, sickness, and death is vividly present before your very eyes. All of you, try to examine yourselves:
from youth to old age, from birth to death, you have rolled into a single mass with the consciousness of worldly toil and karma, fused into one whole. Ultimately...
How can this be brought to fruition? Ultimately, when will there be an end? What is that one turn of the head?
What is that single step of the body? Suddenly, when the three-inch breath is extinguished and the light of the eyes falls to the ground, the hundred limbs disperse and all affairs cease.
A solitary wandering soul follows its karma to receive retribution—is this not a life lived in vain and a death met in delusion, willingly enduring the cycle of rebirth?

How remarkable! Why not look back at our predecessors among the scholar-officials, who all attained enlightenment regarding the mind-ground under the lineage of the Chan school and broke through the barriers of Zen?
There were great karmic conditions and many exemplary models. Let me cite one or two instances to illustrate:

Retiring from his meal in the public hall, he leaned upon his desk; Unmoving and unshaken, his mind was like water. A single clap of thunder pierced the gate of his crown— Thus did he attain realization.
"Startled awake, [he realized] that which was originally his own. These are the words of Lord Zhao Qingxian, who broke through the Zen barrier.
"In the intervals between official duties, he delighted in sitting in meditation; he never once allowed his side to touch the bed.

Although he manifested the appearance of a civil official, his reputation as a "Venerable Elder" spread throughout the four seas. These are the words of Official Feng, describing his diligent application in the study of the Way.
Furthermore, for example, Vice Minister Zhang Zishao had long attended upon Master Dahui of Mount Jing.
Whenever he visited Mount Jing, he would remain there for a month or two; though his period of study and attendance was long, he had not yet attained enlightenment.

One day, while discussing the Way with Dahui at leisure, they reached the Confucianist principles of "extending knowledge" (*zhìzhī*) and "investigating things" (*gēwù*). Dahui laughed and said, "You only know how to investigate things."
Zi Shao did not understand the term "investigation of things" (wu ge).

Da Hui said, "What I call the investigation of things contains a subtle principle that is beyond the comprehension of Confucian scholars. Zi Shao was skeptical, yet he earnestly requested an explanation.

Mahāmati said: "This is a difficult point to express; please clarify it through an analogy. During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, there was an official whose name has been lost to history.
He once served as the Governor of Langzhou in Shu and administered the region with considerable virtue and merit.

Upon his retirement, the people of Langzhou held him in such high regard that they fashioned an image of him and established a temple to enshrine it for worship. Later, however, this man conspired with An Lushan to rebel."
The capital fell. Emperor Xuanzong fled westward into Shu. Upon reaching a temple in Langzhou, he beheld the statue and, filled with wrath, drew his sword and severed its head.
At that very moment, the person [who had been the statue] was in the army at Chang’an when his head suddenly fell to the ground for no apparent reason.

This is the subtle wonder of the investigation of things (*wu-ge*). It simply does not admit of conjecture or deliberation; one must merely investigate and examine within the context of one’s own primary practice (*ben-can-shi*).
Once awakening occurs, this principle will become clear of itself. Zishao became increasingly suspicious of this. From then on, he exerted himself with all his might to maintain mindfulness.
Suddenly, there was a realization, and he composed a verse, saying: "Zishao investigates things (*wu-ge*); Miaoxi [says] things are investigated (*wu-ge*). If you wish to know the One..."
Guan. Two *wubo* (five hundred). Da Hui approved of this. This is precisely the karmic occasion for Vice Minister Zhang’s realization of his own fundamental matter (*jishi*).
Others such as Lord Pei Mei, Bai Juyi, Liu Zongyuan, Zhang Wujin, Yang Yi, Yang Wuhui, Prince Fu, Lord Fan Wenzheng, and Lord Wang Jinggong were all masters of the Confucian tradition and sages.

Truly, these words are true. Now, Master Junxiang Qian of Mount Maji in Pilin has cultivated the seeds of goodness over many lifetimes.

Possessing the faculty of faith, he was able to resolve difficulties and settle disputes among his neighbors and fellow villagers, bestowing kindness and grace such that those both near and far were without exception pleased and submissive.
In recent years, he has further traveled extensively to famous mountains, where he has encountered many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
He is capable of performing what others cannot perform and renouncing what others cannot renounce.

Could one who has not been perfumed by the seeds of past goodness act in such a way? Now, once again, you have extensively convened this Dharma assembly, leading the present multitude to seek instruction on the method of Chan meditation;

Turn over and completely overturn all deluded thoughts, false notions, evil cognitions, and perverse perceptions within your breast;
cut them with a single stroke into two pieces until you are utterly bare, naked, and clear, standing solitary, remote, and toweringly sublime.

Only then, take up a single koan of the Patriarchs and hold it up with fierce intensity, so that its constant radiance manifests before you, standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. Act likewise in this manner while walking.
Sitting is thus; donning robes and eating meals are thus; welcoming guests and seeing them off are thus; today is thus; tomorrow is thus.
Thus and thus, one presses on until reaching the point where the patterns of the fabric meet at the corners;

when one arrives where the water ends and the mountains exhaust themselves, with a sudden "thump" of the staff, one attains sudden, expansive awakening. This very moment is the manifestation of the Great [Way].

This is the time for action. After having clarified the principle, you must further undergo refinement once more in the furnace of a master and by the tongs and hammers of your own fundamental practice.
Only when there is not even a hair’s breadth of leakage may you be permitted to untangle the entanglements and cast off the bonds.

Once you have untangled the entanglements and cast off the bonds, you will naturally realize life and transcend death. Once you have realized life and transcended death, you will naturally transform the mundane into the sacred. Once this is attained...
Transforming the mundane into the sacred is like a person arriving home. With authority in hand, a single call from the hall above is answered by a hundred responses below;
as the wind blows, the grass bends, and as the water flows, the channel is formed. One opens their own inexhaustible treasury, taking from it without limit and using it without depletion.
Only then does one believe that mountains, rivers, and the great earth are the Dharma King’s body, fully revealed before one’s eyes, even down to the grasses and trees.
The entire forest simultaneously let out a lion’s roar. Whether speaking horizontally or vertically, there was nothing spoken that did not penetrate;

whether acting in reverse or in accord, there was nothing performed that did not reach its goal. With mastery in rolling up or unfolding and freedom in bestowing or taking away, he even manifested great supernormal powers and displayed sublime functions:
from the tip of a single hand he spat forth the waters of the great ocean, and he took a single mustard seed and...
To overturn Mount Sumeru is entirely ordinary and by no means extraordinary;
it is, from the very outset, identical to the realization, identical to the liberation, identical to the enjoyment, and identical to the sovereignty of all Buddhas and patriarchs.
All manner of marks and signs, all manner of adornments, all manner of merit, and all manner of wisdom are each fully complete and each manifestly perfected. Each and every one...

Without distinction, each and every thing proceeds in equality. When I, this mountain monk, raise up [the Dharma] in this manner, it is much like prematurely fanning the wind of joy—greedily grasping for what is ahead while losing what is behind;
it is like painted cakes that do not satisfy hunger, or spoken medicines that do not cure illness.

It would be better instead to extract the very koan you are investigating from beneath your own heels and recognize the true host. You must by no means follow along with the flow of external conditions.
You run outward in pursuit. If you were to turn the light back for even a single thought-moment, the true host would not be far away.
If you abandon yourself to seek elsewhere, you will only become further estranged from it. Nowadays, many speak much while knowing little; listen to this verse:

The mind is in the sky; it is not in the waves.
At the request of Lord Fei of Shanghai County, [the Master] ascended the seat at Zhenru Hermitage to perform the full distribution and dispersal of the Tripitaka. A monk asked:
"From the Deer Park in the beginning, until the Bahudhita River in the end—within these two intervals, you have never uttered a single word. Is this still the ultimate?"
The Master said, "I thought you had forgotten, Venerable Sir. The student replied, "If that is so, then the World-Honored One did not speak what was spoken, and Kāśyapa did not hear what was heard.
The Master said, "What about the Great Canon of Sutras? The student replied, "When the benevolent see it, they call it benevolence;
when the wise see it, they call it wisdom. The Master said, "And when you, Venerable Sir, see it, what do you call it?"
The monk prepared to respond. The Master then gave a shout. The monk said, "I have words. The Master said, "You say again that 'he who does not speak speaks, and he who does not hear hears.
The monk bowed. The Master then addressed the assembly, saying: "The World-Honored One spoke what was unspeakable;
Kāśyapa heard what was unheard. What a perfectly realized Great Canon! It fills the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and is scattered across all the hundred grasses."
At the edge of one's head, night is dark and day is bright; Yunmen’s rain falls and the wind rises, the water surges, the magpies screech and the crows caw—even down to the walls and the rubble.
Throughout the twelve hours of the day and night, they proclaim this teaching with blazing intensity, without interval, without interruption, without confusion, and without destruction.
Each has its own name, its own appearance, its own phrasing, and its own sentences; or by means of a single sentence, it unfolds a thousand or ten thousand verses.

One may utter ten thousand phrases or a thousand phrases without perceiving them as many; or one may expound ten thousand phrases and a thousand phrases so as to enter into a single phrase without perceiving it as few.

What is called the unimpededness of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the unimpededness of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the unimpededness of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the unimpededness of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*) are all contained therein.
Indeed, it does not depend on the World-Honored One’s speaking or Kāśyapa’s hearing; rather, the sentient and the non-sentient respond according to their kind.
It has been circulated and passed on. Suddenly, there might be a faceless fellow who comes forth and says: "Not so, not so!

In the ground of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is admitted; all Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky.
To conceptualize them as existing phenomena is to be called a person of false views. When I, this mountain monk, arrive here, I am simply unable to distinguish anything.
To say they exist is not permitted; to say they do not exist is not permitted; to say they are neither existent nor non-existent is not permitted. Even if one were to [employ] a thousand...
The Buddha emerges with his head; he has a mouth that is fit only for hanging on a wall. Holding up his staff, he says: "Lower your voices, lower your voices! Śākyamuni the Old Man is coming!
He is now upon the tip of this staff to adjudicate this matter. Do you wish to know if there is any dharma to be spoken?"
Pointing to the left side of the main table, he said: "Receive [the truth] here. Do you wish to know that there is no dharma to be spoken?

Pointing to the right side of the table, he said: "Receive [the truth] here. Do you wish to know that it is neither existent nor non-existent? Pointing to the center of the table, he said: [The same.]
Recommend this point here! To recommend it, recommend it immediately; do not allow for a moment’s hesitation.

If you cannot do so, then I ask the Master of the Staff to cut off both ends and open up another path. (He draws a line and says: "Venerable ones, there is no dharma apart from the mind, and no mind apart from dharmas.

If this mind is awakened, then whether speaking or not speaking, and whether in affairs or at rest, all are of one house. It is not that arising from principle to manifest affairs, or manifesting principle through affairs, precludes this;
there is both substance and function, and we discuss the real rather than the empty. Take for instance Master Tao:

having awakened to the mind seven kalpas ago, he has come from within the Buddha-dharma. Since his emergence into the world, he has possessed spiritual transformations. In recent years, he has frequently manifested [his power].
He thought: "I simply wish to manifest the Jewel-King Realm and turn the Great Dharma Wheel. Thereupon, he opened his own treasure-trove and brought forth the rare jewels of his own house.
He constructed a *araṇya* of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and manifested the Spirit Mountain (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) for this single assembly.
He created various adornments and offered various forms of worship. Then, he again commanded the monks to take the forty-nine years of Śākyamuni’s teaching...
The Dharma taught throughout more than three hundred assemblies— from a single word, a single phrase, a single fascicle, or a single case, up to the entire Great Canon—
is thoroughly overturned from its very depths. Within it, there is nothing that does not include the provisional and the real,
the sudden and the gradual, the partial and the perfect, the half and the full, as well as faith, understanding, cultivation, realization, cause and effect, the stages of the path, and so forth.
To proclaim and disseminate it is like opening wide the eight characters of these immeasurable treasures accumulated by this Elder over countless kalpas and bestowing them as gifts upon all people.
For this reason, the various Bodhisattvas— both those prior to and those on the stages— as well as the practitioners of the Two Vehicles,
both with and without further training, receive this gift of Dharma and, according to their respective doors of practice, proceed toward the *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇas.

According to their respective capacities, they have realized and entered [this truth]. All the great devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the eight classes of beings throughout the entire dharma-realm—whether hidden or manifest, saintly or ordinary—receiving this gift of Dharma, increase their great majestic power to protect the wheel of the True Dharma. Now, as for this present assembly before me:
Some uphold, recite, and chant [this scripture]; some rejoice upon seeing or hearing it; and some provide for those who serve as messengers, attendants, or laborers.
By virtue of this gift of Dharma, they all together resolve to attain Bodhicitta and enter the ocean of wisdom. Next was the Layman Wuxin:
his paternal clan was Tao, his maternal clan was Tong, and his husband’s clan was Fei. Among these three clans, one...
He transformed all his kinsmen and relatives, extending his influence to his fellow villagers and neighbors;

furthermore, the sons of the Buddha, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, received this Dharma-gift, thereby escaping the wheel of birth-and-death suffering and transcending into the realm of the Tathāgata. Subsequently, the layman attained great *dhāraṇī* and great enjoyment;
the obstacles of karma, the obstacles of retribution, and the obstacles of affliction were here eliminated, along with the roots of precepts and concentration.
The faculty of wisdom grows here; the treasury of the true Dharma-eye is revealed here; the wondrous mind of nirvana is awakened to here.

From the very first moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment, whatever one has pursued, directed toward, vowed for, or sought after—all of these have been fully and perfectly realized here.
Today, this mountain monk ascends this seat to proclaim that initial aspiration.
Through the merit of a single thought, one will realize the final stage of glory.

I dare guarantee that from this moment until the very shore of birth and death, you shall achieve the eighty thousand gates in a single snap of the fingers, leaping directly into the ground of the Tathāgata.

With each exhalation, do not involve yourself in worldly toil; constantly turn this sutra a hundred thousand, ten million, or even billions of times.

it resides precisely where you, Layman, hold the *huatou* and apply effort. Nor does the practice of the *huatou* reside elsewhere; it resides precisely within you, Layman...
