Striking the meditation seat with his hand, he said: "The daily practice leaves no room for concealment; upon hearing these words, one should readily take up the realization of the mind.
Cast aside both the sutras and the ocean of the Tripitaka; the flower of the mind wells forth, illuminating the ten directions."
At the residence of Lü Zirun in Songjiang, various mountain masters assembled for a seven-day *Huayan* (Avataṃsaka) assembly to offer merit for the deceased, the lay practitioner Xu Shì Liǎoxīn.
Each day, the Master was invited to ascend the seat to proclaim the essential meaning of the *Huayan*.

On the first day, as he ascended the seat, a monk asked: "The realms of boundless lands are not separated by so much as a hair’s tip from one another; yet since there are 'self' and 'other,' for what reason..."
"Not at all separated. The Master said, "The ox in Huai Prefecture eats the grain; the horse in Yi Prefecture has a bloated belly.

[The student] asked, "Throughout ten generations of past and present, beginning and end are never apart from the present thought. Since there is a beginning and an end, why are they not apart? The Master said, "Seeking a physician throughout the world, one applies moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig.
[The student] further said, "In this assembly, we should rather propagate the scriptural teachings; there is no need for you to trouble yourself with speaking of Chan. Furthermore, I hope—"
The Chan Master spoke directly on the meaning of the teachings. The Master said, "How could this mountain monk ever have two tongues? Question:
"Within the one true dharma-realm and its ten profound gates, are there still self and other, or beginning and end? The Master shouted, "How could you bring so much clutter here?
The questioner pressed further: "Since there is no such clutter, what exactly is the meaning of that which the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra describes?"
The Master said, "I am lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. A monk asked, "Apart from the profound gate of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), where does the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* reside?

The Master said, "It is in the hands of everyone present. The monk further asked, "If that is so, then those who see it, hear it, preserve it, or lose it will all be able to receive it with faith and put it into practice.
The Master said, "I give you three coins to buy straw sandals. The monk bowed.
The Master then said: "A Zen guest asks about Zen, yet charges this mountain monk to speak directly on the meaning of the teachings.
This mountain monk has but one tongue, while the Zen guest has two ears. Now, to comply with human sentiment, I shall offer some ready-made words. O Great Assembly!
Within the single true Dharma-realm, boundless worlds are all encompassed; within the ten profound gates..."
It universally encompasses immeasurable Dharma gates: it is both phenomenon and principle; both essence and appearance; both the conventional and the ultimate;
both cause and fruit; both the principal and the attendant; both the holy and the ordinary; both the primary and the dependent; both the many and the one.

It manifests in successive layers like the jewels of Indra’s net, and contains all within itself everywhere like a sea of fragrant water—not by the power of supernatural faculties, but by its very nature.
This is simply the natural law (*dharmatā*). For those who are deluded, every path they encounter becomes an obstruction; for those who have awakened, it is fully manifest right where they stand.
This is the discourse of the *Avataṃsaka*’s sudden and perfect teaching that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

The *Avataṃsaka* is the sūtra spoken by our World-Honored One across seven locations and nine assemblies. As for these seven locations and nine assemblies: the first was at the Bodhimaṇḍa; the second was at the Universal Radiance [Hall].
The Bright Hall; the third is the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the fourth is the Yāma Heaven; the fifth is the Tuṣita Heaven; the sixth is the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
the seventh and eighth are the Universal Radiance Halls of the Double Assembly; and the ninth is the Jetavana Grove.

In the first assembly, the Tathāgata’s dependent retribution and primary retribution were expounded; in the second assembly, the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) were expounded; and in the third assembly, the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) were expounded.
In the fourth assembly, the Ten Practices were taught; in the fifth assembly, the Ten Dedications; in the sixth assembly, the Ten Grounds;

and in the seventh assembly, Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment. These seven assemblies above are all taught in sequential order, which is called the "Dharma-gate of Sequential Arrangement" (*xingbu famen*).
In the eighth and ninth assemblies, the Universal Wisdom [Bodhisattvas] raised two hundred questions, and Universal Worthy [responded with] the Vase...
I shall grant two thousand in recompense for this exposition. Generally speaking, when one dharma is taught, all dharmas are entirely contained within it;

this is called the "Dharma-gate of Perfect Interfusion" (*yuanrong*). Sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) is like peach and plum blossoms: first the flower, then the fruit. Perfect Interfusion is like the lotus flower:

the flower and the fruit exist simultaneously. Furthermore, Perfect Interfusion has two meanings: first, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition; second, the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause. As for the cause encompassing...

"The ocean of fruition" refers to the ten faiths; at that time, the ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment are all contained therein.
"The fruition penetrates to the source of the cause" refers to the time of equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment;

at that time, the ten stages, ten transferences, ten practices, ten abidings, and ten faiths are likewise all contained therein. Therefore it is said: "In its outward deployment, it constitutes the characteristics of the teachings."

They are distinct. In their perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), essence and appearance are without obstruction. Since appearance is appearance that is identical to essence, the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) does not obstruct perfect interfusion.
Since essence is essence that is identical to appearance, perfect interfusion does not obstruct the sequential arrangement.

Because perfect interfusion does not obstruct the sequential arrangement, the one becomes the immeasurable. Because the sequential arrangement does not obstruct perfect interfusion, the immeasurable becomes the one. Immeasurable...
When unified, they are harmoniously integrated; when one becomes infinite, they enter into one another in layers upon layers.

Thus, the sutras of the nine assemblies together comprise eighty fascicles. Furthermore, these eighty fascicles are divided into four sections, known as Faith, Understanding, Practice, and Realization.
First, there are eleven fascicles which open the gateway of faith for sentient beings. Next...
There are forty-one fascicles that open up the gate of understanding for sentient beings. Following those, there are seven fascicles that open up the gate of practice for sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are twenty-one fascicles that open up the gate of realization for sentient beings.
A certain great scripture does not go beyond the four divisions of faith, understanding, practice, and realization.

The meanings elucidated by these four divisions do not exceed the five cycles, the six characteristics, the ten mysterious gates, and the four dharma realms. One understands through faith; one practices through understanding.
Realization is attained through practice; this is the fundamental purport from beginning to end of this single sutra. Since the great purport of the sutra is now clearly manifest, one may ask:
what is the meaning of the previous statement that those who are deluded encounter obstructions at every turn?

This refers to those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) present in the assembly at that time—those who had ears but did not hear the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, and who had eyes but did not see the body of Śākyamuni.
It is so. For one who awakens to it, it is fully manifest right where they are. What does this mean?
This refers to the ten profound gateways pointed out by the great virtuous ones currently present for the lay practitioner Xu Shìliǎoxīn, which serve to reveal and exalt the single true Dharma-realm.
Have you not heard the Way taught: "Within every single atom of all the worlds in the Flower Treasury, one sees..."
The Dharma-realm. Do you all see it yet? [He strikes with the whisk to the left. The ten profound gates have been opened. [He strikes to the right.

The one true Dharma-realm has manifested. If you can see it thus, you will see that the inexhaustible treasury of merit and boundless radiance, filling the void and pervading the Dharma-realm, is present here and now—bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field.
The ocean-like assembly is also here. The spiritual friends and the eight classes of gods and dragons, as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, are also here.
The thrones, couches, jeweled nets, jeweled canopies, jeweled trees, jeweled lotuses, jeweled flower garlands, and jeweled necklaces, as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, are also here.
The clouds of fragrant flames and clouds of flower-flames, as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, are also here.
The clouds of lamp-flames, the clouds of mani-jewels, and the clouds of lion-banners are also here. Question: Are they also here? Answer:
They are also here. Perfect interfusion is also here; sequential arrangement is also here.
Faith is also here; understanding is also here; practice is also here; realization is also here. Maitreya snapped his fingers.
The opening of the gates of the pavilion is right here. Mañjuśrī extending his hand to stroke the crown of Sudhana’s head is also right here.
Even the five cycles, the six aspects, the ten mysterious gates, and the four dharma-realms are all right here.
Is this not the total manifestation of reality in its very place? Now, for your sakes, I shall further summarize [the teaching] at the point that is most intimate and essential.
He gathers them in. Striking and waving his whisk, he says: "The World-Honored One had seven locations; here, we have but one location. The World-Honored One had nine assemblies;
here, we have but one assembly. The World-Honored One preached eighty fascicles of sutras; here, we have but a single phrase. Everyone, tell me: what is that one phrase?
He then speaks in a loud voice: "To realize the mind! Again, he strikes the floor with his staff and says: "To realize—that is realization."
Indeed! Ultimately, where do all people meet with the layman? Listen to this verse: The mind that realizes the mind is utterly mindless;
Right there, the meaning is fully revealed and becomes ever more profound. The muddy waters of supplication transform into the Flower Treasury Ocean;
The flowers of awakening bloom everywhere throughout the groves of manifold blossoms.
On the second day, he ascended the seat. The Flower Treasury World of Vairocana’s Adorned Ocean pervades all places;
the Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra encompasses all phenomena. Since the Flower Treasury Ocean already pervades every location, tell me:
what of those foul and evil realms such as cattle pens, horse stables, wine shops, brothels, the sword-trees, the knife-mountains, the cauldrons of boiling water, and the furnaces of glowing coals?

Furthermore, where could it be established? Since there is no place for it to be established, can one then take glowing coals, boiling cauldrons, mountains of knives, and forests of swords and call them the Flower Treasury Ocean (*Kusumagarbha-sāgara*)?
Can one then take brothels, wine shops, horse stables, and cow pens and call them the Flower Treasury Ocean?
If one does not call these the Flower Treasury Ocean, then one cannot say that it pervades all places.
It is the locus of all things. Since the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* encompasses all phenomena, tell me:
where do you distinguish the foul and evil sounds of spirits wailing, ghosts crying, the sound of water, the sound of wind, dogs barking, chickens crowing, donkeys braying, and horses neighing?

Since there is no place of conceptual discrimination, can one then take the neighing of horses, the braying of donkeys, the crowing of chickens, and the barking of dogs and call them the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*?
Can one then take the sound of the wind, the noise of water, the wailing of ghosts, and the clamor of spirits and call them the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*?
If these are not called the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, then it cannot be said to "pervasively encompass all phenomena. O sharp-witted one!
Now, those men of superior talent and virtue were unable to point it out from within, nor could they discern its distinctions.
Today, this mountain monk shall point it out for you all: there are immeasurable and innumerable oceans of fragrant water with floating pavilions;
immeasurable and innumerable world-systems with their surrounding mountain ranges; immeasurable and innumerable sites of liberation and enlightenment; and immeasurable and innumerable mani-jewels.
A mass of jewel-light; clouds of immeasurable and innumerable palaces and towers; immeasurable and innumerable lotus lion-thrones;
immeasurable and innumerable manifested and adorned bodies; and immeasurable and innumerable cities, kingdoms, and spiritual friends.
Holding up his whisk, he said: "Right now, they are all simultaneously revealed upon the tip of this whisk. The Teacher Vairocana..."
That which is spoken by the mouth; that which is spoken by Samantabhadra, the King of Vows Bodhisattva; that which is spoken by Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva of Great Wisdom;
that which is spoken by the Bodhisattvas present in the seven locations and nine assemblies;

that which is spoken by the assembly of all great-minded sentient beings, devas, nāgas, asuras, and the forty-one stages of Dharma-body Mahāsattvas; and that which is spoken by the earth spirits and water spirits.
The Fire Deity speaks; the Wind Deity speaks; the Mountain Deities, Forest Deities, Tree Deities, and Deities of the *bodhimaṇḍa* speak.
Even the Cloud Terrace speaks, the Jewel Net speaks, the Dust speaks, the World-System speaks, and the Blazing Radiance speaks. The Master of the Staff says:
"Right now, at the very bottom of this staff, it has been simultaneously proclaimed. But tell me, why is it that the staff and the whisk are thus?
How extraordinary! If one knows the extraordinary places of others, one then knows the places where they manifest transformations and achieve unimpeded fusion.
If one knows the places where they manifest transformations and achieve unimpeded fusion, one then knows that they pervade all places and encompass all phenomena.

Only by knowing it in this way can one understand the divine cries and ghostly wails, the sounds of water and wind, and the barking of dogs, the crowing of roosters, the braying of donkeys, and the neighing of horses.

There is not a single dharma that is not the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Whether it be a cowshed, a stable, a tavern, a brothel, a forest of sword-trees, a mountain of knives, a cauldron of boiling water, or a brazier of burning coals—there is not a single place that is not the Flower-Treasury Ocean (*Puṣpakaraṇḍa-sāgara*).
If this mind is not yet realized, names and forms appear in myriad variations; once this mind is realized, essence and function are one. The samādhi of realizing the mind can be thus.
"It is so. Those who have not realized their minds do not know this.
He then struck the sounding block, descended from the seat, and on the third day ascended the seat again, saying: "The fifty-three patriarchs are upon your eyebrows and eyelashes;
the eighty-one fascicles of the Great Sutra are at the tip of your nostrils and around your lips. If you wish to act upon these eyebrows and eyelashes..."
If you seek it, you will have missed it by thousands and tens of thousands of miles.

If you try to seek it at the nostrils or the lips, you will lose it through a thousand errors and ten thousand deviations. Have you not heard it said that there is a great scripture within a single mote of dust?
There is a wise person who breaks open this minute speck of dust to bring forth the great scripture. If you can see this great scripture—
Then all eighty-one volumes would become nothing but idle scrap paper.
Furthermore, have you not heard it said that true spiritual friends are not separate from one's own self? That the Way is sought within oneself and not found by seeking elsewhere?
If you can see this very spiritual friend, then those fifty-three patriarchs are all merely people by the roadside. If you are not yet able to accept this in such a manner, then you must not wait.
Let us pass through this at leisure. This eighty-one fascicle work has a beginning and an end;
it is best to read it from the start. These fifty-three members have their own sequence; one may proceed by examining each position in turn.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) nurtures all roots of goodness, just as the Snowy Mountains nurture all medicinal herbs. A spiritual friend is a locus of merit.
Just as the great ocean gives birth to all manner of jewels, so too the spiritual friend is unstained by worldly dharmas.

Just as the lotus flower is not adhered to by water, so too the spiritual friend does not accept any evils. Just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse, [so too the spiritual friend does not harbor evil].
A spiritual friend illuminates the dharma-realm, like the blazing sun shining upon the four continents.
A spiritual friend causes the body of a bodhisattva to grow, like parents nurturing their children. Furthermore, it is said that seeing a spiritual friend prevents the mind from becoming distracted;
seeing a spiritual friend shatters the mountains of obstacles; and seeing a spiritual friend enters the ocean of great compassion to provide protection and rescue.
Sentient beings, upon seeing spiritual friends, obtain the light of wisdom that universally illumines the dharma-realm;

they see spiritual friends as being able to universally behold the ocean of Buddhas of the ten directions; they see spiritual friends as enabling them to behold all Buddhas turning the wheel of Dharma.
It is further said that by associating with spiritual friends, one is able to courageously and diligently cultivate the path to omniscience; through associating with spiritual friends...
Consciousness can swiftly give birth to an ocean of great vows. By associating with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), one can undergo immeasurable suffering on behalf of all sentient beings;
by associating with spiritual friends, the sound of the Dharma taught within a single atom can pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
and by associating with spiritual friends, one brings the practice of a bodhisattva to ultimate completion in every moment of thought.
They abide on the stage of omniscience. By associating with spiritual friends, they are able to travel throughout the lands of the ten directions.
Excellent, excellent! Such is the benefit of spiritual friends. Nevertheless, even so...
To meet a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) requires great karmic conditions. Those with such conditions encounter them even across a thousand li;
those without such conditions pass them by despite being face-to-face. An utpala flower is easy to see, but a great virtuous friend is most difficult to encounter.
How could these words deceive anyone? It is simply that this lay practitioner of the Xu family has long possessed great karmic affinity and has encountered many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Furthermore, although this mountain monk certainly possesses no outstanding qualities, the lay practitioner once offered incense, sought the Way, and presented his inquiries for my instruction.
Now, though this illusory body composed of the four elements is said to be dead, his spirit of seeking instruction and inquiring about the Way—
The mind is luminous, numinous, clear, and vivid. Eye meets eye—where has there ever been birth or death?
What was previously called a "true spiritual friend" is not separate from oneself. Now that you have encountered external teachers, go and seek the teacher within yourself.
Layman, do you understand? Amidst vast mists and waters across more than a hundred cities, who is willing to follow?
A person walks behind; before their feet have even crossed the threshold, they have already met. Upon arriving home, one has never actually traveled the road.
On the fourth day, he ascended the seat and said: "If anyone wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm."
"All is created by mind alone. This single verse encompasses, without exception, all realms of the mundane and supramundane, as well as those of the sages and the ordinary.
What is called the "Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) consists of the four realms of the sages and the six realms of the ordinary;
these four and six together constitute the ten Dharma-realms. The four sages are the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas. The six ordinary...
These are the realms of devas, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings. Thus, these ten dharma-realms originally have no self-substance and originally have no self-nature.
They have neither seeds of their own nor roots of their own; they are all created solely by the single mind.
What is called "mind" is like the great void: fundamentally pure and fundamentally vast and transparent, without direction and without...

It is without marks and without form; it neither perishes nor arises, neither moves nor changes. Not knowing for what reason [you say this], you claim that the dharma-realm is created solely by the mind.
To examine the origin of this mind: although it is said to be unchanging, it also follows conditions (*pratyaya*).
Because it follows conditions, it is said to be "capable of creating. That which follows conditions may arise from a fleeting thought, or it may arise from contact with external objects.

Because internal and external factors interact through contact, they are called causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). As soon as causes and conditions exist, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is formed.
To clarify this by means of a metaphor: the mind is like water, and the Dharma-realm is like waves.

When the substance of the water is originally still, before there is any contact with external stimuli, it is profoundly clear and limpid, neither shaking nor moving. Yet, when it happens to encounter the touch of the wind, a thousand waves arise.
Ten thousand waves arise according to whatever they encounter; hence it is said that water can create waves, and waves exist because of water.

The mind can create the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and the dharma-realm exists because of the mind. Thus, that which is spontaneously adorned with ten thousand virtues through the One Vehicle is the dharma-realm of all Buddhas.
That which perfectly cultivates the six perfections and universally encompasses ten thousand practices is the [path] of the Bodhisattvas.
The dharma-realm of the Bodhisattva; the dharma-realm of the Pratyekabuddha, who limits their vision to causes and conditions and realizes the principle of partial emptiness;
the dharma-realm of the Śrāvaka, who accomplishes the Four Noble Truths and returns to the Lesser Nirvana;

the dharma-realm of the Heavenly Path, which extensively cultivates precepts and virtues as causes for outflowing existence; and the realm of humans, where defiled attachments do not cease while various wholesome conditions are intermingled.
The Dharma-realm of the Path. Those who stubbornly cling to a sense of superiority and constantly harbor anger and strife constitute the Dharma-realm of the asuras.

Those whose roots are love and views, and whose karma is stinginess and greed, constitute the Dharma-realm of the hungry ghosts. Those whose desire and greed do not cease and whose deluded thoughts arise recklessly constitute the Dharma-realm of the animals.
Those who create the ten causes of habituation and undergo the sixfold retributive interactions constitute the [Dharma-realm] of the earth...
The Dharma-realm is the nature of the prison. To discuss it in its vastness:
the twentyfold Flower-Treasury World-Ocean is manifested and constructed based on this mind; the boundless seas of fragrant water flow forth based on this mind;
the great and small Iron Ring Mountains abide based on this mind; and the sun, moon, and stars revolve based on this mind.
It is practice. All the jeweled rows of trees grow in dependence upon this mind. All the great lotus flowers bloom in dependence upon this mind.
That which all sentient beings are deluded about is this very mind. That which the worthy and holy ones of the Three Vehicles awaken to is this very mind.
That which the entire Great Canon of Teachings elucidates and guides is this very mind. Throughout...
What the successive patriarchs have pointed out is this very mind. The three contemplations are the contemplation of this very mind. The single transmission is the transmission of this very mind.
Cultivating through successive kalpas is the cultivation of this very mind. Realizing through successive stages is the realization of this very mind.
It is precisely because this mind transforms and creates in accordance with conditions that there exist the various realms of reality (dharmadhātus). If one can...
When one realizes and attains enlightenment through single-minded non-arising, then the various dharma-realms are empty according to that realization.
Therefore, once the ten habitual tendencies are severed and the six intersections do not arise, the mind of hell is extinguished.

Once desire and greed are severed and deluded thoughts do not arise, the mind of animals is extinguished. Once craving and views are severed and stinginess and greed do not arise, the [mind of] hungry ghosts...
When the mind of victory is extinguished, anger and strife do not arise; this is the extinction of the asura-mind.

When attachment is severed and right mindfulness manifests before one, this is the extinction of the human mind. Abandoning the causes of outflows and cultivating untainted karma—this is the extinction of the heavenly mind.
The mind of the Way of Heaven is realized. Not clinging to the Four Noble Truths and not guarding at the emptiness of the absolute—this is the realization of the Śrāvaka mind.
Not being confined by causes and conditions, turning the mind to enter the Great Vehicle—this is the realization of the Pratyekabuddha mind.

When the merit of the Six Perfections is perfected and one suddenly transcends the stages and positions—this is the realization of the Bodhisattva mind. Perfecting Bodhi and returning to non-attainment—this is the mind of all Buddhas.
"I have understood. Now, Layman Liaoxin has spent his life investigating this mind, vowing to seek its realization.
Within the six realms of ordinary beings, he must surely have already realized it and harbors no doubts. But tell me:
within the four realms of the noble ones, in which realm does the mind he has realized fall? He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
On the fifth day, he ascended the seat. "If one wishes to know the realm of the Buddha, one should purify the mind so that it is like empty space;
far removed from deluded thoughts and all grasping, let the mind be unimpeded wherever it turns. What is called the realm of the Buddha?

It refers to those who, while alive, encounter calamities from kings, and at death, fall into the three miserable realms—the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals—where they undergo suffering and punishment. These three obstacles are like hooks.
Like interlocking rings bound together without interruption, it is therefore called saṃsāra.
At this time, the bright and luminous ancient mirror transforms into dust and grime; the clear, translucent, and still water solidifies into cold ice.

Hell is fundamentally empty; it is created by the stirring of a single thought of delusion. Therefore, it is said: "All phenomena arise from the mind; all transgressions arise from the mind.

By removing dust and grime, the light of the ancient mirror is revealed once more; it is like relying on the bright sun to melt away the cold ice, thereby restoring the nature of still water.
Thus it is said: "All phenomena are extinguished through the mind; all transgressions perish through the mind.

If the offense is grave, one will be reborn in a Buddha-land; compared to this, what difference is there between this and merely escaping one's original transgression? It is more than a distinction as vast as that between heaven and earth.

Let it go. Let this discourse cease for now. To exhaustively fathom its spiritual subtlety is as the sutras describe: manifesting jeweled lands upon the tip of a single hair.
He turns the Wheel of Dharma within the mundane dust and casts the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters. He contains Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed;

there is not a single of the hundreds of thousands of samādhis that does not manifest through this. The essence of the mind is fundamentally one, yet at the moment of responding to affairs and interacting with others, one may occasionally lose its sovereign mastery, thereby giving rise to the distinctions between the heterodox and the orthodox, or the true and the false. What is the true mind? It is the original...

It is called being primordially pure and undefiled; it is called being primordially liberated and unimpeded; it is called the wondrous responsiveness that follows conditions with sovereign mastery in both vertical and horizontal dimensions.
What is meant by "deluded mind"? It refers to that which, due to delusion regarding true awakening, undergoes transformation according to thoughts;

wherein consciousness and perception fly about in confusion, and the sense organs and their objects become entangled and disturbed, such that there is no state of inversion and disorder to which it does not reach. It is like this:
It is like a mirror. Its fundamental substance is luminous and pure; when a Hu person comes, it reflects a Hu person; when a Han person comes, it reflects a Han person.

It responds to the myriad variations of beauty and ugliness without the slightest error. Yet, if one cannot protect its original truth and defiles it with the dust of delusion, which accumulates day by day and grows ever thicker, then that which is fundamentally luminous and pure becomes obscured.
Once there is a deluded mind, everything one pursues and everything one does is termed deluded karma. Thus it is said: [text continues].
Where there is deluded karma, there is deluded retribution; karma and its retribution follow one another like a form and its shadow, never parting.
Thus, the cycle of birth and death through the three miserable realms and five sufferings cannot be avoided.

To investigate the extent to which turning one's back on the Truth and following after delusion leads—how could the harm be anything but endless if there were no method for treatment? Therefore, our Buddha contemplated the means by which...
To treat it, one manifests the entire Great Canon of Teachings and extensively employs various skillful means; these are all methods for discarding delusion and attaining truth.

They are like the medicinal prescriptions used to polish a mirror, intended to ensure that it is polished and cleansed day by day until the defilements are exhausted and its brilliance appears, at which point the process ceases.
If one understands that treating the mind is like polishing a mirror, then every person can be made into a sage or a worthy.

Return! Let every person take the sages and worthies as their refuge. Then would the Buddha’s way of governing the mind be a strange, eccentric, or heterodox art, or a practice steeped in perilous, lofty, and obscure mysteries?
Those who are deluded in this world may cling to the words they first encountered or be confined by one-sided views;
thus they are unable to clear their eyes for the Buddhist scriptures or devote their minds to the Buddha-way. Since they do not know—
To believe and yet be slandered in return is like a blind man slandering the sun; who could possibly add to or detract from its impartial illumination?

Since the Dharma flowed eastward, those who have received its bounty have filled the world. Yet, in later times, circumstances diverged and the Dharma grew stale over the long duration, leading to the emergence of various corruptions.
Those who rely on the literal text to explain the meaning are many, while those who practice and cultivate it are few. For this reason:
Bodhidharma came once more to sweep away all antiquated dross. He pointed directly to the human mind and did not establish reliance on words and letters.

The essence lies in taking full responsibility for one's own being prior to the stimulus and beyond words; this is called the "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings," which is the ultimate in brevity, essentiality, and directness.
From this point on, the school of the separate transmission (biezhuan) spread throughout the land, and even renowned statesmen and eminent scholars all turned toward it.

Such as Prime Minister Pei, Prime Minister Zhang, Vice President Bai, Prefect Liu, Palace Secretary Yang, Yang Cigong, Duke Zhao Qingxian, Duke Fu Zheng, Imperial Annalist Huang, and Academician Su; none of them abandoned their wealth, honor, or official duties.
His literary works are renowned, yet he was able to elucidate the Way of Direct Pointing. His spirit swallowed the Buddhas and Patriarchs; his voice shook heaven and earth.
Is this not one who settled the matter in a single lifetime, bringing joy and liberation for a thousand ages?
Now, Lord Di of Xicun in Guangping is also one who deeply believes in our school. During the years of Tai ding (1325–1326), while I was staying at the Huan... in Wumen—
While residing at An, Xicun was observing the mourning period for his mother. He built a thatched hut (ilü) at the tomb outside Changguan, and his filial conduct was widely praised at the time.
I once composed a preface for his hut-dwelling, citing extensively from the Confucian classics; however, Xicun questioned me regarding the Buddha-dharma.
I then granted him permission, saying, "It will not be too late to speak of the Buddha-dharma for Xicun on another day. Thus, like swallows and wild geese, we parted.
North and South have been separated by a vast distance for sixteen years without hearing from one another.
Recently, I returned once more to Huanzhu, and Xicun also returned from the capital. Having reached the age of fifty, prosperity and honor are now coming his way;

yet he suddenly produced two long scrolls requesting words for his progress on the Path, citing the promises I had previously made to him as if demanding the payment of an old debt. However, our school...
There are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma to be given to others; it depends solely upon one’s own investigation, one’s own awakening, and one’s own realization.

As for the method of self-investigation and self-awakening, one must first illuminate through insight and shatter the world’s empty names, fleeting profits, attachments of affection, and worldly splendor.

The myriad realms and myriad conditions are one and the same as a dream or an illusion. Next, you must earnestly reflect that the passing of time is like a flying arrow and that time does not wait for man;
at the brink of birth and death, there is no foundation upon which to rely. Only then should you, moment by moment, maintain the essential points of the Chan school through constant mindfulness.

Precisely while maintaining this mindfulness, regarding the cultivation of the self, the regulation of the family, the hearing of lawsuits, the administration of justice, rites and music, and penal governance—[all these are seen as such].
The dissemination of this [teaching], the exchange of official documents and records—all these are mutually unimpeded; they are all points where one gains effective power upon application.
If one can truly act in this way, one’s efforts will not be in vain and one’s thoughts will not be wasted.
Suddenly, if the barriers are shattered and the very core of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is grasped, how could one then be surpassed by those such as Pei, Zhang, Su, and Huang? Now, Xicun requests...
"I have already settled my debt to him. Having elucidated the Way of Direct Pointing, I too have high hopes for you, Xicun.
When we meet again in the future, I shall demand payment of my debt from you; you must practice this with vigor and cultivate it to its ultimate depth."

At Zhen Dian Temple, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the Buddha? Zhaozhou replied, "The one in the hall. This single turning word is as light as a thread drifting through space, requiring not the slightest exertion of effort;
it is as swift as a hair-cutting blade, sweeping away all myriad distinctions and differences. From...
When the Buddhas and Patriarchs arrive here, even the sparks of flint and flashes of lightning cannot be grasped.

When the Treasury of the True Dharma-Eye arrives here, it dissolves like crumbling walls or melting ice; it cannot be lifted up. The ten directions are empty and desolate; not a single dharma accords with the mind.
There is nothing adhering that is not resolved, and no bondage that is not removed. Those of recent times who merely study words do not recognize the tongue of the ancients.
At the moment the head falls, upon hearing him say "the one within the hall," one immediately gives rise to conceptual deliberation.
Some claim that the Buddha is manifest before one's eyes, that sentient and insentient beings share the same enlightened essence; others claim that the Buddha is merely a construction of the mind.
To claim that wooden carvings and clay sculptures can manifest the Dharma-body is a peripheral indication;

to say this reveals the true mechanism apart from sound and beyond the mind is an extra-ordinary holding-up. To say it is the manifestation of the signless within signs, yet neither separate from nor identical to them—to examine these claims, they are all misunderstandings.
Since they are misunderstandings, one cannot avoid becoming stuck, layering further attachment upon bondage.
This is a supreme bondage; it brings the profound and wondrous words of the ancient masters into the realm of frivolous discourse. Is this not a grievous matter?

Even if one were to set aside the aforementioned misunderstandings and attain a distinct path through intellectual comprehension and practice, what can be done when, upon encountering conditions and confronting objects, one still fails to break through?
This is for no other reason than that, within one's own sphere, one has never yet penetrated through.
To penetrate from top to bottom and cast it off once and for all is, for the most part, like scratching an itch through a boot; what benefit does it provide?
Now, if you wish to cast it off once and for all, there is no difficulty: you need only apply intense energy to the point where your primary koan is intimate and direct.
Whether viewed horizontally or vertically, when you suddenly see through it, you will finally understand the story of "the one inside the hall.
Even the four kinds of horizontal deliberations mentioned above cannot deceive you anywhere. The Chan practitioner Zhen of Wuxing is the son of Master Wanshi;
he hangs his staff at Dacheng Temple and serves as the Hall Master. His mind for the sake of the assembly and for himself has been forged into a single whole.
This one fellow is truly a patch-robed monk who yearns for the Way. Having received the command of Chuan Wanshi, he came to me seeking words.
I therefore showed him my previous discourse and offered him this verse: "What is that which is within the Buddha Hall?
The Tathāgatas of the three periods have their eyesight clouded; The lanterns and the pillars break into smiles, Smiling until half the sky is split asunder. Tsk!"

He showed Master Guo of Shu that what is called "Teaching" (Jiao) refers to words and letters, while what is called "Chan" refers to being apart from words and letters. Chan is not a teaching external to Chan;
Teaching is not a Chan external to Teaching. Teaching is Chan with words and letters; Chan is Teaching without words and letters. Thus it is called Chan.
It is said that while the names of their teachings differ, their substance is the same; they are merely identical skillful means for the purpose of governing the mind.
The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to deliver all states of mind. Since I have no such states of mind, what use have I for all dharmas?

It is also like the myriad types of medical prescriptions, which are established for the sake of the myriad differences in illnesses. If the illness is removed, then whether [the medicine is] warm or cool, deficient or replete—[it is no longer needed].
To what end, then, would the medicinal powder be applied? Those who have not yet attained mastery of the principle of skillful means each privately cling to their own school.

Regarding the teachings (*jiao*), they hold it as supreme to memorize, recite, and study, interpreting the meaning strictly according to the literal text. Regarding meditation (*chan*), they consider it lofty to sit blankly like a blind man, refusing to enter the path of meaning.
Each clings to their own "one is," and they mutually condemn one another. Unless one attains thorough awakening to one’s own mind...
For one who perceives the meaning of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), how could right and wrong ever cease to exist?

Formerly, Master Deshan, with his keen intelligence and eloquence, expounded the profound meanings of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* until he had swallowed the rivers and seas in his spirit.
Yet, upon first seeing Longtan after leaving the gorges, he suddenly said: "The dragon does not appear, and the pool is not to be seen; I have already groped about in vain."
At night, when the paper candle was extinguished during the third session of meditation, he suddenly lost his eyesight; only then did he finally consent to say:
"Exhausting all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the great void; exhausting all worldly pivot-points is like casting a single drop into a vast abyss.
From this point on, he wielded a white staff to strike through wind and rain. How could this be the work of one who relies on memorization, recitation, or literal interpretation of the texts?
This is indeed a realm of realization! Furthermore, when Master Yuanwu first tasted the essence of Chan, his vision surpassed all quarters;
when the great elders who had traveled ten thousand *li* from the south came to him, there was none who did not marvel at him and nod in approval.
Later, however, upon meeting Dongshan Enzu, he presented his full understanding. The Patriarch said, "Upādyāya Qin, what you have spoken is the 'Chan of the Dharma-seat'; it cannot save anyone."
Dongshan did not approve of his explanation. He shook out his sleeves and departed.

Later, while at Jinshan Temple, amidst a fever, he examined all that he had understood throughout his life and found that none of it was effective. He then reflected upon himself with remorse and went back to Dongshan to study further.
Having heard the story of frequently calling for "Little Jade," he harbored doubts; before long, upon hearing the sound of a cock, he was suddenly liberated and transcended all constraints.

Only then did he realize his previous errors. How could this state possibly be reached by those who sit in dull-witted, stagnant meditation? Indeed, these two elders— (Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "夫此二老" [As for these two elders].)
In the beginning, he considered himself a fine falcon or a swift hawk that would not submit to a cage.

Fortunately, he encountered a master of the true lineage who, with a harsh and pungent hand, stripped away his blindfold to reveal the true eye at the crown of his head. Thereafter, he was like an elephant king breaking free from its shackles.

Roaming across the sea like a fierce dragon leaping through the nine heavens, raising clouds and raining down as if in play—at such a time, mind and dharmas are both extinguished, medicine and illness are both forgotten;
even if Buddhas or Patriarchs were to arrive, there would be cause for them to step back.
What further need is there to debate the teachings of Chan? The Dharma Master Guo of Shu was a fellow villager of the two great elders mentioned above;

he abandoned the scholastic teachings for Chan and was resolute in his pursuit of progress. As I was about to take my boat home after the summer retreat at Tianmu, he requested words of parting, and I have offered these as a response.
Should you, however, be overcome by impulsive indignation, you might stumble and fall, tumbling over the Yanyu Rock.
Having severed the road of the Three Gorges, even Yuanwu and Deshan would have to bow in respect upon seeing his dust. You must exert yourself in this!
To Master Zangzhu Yushu:

The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is from the beginning not a matter of artificially creating categories, nor is it a heterodox fabrication of the strange; furthermore, it is not...
That which is exceedingly lofty and difficult to practice is simply what you employ daily and constantly as your established experience.
To give it a name by force, we call it the "Self-Nature True Buddha," and we also call it "one's own Lord.
Speaking more closely, at all times and in all places, you use the eyes and ears of Śākyamuni to see forms and hear sounds.

Regarding these sounds: when the Great Master Daruma uses his tongue and nostrils to speak and breathe, if one discusses this to its ultimate limit, the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the ten directions are each utterly destitute;
their very lives and natures are entirely within your grasp. Whether they are gathered together or released, it is none other than you who directs them.
If you truly possess such a skillful strategy, you can take for granted that the Buddhas and Patriarchs will [submit] before you.
You have no chance to surrender before me; there is no way for you to beg for your life from my hands.

If you do not yet possess eyes that transcend the school and surpass the conventional, nor the skillful means to bind tigers and seize dragons, you will inevitably, at all places and at all times, be obstructed by forms when seeing them and obstructed by sounds when hearing them, such that even your speech and breath will be hindered.
This is to speak with one's eyes open while dreaming in broad daylight under a clear blue sky. Therefore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says:
"Due to the beginningless, fundamental ignorance that has arisen from the outset, once born, it presides over all things. Beings are born without the eye of wisdom;
the nature of body and mind is entirely ignorance. How true these words are! Having already lost its own mastery, it furthermore submits to the command of that which is non-existent.
Clear! Because of this, you cannot turn things; instead, you are turned by things. A single skull born of a mother has been pierced through by him;
a single life-vein, both living and dying, has been seized and controlled by him.
Yet you willingly submit to this dense forest of darkness, with hands and feet stuck fast, having no share of freedom. Within this surging sea of suffering, you bob up and down without end.
This period of liberation is described in the teachings as truly pitiable. Out of compassion, the ancient Buddhas and World-Honored Ones could not bear to sit idly by;
they waded through the mud and water, establishing many skillful means to untangle your adhesions and remove your fetters.

Furthermore, the patriarchs below them did not spare their own eyebrows, demonstrating to you a single function, a single realm, a single push, and a single squeeze—like sparks struck from flint, like a flash of lightning.
The light is like a swift flame passing through the wind, like a rushing torrent crossing a blade, like a circle of vajra, and like an iron cauldron of acid.
In a hundred ways and a thousand manners, each one brings you face-to-face with the path by which you may emerge.

If you are a man of bronze head and iron brow, you will turn away the moment you are touched—just as a lion cub, upon being pressed against a precipice ten thousand fathoms high, knows how to flip itself over.
With a single roar, the skulls of all beasts are split asunder; only then does one possess even a fraction of the spirit and bearing of a patch-robed monk.
Have you not seen how the Great Master Linji asked Huangbo three times about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma and received three times the painful staff?
Later, having been pointed out by Dayu, he suddenly smashed his lacquer bucket and said, "It turns out that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma was not so much after all."
"Son, this is precisely the manner of turning one's body with a single squeeze.
From this point on, one shall roam freely across the sea, acting as a tree of cool shade to shelter all descendants under heaven. Later, Master Baiyun said:
"With one punch, I toppled Yellow Crane Tower; with one kick, I overturned Parrot Isle. When there is spirit, add more spirit; when not..."
This is the place of the flowing breeze; this is the state of total, thorough exhilaration. It is the very model of one who does not disgrace the lineage of Linji’s descendants.
My own preceptor, the Librarian Sun Yu, was resolute in his commitment to Zen practice; he was indeed able to exert himself with courageous determination.
Do not say that Baiyun was Linji; you should know that Master Bodhidharma and the Elder Śākyamuni are both right under the tips of your toes.
Take care not to let them slip away through negligence.
To the Abbot Dayu:
Great rest and great cessation are the places where the Buddhas and Patriarchs have personally arrived through diligent practice.
They are called the Ocean of Great Nirvana, the Ground of Reality, and the person of leisure who has transcended study and attained non-action; these are all different names for Great Rest.
Thus, such great rest lies in awakening and realization; it is certainly not a matter of merely speaking of it and then stopping.
As the ancients said: "Do not study the Buddha-dharma; strive only for the resting of the mind. For every portion of the mind that is rested, one portion of the Buddha-dharma is mastered.
When the resting of the mind reaches its ultimate limit, that is when the mastery of the Buddha-dharma reaches its ultimate limit. Therefore, there is nothing else in the Buddha-dharma to be studied.
It is solely by means of resting the mind that one studies. To investigate the origin of this:

all Buddhas and sentient beings equally possess the substance of the Great Mind, which pervades the entire dharma-realm, being unmoving and unchanging. It is like the great void of space, which contains all phenomena;
whether called Patriarchs or Buddhas, none are established apart from it. Who, then, could ever cause it to rest? That which is currently called "resting" is, in fact, false and illusory.

It is merely the mind that clings to the cycle of birth and death. From antiquity until now, it has raced and sought without ceasing, like the flickering of a lamp’s flame or the dripping of water from a spring.
If this mind does not come to rest, the principle of awakening and realization will be severed.

To bring the mind to rest, one must possess the correct eye at the crown of the head (*dharmodaya*) to pierce through the defilements of worldly toil and karmic consciousness; only then can one let go completely, even unto...
Put it down, and put it down again. Put down even that which puts things down. Even if sense organs and objects are simultaneously extinguished and weary anxieties are forever stilled;
even if one awakens in vast clarity and the entire body of reality manifests before them—this is still merely a place of minor rest and temporary repose.

One must wait until the old nests are overturned and the rungs of the ladder are swept away, such that delusion and awakening are both forgotten, and mastery over giving and taking is attained, no longer clinging to a single state.

Traversing the path of skillful means, he turns his body to move among those of different species; his vigorous activity functions without the involvement of discursive thought, responding perfectly to the Dharma-realm without stirring from the true source.
Only when one reaches such a state does there begin to be a portion of great rest. This is the case for Master Yong of Huating.
He was a disciple of the Venerable Dayuan of Tianmu.

Since he had taken "Great Rest" (Daxiu) as his title, it was necessary that his name be Great Rest, his reality be Great Rest, his speech be Great Rest, and his conduct be Great Rest. Every thought-moment was rest; every step was rest.
Upon attaining rest, he rested; with a single rest, there was eternal rest. Eternal rest must indeed be eternal Great Rest. He vowed never to cease until he reached Great Rest.
Stop! To show you, Venerable Shou,
that the entire Tripitaka is like casting a net to catch the wind, and the seventeen hundred cases are like swinging a staff to strike at the moon— these are mere words.
For those who study, to present the teaching face-to-face in its entirety is the most direct and appropriate method.

Were it not for a monk of fiery temperament who, having shattered his mother-born skull, can fix a single eye upon the ground where there is no reliance, he would be unable to take responsibility at this point.
One cannot avoid being further entangled by the vines and nets of the teachings, becoming bogged down at every turn.
Or, one may attempt to grasp it through the intellect, consciousness, and mind, attaining only a partial understanding; this clings to the skin and flesh, obstructing the gate of self-awakening.
This is called "poisoned dregs entering the heart," like being possessed by a demon, or like mistaking a thief for one's own son. Having been thus seized by demonic thieves, [one is lost].
Holding [onto these], they play with light and shadows at the gates of the six sense organs; with mouths full of heterodox words and deviant talk, they disturb and confuse good people.
When their three-inch breath finally fades one day, those who merely "hold" will be like a crab falling into boiling water.

Yet, the old man of the Yama realm will settle the bill for their meal, refusing to let them off by even a hair's breadth. Furthermore, as for the patriarchal gate’s reaching out of hand, its dynamic function is not...
It is the same. As for those who are most thoroughgoing and most direct, none surpass Linji and Deshan.

When Linji saw a monk enter the gate, he would immediately shout; when Deshan saw a monk enter the gate, he would immediately strike. This was truly to overturn everything to the very bottom and present it whole.
To seek understanding only after he has already shouted or struck is to miss the mark by a long way—the sword has long since been lost. How so?
How much more so when, having missed the mark face-to-face, one comes to calculate and speculate in secret;

taking a single blow of the staff or a shout and calling it a "pedagogical device," or calling it "adapting to circumstances," or calling it a "temporary expedient," thereby choking the throats and mouths of students.
To hope to see Linji or Deshan in such a manner is not merely a matter of sixty kalpas over three lifetimes—it will, moreover, cause...

When the two elders heard this, they beat their breasts, saying, "It is settled. Generally speaking, a student of the Way should regard the unresolved matter of birth and death as the most urgent and vital affair.
As for all other matters—whether they be evil knowledge or evil interpretations—they are like water in a region infested with poison;
do not touch even a single drop. Simply take the koan you are investigating and, from beginning to end, hammer it into a single unified whole. Even while amidst the vast...

Within this assembly, dragons and snakes dwell together, and demons and Buddhas intermingle. Amidst laughter and jesting, anger and abuse, and the free play of the favorable and the adverse, there is a point of turning at every step.
Suddenly, the black lacquer bucket is stripped down to its very bottom;

then, when one casually opens the mouth or moves the tongue, it covers heaven and earth—all of it flowing forth from within one’s own breast. Yet, as for the great treasury of the teachings and the thousands...
To scrutinize the failures and shortcomings of the Buddhas and patriarchs seven hundred times over is precisely where the extraordinary character of a monk lies.
How could one ever be willing to fall into their tracks and emulate the muddled practitioners of the present day? The Venerable Shou of Dongshan in Guangde is the grandson of Master Tieshan.
If you rely upon my words and practice them with diligence, then in the future you will greatly revive the reputation of your ancestral house.
This is not difficult.
The ancient master Qianzang said:
"In practicing Chan, one must give rise to the 'doubt-mind' (*yiqing*). Great doubt leads to great awakening; small doubt leads to small awakening. Without doubt," [there is no awakening].
One does not awaken. Yet this state of doubt has from the beginning no instruction, nor any expedient means of contrivance or fabrication;
it arises solely because one’s own birth-and-death remains unclarified. From vast eons until now, one has wandered on and on;
living, one knows not whence one comes, and dying, one knows not whither one goes. Is this not precisely the point where one must truly and earnestly give rise to doubt? From...
Although the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old did not engage with public cases (*gongan*) or *huatou*, they were solely and earnestly preoccupied with the matter of birth and death.

By doubting this incessantly, one naturally causes emotional attachments to dissolve, the pathways of the mind to be severed, intellectual understanding to vanish, and subject-object duality to be forgotten.
Without conscious effort or awareness, one suddenly attains clarity; this is precisely the moment when the mass of doubt is shattered and one penetrates beyond birth and death.
Modern masters, observing that students do not maintain right mindfulness nor possess right faith,

and that their doubts regarding birth and death are neither genuine nor urgent, have therefore taught the practice of the *huatou*. They value having students let go of all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—
including all mundane and supramundane conditions and affairs— and direct them to investigate with nothing but the arousal of a great state of doubt.
Apart from the *huatou*, there is no birth-and-death; apart from birth-and-death, there is no *huatou*. Once the *huatou* is penetrated, birth-and-death is also clarified.

Thus, while the patriarchs and Buddhas of the past awakened to the Way by doubting birth-and-death, and students of recent times awaken to the Way by doubting the *huatou*, although what they doubt appears to differ, the Way they awaken to is no different.
Furthermore, the reason why Chan practice today lacks efficacy lies in the failure to give rise to the "doubting mind" (*yiqing*).

The reason the doubting mind does not arise lies in the fact that the matter of birth and death is not felt as urgent. Because of this lack of doubt and urgency, one gradually becomes estranged and distant from the *huatou*.
For instance, as Doushuai said: "Tearing through the weeds and gazing at the wind is intended solely for the purpose of seeing one's nature. Now, as for the nature of the person above—
In what place? Having already seen that one must realize one's nature in order to escape birth and death, how does one escape when the light of the eyes falls to the ground?
To escape birth and death, one must know the point of descent: where do the four elements separate and go? Have you ever penetrated each of these three barriers?
If you have not yet penetrated them, you cannot avoid a life lived in vain and a death in the waves. If you can indeed, at...

When this is penetrated, there is not a single hair’s breadth of obstruction. Even that which was being investigated, that which was doubted, and that which was penetrated—including the very koan itself—are brought back to one's own self.
Thus, there is no longer a single dharma confronting the mind, nor is there a single dharma to be considered either realized or unrealized.
Only then can one truly arrive at the ground of non-doubt.
This reveals to the superior person that the single stroke beneath the monk’s own robe and bowl encompasses heaven and earth and penetrates through past and present. Although it is said:
It is brilliantly manifest before one, without a single thread or speck of leakage. Yet, alas, one cannot settle upon it; one cannot grasp it by touch.
Therefore, the Buddhas of the three periods have exhausted their verbal karma, explaining it horizontally and vertically without ever reaching a definitive conclusion.

The patriarchs of successive generations have spent all their effort, practicing in both reverse and direct ways without ever reaching a fixed course. Since neither Buddhas nor patriarchs can establish it, how can you?
This inevitably leads to misleading students, causing their mental paths to become increasingly convoluted and their koans to become increasingly cluttered.

From this, a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions arise, such that there will never be a day of certain resolution. If one examines the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, how could they have intended to deliberately deceive people?
It is simply because this one point does not admit of being arranged by others nor of being pointed out or annotated by others. You must act in this way...

"Ma! He does not act like that; you do not act like that, yet he acts like that. Even if one possesses hundreds or thousands of supernatural powers, one cannot bring him to a state of fixed certainty.
Therefore, what he says and what he practices are nothing more than provisional expedients for a single period, employed only because there was no other way.
Thus, the teachings of all Buddhas and the karmic conditions of all Patriarchs that circulate in the world are, in their entirety,"
It is a matter of ghosts and spirits; what connection does it have to the individual practitioner themselves?
The Venerable Ding of Jinling bears the ambition of a great man, vowing to settle this one pivotal point. His resolve is truly commendable.
Furthermore, even that which the Buddhas and Patriarchs spoke and practiced was not yet sufficient for their own use;
how much less so the talk of recent monasteries, recent masters, recent models, and those from the mountains and fields—how could these be taken up and used?
If you truly possess the spirit and ambition of a great man, it will not be difficult to settle [the mind]. Simply take all the miscellaneous bones from the past until now...
Dong Qing swept everything toward one wall; fists clenched, teeth gnashed, and feet planted firmly.
Relying solely upon himself, he projected the Vajra Eye from the crown of his head, scrutinizing closely from top to bottom that which cannot be fixed.
Suddenly, when you see through it, you should know what the Buddhas and Patriarchs have said.
The bottom and the practice are both one's own livelihood. I may hold it sideways or use it upside down; it is acceptable to say it is fixed, and it is also acceptable to say it is not fixed.

I am the Dharma King, sovereign over all dharmas—is this not the mark of a true great man who, having accomplished the great task of a great man, stands out as preeminent? If you depart from yourself and rely on something else...
To seek understanding through mere intellectual attachment—I most certainly dare not grant such permission.
I have shown this record for Zen practitioners regarding the Way of the Patriarchs: one must practice true practice; one must realize true realization. King Yama does not fear much talk. Furthermore—
It is said: "A single thought tied to even a hair's breadth becomes the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting stir of emotion leads to shackling for ten thousand kalpas.
This has already been spoken by me with a heart of pain and bitter words, as if every drop of blood were falling for you, to serve as a warning.

What more need be sought elsewhere? For the purpose of Zen practice is to resolve the matter of birth and death, to escape the cycle of transmigration within the triple world, and to penetrate through to the patriarchs.
The dark gate. Only after this can one act in reverse to transform others according to their needs, thereby receiving beings and benefiting life. How could this be a trivial or minor matter?
This is why it is necessary to engage in true inquiry and achieve actual realization.

If you inquire without sincerity or realize without substance, you will inevitably keep your eyes wide open while sitting inside a ghost cave, giving rise to all manner of heterodox views and erroneous interpretations, prattling on about "yellows" and "blacks."

It is not merely a matter of slandering the True Dharma Wheel; it also causes one’s fundamental involvement in the cycle of birth and death to become ever deeper and heavier, such that the time for liberation will never come.
For one who has attained true awakening, it is like a fish drinking water or a mute person having a dream—it cannot be demonstrated to others, nor can it be explained to them.
It is like cutting a bundle of silk threads: with each cut, one [strand]...
It is like being suddenly confronted by one's own father at a crossroads: upon seeing him, one sees him; upon recognizing him, one recognizes him.
How could one wait to ask others before determining whether it is so or not? Students today suffer only from a lack of genuine inquiry;
they do not suffer from a lack of true realization. Even if one has practiced for a long time without attaining awakening, [the fault lies in the inquiry, not the potential for realization].
Simply ensure that your mind of genuine inquiry becomes ever more authentic, ever more substantial, and ever more enduring so that you never regress;
naturally, a sign of progress will emerge. Chan practitioner Shanji has come seeking admonition regarding his differing views and understandings.

I have four lines for you; take them well to heart. Thoroughly penetrate the teachings through inquiry, and fully realize the teachings through awakening. When the Buddhas and Patriarchs bring them forth—
On one hand, do not follow those who are ignorant of cause and effect and recklessly discourse on Prajñā, for their sins would fill the heavens.
To reveal the source of the mind and gather [the community] is the duty of a *karmadāna*;
because they realize the mind and reach the fundamental source, they are called *śramaṇas*. The instructions and admonitions bestowed by our Buddha are concise yet profoundly pertinent.

Although the vast treasury of the Buddha’s teachings contains manifold citations and subtle metaphors—surging like billowing waves and extending to boundless horizons—in their ultimate intent, none transcend this.
Now that one has become a follower of the Buddha, if the mind does not recognize its source and the mind does not reach its origin, can one not feel ashamed of the title of *śramaṇa*?
Nature (*prakṛti*) is the source of the mind; the mind is the source of the Dharma.
Surveying all things throughout the vessel-world—whether high or low, vast or minute; whether the myriad events of suffering or joy, adversity or favor;
or the myriad thoughts of good, evil, or neutrality—not a single phenomenon fails to be a manifestation from the source of the mind.
It is like the rivers, streams, lakes, and seas: they are all called "water," yet how could there be water in the world that lacks a source? Thus it is with the mind.

The source and root are empty; the myriad phenomena are delusory transformations. Therefore, students, by means of their thoughts and concerns regarding things, accumulate delusions and become lost in confusion.
Internally and externally they rush about, drifting and wandering until they forget their way back. Among those who seek to know the mind-source, there are few.

Now, if one wishes to recognize and reach the mind-source, there is no other extraordinary technique: it is simply to employ the "mechanism that cuts the current" right at the moment when thoughts and concerns surge forth.
Severing all attachments: when confronted by the entanglements of sensory objects, one must possess the eye that penetrates the barrier and thoroughly illuminate them through and through.

Suddenly, one will see the source of the mind clearly, as if feeling for one’s own nostrils with one's lips; naturally, everything becomes a thousandfold secure and a hundredfold certain, requiring no further questioning of others.
Precisely at such a time, there is no Śākyamuni before and no Maitreya behind; above, there is nothing to grasp or look up to; below, there is nothing to rely upon.

To sever one's own person and call it the "source of the mind" is already like painting empty space; to further claim that consciousness has attained realization is no different from adding five colors to it.
Before those with clear eyes, this is not worth even a single laugh.
The monk Shixin, acting as *karmadāna*, asked Guizong, “What is the Buddha? Guizong said, “I tell you: do you believe me?
The monk replied, “Since the Master speaks with such gravity, how could I not believe? Guizong said, “It is you yourself. The monk asked, “How can this be guaranteed?”
Ren. Guizong said, "A single film obstructs the eye, and empty flowers fall in confusion. This monk can truly be said to possess great power of faith;
as soon as he heard the mention [of the truth], he immediately took it up and accepted it directly, attaining great realization.
Nowadays, the capacities of students are not uniform. Regarding the talk that "you yourself are it," everyone knows it and everyone understands it. But...
People can speak of it, yet they cannot truly take it up. When it comes to being instructed to hold the *huatou*, they cannot raise the *huatou*;
when instructed to practice the work, they cannot apply themselves to the work. Their ailment grows deeper, and the medicine becomes increasingly ineffective.
This is due to nothing other than the fact that their mind of true faith is neither genuine nor earnest. Faith is the root; all...
The Buddha-dharma arises from this. Faith is the gateway; all sages and worthies enter through it. What is meant by faith? There are three kinds.
First, one must believe that oneself and all Buddhas and patriarchs are fundamentally of one and the same essence, fully realized from the very beginning.
If one has not once awakened to and realized this, one remains merely a deluded ordinary person caught in the cycle of birth and death.

First, you must resolve that [the meaning] cannot be determined by mere intellectual speculation. Second, you must have faith that the Buddhas and Patriarchs have left behind words and phrases that clearly provide a point of awakening;
unless one practices genuine investigation with courageous and diligent effort, there is absolutely no principle for attaining self-awakening.
Third, you must have faith that worldly fame, profit, and the攀缘 (pān-yuán) of delusive thoughts are precisely the root of obstacles to the Way. If...
If one does not overturn the seat of harmony and sweep away all traces, there will certainly be no possibility of progress in study.
If one can attain such faith with complete stability and confidence— like a single mountain of iron— so that all false conditions and delusive objects cannot penetrate it and it remains unshakable,
you may take it for granted that you will naturally gain power in daily life and realize the Great Matter.
It has been some days since I showed this to Layman Yang Zhuo.
Layman Yang Zhuo places himself amidst the sticky entanglements of various conditions, applying his mind to responding to challenges from all eight directions.

At that time, his right mindfulness was not swayed by external things. Daily he studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*, inquiring into their definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

As for "definitive meaning," it does not refer to the provisional teachings of the partial or lesser vehicles; rather, it is taught in accordance with the nature of reality for those of the highest capacity through the Perfect and Sudden path.
It exhaustively investigates deluded thoughts, reveals the true mind, reaches the ultimate source, and elucidates the profound mysteries. One—
This is what is meant by the "Dharma without remainder. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have experienced the continuous succession of birth and death because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. By employing various false thoughts, and because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic wandering.
Thus, false thoughts are the very root of the cycle of birth and death; they are also called "grasping at conditions" (*pāra-tantra*).

The mind is also called inverted perception (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*). Such deluded conceptualization exists only at the gateway of the six sense faculties of people, at the point where the objective field and the subjective state intersect.
For instance, when the eye sees a form, it gives rise to a perception following that form; when the ear hears a sound, it gives rise to a perception following that sound.

All of this arises because one has lost the eternally abiding true mind and instead revolves according to external objects. When an object is favorable, there is attachment; when an object is adverse, [there is aversion].
Thus one hates. From love arises craving; from hatred arises aversion. By means of these false cravings and false aversions, false karma is perfumed and formed.

By means of this false karma, false retribution is summoned and experienced. Consequently, within the three realms and amidst the seven destinies, false states follow one another in succession as one undergoes false birth and false death.
From the beginningless kalpas above down to the end of the future below, one falsely undergoes [existence].
Samsara revolves without end. Therefore, when our Buddha interrogated the mind from seven perspectives, he was interrogating this deluded mind.
When he analyzed the vision through the "eight returns," he was analyzing this deluded vision.

Thereafter, employing numerous analogies and various elucidations, he extensively refuted [the notion of a self] from the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve spheres, and the eighteen elements, up to the seven great elements.
Regarding dharmas such as causes and conditions, arising and ceasing, and so forth, there is not one that does not exhaust delusive thought and reveal the true mind.
It is the firm desire that sentient beings turn back from delusion to return to truth, attaining sudden awakening to their Buddha-nature, before it shall cease.

Yet, truth and delusion share the same source and originally possess no dual substance; they are distinguished only because of confusion and inversion. When deluded, one gives rise to delusion based upon the truth, like binding water into...
It forms ice. To awaken is to return the delusive to the true, just as ice melts back into water. The *Awakening of Faith* says:
"The various illusory transformations of all sentient beings all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment, just as flowers in the sky appear from empty space.
Although the illusory flowers vanish, the nature of emptiness is not destroyed; the illusory minds of sentient beings likewise vanish by relying on that very illusion. All illusions...
When the mind of awakening is extinguished, it is immovable. The preface to that [text] also says: "To be deluded is the beginning of birth and death;
to awaken is the cessation of saṃsāra. What both sutras discuss is the same definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and the same intended purpose.

The essential point lies solely in awakening the mind. Therefore, any practitioner of the Way must seek authentic awakening. If one attains authentic awakening, then all that is delusory becomes true, and whatever one encounters...

Abiding in the integration of all things, one attains liberation according to conditions. Pervading the entirety of empty space and the Dharma-realm—mountains, rivers, grasses, trees, sun, moon, mist, and clouds—though the myriad phenomena are vast and manifold, every single dharma is the wondrous essence of the *Śūraṅgama*.

Amidst the thicket of sounds and forms, within the sea of right and wrong, love and hate follow their nature, and acceptance and rejection accord with conditions. Though ten thousand thoughts race across one another, in every single thought there is perfect enlightenment.

It is the wondrous mind. If one turns back to contemplate the subtle words and profound meanings of these two sutras, as well as the various patriarchs’ Zen commentaries throughout the entire Tripitaka, all that has been obstructing the chest can be resolved with a single laugh—how much more so for the two characters "nurturing simplicity" (yangzhuo).

This is also the method for once again returning from delusion to truth. If one can truly abandon cleverness and employ simplicity, and deepen the practice of preservation and cultivation, then the time for authentic awakening may be awaited while sitting.
This mountain monk does not begrudge the length of his tongue; he shall speak another verse as a prophetic prediction:
The *Awakening of Mahāyāna* and the *Śūraṅgama* reveal the secret cause; The practitioner nurtures simplicity to accord with true nature. Whether obstructed or unobstructed...
Transcending both objects and subject simultaneously, one attains the Dharma-body without passing through the kalpas of the śrāvakas.

To demonstrate the emptiness of nature, it is revealed that the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened nature of the practitioner is fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning; it is equal, pure, and as vast as the great void, such that it cannot be described by any physical form or state.
To describe it with the finger: it is not a place that can be approached, nor a path by which one may enter; it cannot be depicted with the five colors.
It is vast and silent, such that not a single thing can be grasped; it is expansive and open, such that not a single dharma can be applied.
