It transcends past and present and is free from all arising and ceasing; it is impossible to describe or conceive through thought.
Impelled by karma and brought together by conditions, that which was ultimately non-existent becomes ultimately existent. Once a single thing is established, all phenomena follow and arise.
From this point on, the myriad realms manifest and the ten thousand images are laid out;

from the great earth, mountains, and rivers to the finest motes of dust and all Buddha-lands, there is nothing that does not exist. Yet that which exists is not the original possession of the enlightened nature; rather, it is the product of emotional consciousness.
It exists falsely through the convergence of conditions and karma. That which exists falsely is like a dream, an illusion, a shadow, or an echo;
like a mirage or flowers in the sky. It fills the world, arising and ceasing in disorder. When observed before one's eyes, it cannot be said to be non-existent;
yet when its beginning and end are investigated, it is not truly existent. For emotional consciousness arises from the transformation of the awakened nature. Emotional consciousness...
As with a form, karma conditions it like a shadow. As soon as the consciousness of a sentient being arises, karma immediately manifests.
There has never been a form that does not manifest a shadow, nor a shadow that does not follow a form. Although my enlightened nature can transform and manifest consciousness, [it remains so].
Yet it does not undergo transformation along with mental consciousness. Therefore it is said that the nature of awakening is like empty space: equal, unmoving, and unchanging.
It is also like the substance of a great round mirror, which is fundamentally pure and fundamentally empty; yet all images of beauty and ugliness appear as they arrive.
Although these images have beauty and ugliness, and come and go, the substance of the mirror never follows after their beauty and ugliness, nor their coming and going. Such is the case.
This is what is called the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have realized this emptiness of nature to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
All Bodhisattvas rely upon this emptiness of nature to perfectly cultivate the holy path. Boundless sentient beings, deluded regarding this emptiness of nature, sink and fall into birth and death;
within this cycle of birth and death, they give rise to all manner of hatred and love, all manner of attachments, and follow along with conditions arising from their emotional consciousnesses.
Karma. Driven by the conditions of karma, the emotional consciousnesses stir and become entangled with one another, revolving and binding in a continuous cycle.
Through the accumulation of births and kalpas, beings wander back and forth within the three realms, unaware of the liberation of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

Thereupon, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas arise in the world to rescue them, manifesting through speech and appearing in their deeds to clarify the nature of karmic conditions amidst the defilements of worldly toil.

Within the midst of afflictions, he reveals that within the very moment of sensory perception—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—one may cause that which is delusory to immediately reveal the true, thereby together reaching the principle of the emptiness of nature.
One who can reach this principle is, according to their capacity, liberated and agile;
with right mindfulness vividly clear, they are neither stained nor attached to phenomena or sense objects, and do not depart from sensory awareness, but rather transform it into purity.
Through the contemplation of wisdom, one does not abandon the afflictions of worldly toil, yet brings them forth as wondrous and sublime functions.
To examine it thus, the Way of the emptiness of my own nature will be indistinguishable in essence from that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; how could it be merely a matter of attaining proficiency?
I show my fellow practitioners at the Xizi Assembly that the Pure Land is mind-only;
there is no land apart from the mind. This land of mind-only has no "east" to its east and no "west" to its west.

It encompasses the four intermediate directions, above, and below without exception. What are called the Buddha-fields as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions are, in truth, my own Pure Land.
It is a land within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the three periods of time are the Buddhas within my Pure Land.
Even the World-Honored One Amitābha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is merely one land and one Buddha within my own Pure Land.

That all phenomena are non-existent is called "Pure"; that all phenomena are not non-existent is called "Land. It is both the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*); it is neither one nor [many].
Its functions are constantly and profusely active, yet its essence is inherently pure. It is defiled yet not defiled; it is cultivated yet not cultivated.
Fundamentally, there is no mental state to which one can be bound. It departs yet does not depart; it arises yet does not arise. Furthermore, how could any location or direction be pointed out?

Because sentient beings do not realize that all is but mind, they are restricted to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Since their faculties and capacities are unequal, their realizations differ vastly;

therefore, within a single pure land, four types are distinguished: the Constantly Quiescent Light (*nityapraśāntābhāsa*), the True Reward (*vipākaphala*), the Expedient Means (*upāya*), and the Co-residence (*sahā*).

Within the Co-residence, there are two further divisions: the defiled and the pure. The Constantly Quiescent Light is the general [category], while the remaining lands are the specific ones. The Constantly Quiescent...
In that regard, they are one; in other lands, they are many. That Amitābha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss is but one among the pure lands of the *sahā* realm.
Yet, Śākyamuni Buddha specifically designates that Buddha as the object of focused mindfulness and uniquely points to that land as the method for rebirth.
This is because Amitābha’s vows are profound and he especially receives sentient beings from the *Saha* world, thereby causing those beings to focus their minds [upon him].
When the mind is focused on a single point, recollection is easily accomplished. In the near term, this can induce rebirth in a pure land of shared enjoyment;

in the distant term, it can serve as the cause for the three higher lands. For this reason, within the various teachings of the One Vehicle, how many times has the Buddha earnestly pointed the way and exhorted others to go there?
As evidenced by the citations of the broad and long tongues of the Buddhas of the six directions praising [this practice], one’s rebirth therein is verified.

This is indeed true. For instance, in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, it is recorded that Śuddhodana and seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan were granted the assurance (*vyākaraṇa*) of being born together in Sukhāvatī;

this demonstrates the verification of their rebirth there. Furthermore, in the final assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Samantabhadra exhorted Sudhana and the great multitude of the ocean-like assembly to return to An-yang (Sukhāvatī) by means of the Great King of Vows. This is also the case with the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.
In the sutra, Mañjuśrī himself recounts his past causes, stating that he attained the Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha and is constantly reborn in the Pure Land.

Thus, he acts as a principal figure supported by associates to propagate the teaching of rebirth there. These individuals were all members of the assembly who had perfected their faith and understanding and had transcended to the stages (bhūmis) of realization;
yet even they still aspired to take birth in that land. If this is so, then those of middling faculties and inferior vessels might well fail to believe.
How admirable! From Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu in the eastern lands, through Tiantai and Xianshou, the holy masters of successive generations have inherited this teaching.
Whether monastics or laypeople, those who have attained rebirth through their own practice and their transformation of others are recorded in such abundance that they cannot be fully enumerated.
Yet, among the practitioners of Chan, there have occasionally been doubts; thus, Chan Master Yongming Shou...
The Master received the teaching of the direct pointing to the human heart through single transmission; he also used the Pure Land method to transform others.
He thus composed the "Four Selections," the gist of which is stated in verse: "If one has Chan but no Pure Land, nine out of ten will go astray. If one has no Chan but has the Pure Land..."
"Ten thousand practice, ten thousand depart. How could this be a deprecation of Chan?

It is simply the establishment of teachings according to the capacities of beings, sometimes suppressing and sometimes exalting, so as to ensure that practitioners of Chan do not harbor doubts regarding the Pure Land.
As for the great Chan masters such as Tiantai Yihuai, Zhenxie Qingliao, Siji Xinyue, Changlu Zongze, and Yuanzhao Daoben, they all practiced the Pure Land path concurrently with their Chan training.
Transformations may differ yet remain identical; these are all instances of those who have skillfully realized that "mind-only" and are not confined to the school of Chan alone.
Now, Master Zhang of Huishì at the West Hermitage on Mount Tiānmù establishes a monthly "West-Resource Assembly.

He gathers various Chan practitioners to uphold the rules of Baizhang’s "Ten Recitations at Cremation," expanding them into a practice of mindfulness through the Buddha’s name performed during the three periods of the day. This is clearly derived from the tradition of Yongming.
Is this not the intention of the elders? The Venerable Yuansou of Mount Jing and Master Yixi of Zhongzhu each contributed words of praise for him.
Unable to decline, I have thus cited the doctrine of "Mind-Only" to corroborate it.
To the layman Zhou Zhongxiang, [the Master] showed that among things of the same category there are those whose capacities differ; this is rooted in the fixed decree of Heaven.

The great Peng bird soars ninety thousand li with a single bound, soaring above the Milky Way and regarding the Nine Provinces as too narrow; yet when compared to the flight of the common wren (*chìyàn*), [its vastness is inconceivable].
They do not exceed a few paces, soaring only amidst the weeds and thistles; yet each exerts its full strength and fulfills its own lot. It is the same for human beings:
the distinction between wealth and honor, poverty and lowliness, failure and success, or gain and loss, is determined by Heaven, allowing not even a hair’s breadth of increase or decrease.
Those who are ignorant of this distinction may seek glory while abandoning disgrace, or rush toward...
Seeking profit while avoiding harm, those below scramble for the heights, and those nearby covet what is distant.

To the point where they exhaust their minds and wither their thoughts, there are those who spend their entire lives without succeeding in their ambitions. Not only do they fail to achieve their aims, but they also increase the root of their karma.
From this, we know that what is called "the fixed allotment of Heaven" is not truly fixed by Heaven; rather, it is one's own karma.
It is through the power [of karma] that one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The power of karma induces the result beforehand; the portion of concentration corresponds to it afterwards.
Karma is like the cause; the portion is like the fruit. Because the power of karma varies in ten thousand ways, how could the excellence or inferiority of these portions ever be the same?
While the portions induced by karma can certainly not be identical, the Way of wondrous, perfect, and true awakening has never failed to be so.
It is the same. Now, as for the Way (*dào*), it encompasses heaven and earth and spans all time from antiquity to the present. Neither sage nor ordinary person, neither fool nor wise man, lacks it;
yet by turning inward to seek it, one finds that there is nowhere it does not penetrate. Those who have mastered the Way exhaust their inherent nature (*xing*) to rest content within their own lot.
Abiding in lowliness, filth, poverty, and meanness, they remain placid; nothing can shift their steadfastness. Regarding wealth, honor, fame, and profit, they view them with detachment.
Their minds remain unmoved. Since they are not enticed by worldly desires, they are not dragged along by the power of karma.
They roam at ease at the origin of all things and soar beyond the three realms. Neither affinities of nature can constrain them, nor can distinctions of status equalize them.
How could those who soar through the Milky Way and look down upon the nine provinces be worthy of comparison?
It is by knowing this that it is shown:
when the elder Zhizhao calms all thoughts, still wisdom arises, and the minds of all Tathāgatas manifest therein. This is the teaching on *śamatha*.

Is this not what is meant by "illumination"? Now, the ocean of the nature of all phenomena returns to a single source; its essence merges with sound and vanishes, remaining eternally clear and eternally profound.
Yet, when it is stirred by the winds of the eight objects of perception, the waves of emotion and the surges of consciousness arise in myriad ways.

It is through non-attachment that one can clarify this clarity and deepen this profundity. In the Dharma-realm where the single nature is perfectly manifest, views vanish and objects dissolve, remaining eternally as they are.
The constant luminosity is revealed. When it is slightly obscured by the dust of the two hindrances, the mists of delusion and the clouds of confusion intersect in myriad forms;

without illumination, there would be no way to manifest its revelation or clarify its clarity. Once all movement has ceased and not a single wave arises, the myriad phenomena are clearly manifest, unmixed and unobstructed;
thus, illumination does not depart from within stillness. When the profound darkness is cleared and the single film [of ignorance] is removed...
It does not arise. The ten directions are vast and empty, without movement or agitation. Thus, cessation does not abide outside of illumination.

"Cessation" (zhi) is like meditative concentration (*samādhi*); "illumination" (zhào) is like wisdom (*prajñā*). Illuminating by means of cessation means that concentration is the manifestation of wisdom; ceasing by means of illumination means that wisdom is the basis for concentration.

When wisdom manifests, it does not wither; cessation is sufficient to support the function of illumination. When concentration provides its basis, it is never lacking; illumination is thereby fulfilled.

This is to achieve the perfection of stillness (*śamatha*). If one remains in stillness while neglecting illumination (*vipaśyanā*), one may fall into the error of sinking into emptiness or stagnating in quiescence.
If one remains in illumination while neglecting stillness, one may flow into the弊 (shortcoming) of discursive awareness and analytical observation.

For stillness is indeed the cessation of movement, yet it is also the root of movement; therefore, a stillness that neglects illumination is not a falling into empty quiescence, but rather gives rise to distraction.

Illumination indeed illuminates the obscure; yet it is also the very root of that obscurity. Therefore, if one sets aside the illumination of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and fails to practice the flowing awareness of *vipaśyanā* (insight), then delusion and attachment will manifest.
For this reason, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* must be mutually complementary, and neither may be neglected.

However, this "stopping" (*śamatha*) is not the inherently present stopping; its efficacy is manifested through the contrast of movement and stillness. This "illumination" (*vipaśyanā*), likewise, is not [independent] freedom...

Illumination (*zhào*) relies upon the conditions of darkness and light to manifest its function. Since it has not yet transcended the realm of functional utility, how can it be called true stillness (*zhēn zhǐ*) or true illumination?

As for that wherein the effort of stillness does not arise and the function of illumination is forgotten—only then is "movement itself" stillness as the stillness of true illumination, and "darkness itself" light as the illumination of true stillness. This stillness of true illumination merges with...
In movement and stillness, hundreds of thousands of Buddhas enter right concentration amidst the surging tides of emotion and the waves of consciousness,
yet this does not hinder their embodiment of the essence or the dissolution of sound. When the illumination of true cessation merges with both darkness and light,

the eighty thousand gates of practice manifest right wisdom amidst the mists of delusion and the clouds of confusion, yet this does not obstruct the disappearance of views or the vanishing of objects.
It is precisely this. At this point, all thoughts are not clear yet they are clear; still wisdom does not arise yet it arises;
the minds of all Tathāgatas do not manifest yet they manifest. Even if one wished to use the substance of the great void or the light of a thousand suns as a metaphor for it, [it would fall short].

How could the difference between them be anything less than that between heaven and earth? The Elder Zhijiao Xiangjian of Qujiang requested my words regarding "stopping and reflecting," and I have thus provided this general discussion.
May he examine and choose from it.
An Exhortation to Layman Cao Miaojing (In Response to His Inquiry on the Causes and Conditions for Abstaining from Killing in the Three Teachings):
To "abstain from killing" means to exhort others not to take the lives of sentient beings. When it comes to living things, their life-force (*xingming*) must not be killed.
The principle of retribution follows one like a shadow follows a form; if one kills, one will inevitably receive its retribution. Pei Gongmei said: "As for those with blood and breath..."
That which possesses attributes must necessarily possess cognition. All that possesses cognition must be of the same substance. Zhang Hengqu said: "The people are my fellow brothers;
all things are my companions. Examining the words of the ancient gentlemen throughout history, this refers to the fact that all things and humans alike receive the nature of spiritual cognition.
Although things are not as supremely intelligent as humans, their feelings of cherishing their own bodies and sparing their own lives—and their fear [of harm]—are the same.

If one harbors thoughts of craving life while facing death, then one is no different from ordinary people. Since their spiritual awareness is the same and their emotional dispositions are likewise the same, they are said to be of the "same substance" (*tongti*).
Thus, they are called our "fellow beings" (*wuyuye*). Fellow beings refers to those of our own kind.
Now that we are fellow beings of the same substance, how could it be right to kill and eat them? How can it be that the most spiritually endowed human being—
They are able to restrain the desires of their mouths and bellies, yet they cannot extend the thought that [all beings] share the same essence.

They disregard the affection for their own bodies and show no compassion for the fear of death inherent in others. Often they kill and eat them on purpose—killing another’s body to nourish their own, and harming another’s life to sustain their own.
Where, indeed, is the heart of benevolence and forgiveness? Confucius said: [“Do not do unto others what you would not have done unto yourself”].

The Master said, "On the mountain beam, a female pheasant! 'The time has come! The time has come! Subsequently, Zi Lu offered it respectfully, whereupon [the Master] smelled its scent three times and rose.
Zhu Xi, citing the commentary of Xing [Xuan], says: 'The time has come' means that the pheasant’s drinking and pecking were in accord with the proper season.
Zi Lu did not understand this and thought it was a timely delicacy, so he prepared it for offering. Confucius did not eat it; he smelled its odor three times and then stood up. Regarding Confucius—
Not eating [meat] is likely due to an inability to bear [the sight]. Mencius said: "Seeing it alive, one cannot bear to see it die;
hearing its cries, one cannot bear to eat its flesh. If one cannot even bear to eat the meat, and cannot even bear to see it dead, how could one bear to kill it for that purpose?
Confucius and Mencius were sages and worthies. It is in this that the compassionate and forgiving hearts of these sages and worthies are revealed.
Laozi said: "Chasing and hunting causes the human mind to go mad. He further said:

"Shooting at birds in flight, pursuing fleeing beasts, disturbing those emerging from hibernation, startling those perched in nests, indulging in violence and slaughter, and cooking animals in ways contrary to principle—sins such as these, the Lord of Life (Siming) shall, according to their gravity, subtract from one's allotted years (*jisu*).
When the years are exhausted, death occurs; if there are remaining charges, the calamity shall extend to one's descendants. Thus it is for all [the transgressions of] Confucius...

The second elder taught them through the sages and worthies. Although the methods established to transform the world differ, there is no difference in their words regarding the love of life and the loathing of killing.
As for our Buddha, the World-Honored One, he further demonstrated in detail the matters of karmic retribution, cause and effect, and the cycle of birth and death, while strictly forbidding them.
The Buddha’s teaching says: "The commissioning of karma is the cause; one receives retribution."
They act as the fruit [of karma]. Through death and rebirth, they receive retribution according to their karma, repaying one another like the revolving of a wheel.
Regarding the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), non-killing is considered the foremost; regarding the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*), killing is considered the gravest.
Through the karma of killing, one falls into hell after death. When the punishment in hell is finished, one falls again into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Hungry...
When their karmic retribution as ghosts is exhausted, they fall again into the realm of animals. Within that animal realm, they undergo the retribution for their past deeds:
those who committed killing receive the retribution of being killed; those who devoured others receive the retribution of being devoured.

Once this retribution has been fully paid, even if they should obtain a human body, it will be short-lived or plagued by many illnesses, or they may suffer from blindness, deafness, muteness, leprosy, carbuncles, and various other such undesirable conditions. This is so.
All of these are the residual retributions of the karma of killing. Thus, a sutra says: "Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created does not perish.

When the causes and conditions meet, the fruit of retribution returns to be experienced by oneself. This principle is clear and can be observed; how could the Buddha’s words ever deceive people? It further states:
"If one kills the life of a sentient being, it is as if one were killing a Buddha. This is because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have vowed to deliver all beings.
Because they manifest transformation bodies according to their kind through the power of their vows, within feathers, fur, scales, and shells there exist the bodies of Bodhisattvas and holy sages.
How much more so for all living beings, who are all endowed with Buddha-nature; if you kill them, it is to kill Buddhas and holy sages.
It is further said: "To harm the life of a creature is equivalent to harming one's parents and kinsmen."
Why is this so? Because since time immemorial, throughout countless and incalculable kalpas, you have undergone immeasurable births and deaths.
In each birth, you have had parents, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen;

yet these immeasurable and incalculable parents and kinsmen have revolved within the cycle of birth and death without attaining liberation. At times they were born as beings with massive bodies, or at times...
Small-bodied sentient beings—whether aquatic, terrestrial, or aerial—fill my eyes; they have changed their heads and faces so that none recognize one another.
If you were to harm them, it would be as if you were harming your own parents and kinsmen.

Even if you do not kill them yourself but instead cause others to do so, this is likewise causing others to harm my kin. How lamentable! How painful! Having thus explained the karma of killing, [he continued:]
The retribution of saṃsāra is further illustrated by the bodies of the retinues of sages and worthies; this may be called a detailed demonstration and a strict admonition.
Can one who understands this principle fail to believe the words of the Buddha? Can one who believes these words kill living beings?
For those among people today who have not yet been able to suddenly sever their craving for flesh and blood, let them eat [for now].
The three kinds of pure meat were established to gradually restrain one’s passions and gradually diminish karmic activity. As for the "three purities," they are what our Buddha called:
not seeing the killing, not hearing of the killing, and not suspecting that it was killed specifically for oneself. These three types are termed "pure meat" and were provisionally permitted as food.
This was a skillful means provisionally bestowed for those whose deluded attachments are too heavy and whose greedy desires are too deep.

These are my words. As for the rest—whether laypeople or monastics who are called disciples of the Noble Ones—you should cultivate a heart of benevolence and forbearance, give rise to thoughts of compassion, and it is only right that you suddenly sever the craving for flesh and blood and completely cut off the karma of killing.
Only then can you suddenly empty the retribution of your offenses and suddenly escape from saṃsāra. And then...

This is for the purpose of creating the realm of the Buddhas, Patriarchs, Sages, and Worthies. An ancient master said: "Whenever one wishes to kill a living being, one should contemplate it as oneself.
One's own person cannot be killed; the life-force of other beings is no different from one's own. Be cautious! Be cautious! The life-force of other beings must never be taken.
Thus, one must absolutely not kill living beings.
Cihushe, the attendant of Master Shizi, instructed his disciple:
"Go straight toward the precipice and apply pressure; you must turn yourself around from that very point of pressure. Whether alive or dead, there is no room for even a blink of an eye.
These few words may serve as a metaphor for the method of study in our school. The venerable masters of old—
With a profound and subtle mechanism, he reaches out his hand to receive people; yet he often cuts off their paths and removes their habitual molds.
He allows no resting place and permits no climbing. It is as if he were pushing one down into a thousand-fathom well and, without providing even an inch of rope, leaving them to emerge by themselves.
How could he ever have bestowed a single dharma upon others? If a student can thus investigate and examine for themselves, they will—
Only when one can revive the dead may one be permitted to be considered a true seedling who has traveled the path of Chan and sought the Way.
Apart from this, some lead people into the weeds by harmonizing机缘 (karmic conditions) and anecdotes; others blind people’s eyes with their own analytical intellectualizations.
At worst, being half-ripe and half-raw, they enter the retinue of Māra. As the ancients said: "The clarified butter..."
That which is of supreme flavor is prized by the world; yet when encountered by such people as these, it turns instead into a poisonous drug.

This is a great affliction within our school, and students ought to guard against it deeply and maintain strict vigilance. I, having received my training at the temple, came to Siṃhalavana accompanied by the attendant Cihù, the disciple of my teacher.
Having followed the crowd for nearly a year, I suddenly felt a profound desire to return home, and thus produced this scroll.
Seeking words of exhortation, he cites the previous analogy and further demonstrates it with this verse: "Old fellow, you have lost your wits;
you follow others blindly in your delusions. You do not know how to 'strike the grass to startle the snake,' nor do you know how to 'press the ox to graze.'"
In the lion’s den are lion cubs; the large are large and the small are small. They cannot be chased away nor summoned to come.
Increasing them does not make them many, nor does decreasing them make them few. I have not a single dharma to teach them; such teaching is merely an external entanglement.
Wait until he can turn himself over on his own from a precipice ten thousand fathoms high, and it will be finished. When the earth is dark and the sky is gloomy, let out a single roar:
"Upon the coral branches, the sun shines bright.
This is shown to those of like study.

In the Way there are fellow students; in Chan there are fellow practitioners (*tóngcān*). That which is shared among fellow practitioners is Chan; that which is shared among fellow students is the Way.
Tell me, is the meaning of the former master the same or different? Textual study fails at learning; investigative inquiry lacks realization and clarity.
Tell me, is this statement of the former master a praise or a censure? When the World-Honored One was in samādhi, Kāśyapa did not know it; when Kāśyapa was in [samādhi], the World-Honored One...
Ānanda was ignorant and did not know. But tell me: is the nose of Elder Ze horizontal or vertical? While alive, one does not know where one comes from;
when dead, one does not know where one goes. Tell me: what is this thing called birth and death? And who is it that undergoes birth and death?
The Master has no choice but to speak of birth and death, yet this is already creating trouble where there was none.

To further speak of "investigating Zen" and "studying the Way" is clearly like gouging out flesh to treat a sore. He hopes that your spiritual faculty will awaken of its own accord and that you will find a path for yourself to turn back;
since you yourself lack such transformative ingenuity, you cannot avoid burdening him and causing him to wound his hand on a sharp edge. Sometimes he breaks through [the barrier] and begs...
The child’s rice bowl. Sometimes, seeing you nodding off, I give you a pillow; sometimes I prick you with an awl; sometimes I hook you with a hook;
sometimes I use a wedge to extract a wedge; sometimes I use one poison to counteract another;
sometimes I trade black beans for your eyes; sometimes I use arsenic to save your life—all of these are divine manifestations of adapting to circumstances.

The pivot. How could there ever have been a fixed dharma? It depends on the student to personally recognize the root of their own ailment, to personally know how to transform and realize [the truth], to personally give rise to transformative wisdom, and to personally attain wondrous function.
For one who is skilled in its application, even mouse droppings surpass the liver of a dragon;
for one who is not skilled in its application, lion’s milk is no better than donkey urine. Thus it is said: "Only by burning the medical treatises can one become a Lu-physician."

Bian Que. For what reason do students fail to penetrate the living meaning beyond words? Often they speak of life and death while clinging to life and death; they speak of Chan and the Way while clinging to Chan and the Way;
they speak of inquiry and study while clinging to inquiry and study; they speak of Buddhas and Patriarchs while clinging to Buddhas and Patriarchs.
It is just like a ball of sticky glue that sticks here and there, never becoming clean again. When a Master reaches this point, his bow snaps and his arrows are spent.
[The Master] finished speaking. He then said: "Dharma is but an old, hairy barbarian; Śākyamuni is but a dried-up dung-club;

the twelve divisions of the teachings are but paper for wiping sores. There is no other Chan or Way to be learned. Those who have something to learn all fall into the ranks of demons and external paths.
It is better to be without affairs. When the students heard this, they fell into a pit and dropped into a ditch at the very place of "no affairs."
Not found on the left; not found on the right. One merely speaks of the length of the thatch; how could one know the ground is not level?

This old man, throughout his lifelong study of the Way, has suffered so many deceptions and misleadings. Having once endured the bitter cries of monkeys in the Gorges of Ba, even hearing a donkey bray now breaks my heart.
Today, ill-fated as I am, I have run into you, who again speaks of birth and death, of delusion and [awakening].

Awakened! Consider, for instance, how Yajñadatta, deluded about his own head, ran about in a frenzy. When he was deluded, his head was never lost; when he awakened, his head was not acquired from without.
This single awakening and this single delusion have no connection whatsoever with his head. You should know that this matter is like the vast void;
not even a hair’s breadth can be added to or subtracted from it. What relevance do birth-and-death, delusion, and awakening have to it? Even if...
You have indeed realized and awakened to it. If even the slightest trace of this view of realization has not been forgotten, that is precisely the seed of hell;
you have not even dreamed of the late Master’s intent. If you encounter the hands and feet of a pig-eating dog, a heavy blow breaking your donkey-waist would not be an overreaction.
Now, if you wish to understand the late Master’s intent, what difficulty could there be? Simply take—
The three eaves and two buckets of the foul, stinking, and evil water of birth-and-death, delusion, and awakening—turn them all over until not a single drop remains.
Thereafter, apply yourself with intense vigor and examine directly: in every movement and stillness, in every word and silence.
After all, whose hands hold this single life? *Hūṃ, hūṃ!* This is no place for play.
If you cannot discern it, I shall strike you with a painful blow that breaks your donkey’s waist. If you can discern it, I shall strike you with a painful blow that breaks your donkey’s waist.
Apart from these two lines, if there is another message, I shall strike you with a painful blow that breaks your donkey’s waist. Why?
It is thus. It is because you have not yet realized the intent of the former master. Now tell me, what exactly was the intent of the former master?
*Dot!* (A shout).
From the Recorded Sayings of Master Rintai of Shishinden, Volume Three.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Rulin Tianru, Volume Four,
Compiled by the Junior Disciple Shanyu:
Verses and Eulogies.
The idle person loves song;
when guests come, they love the idle one even more. With cold eyes, they watch others’ busyness never ending.

They say they have fashioned the treasures of an idle household, enjoying a lifetime of idleness without lack. How long can the shadow of a skull last? The days gone by are already far distant, and those yet to come...

Not much. The path to the gate of benefit is called a road of suffering that does not penetrate through. Who recognizes that I have leisure in this Sahā world? When at leisure, even a Buddha has no mind to act.
Of what use are meditation boards and rush cushions to pass the time? The sand pot’s water is warm, boiling with pine waves; I stew white clouds mixed with pine powder.
Everywhere else there is clamor as they boast of discussing the profound; I have already washed my ears at the Cold Mountain spring. I only crave—
In a dream, it is best to speak of dreams; once asleep, one need not fear three thousand years. There is another kind of idleness that is not like this:
it is not subject to the constraints of the twelve hours of the day. Extending the fist, one releases the flowers of empty space; struck, they shatter both nirvana and birth-and-death.
One can then dig into the earth to seek the blue sky; pressing upon the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one becomes a madman of the wind.
One strikes one’s head into the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse, lying across the sword-trees and iron nets. One laughs at others who sit in withered stillness, forgetting dawn and dusk;
outwardly they seem idle, yet within they are restless. It is all because they cannot manage the ox; led by the nose, it returns to the weeds. Who would have known that in such a dead-end?

There is the vital spark of life. Stillness quells the clamor; it is hushed and quiet. Sometimes one hides one’s form within a round mirror; though Śakra scatters flowers, there is nowhere to find it.
Sometimes one pushes through the crowds in a bustling marketplace; even iron walls and silver mountains can simply be toppled by leaning against them.
This is the extraordinary leisure of our kind. To seek it elsewhere apart from this—I do not guarantee it. There was also a man of leisure in Luling who understood.
His own person was surrounded by idlers; in a casual word, they suddenly found common ground. For their sake, he sang: "It is good to be an idle man.
The Master Juezhao abandoned the teachings to practice Chan.
Where there are sutras, there are sutra masters; where there are treatises, there are treatise masters. "In the Great Tang, there are no Chan masters. An ancient struck once—
The palm is bleeding; who has ever known this pain or this itch? At that time, Deshan was a fine fellow indeed, yet before those with clear eyes, he was three feet in darkness.
Where the paper lamp is extinguished, the spirit is lost. Treat the sutras and śāstras as enemies!
Have you not seen how Caoqi deceived old Yongjia, causing him to ruin his home and scatter his estate in search of a livelihood? The entanglements and proclamations cannot be shaken off.

Freed from constraints, he entered the sea and followed his predecessors to count the sands. What, then, are Chan and the scriptures and treatises? Whether there is a teacher or no teacher, who can discern the truth?
The diamond ring on the heel of the straw sandals—neither Buddhas nor patriarchs can leap out of it.

The Master Juezhao’s place of birth was ancient Jingzhou; with neither Buddha nor patriarch, he roamed freely across the sea. Sometimes, when asked about Chan, he would answer with the teachings. Thoroughly.
Bones exhausted, he comes to contemplate ancient tombs; sometimes when asked about the Teaching, he instead answers with Chan. Three monkeys toss coins at night;
sometimes he says to all people: "The Teaching and Chan are both merely idle entanglements.
Wait until I blow out the lamp of discarded paper, and let us see how thick the skin on the faces of Longtan and Deshan is."
The "Great Collection of the Buddha's Teachings" (Tripitaka) is a mere phonetic rhyme; when has that word ever truly captured its meaning?
To answer the question posed to him with a single silence is entirely to remain muddled and indistinct. Since it is neither silence nor speech, it is simply valued in the nodding of one’s own head.
"I agree. This is a nod of self-approval; otherwise, one is like a "board-carrying" Chan practitioner who sees only one side.
When this side and that side are not in harmony, if one has not yet reached the home of realization, nothing will be resolved. The Chan practitioners of Cuiyan do not allow themselves to be deceived;
setting aside this very thing, they look with another eye. This ready-made phrase is not a matter of mind or境 (objects). The gate is near Hongya’s thousand-fathom well.
It is neither an object nor a mind—how can one investigate it? The stone bridge divides the waters as they wind around the pines and cypresses. To proceed in such a manner is to become entangled;
not to proceed in such a manner makes it difficult to find a foothold. How much better to pivot suddenly upon a single turning point, letting it flow with unimpeded ease and clarity!
"What is this? Running westward into Tengwang Pavilion.
A gift to Master Wugaidian of the Tiantai school:
"The entire ten directions is this very self; Standing alone and manifest, majestic and beyond compare, It has existed throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
In the space of a single snap of the fingers, the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time reside within a single pore.
In the ordinary blink of an eye, it is already ten thousand miles of white clouds. Earth is earth; heaven is heaven; mountains are mountains; waters are waters.
Who is it that possesses this fundamentally? Who is it that creates these transformations? You are not like them; they are not like you. [They speak of] mind, Buddha, and the assembly.

Birth! From this point on, ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences began. It has even come to affect the Yellow-Faced Gautama, who does nothing but patch heads and join tails, speaking of the real and the provisional, pointing to phenomena and the principle.
This has led the old fellow Nāgārjuna to discourse on the conventional and the empty, and caused Master Bodhidharma to distinguish between the skin and the marrow.
Without cause, he has carved sores into healthy flesh; in broad daylight, the blue-eyed one’s vision has blossomed with cataracts.
A mass of doubt! Like a winnowing basket, hooks, locks, and interlocking rings, they have mistakenly led students astray to scramble and climb in confusion.

To take a step forward is to face silver mountains and iron walls; to take a step back is to face iron walls and silver mountains. Neither advancing nor retreating, one encounters a formidable barrier on level ground.
If you are a monk who can remain steadfast amidst movement, how could you be content to follow the herd like a blind donkey? As for the Buddha-dharma and the Patriarchal-dharma, believe...
Picking it up with the hand, it shatters into a hundred fragments. There is no obstruction in principle; there is no obstruction in phenomena;
there is no obstruction in the realm of truth; there is no obstruction in contemplative wisdom. Even so, there is no obstruction in the unimpededness of expression and the unimpededness of meaning.

All the myriad differences are equally unimpeded. Even this "unimpededness" is itself non-existent. This is called absolute, ultimate non-obstruction. When one reaches such a state, one must still apply the final point.
Examine whether or not Master Wang’s eyebrows beneath his chin are still there. If you take up the burden at the point of absolute transcendence, the practitioner remains outside the thousand peaks.
(A Song from the Chamber of Preserving the Mind)
The mind cannot be maintained; that which can be maintained is not the mind. To drive a wooden stake into the back of empty space—Sāgara, the Dragon King, cannot bear the pain.
The mind has no fixed location; if you grasp it, it remains. A mosquito might suck dry the waters of the Eastern Sea; a lotus fiber might move Mount Kailash.
Such is not the way to maintain [the mind] beyond the norm. If you let go, it does not function; if you try to hold it, you cannot. This single body—
Universally manifesting all bodies, a single place universally encompasses all places. At Shaolin, the direct pointing is like a hot bowl clinking;
when the Second Patriarch sought peace, a strange thing was produced. What is that which Niu-tou contemplates at the bottom? He has struck out his own pair of eyes.

The Wayman built his hermitage atop Mount Tianmu. He used the environment to reveal the mind, and the mind to reveal the environment; though both mind and environment coexist, people do not perceive it.

It is like a well looking at a donkey, or a donkey looking into a well. A mass of fire, a forest of swords, the banner of the True Dharma, the palaces of Māras and the realms of ghosts—all these are the site of Bodhi.
When discursive thoughts swirl about, one enters right concentration; the various trees are transformed into the fragrance of sandalwood. Whether they exist or do not exist—[it is all the same].
There is nothing that cannot be. The Buddha-mind completely envelops all sentient beings. When a guest arrives, do not attempt further to resolve the contradictions.
Pick up a piece of orange peel and call it fire; let water enter the ears and sand enter the eyes. Do not ask whether it is so or not; do not ask whether it is right or wrong.
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, do not wander aimlessly; nor should you hide your body within the Big Dipper. Ten-thousand-fathom heights.
When letting go at the edge of the cliff, listen to a single roar of the lion.
As the Master An returns to Kuaniu Hermitage in Luling, what is the price of rice in Luling?
The local people have eyes that look across the four quarters of the world. If you call this a "Chan device," you are merely poking your head into it.
There is no seam or fissure. If you do not call this the pivot of Chan, it is already like forcing a tortoise to form hexagrams.
To cut off both ends and be able to take responsibility—only then may I allow you to ride an iron ox upside down. You are a man from Luling; I speak the dialect of Luling.
If you say I am being partial to my hometown, you will be reviled by people three thousand miles away.
Inscription for Master Liaotang’s “Pine and Wind Hall” Painting:
If there is pine but no wind, the sound does not emerge. If there is wind but no pine, it does not form speech. To say that the pine has sentience is to ignore its nature;
To say that it lacks sentience is to deny its reality. Sound does not arise in isolation; it is born of conditions. Its hearing is not self-evident; it depends on causes.
As for that sound: the ultimate nature of the śrāvaka is fundamentally identical [to the Buddha]. Who can distinguish between self and other, or between the sentient and the insentient?

The dragon roars from a withered tree; the angry tide surges forth. Ten thousand cranes dance as the immortal’s jade bells ring. At night, the army marches in solemnity, its clashing metal resonating. The swords of the warriors roar, startling gods and ghosts.
Some say that upon entering the ear, the mind immediately becomes tranquil; others say that listening in stillness makes the sound even better. Stillness and clamor—[are they not one?]
Cutting it into two ends creates a mechanism; both are equally delusions following the nature of sensory objects. Only the pines in the hall are different.
When the pine hall is subsumed within the painting, the painted pines in the hall remain silent and speechless. Those who come merely part the grass to gaze at the wind in vain.
The wind has no form; who has ever known it? The characteristic of sound is fundamentally empty, without arising or ceasing.
Where there is no arising or ceasing, the eye can hear. Set aside this pair of fresh curled leaves.
The Song of the Spirit Stream:
The source of the spirit stream is vast and boundless, with no east or west. Its depths are like those of the Nine Abysses, yet they are not uniform.

Seizing upon opportunity and momentum, it suddenly surges forth, flowing out as a single current to become the Spirit Stream. This Spirit Stream comes from ten thousand *li* to the west; it cleaves rocks and displaces mountains—who can [contain it]?
I venture to propose this: rushing torrents overflow as they pass Caoqi; at the eighteen rapids, all the waters swell.

The stillness of Lingxi is like the light contained within an ancient mirror; it reflects people’s faces so that they cannot be concealed. The resonance of Lingxi is like the sounding of ten thousand drums;
its clamor shakes mountains and rivers, its waves surging and rolling. Deshan’s staff brings forth a tempest of wind and rain, stirring it up.
Turbidity is stirred up while clarity is not yet lightly granted; Linji’s shout startles like thunder. Chasing waves and following ripples results in a mistaken display;

Yancui’s way of entry was not true hearing. The tongue-mark at Tiger Creek is even more falsely transmitted. At the ancient ford, he drenched Dongshan’s feet; at the shallow滩, he overturned Huating’s boat.
The myriad spirits of the great earth are like bubbles arising and vanishing; so it is with the Buddhas of the three periods.
Emerging from the water and submerging back into it; there was no prior opportunity for a bold retreat from the swift current. How many more than seventeen hundred have been submerged and drowned?

Some say the stream has no spiritual power; yet the stream’s malice is difficult to fully describe. Others say the stream possesses spiritual power; yet the stream’s wondrous function seems as if by divine means.
Whether the stream is spiritual or not, I cannot know it through intellect nor recognize it through consciousness. You must go and ask the pines.
The Venerable Lingxiyuan of Jiangjiang: An Inscription by the Venerable Jin on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* Written in Blood, Depicting the Body of Vairocana Abiding in the Realm of Space.
Amidst a heap of refuse, a cluster of jewel-light; a spiritual friend for the ocean-like conduct of Samantabhadra.

The Gate: Ten thousand streams and a hundred rivers share a single source. At the seven locations and nine assemblies, one stumbles through practice; in the four divisions and five cycles, one gazes at the tower and strikes the tower.
Speaking in every dust mote and every world-system, speaking with blazing intensity—the True Buddha appears before one, yet it is difficult to discern.
Taking the waters of the ocean for ink and Mount Sumeru for a brush, from antiquity until now, nothing has been written. That superior man displays his spiritual powers in a different manner.
Having fully realized that the sequential unfolding of practice does not obstruct perfect interfusion: the body and lands of Vairocana are gathered within the tips of ten fingers;
the realm of Samantabhadra is contained within a single pore. A single prick with the point of a needle reveals the full brilliance of the painting;

drop by drop of blood, one speaks of the Perfect Teaching. Purple clouds move through the sky as pavilions appear; rain dyes the various flowers and the spring trees turn red. The fifty-three [sages].
Hanging from the wall, he seems about to kill the youth Sudhana before the wind.
The Song of the Lazy Ox:
the laziness of this lazy ox has entered his very bones; it is his natural, innate disposition. Magnificent, he stands revealed in the open field for thirty years.
A year passes; his towering horns are yet unrecognized by men. Having not entered the herd at Peach Grove, how could he ever submit to the whip and spur of Mount Mui?
Long since devoid of intent to violate the crops, his nostrils reach toward heaven—no one can pierce them. The spring mountains are verdant and vast, the waters boundless;
amidst the misty reeds and dewy grasses, the scent of hooves lingers in spring. Thirsty, they drink; hungry, they eat, each according to their lot. The sound of the bamboo flute rolls on.
Outside, one sleeps in the slanting sun; shaking out one’s entire body, it is utterly empty and hollow. Precious treasures and great chariots are difficult to bind or tether.

With no home in the three realms, what use is there in returning? Recognizing the path on level fields results only in error. The five thousand and four hundred and eighty scrolls are but idle ropes at the head of a line;
touched by even a hair’s breadth of them, one has no freedom. These seventeen hundred "unresolved fellows" are merely those who pull the plow and drag the harrow.

When will it cease? People say that laziness is a scheme for seeking ease; how could my laziness allow others to make such arbitrary conjectures? Sometimes one’s strength pulls back but cannot turn it around; sometimes inspiration arises spontaneously. It shatters the lands of even the finest dust motes, leaving no gate to enclose them; it tramples over the ancestral fields and gardens, until the void has no bottom. At such a time, it is not inappropriate to send word to Old Dongshan: "When will it cease? People say laziness is a scheme for seeking ease;

How could my laziness allow others to make such arbitrary conjectures? Sometimes one’s strength pulls back but cannot turn it around; Sometimes inspiration arises spontaneously. It shatters the lands of even the finest dust motes, Leaving no gate to enclose them; It tramples over the ancestral fields and gardens, Until the void has no bottom. At such a time, It is not inappropriate to send word to Old Dongshan."* *Note:

This is a poetic rendering of the famous verse by Dongshan Liangjie (807–869) concerning his "laziness" (懶). The original Chinese text contains the character 欄 (lán), which is a variant or error for 欄 (lán, meaning "railing" or "enclosure"), and the character [木*圈] (mùquān), which is a graphic representation of 欄 (lán, meaning "enclosure" or "fence"). The translation reflects the intended meaning of these characters.*
The tail is not inside the window lattice.
Sending off Secretary Dōrin Kuni and the monk Nanpian:
they have no skillful means. Having harbored doubts about Dongshan’s three blows of the staff, they instead come to annotate Zhaozhou’s “old woman.”
To argue over whether the Way exists or does not exist is merely stubbornness. Little do they realize that the root source of all dharmas lies upon the tip of a single hair.
To perceive the root source upon the tip of a single hair is still like a group of blind men collectively feeling an elephant.
This is why Master Ma gave Baizhang such a twist that he broke his nasal bridge, and gave Shuilao such a kick that he fell prostrate. Furthermore, it is said since the Hu...
After the turmoil, for thirty years there was no shortage of salt and sauce. Total letting go is gathering; total gathering is letting go.

Had anyone understood this pivotal moment at that time, let alone old Ciming—even a Buddha would have had difficulty approaching him. When I, this mountain monk, point this out in such a way, I dare ask:
is Secretary Dulin praising me or slandering me? If you cannot distinguish between black and white, it is the Buddha’s hand.
The story of the donkey’s hoof. He offered yet another portion as an offering;
the courtyard where Keting Ge and Keshi stood was covered in snow. The soles of their vajra-feet were frozen to the point of cracking. Unable to find the mind, he [realized] it was simply the mind.

Peace. I dare say that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate realization. "A single bright moon may be in the courtyard"—this is a false recognition of fleeting light that obscures one's own spiritual essence.

You have not yet understood the saying: "When light and its object both vanish. Peering at the sky from within the house, the heavens are vast and profound. There is another "courtyard" that is not of this kind;
by taking the "may be" as the courtyard, there is no facing or turning away. When the myriad phenomena intersect, they all nod their heads in agreement—who would dare say otherwise?
The Patriarch had no intention of complying. At times he clenches the Cakravāḍa mountains so that Mount Sumeru, the King of Floating Banners, can be grasped by hand;
the Buddhas and Patriarchs fall down the steps, remaining only within the surrounding eaves and corridors. At times he lets go, leaving everything empty and desolate;

the ten directions are transparently clear, without walls or barriers. When one calls out from atop the hall, no one hears; yet the Śūnyatā-deva (Śunyatā-deva) responds with a "Yes" in accordance with the situation.
Yellow leaves flutter amidst the mortars and pestles; along the vast corridors, the pines sing in the wind. On the platform for living beings, birds find joy in their food;
each one discourses for me upon the Heart-Essence. People today do not believe my words are straightforward; ten thousand divergences at the gates are difficult to fathom.
Empty space has already fallen to the ground long ago; the cypress tree refuses to become a Buddha—instead, I request the coiled dragon.
How could it be possible? For his sake, I shall reveal a true message:
"In the middle continent, I hear the song of the Vairocana Flower Treasury Ocean. From the surface of the ocean, a Lotus King emerges; within the flower, the Earth-Holding One is like a continent."
*Tan*. Its ground is firm and thick, composed entirely of vajra. Within the continent, countless oceans appear; within these oceans, flowers appear like spreading clouds.
Each flower supports a land as vast as a continent, and within each continent there resides a world-system (*kṣetra-vyañjana*).

Within those systems, the number of worlds that appear is even more numerous. These worlds support one another like a honeycomb; in each world is a Buddha and a single assembly, each manifesting its own characteristics.
The interlacing of radiant light is wondrous. Yet I have heard it said that it is not thus: in the characteristics of all phenomena, there is no grasping at all.
The great ocean is swallowed within the tip of a single hair; the Buddhas dwell with no fixed location. To cling to the existence of marks is not the work of a master;
the separation between heaven and earth lies in a mere hair’s breadth. The islands and seas of the ocean are fundamentally not real; all worlds are like flowers in the sky.
Furthermore, it is heard that it is neither empty nor existent; having grasped the nostrils, one loses the mouth. It all resides within a single thought-moment of the person themselves.
Because two arise from one, do not cling to even one. There was a Chan practitioner from the land of Chu named Hai, who received the title Zhongzhou because of his name Hai.
I hold these three kinds of meanings mentioned above and ask: do you understand, Zhongzhou? Zhongzhou said, "In this way..."
"It is not so," he said, "nor is it not so. 'So' and 'not so'—neither is acceptable.
Laughing at the heavens, he suddenly forgot words; the clouds have vanished over Xiangtan, and the evening mountains emerge.

The "Jinling Xing" has one line that is twisted and strange: "Mountains encircle the old kingdom, standing all around. It has another line that is rugged and imposing: "Tides strike the empty city and return in silence.
The mountains are mountains; the waters are waters. On level ground, there is no cause for a heap of bones to rise up. The waters...
It is not water; the mountain is not a mountain. A five-flower cat has no spots on its body. Zen monks have a special function beyond the ordinary:
they sweep away both "is" and "is not. They can grasp at emptiness and fill it up; they can take error and turn it into correctness.
When a Han comes, they manifest as a Han; when a Hu comes, they manifest as a Hu. Even Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his slaves. He empties the alms-bag and pours out the four great elements.
The Ocean: A straw sandal kicks over Mount Sumeru; it is neither mind, nor object, nor samādhi.

If the Lecturer Juezhao understood this meaning, he would have overturned both the Buddhist scholastic caves and the Zen hermitages, yet he instead said that the ancients had not realized it at all. First, one must ask Niu-t’ou T’ung;
second, one must ask the Elder of the Eagle’s Nest. From the tip of his staff, the diamond drill rises in combat—a display of vigorous power.
If the dragon soars through the sky, I am like a tiger watching a water mill, or like an ox passing through a window lattice.
Although the debt for my feet has not yet been cleared, I have learned to sit in daze like a man from Suzhou. This one, this one, and that one; thus it is, and yet not thus.
Wait until you have finished your investigation and returned, then explain each and every point to me.
Master Qing of Wumen traveled to the other side of the Stone Bridge at Tiantai.
There is a path that lies precisely where one turns around and steps off the bed;

if one can tread firmly upon the void with one's heels, who has time to look back at the flowing bridge and the flowing water? Before Mount Huading there is a barrier; it lies precisely where one pushes open the door and falls through.
In the mortar’s space, ask neither of what is within the gate nor without; simply see that before one’s eyes, all is green mountain. A patch-robed monk can both let go and take up;
though he gathers up the great earth, not an inch of soil remains. At times, across billions of Jambudvīpas, he lets it loose, yet it occupies no more than the tip of an autumn hair.
Though this talk is numinous, those who believe it are rare; people today do not suffer the deception of the ancients. High are the mountains!
The waters are deep and the road is long; only upon arriving once does the mind find peace. The dragon of the waterfall roars so that the empty mountains seem to tremble;
ten thousand thunders beat like drums as they rush together in pursuit. Spray flies up to the steamed-bread peak; even in the sixth month, the shaded cliffs are frozen with snow and frost.

Clouds lock the path to the profound mystery; it cannot be traversed. Since the National Teacher departed, no trace remains. The *dhūta* practitioner sits upon the rock, yet his portrait is difficult to complete.
The bright moon is in the spring, and the mist rests upon the pines. How can one meet the Venerable Banzhan? Mirage and empty flowers are the palace itself.
When serving tea, do not mistake the flower in the tea for the truth; before the flower, recognize your mother’s face. When the兴致 (xìngzhì—spiritual resonance) ends, the matter truly lies therein.

When descending the mountain, not a speck of water or a grain of earth can be moved. Having attained the news through non-hearing and non-seeing, who goes and who comes—you should know this for yourself.
If someone asks, "Is the Stone Bridge still in good condition? at that moment, you must most certainly refrain from opening your mouth lightly.
Again, if asked, "How is it now at Mount Huading? shake off your sleeves and walk away without looking back. If asked about Lingyan or Tiger Hill, do not—

the Abbot of the Treasury, back to Hunan to erect a stupa inscription for his teacher,
Iron Ox (Tienu) Worthy.
I would not speak of Chan either. Even thirty years of "nailing down the post and rowing the oars" is not Chan.
I say that a red-eyed turtle is called a soft-shelled turtle; it resembles an old Persian from the South Sea, its teeth missing half since birth.
Stupidly chewing on the dregs of empty space until they are rotten; spat out as three feet of snow in the Heavens of Blazing Fire.

"Dongshan’s three pounds of hemp," "Yunmen’s dried-up shit-stick"—take these up together and look: before you know it, your skull splits open. How much more distinct is the mechanism of another stream?
The offspring of the Iron Ox has golden flanks. Treading the wrong step, he overturns the Lake of West Zi; he pulls out the *maṇi* jewel from its treasury.
The middle wedge! The Buddhas of the three periods have been swallowed crosswise by him; as soon as the seam of his mouth opens, thunder rolls and lightning flashes.
On this journey back to Lingyun Mountain, he intends to grind out the Vajra-eye of the former master upon the precipitous cliffs.
He then set aside all the skulls. As he was about to depart, he asked me for a turning word; I had no words.
A thousand miles, ten thousand miles—a single iron rod.
(Master Wuwen Kui, Abbot of the Zang)
"I have finished eating congee; I am going to wash the bowl. Zhaozhou’s "dead word" is his "living word. One must take it up at the very moment he opens his mouth.
This monk says, "What awakening has he ever awakened to? This matter is fundamentally not something to be awakened to, nor is it something that is immediately manifest.
It is like arsenic hidden within cotton or thorns hidden within silk; if one stirs it even by a hair’s breadth, disaster arises. The entire Tripitaka is but stinking meat and rotten pickles;
the seventeen hundred koans are like mistaking a crow for a horse. When Yangshan uses his rattan cane, it is all merely "zhi-hu-ye-zhe" (the particles of Chinese grammar).
With one hand I grasp and with the other I lift; let go and it will not stay, try to hold it and it will not come. Furthermore, there is not a single dharma.
I bind you fast. Wait until another time when your eyes open of themselves. When the eyes open, lift up the Seal Without Words; the myriad phenomena, as vast as they are, are all sealed therein.
Once the Seal breaks, the iron-skinned face of the King of Emptiness shall beg for its life from the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
Return home and push aside the Peak of the Six Characters; receive it within the eye-lashes of a gnat. Pick up a single blade of grass and strike a sneeze—ten thousand...
The ravines are solemn, giving rise to a pure breeze. If someone asks where we dwell, I tell them there is nothing for you to grasp.
The Dragon King has swallowed the night-bright pearl; the mud ox at the bottom of the sea fights until its horns are broken.

The Master of the Treasury of Peerless Merit opens his mouth and bites his tongue; he washes his face and touches his nose. Clearly manifest at the tips of the hundred grasses, clearly manifest is the meaning of the Patriarch.
In those days, Huangbo had eyes; with sixty painful blows, he struck Linji until Linji was driven to madness.
Drunken and staggering, he meets people and spits out the scent of gruel and rice. Daoyu calls this "the grandmotherly heart," yet it exhausts the poor livelihood of the patch-robed monk.
Striking the south, the north shakes; when Mr. Zhang drinks, Mr. Li gets drunk.
If one were a heroic great man, how could they ever ask others for an explanation? To gather together the mirages of a sunbeam and the flowers of the sky, and then squeeze them into nothingness.
The void is as if shattered to pieces, yet it flows forth from within one’s own breast, covering heaven and earth.

At times, he reveals a single pivot that transcends all categories, churning the monastic groves into a seething cauldron; he rolls thorns into flower-balls, wielding them crosswise and upside down like a game.
This is called the "Incomparable Merit," and it is also called the "Incomparable Samādhi. Even were one to...
Even if Bodhidharma were to return once more to display hundreds of thousands of ghostly arts, it would suffice simply to wave one's hand and say to him: "Old brother, old brother,
where have you come from?"— Master Xi Yun Yue, Curator of the Tripitaka.

Yunfeng’s Delight saw ghosts with his own eyes; his spirit fell into the rim of a bucket. He pointed to the quicksilver and silver of others’ medicines, yet he could not lift the broken bucket himself.
Although Xiyun shares the same name as Delight, her nose is naturally straight and her two eyes are wide-set.
She stands firm under heaven and upon earth, making her living; she refuses to follow another’s path for even a single step. Once, at Lion Rock...
Encountering a single squeeze, he mastered the art of the somersault before the pivot; grasping his staff upside down, he traversed the Yangtze from east to west.
Blindly stumbling, he knocked over Zhang Sanba; Stone Ear Peak joins with Horse Ear Peak—three calls like thunder, yet he hears as if deaf.
The *maṇi* jewels of the ocean treasury were all scattered; Longxiang provoked the dragon among monks. This journey meets me on the road of Wumen; it is narrow.
Meeting on the road, there is no room for evasion; he hangs up his frost-and-dew iron mask.
To examine the words of fellow practitioners, he blocks off the ready-made path and strips away the old way of life. He even knows how to extract the bone from empty space;
seeing Buddhas and Patriarchs, he treats them like enemies. His brand-new commands transcend past and present; there is another mechanism that must be realized.
Tearing it open, the dog licks the hot oil cauldron; struck as the "Poison-Coated Drum" of the Forest.

As for the Master Ji, his travels to Wutai Shan were characterized by stillness that is ever-illuminating, and illumination that is ever-still. Within the tip of every single hair there are ten billion lions; within the tip of every lion’s hair there are ten billion hairs.
I am truly Mañjuśrī; yet there is no such Mañjuśrī. When presented before the opportune moment, they fail to realize it; though right before their eyes, they are separated by a vast distance.
It is just like when a monk asked about the road to Mount Tai, and the old woman told him to go straight ahead—Zhaozhou saw through her with no room for excuse.
Throughout antiquity and the present, this has killed countless people with doubt. You, superior man, as you depart now, cannot be held back; you must examine Mañjuśrī and...
Zhaozhou carries his knotted staff across his shoulder, as vigorous as a tiger; his tattered patchwork robe is worth more than a cloak of a thousand pieces of gold.

Upon the Stone of Coolness, the clouds are like water; in the sixth month, a cold wind freezes the very marrow of one's bones. Within the light that gathers his body, he beholds Mañjuśrī; he bows down along with others and rises up along with them.
"Three times three before, and three times three after"—having seen Mañjuśrī, one should truly investigate this further. If you should encounter...
Do not mock each other, Shancai; the ox-head faces north while the horse-head faces south.
Composed in the rhyme of Scholar Yu of Shao’an to see off Chan Master Chushi, the Head Seat, on his journey—wherever he travels is home.
He has also spent the remnants of three summers in various places. This was recognized by the Layman of Shao’an.
The pivot: He laughs at those who sit until their meditation cushions are worn through. The great trichiliocosm is squeezed into the tip of a single hair;

ten-thousand bushels of dragon pearls are scattered at will. An iron snake lies across the road, blocking the passage of men; a mountain-shattering thunder roars through the spring night. Once, in Vaiśālī, he feigned illness;
the manifestation of the aggregates is neither grasped nor abandoned. When worldly people probe for depth beneath his words, the hare crosses the river.
The River doubts elephants and horses; he calls himself a blind man with flowers blooming before his eyes. Even the Buddha was deceived by him.
Chushu knows where he applies his means. Going hence, he ascends once more to the cool summer pavilion;
from between his brows, he draws forth the Vajra King, cutting off the long-legged talk of old.
I present this to the Abbot of Dongshan, offering him a "Bharaṇī" from the Eastern Mountain: swallow the entire Great Canon in one gulp; Yunmen cast down a piece of firewood.
This raw-iron caltrop is difficult to approach. Who would have known that playing with it until now has resulted in an unresolved koan?
A swift and capable monk cuts off immediately when it is time to cut off. If you can grasp the first stroke at the very beginning, it is the same as the final segment;
where there is no place for confusion, there is yet confusion. Killing and giving life according to the occasion—there is no fixed pattern.
Have you not seen how Ciming inspired Nanpintou? It took nothing more than three blows of Dongshan’s staff.
Next, regarding the rhyme of the character *péng* (篷):
the monastic secretary Daolin and two or three fellow practitioners from Lì Zhuófēng exchanged verses once or twice using this rhyme.
Now that the collection is complete, they have requested something from me; thus, I offer these two rhyming poems on "tents" as a token of my sympathetic joy to serve as a parting gift.
The Boatman lacked eyes; he crossed the water seeking the tracks of fish. He hewed away all the bamboo for his fishing rods and trampled over the sail upon the waves.
In recent years there has been a fine carp that did not fall into the pickle jar; it split the waves of the Dragon Gate and, with its scales marked, became a "marked-chest" (a leaping dragon).
Turning my head, I laugh at my own laziness; I have sat until I have worn out the remains of Cien and Rong. When asked about my former path, I say: "Who provides the funds for the rice gruel?

I gather the waters of hundreds of thousands of oceans; a single hair swallows the vast expanse with room to spare. Toilsome are you to probe its depths; from the West, you have traveled back to the East.

The ancients used the staff and the shout; like a horned sheep leaping over a cliff, there is no trace left behind. It is like crossing a sea of virulent poison: the oars and rudders follow the pole and sail.
If you miss it face-to-face by even a hair’s breadth, you will hide away within the old nest. When the lacquer bucket is not yet overturned, changing hands and merely beating one's breast is in vain.
Dàolín broke free from the net of teachings; his spirit overwhelmed those of Shēng, Zhào, and Róng. When you ask me for words on "staff and shout," I have no excrement or entrails to offer.
In my old age, I understand the discourse of Māra; there is not the slightest room for human sentiment. The Big Dipper faces south, yet Jambudvīpa lies to the east.
In the style of Master Yuejiang, I compose this to see off the Abbot Cangeru:
Last night the west wind shook the door panels; the pivot of Mount Mao’s gate is deep and difficult to perceive.

Twenty years later, Elder Songyue shall for his sake once again turn the millstone. Cangeru, brandishing his staff, has often visited my door; he immediately understood the "thorny chestnut" and cast it away entirely.
Lun-tun! He plucks the whiskers of a fierce tiger and leaps about wildly; he tramples the water-mill wheel right where he stands.
Last year, on the path before the Drunken Stone Cliff, he brought forth the "cutting-foot" phrase of Dongshan. The ten-thousand-fathom dragon abyss was dried to its very bottom;

having seized the pearl from the black dragon’s head, he descended the mountain. Within his bowl-bag he hides a vessel of venomous poison; that he devours Buddhas and Patriarchs is truly no exaggeration. Returning once more—
Beholding the pine-moon upon the river, looking down, the dragons and elephants are all but black donkeys. The old shrimp’s submission serves only its own offspring;
talk that falls into the weeds does not form a coherent word. The customs of Min and Shu are the same; speak of the spiritual with reverence. From now on, when meeting people, do not act with levity.
I see off my Dharma relative Suan-an as he returns to Baiyun Peak at Heshan.
Sitting and reclining are not Chan; Chan is not sitting and reclining. Before the seams of the mouth have even opened, one has already fallen into idle chatter.
Atop the Six-Character Peak lies a single pivot, which our ancestors never deigned to break open. It has caused you and me to run abroad in search of it; there is a Buddha...
There has never been a Buddha who has not passed through this; for twenty years we have met twice. Our teeth are chattering and our jaws are sagging—we are both grown old.
Since you already know that when the water rises the boat floats, I too shall say that rice is made from grain. Amidst the vast clamor of all quarters, what are you doing now?
The Great Wheel of Dharma turns like a millstone driven by water; quicksilver cannot rival the authenticity of *arura*.

To take a vulgar song and harmonize it with the "Yangchun" melody—what can be done? What can be done about this? At such a time as this, what is there to be done? Beneath the White Cloud Peak, you should sweep away all traces and return;
within the Lion’s Grove, I too shall sit cross-legged, body at ease. Do not follow in the footsteps of your ancestors.
This is no different from peddling old, stale merchandise. Have you not seen how Dao-wu brandished his ritual tablet and He-shan beat his drum?

These were all instances of inviting thieves to ruin one’s house or lighting incense to invite disaster. The Buddhas of the three periods swallow it all in a single gulp; among thousands and tens of thousands of people, there is not even half a person who understands.
Song of the Guishan Room, composed by Junxiang Qian.
On Mount Taihu, I have built the Guishan Room to lodge my Chan practice. Upon entering the door and seeing it for the first time, my eyes were struck with clarity;
sitting for a long while, I gradually felt my body become at ease. People say that good and evil originally have no inherent nature; all choosing and rejecting arise solely from emotion.
Transformation. To abandon evil and take up good is called "returning to the good. When evil has departed and good remains, this is still partial.
When one returns to the ultimate good and abandons even that goodness, one arrives at the state of no-return; only then is the nature perfected. It is like administering medicine to treat an illness:

when the illness ceases and the medicine is discarded, the spirit is naturally restored. My way of practice is not like this: there is no discrimination between the taking and abandoning of good and evil. Seeing the Buddha.
I do not rejoice in Māra, nor do I loathe him. Birth and death are both followed according to conditions. The Master sits with me within the room;
once my sitting grows weary, I return to sleep again. When inspiration arises, I take up my staff and go out the gate, rubbing my aged eyes upon the peaks of the lakes and mountains.

The lake and mountains press down upon the heavens, while the sky and water merge with the moonlight. Looking up and observing below, heaven and earth are vast; the myriad phenomena stand clearly and solemnly before me.
At first, I wondered if the lake and mountains shared a single chamber; then I wondered if that single chamber could contain the great chiliocosm.
The great chiliocosm is expansive and pervades the entire Dharma-realm; within this pervasive realm, all the deluded masses are simultaneously made clear. The Buddha-dharma has no [fixed location].
If one employs such a doctrine, the ancestral lamp has no basis for its transmission; people do not see it on either bank or in the middle of the stream.
Before the mountain, the boat that crosses the lake remains idle.
[This is] the verse for seeing off the Head Seat Yujian as he pays homage to the Patriarch.

Regarding that one critical point of Bodhidharma’s future: the universe stands alone, bare and desolate. Without cause, they seek the mind and seek out sin, drilling through layer after layer of the sacred tortoise’s shell.
Do you not see? With the mattock for planting pines beneath Mount Pòtóu, he crashed headlong into a calamity, exposing his own ugliness.
To this day, the waters of the turbid stream flow crosswise; travelers on both banks find it difficult to find a mooring. Furthermore—
He was not seen. At midnight at Huangmei, gods and ghosts clamored; the waist-stone remains, yet no one transmits it.
