Later generations called it "Iron Sour Filling"—who in this world has a mouth capable of swallowing it? How much less could Niu-tou Rong or He-lin Su have done so?
A branch extends horizontally, idly displaying a proclamation; a solid iron hammer is cast recklessly. It shatters the void and its heavy shackles;
receiving the echo in emptiness, the blazing disputes of "same" and "different" persist. Since the True Dharma has been swept from the ground, every eye beholds only the sects of Mara.
You, too, possess a spirit as vast as an autumn rainbow; you have long since leveled the twin peaks of Emei. Now, for my sake, pull down this fortress of Mara.
Holding the staff in hand like a fierce dragon, he cannot be blocked by a single barrier at the sea gate. Thunder and lightning stir as he roars against the wind;
outside the city of Shitou, he leaps and bounds. Furious waves sweep across the void of the Yangtze River.
Otherwise, he cleaves the road to Huaiyang and turns his body straight up toward Mount Kuanglu. Sitting, he watches the Milky Way fall from the Nine Heavens. Clouds rise over the Southern Mountain.
Rain on the Northern Mountains.
A song for alms-begging by a monk:
we have no livelihood, nor do we possess the ancestral fields of our forefathers; we rely solely upon this black alms bowl that follows us everywhere.
When hunger comes, eat; when weariness comes, sleep. The ancient Buddhas cast aside their golden wheels and wandered through city gates begging for food with their disciples.
With hands of *tūla* cotton they held forth their alms bowls, and the majestic radiance of twelve hundred beings shone forth.

They called the alms bowl the "Treasury of Many Jewels"; their daily livelihood was boundless. They enjoyed what was already present, practicing non-action. Thus did the Buddhas and their descendants act.
As a model, he called his almsbowl the Changshu Estate. When ancient Buddhas transformed food, I transform grain. Transforming grain, I make porridge and rice as I please;
rain, dampness, wind, and cold do not hinder me at all. The almsbowl is simply one mouth; its capacity does not exceed one peck.
Yet sometimes it swallows the vast void, leaving ten thousand granaries and myriad storehouses with no way to escape. At night...
Half of it was once entrusted to Old Lu; the assembly at Huangmei called out to one another in astonishment. Caoxi subdued the fierce dragon and kept him there;

with every beat of his staff, the true command was carried out across rivers and lakes. When Zhaozhou finished eating his gruel and went off to wash his bowl, the doubts of the meditators were instantly resolved.
When Deshan took up his bowl and descended from the hall, they understood Yantou’s final word. Vimalakīrti took up his bowl and returned.
Above, rice grains like pearls vie in their brilliance; a million great Bodhisattvas are sated at once, and for seven days, fragrance still emanates from their pores.
The wondrous efficacy of the alms bowl is beyond description; Buddhas and Patriarchs rely upon it to prolong the life of wisdom.
Holding this forth, it breaks down my banner of pride and awakens your spirit of giving to produce right faith. Having given this year, you shall give again next year—year after year.
I have come to establish the conditions for providing food to the Sangha. I carry this bowl because I seek to achieve the Way; once the Way is achieved, it shall increase your field of merit.

This matter has its cause and will surely have its fruit. Whether the gift be small or great, there is no way it cannot be accepted. If you are stingy and refuse to open your purse, [you shall suffer the consequences].
It is you who, lacking the necessary conditions, have missed me. I do not compose commentaries on transformation, nor do I carry a basket of rice.

I have merely taken the intent with which the Buddhas and Patriarchs sought the Way and written it as a long poem—a song for begging alms. Should someone point out a flaw within my song, they might laugh at me for not yet being empty of the nature of words.
They would say that because my speech is excessive and the Way is distant, Buddhahood is difficult to achieve; they would ask why I need to attach a new handle to my alms bowl. I—

Laughing at others' illnesses, one's own ailments increase further. The handleless alms bowl is indeed a source of confusion. If you can grasp its handle with your own hands, what need would there be for even a single kṣaṇa to become a Buddha?
Ten Verses of Exhortation to the World:
All know that there is birth and death; yet to know this and not turn back is folly.
One may never tire of watching a stage of puppets, but alas, there will come a time when the curtain falls.
The donkey’s business is not yet finished when the horse’s arrives; hooks and chains link together without end.
Merely waiting for today and then tomorrow, one carelessly wastes a lifetime in vain.
The dung beetle carries its manure, never deeming it too much; the rat moves its gold, never fearing it too heavy.
They think only that they can take these things with them at the end of life, yet when the end comes, nothing can be done about them.
To take one's illness as the very realization of death—this is the secret, single-lineage prescription.
If you lack a sovereign master within your own presence, you will be like a crab falling into boiling water, with no way to deliberate or escape.
When you have attained rest, simply rest; let go and gather it back, for all is free. In the end, this weary life is no lasting plan;
do not hang delusive thoughts upon your mind.
Cultivating practice is like purchasing worldly goods; if one is willing to break open the bag of stinginess, the matter will be perfected.
To merely engage in idle talk with the mouth is exactly like having paid the price but not yet returned the money.
Not knowing which of these is my own nature, I turn it over and over again, asking: who is this "it"? Suddenly meeting it face-to-face, I recognize it intimately;
like a fish drinking water, I know it for myself.
With diligent effort, step by step it becomes tighter; even a forge-cast iron barrier is squeezed open.
As for the face prior to the birth of one's parents, let him see it directly once more.
The secret intent has always been with you; your entire being is entirely the Zen of the Patriarchs.
Suddenly, when you scratch your own itch, the toad from the bottom of the sea flies up into the sky.
A single thought-moment unarisen gives birth to perfect enlightenment. When the ancients opened their mouths, one saw their very heart and liver.
If you can take this up before the pivot of action, what need is there for a swift gesture like snapping a finger?
Parting from Master Muhuàn at Wumen for Jiangling: Ten Verses I have realized the "Six Non-acceptances" of Yunmen;
Wherever one acts or withdraws, there is no place to find a trace. The meaning of hearing the bell outside the city of Gusu Resides, in truth, at the head of the stone horse in Jiangling.
An octagonal grinding stone cast of cast iron; were a single hair-tip to stir, Mount Tai would topple.
Even if Naluo exerts all the strength in his wrists, when he cannot hold it back, one must let it go.
There is [good wine] in Suzhou and there is [good wine] in Changzhou; who would say it is not found in North or South Xiang? One need not concern oneself with whether the wine is in a deep alley;
why must vinegar necessarily come from a large gourd?
Longtan extinguished the candle, his lips parched; Nanyue ground the brick, his arm bones weary. The Daoist who herds illusions has no leisure;
when the waters of Jiangling rise, he watches the boat’s height.
Tending the real and tending the illusory is beyond all deliberation; grasping the *maṇi* jewel, he releases its radiance.
Having cast aside Panshan’s talk of light and objects, his excellent reputation has since spread throughout all quarters.
The sixteen-foot golden body is but a single blade of grass; upon that single blade of grass, a jade tower appears. An old case suddenly proves efficacious;
even a stubborn stone nods its head at the sound of the wind.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods swallow it all in a single mouth; the ancients acted with such urgency for the sake of their lineage.
Yet they took up the task of teaching and transforming sentient beings, passing it down through a thousand years to burden their descendants.
White Lotus Peak and White Lotus Bridge—how many times have they met to converse in silence? A single phrase, already manifest, has been brought forth;
it is like scraping tortoise hair from the back of an iron ox.
With azure eyes they gaze at one another, neither harboring any doubt. Shaking off the excrement and entrails, they reveal their own private treasure.
Even if there were something worthy of being gifted upon departure, it would only serve to add more eyebrows to their eyes.
Those who are not karmic enemies do not meet. Travelers, do not treat the road as your enemy.
Though a simple friendship may seem as powerless as water, it can nonetheless carry ten thousand loads.
Ten Verses on Miscellaneous Sayings from Mountain Dwelling:
Having secured this pointed little hut, the masters of all quarters raise it with no doubt.
Sometimes when the earth is dark and the sky overcast, even then the clouds come to take charge as abbot.
Not a single word of Buddhist dharma or literature; facing guests from his wooden bed, he is utterly at ease. What flows forth from his breast covers heaven and earth;
old and decrepit, Yantou’s teeth are sparse.
I recall passing the Six Bridges along the Su Embankment; my small *fan* and *luo* caps were blown away by the wind.
Covered head to toe in the snow of the lake and mountains, it took many instances of scorching heat to melt them away.
Teeth waver, face wrinkles, and hair turns streaked with white; within the eyes, green and yellow flicker without ceasing. Yet there is that which does not follow these changes:
the local dialect remains as it was in Luling.
Clearing the weeds reveals a mistaken application of mind; turning one's head before the hall, the green forest stands dense. Effort is applied only to the surface of the skin;
who has ever seen the depth of the roots?
Hair grows upon the Way; my Dharma-wealth is vast. I present this white paper, entreating you to break through stinginess. Who would believe that this mountain monk is merely here for fine views?
The money for shaving one's head is to be returned to others.
Linguistic analysis only serves to dally with doubt; do not waste your time in forced memorization.
How many brilliant spirits have been buried by this—white-haired, they forget the moment they left the household life.
The wild buffalo roams at will, having no fixed home; as soon as one attempts to block its path, matters go awry. The entire realm is the king’s pasture and water;
let it enjoy whatever portion it takes according to its own nature.

The guest within the host is precisely the host within the guest; whether moving against or with the current, vertically or horizontally, do not take them as real. Meeting on a narrow path, they understand how to intermingle;
in the midst of a bustling basket, it is precisely fitting for idle people to dwell.
Within the nostrils there are three inches of breath; beneath the eyebrows there are three inches of radiance. What a fine expression of the meaning of the Western-Come Patriarch!
Yet everyone who asks about it deliberates it incorrectly.

When Nengshangren returned to Mount Lu to visit his former teacher, he looked upon the old sights of Mount Lu as they were in the past. "What is there about you, Master, that is not at peace? Let the flies go; do not strike and break the paper window.
With wind and rain, the falling flowers signal the spring's very chill."
Dream-Absorbed:
The eye of the Tathāgatas of the three ages has not yet awakened; through dullness and delusive thoughts, he establishes his own school. When guests arrive, he does not raise his fist;
let him listen to his sleep-talking from next door.

In the Jade Garden, the stubborn raw stone was carved open to reveal this "Qiezi" (the child); the jade tree and its precious flowers fill the grove. Yet one laughs at the site where Jetavana was spread with gold:
in recent years, the weeds have grown so deep they bury the head.
The Venerable Tientu Chunsan returned to Wanfeng Hermitage;
brewing tea in a ceramic cauldron, he swallowed yam tubers. A record of his travels at the thatched hut of Wanfeng:
opening the door, he drove the demon of sleep away, letting in a single hook of moonlight through the pines and vines.
Before the cliff of withered trees lies the old path; pine blossoms cover the ground, yet no one gathers them. There is not much more to the Buddha-dharma of the monastic groves:
take the black staff in hand, turn back, and rest.
Venerable Fú bows to Mañjuśrī;

Mañjuśrī meets Fú at the eastern gate of the City of Blessings (*Puṇyapura*). There is a saying one must beware of as mere empty talk: "It was said that in the south there is a spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*);
Sudhana the youth has run through a hundred cities to find him."
The Spirit-Dhūta went to Mount Wutai and said that Mañjuśrī was there; yet how many who reached it returned empty-handed?
The Dhūta’s staff possesses spiritual transformations—pick up one shoulder-load for me and bring it here!
In ancient times at Sekigawa, the school’s style was established beyond two thousand years ago; it firmly grasps the first barrier of the Zen gate.
Seventeen hundred men risked their lives to press against it, yet to this day the path back has never been opened.
Master Guan goes to pay homage at Potalaka;
what does he seek along the slopes of the cliff? He will not cease until he beholds Avalokiteśvara. Once he has seen Avalokiteśvara, he shall laugh to himself:
"It turns out the 'hu-bing' was actually a *mántóu*."
Master Long returned to Luling;
that old fellow from Qingyuan is truly detested by all. He was accustomed to using life-and-death crises to discern monks. To this day, the price of rice remains undecided.
When you meet him, do not say it is Luling.

Master Wuyan Yan finished reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and realized that mind is not the Dharma and the Dharma is not the object of study. He thoroughly penetrated the fifty-three stages and traveled through the hundred cities of smoke and water in the South;
he knew that those who truly understood were few, as each lowered their head and spoke only their own local dialect.
Baoning’s Iron Boat Head Seat returned to Silla.
Baoning possessed a diamond drill; the Head Seat transmitted it and put it to many uses.
It was transformed into a hairless iron hawk, which Iron Boat took with him back to Silla.
Within the empty hermitage, all is bright and clear; there is not a single thing. It can contain the Dharma-realm, yet it is but a hollow reputation.
Zhaozhou lacked the eye of discernment before the pivot; he was blocked by this very fist.
Presented to Liu Hexin:
How many books can one truly digest through reading? Though Zeng Cong was as wise as Yanzi, he appeared as if he were dull-witted. A man of integrity must not be driven by his own cleverness;
rather, it is the man of integrity who is able to master his own intelligence.
All the people of the entire earth suffer from malaria; from birth until death, they never have a moment’s rest. Once a year, they experience chills and fever;
you, however, will suffer fifty bouts of malaria next year.
I heard earlier that when encountering a wind on Lake Pengli, a great vessel was about to sink and gods and ghosts cried out.
In the shock of escaping death with a disordered soul, one night three tufts of white beard grew upon his chin.
The ocean is likened to the vast blue sea that receives all streams; yet the blue sea is fundamentally not its peer. What thing in the world can truly resemble it?
Only empty space is like a single bubble.

In ancient times, during the era of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvara, he plowed the wilderness; he left it for his descendants to sow and reap. In this present age, people do not know the method of cultivation;
it teaches them to hold a hoe in their empty hands.
A Gift for Fei Zirun (with Preface) Fei Zirun was a native of Shanghai County in Songjiang. His father, Qianfu, once suffered a robbery.
A Buddhist laywoman (*upāsikā*) in the village had repeatedly received the kindness of Qianfu’s assistance during times of distress. One day, she came to sell gold and pearls. It was then that—

When the stolen goods were recently discovered, the mistress of the house remained silent and concealed them, refusing to inquire into the matter. She had a favored concubine who said to the old woman, "If you sell these stolen goods from a thief and the matter is exposed, will it not implicate you?
The old woman finally realized the truth and became terrified; she subsequently committed suicide by cutting her own throat. Not long after, the concubine became pregnant.
On the eve of her delivery, she dreamed that the old woman who had cut her throat entered her bedchamber. The concubine rebuked her, but the old woman replied, "I..."
I shared a karmic affinity with Qianfu from a former life; he was destined to become my son. "In five years, you shall repay my life.
Upon waking, a son was born—this was Zhi-run. When he reached the age of five, his mother indeed passed away.
Zhi-run is now over forty years old. At birth, there was a scar on his neck that did not heal; when pressed with the hand, fresh blood would well forth in profusion.

It remains so even to this day; I have witnessed it with my own eyes. The matter is most extraordinary, and I have therefore composed three verses as a gift, so that you may know that the doctrine of karmic retribution is not false, and that the power of karma is inconceivable.

The old woman of the past knew her own body was moist; causes and conditions, like echoes and shadows, skillfully follow one another. The shedding and changing of this skin-sack is called birth and death;
who is it that can die and can live?
Who dies and who is born cannot be truly discerned; entering and exiting the womb is surely not by human will. Alas, the power of karma is inconceivable;
the traces of one's severing [of bonds] are transmitted to future lives.
Emerging from the womb and entering the womb again; thus have they come through hundreds and thousands of births and kalpas. Who can understand this? Before the skull, all is illuminated;
the eye of Maheśvara opens at the crown of the head.
The Chan practitioner presented these verses and requested a response; there are three in all.
Written upon paper, they speak of intimacy; changing the melody and shifting the mode, they become sharp and fresh. People love to hear the words of others;
yet such words have, from the beginning, deceived and slain men.
How could I dare to compose words for long prose Zen verses or short poems? My heart is empty and my mind void of a single stroke of ink;
when I look at others' writings, my eyes are like eyebrows.
To speak of the entire tide and a single bubble—where is the fixed point on the scale when there is no hook? Who has ever inquired about these long-stalled old wares?
At the sheep market, they now hang the head of a dog.
Seeing off Head Seat Yin as he returns to reside at Panlong, I urge him to emerge once more:
In a dream, I ascended to Tuṣita Heaven atop Lingxiao Peak; Upon waking, Huiguang took my hand and beckoned me.
A single speck of dust from the weeds at the bottom of the well Rises upon Dragon Peak, soaring high to pierce the heavens.
Exchange one machine to answer the bubble of inquiry; even a plummet dropped into a well can be made to float.
As for the thirty-six turns of the coiling dragon’s path, you must believe that every turn has its own pivot.
Presented to a man of the sea:
the traces of the hornless antelope already hang suspended; the fine horse that chases the wind brooks no whip.
If one suddenly slips past its head and tail, another ten thousand eight thousand leagues of distance lies between.
To directly accept and take it up is not difficult; when the whole body is filled with joy, the mind finally finds rest. The conduct of a patch-robed monk is like a game;
how could there ever be treacherous barriers on level ground?
Five Poems on Fellow Practitioners at Tianmu Tianmu has fundamentally no Way to transmit;
With divine heads and ghostly faces, it is difficult to recognize them fully. The former master lacked the eye for examining practitioners;
He could only see half of the Patriarch’s nose.
Twisting and coiling around the curved railing is not Chan; the direct pointing of the single transmission is likewise in vain. An ancient was once bitten by a snake;
for twenty or thirty years he harbored doubts about the well’s rim.
In the twelfth month of the Persian calendar, one chews cold ice; cauterizing the space between the eyebrows to relieve toothache. Reflecting on this today, I realize my error from those days:
the source of illness does not lie in the scars of moxibustion.
Rotten vines and creepers fill the paths; the heterodox teachings of all quarters are increasingly difficult to support. Turn over the cauldron of hot oil and look:
does the nature of fire still exist within it now?
The lantern laughs once, its mouth murmuring; the pillar horizontally swallows Lion Rock.
Having received the third phrase of that time, I, the old monk, grant you the status of a fellow practitioner.
Ten Poems on Shuixi Yuan (with Preface).
In the year of Bingxu during the Zhizheng era, I was sixty-one years old.

My monastic and lay dharma friends, mindful that I was unaware old age was approaching, pooled their funds to purchase six or seven mu of mountain land about two li south of Huqiu, establishing [a retreat] for me.

I have made plans for my final resting place as follows: On the day of Wushen in the ninth month of autumn in this year of Dinghai, a gate shall be constructed at the edge of the water and inscribed with the name "Suixiyuan" (Water West Garden).
On the twenty-first day, Gengshen, the burial site shall be determined; it shall be excavated and lined with brick tiles.
The monk Shan’yu has personally engraved this upon stone and deposited it within the grave to record it, saying: "The Elder Founder of Shizilin."
Regarding the funerary monument of the Master: above the excavation, a large stone was placed as the foundation for a stūpa.

The Great Master of Hexi, Suanan, employed his ingenuity to design a model of the stūpa approximately one *zhang* in height. The main body of the stūpa has its entrance facing south with a hollowed-out center, wherein Amitāyus Buddha is enshrined.
The Buddha statue is one foot and six inches in height; it is carved from purple stone and colored yellow.
It was gilded with gold so that devas, humans, ghosts, and spirits might know to look up to it with reverence. On the ninth day of the eleventh month, the pagoda was completed according to the plans.
In front of it was a pavilion shaped like a boat, inscribed with the name "Mountain Boat" (Shanzhou); this was accomplished through the efforts of various friends.
I climbed Zhuofeng Peak and purchased a boat to carry me there to view it. The boat traveled west from Bantang, passing by Jin’s Yuanjue Temple.
"Ān. Furthermore, not far to the west, one passes Liaoxiang Temple; suddenly the water runs out and the boat reaches the gate.
Entering the mountains and walking several hundred paces, the path turns and bends, and from amidst ten thousand pines a pagoda emerges.
Thereupon, some walk along the pagoda, some gaze from high vantage points, some stand leaning against pine trees, some sit crouching upon rocks, and some speak while others remain silent."
Everyone formed the thought that he had already entered parinirvāṇa. Thereupon, he reflected to himself: "Birth is fundamentally without birth;

do I, then, truly have an extinction? Extinction is itself without extinction; do I, then, truly return to this state? Unconsciously, his mind turned toward the inverted [view], and words burst forth from his mouth as he spoke ten verses to record it.
Alas! Among the ancients, there were those who performed sacrifices for themselves, and those who described their own [states].

Among practitioners, there are those who inscribe their own epitaphs upon their stupas; these are all sufficient to be transmitted and recited by others, thereby leaving a transformative influence upon the world.
How could I dare hope to equal the ancients? I merely do so to admonish myself and inform myself.
The waters of the Great Trichiliocosm are the western plains; the ten billion Mount Sumerus are its burial mounds. The True Person of No Rank is buried without fixed location;
yet another pit is added to burden one’s descendants.
Karmic debts are like mountains, indestructible; when death arrives, one follows karma to undergo saṃsāra. Who among us hopes to attain Buddhahood before another?
From level ground, there suddenly arises a heap of bones.
The monkey hangs its heart and liver upon the tree; the spirits of ghosts at play are of two kinds. Before dying, it buries itself to leave a path for life;
even the eyes of dragons and tigers cannot behold it.
The immortal bows to the skeletal ghost; the whip lashes the corpse. Enmity and gratitude are difficult to forget—one must know them both together. Cherish well this skin-bag born of one’s mother:
it is my disciple, and it is my teacher.
With spade and pickaxe in hand, he follows his path without leaving a trace; he digs a cave in empty space to bury empty space.
In a single night, empty space sprouts horns and tusks, piercing through tens of millions of layers of white clouds.
Children find it amusing to watch the living corpse die; they carry it away and call out, but it does not answer.
When it does not answer, one should realize for oneself that while alive, it was originally but a false spirit.
The sky-piercing hawk falls into the Yellow Springs; the shell-shedding turtle flies up to heaven. The half-dead practitioner pays no heed at all;
he beats upon shards of tile to calculate his years.
Once I studied madness from Yanjue; now in my old age, a new kind of stupidity has been added. Madness never ceases within the sea of birth and death;
I have arranged for this madness to ascend the platform of nirvana.
The mountains appear like a formal procession, the waters like a court audience; ten thousand pines encircle the seat like a retinue of children.
As we gaze upon one another, a single thought spans ten thousand years—the patriarch’s lineage remains far from desolate.
The stupas emerging from the earth are not enough to boast of; true elegance must come from those of the authentic lineage.
Within the eyes of the skull, the spring breeze stirs, blowing the five-petaled flower open throughout the entire world.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Tiantu of Shizilin, Volume Four;
The Recorded Sayings of Master Tiantu of Shizilin, Volume Five.
Compiled by the junior disciple Shan Yu.
The monk Zong of Foshi locked the coffin (a native of Taizhou).
As the lantern ascended the wall toward Tiantai, tell me, what principle did he clarify? Master Zong died and yet lived again.
The living word revives the dead word; the adamantine barriers of the Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot hold you back.
He lets the Rear Hall Head preach the Dharma in the Tuṣita Heaven; he lets the First Seat turn his body over on the shore of Nirvāṇa; he seizes the staff from the beginner.
Beyond the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations, one further manifests amidst a mass of blazing flames.
Master Neng drags a corpse here;
its nostrils do not meet its mouth. Both subject and object are utterly extinguished; like a shrimp leaping, it cannot escape the measuring basket.
"Thrusting forth fire," he said. "Now he has leaped out. Fire burns beneath the water, incinerating the void; the entire forest lets out a lion’s roar.
Elder Dìng Bào'ēn turned his bones mid-way (he succeeded Master Gāofēng)."
Daowu moved his stupa to Shishuang. "No one knows a son better than his father. Ba’en shifted his remains back to Tianmu. "A wealthy family breeds a pampered child.
Although it is one and the same bond of affection, how can one avoid the distinct mechanisms of these two houses? He stroked the bones and said:
"Had it not been for this settling and moving, this patch-robed monk would have encountered you on a narrow path; I would not have let you pass."
The *weina* takes a firebrand and draws a circle with it, saying: "Yunfeng broke a cask stave; it was somewhat like this. He then strikes with the firebrand, saying:
"One blow and it shatters into a hundred pieces. Now tell me, what is it? The nature of fire is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true fire.
The Pure Head Seat [performs] the fire-purification of the wondrous Dharma-body. Originally, there is neither arising nor ceasing. Pointing to the funeral niche with his hand, he says:
"As for this—neither mind, nor Buddha, nor thing. It is provisionally named the 'True Person of No Rank. He is called the model for the monastic community. For kalpas..."
When a fire blazes fiercely, it cannot burn others.

The head monk (dusi) Yan was not strict regarding the family laws of the Heavenly Child; he had only two oil lamps. The administrator (zhishi) of Nanshan obtained the right person, which was truly [effective].
A lifetime of carrying a wooden board. Do you wish to see where Abbot Yan carries the board?
Upon the dead firewood, the flames glow bright red, manifesting the three eyes of Maheśvara.
"The Great Elder enters the stupa;
the entire earth is this Great Elder. The entire earth is this skull of death. The entire earth is this seamless stupa.
Now tell me, from where does the gate enter? He let out a shout.
Praising the Head Seat: "A sword hangs from his brow. This may be criticized but not praised. "He beheads the cat. This may be praised but not criticized.
Suddenly, praise and criticism proceed together; what principle is this ultimately? "The fire burns the Persian's beak in the South Sea."
The fire of Master Rui, the Chief Administrator, illuminates both heaven and earth in a single stroke. Oil leaks from the bottom of the bowl and cannot be contained; sparks fly as his eyebrows blink.
He shatters nirvana and birth-and-death alike. Holding up the torch, he asked: "Do you all see? I see the light of the lamp."
The Buddha’s original radiance and auspicious signs were like this.
When the Elder Cong passed away after taking medicinal broth (having died from food poisoning), his wisdom was eclipsed by the brilliance of his clarity.
This bitter medicine is for the patch-robed monks who suffer from ailments deep in their vital organs; it locks the throat shut so they may swallow it down.
"Not falling [into categories]. Elder Cong, you have now forgotten both the medicine and the illness;
feel free to swallow it or spit it out.
Chanter Wen, when the coffin is raised—neither relying on words nor following the conventional path—at such a time as this, what is Chanter Wen’s departure from the gate?
A sentence: it must not exist, nor must it be non-existent. It leaps across Yangqi’s three-legged donkey.
"If the dragon were in the fire, the water could not hide him. Elder Long, do you understand yet? If you do understand, try entering the Fire-Light Samādhi.
In the stone grottoes of the cloud-capped ravines, ten thousand households rise up;
if one’s bones sprout life, one shall receive a fief for meritorious service in war. If one dies, they shall be enshrined in the temple to partake of offerings, manifesting divine intelligence.

Touching the bones, he said: "Furthermore, from this very place, turn your body around; in every dust mote of the Buddha-land, there is a path that leads through. This person was invincible in valor and profound in stillness.

In strategy, he possessed both martial skill and civil wisdom, acting as a "Feng Yi" among the Green Forest rebels; in loyalty and righteousness, he always harbored the spirit of Zhou Yu at Red Cliff.
His worth was extolled by his friends, and his kindness was felt by his soldiers.

Carrying out the King’s mandate to eradicate the Yao and Zhuang tribes, he exerted himself without regard for his own life; wielding military authority, his prestige shook the barbarian frontiers, and those who heard of him were struck with awe.
His spirit ascended; the report of his victory was first transmitted to the heavens. On his journey home, he suddenly grew weary of the human world.

Before the Qingxiang Monastery, he performed a somersault and departed; from the Wu Song River, he welcomed his skeletal casket back. Heaven and earth changed countenance for him; mountains and rivers shed tears for him.
His task being accomplished, what regret could there be in death? The entire nation acclaimed him as a true man of honor.

For thirty-four years, following the teachings has been like a dream. That the family lineage has been transmitted relies upon a remarkable man; for hundreds of thousands of millions of generations, his fragrance shall flow on.
Arriving at this point, exert your spirit intensely and communicate a separate message: tear asunder the net of affliction and smash through the barrier of birth and death.
The illusory form and illusory shadows come and go, like floating clouds emerging from a valley; yet the true nature—
True illumination is neither shifting nor changing, like the bright moon suspended in the sky. This very thing is the source of one's own self; this very thing is the ancestral estate;
this very thing is the place where one establishes a dwelling and sustains life;
this very thing is the moment of becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch. This is certainly so. But tell me, as you now raise your backbone, is there any auspicious omen or not? Yesterday...
The night wind stirs the snowflakes, sweeping the road for your westward return.
Master Zhucuo closed his grave and escaped both life and death;
you must know where he lands. Once the place of landing is clear, let go from the void and cast it down. Let it go.
What follows? Heaven opens and earth parts, revealing his entire being; like a jade phoenix perching at night upon a tree that casts no shadow.

This person is the son of General Mei-zhu and the grandson of Professor Shou-zhai. Looking back to distant times, from the era of Prince Wuhui onwards, successive generations have been chronicled in the annals of history.
Looking more recently, from Lord Wen-gong downward, there has not been a single commoner among his kin. All people admire this grandeur.
Ah! The Duke did not consider this an honor. When he was briefly appointed to a teaching post at a school, he grew weary of the cold autumn maples of Wujiang and shook his sleeves to return home.
Later, when summoned by a provincial decree to inherit a position, he cherished the bamboo groves by the steaming creek and shook his head, refusing to rise.

By nature he was indifferent to wealth and status; though wealthy and noble, he was not corrupted by them. He had no intention of seeking fame or office, yet fame and office came to him of their own accord. With weapons in his left hand and sacrificial vessels in his right...
Dòu has certainly not forgotten the family reputation of the Cáo clan. In the morning he indulges in poetry and wine; in the evening, he attends to the lute and books.

He aspires to emulate the refined demeanor of the people of the Jin dynasty. He once cut flesh from his own thigh to blend with the soup in order to cure his grandfather’s illness, and he once removed his own clothes and gave away his food to provide for the needs of impoverished scholars.
In treating his friends, he was earnest and encouraging; in treating his kinsmen and neighbors, he was磊 (liěi)—[upright and generous].
Majestic and towering, the sons of the Confucian academies look up to him as a great master of literature; the officials of the Jixian Academy style him as a "Pure and Recluse.
Throughout his life, all matters were already complete; at the final moment, his single mechanism was even more sublime.

From the crown of his head, he reveals the adamantine eye; in every stroke, he encounters the pivot of the ancients; from the tip of his brush, the precious treasury of the *Lotus Sūtra* manifests; in every instance, he is fully realized.
Revealing the precious treasures of one’s own house, there is no obstruction whatsoever in words or language; nirvana and birth-and-death do not hinder one another.
Previously, it was only said: "Come forth! Come forth! Come forth quickly! Alas for the burning house of the three realms!

Only upon reaching this point does one know: "Go back! Go back! It is good to go back. This is the very assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Since it is called "knowing the way back," how could it be otherwise?
Yet there is something that cannot be carried away. Since it cannot be carried away, it ought to be concealed. Now, if it is said to be concealed, what evidence is there? [He] scatters soil and says:
"The illusory city and the treasure land are without distinction; every inch of earth has always been an inch of gold."
In self-praise,
the junior master Shan-yu invited Hui-li to first consult with the Elder Hai-yin.
He remarked, "I have learned how to face south and look at the Big Dipper," and upon arriving at Tianmu, he beheld the illusion.
The old man laughs, splitting the mouth of his lantern in half. For thirty years he has hung his alms-bag high;
looking down upon ten thousand peaks as mere hillocks, he refuses to be dragged about by others in all directions. He does not even teach people to follow after him.
Now his true face is revealed in full majesty—try asking the people here if it resembles anything else. When thunder rolls and wind flies, one sees it intimately; throughout the entire forest...
He let out a lion’s roar. Since this teaching has already spread, why wait another thirty years?

He invites the parched seeds and withered grass of those who claim to be "unsurpassed men," and the poisonous roots and sprouts of those who would not even want to be Buddhas. They revile the Buddhas and Patriarchs as if they were hateful enemies and thieves.
Do not dwell in monasteries either; avoid them as you would avoid taxes and corvée labor. When you see others practicing the Way, you can only coldly laugh at them.
Receiving offerings from others, you cannot say they are difficult to digest. Now your portraits and likenesses are painted, and everyone everywhere recognizes you.

Hereafter, with the cangue upon your shoulders and chains upon your feet, who will be willing to show you mercy? Since you know there is guilt, you have no choice but to comply with the regulations. Prepare yourself in advance.
The oral confession has been completed; one must now prepare for the summons of King Yama.

Great clumsiness: Elder Neng once challenged Linji with a shout until his mouth was nearly torn apart; Deshan’s staff left his hands aching. Striking the grass to startle the snake—this is great skill and great clumsiness.
To take a tortoise for a turtle is both extremely easy and extremely difficult. For those beneath the Lion’s Grove, there is not a single such thing;
they have swallowed all the Buddhas of the three periods of time in one gulp, their two eyes shining so brightly that people’s livers and gallbladders turn cold with awe.
The attendant of Jiangxi requested:
"A single draught from the Western River leaves not a drop behind; Tiantu stepped over it and left no trace. He sits fully established, cutting off the Lion’s Grove;
whether demons come or Buddhas come, none can fathom him. He cannot be sketched, he cannot be painted; when his great function manifests, there is no track."
Thus it is said: "If one says this is the Tathāgata, there is an extra eye atop his head.
Standing tall like a peak, the Secretary invites [him] to the Bodhi Aranya tree.
This tree is the king of trees; I come to sit beneath it, and because of this tree, the site of enlightenment is formed."
In winter one seeks warmth; in summer one seeks coolness. Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-dharma are not what he excels in. His nostrils reach toward the heavens with a sense of touch;
every branch and every leaf is sandalwood fragrance.
The fellow practitioner Suizhiyi requested that wood be used for a jeweled canopy and stone for a seat, so as to occupy the void alone and establish a Dharma hall.
The intimate verses transmitted from his ancestors’ house have never been leaked to other quarters.
When Zhuanzi asked about "pervading with one," Dongbai (his sobriquet) replied, "It is Tianru.
This was an error from the start; to say it is not Tianru would be difficult to defend. Turn your head and look within the Great Perfect Mirror;
within the radiance of the myriad phenomena, the whole body is revealed. Someone asked about "pervading with one," and then asked, "Where does the one return?"
Where? It was said: "When the east has turned white, the golden rooster flies up onto the coral tree.
A certain disciple requested:
"The fly-whisk is for beating flies; the staff is for beating dogs. Take not a single step before others; utter not a single word."
Following after others, who would be of the same wind as the correct edict that Bai Zhang has not yet put into practice?

Who could possibly open their mouth to manifest the complete mechanism that Bodhidharma has not yet revealed? This fellow knows it well enough; do you all understand? The mountains, rivers, and great earth are the body of the Dharma King;
the grasses, trees, and forests are the lion’s roar.
The practitioner of the third dhyāna invites you to come and eat a fall before Lion Cliff;
sitting like a fool within the city of Gusu, he has completely forgotten the transformation of wisdom throughout his entire being;
yet when touched by ignorance, his roar is like thunder.
I do not engage in the tangled vines of various quarters; I do not hang my name upon the Lamp of Transmission.
Upon the stone bench beneath the Bodhi tree sits this old monk with white hair and a weathered face.
Resembling heaven or not resembling heaven—it is the same. Whether resembling it or not, there is no intimacy or distance. The nostrils have their apertures; the eyes have their pupils.
Whether as a Buddha or as a demon, it is all this very one.
The Master of the True Lecture at Mount Shōkai in Saikawa expounds the sutras with a mouth like a cascading river;
his responses are as swift as flashing lightning. While all other quarters possess their own achievements, this man alone lacks spiritual transformations.
Tall pines lie prostrate, their emerald foliage draping the clouds; strange rocks slope and rise, their azure surfaces drenched in mist. He idly picks up—
The whisk rests like a mountain; from the tips of its billion hairs, lions appear.
When the layman Fan Jingxin invited Zhaozhou to investigate the "Old Lady of Mount Tai," where there was no confusion, there was confusion. Yuanwu roused and inspired the Layman of Fan County.
"O Master, where there are few words, there are many paths. A pure mind paints me and makes offerings to me. Now tell me, what is the essential meaning of Zhaozhou and Yuanwu?
If you can utter a single turning word here, I will grant you permission to burn incense and make offerings to them."
The Layman Su invited Laozi to stay for his entire life;
facing neither front nor back, whether acting against the grain or with it, all were skillful means.
Returning from begging in a village of three households, he opened a tavern at the crossroads. Whether he was a sage or an ordinary man, no one could tell.
The lay practitioner Cai Guoxiang of Southern Quanzhou requests that the Blind Donkey lead the herd out from Luling.
Deeply poisoned at the summit of Mount Tianmu, he extinguishes the True Dharma Eye of Linji and transforms the ancient forest grove of Baizhang.
From the mouth of a toad, a full moon is spat forth; upon the mane of a lion, ten thousand [hairs] grow.
Two pieces of gold. This matter cannot be concealed even now. In the Buddha-land of Quannan (Fujian), there are those who understand.

At the request of the Venerable Master Zhuang of Yunnan—[whose image is between the forest huts]—whether in bustling markets or mountain forests, from people of different regions, [he gathers them all].
A quiet nook for warming pots and boiling pans; though doors are blocked and gates are filled, they are all here.
The honored guest asks about Mazu within the Plum Pavilion, examining and testing his disciples; he points to Zhaozhou within the Cypress Hall, spreading out his mat for all.
The Old Barbarian (Bodhidharma) was full of spirit as he sat grandly in the Snow Hall, yet that simpleton lacked any sharp wit.
He dwelt in peace within the Cloud Chamber, never having a single dharma to give to others, nor did he himself wish to become a Buddha—only to support those who seek the Ultimate.
The Dharma-vehicle relies upon many masters of learning; why, without cause, do you again manifest a body outside of your own? How can two masters dwell together?
Send him to a place where there is no Buddha for him to honor, and present him with a whisk made of tortoise hair.
The Elder Gudo of the Kingdom of Goryeo (named Da-haeng) requested [this teaching]:

"Han Pak-mung has no understanding; wherever he goes, he never accepts defeat. In his entire life, he has harbored a singular resentment toward Old Chung-bong, who forced me to bow my head and pay three prostrations.
When I struck him, he brandished his ignorance right at my face. This is the family tradition of the 'Tiger-Trapping' device."
It remains as it was. For thirty years he has gazed at the Milky Way; the golden ore refuses to mingle with the sand for sale.
Now, sitting within the city of Helu, he turns his Zen sackcloth inside out from top to bottom. To whoever comes from the south or the north, he asks them to repay their karmic debt of Chan.
What need is there to speak of "that which not even a thousand sages have transmitted"? What need is there to speak of "the lacquer bucket being too slow"? He stands forth grandly.
The great way has been traveled by many; tell those in all quarters to cease their fabrications and oddities.
At the head seat of Linji Temple, someone asked, "What is the Buddha?
To which he replied, "A brush stuck in one's hair. From antiquity until now, there have been seventeen hundred such kōans. Now...
Once again, I add one more point. This one point is precisely the mark; it gathers from all eight directions, and the myriad functions of the mind naturally cease.
Seizing the person and seizing the environment, his shout is like thunder. Even Linji was not a "white-handed thief."
The Elder Wudie of Gaochang Country invited [Master] Shengdang to be born in Luling;
he did not know the price of rice. Starving, he hung his heart and liver upon the tree-tops. Ascending Mount Tianmu, sweat flowed from his entire body;
the stinking falcon-hunter’s robe was completely cast off. At the shore of Lehe Beach, he dipped his brush-point; the ocean of meaning was swept empty and still.
A word! In the forest of lions, he opens his Zen hut. Summoning the seven Buddhas, they enter retreat together.

He does not regard the various quarters with the "right eye. Let the various quarters do as they please—quarreling and reviling him. By having nothing to contend with, he makes it his banner of victory;
this is what is called being "unconquerable under heaven."

The Venerable Qin of Zhenzhou invited a board-carrying fellow who lacked discernment; he was neither conversant with the tradition of the ancient Buddhas nor had he resolved the public cases of the former masters.
Discarding the turnip-head of Zhenzhou and collecting the axle-puncher of the Qin era, one relies solely on a single partiality and refuses further examination.
To praise such a person as a "clever monk" leaves one half-inclined toward doubt; to revile them as a "blunt Chan practitioner" likewise leaves one half-inclined toward doubt.
Is it difficult to discern? One clearly knows that one’s own nature is originally true; names and designations are merely what people call out.
To suddenly call it a "three-legged donkey" is nothing but a chaotic fabrication.

Praise for the Buddha’s Departure from the Mountains, His Entry into the Mountains, and His Departure Again: Having long remained in stillness, he again contemplates movement; though sentient beings have attained the Way for many ages, the Buddha-Dharma remains but a single hair’s breadth [of its full potential].
Useless. A-he-he. Now, reflecting with a cold heart, one sees that six years of hunger and cold were endured in vain.

The fish-basket of Guanyin is empty, for the scaled fish have all been sold and the hands are light. Yet, as she gathers from the rivers and lakes, she still possesses a compassionate heart. Turning her head toward Changsha, she stands upon the shore.
On the road, a rancid wind blows like the sound of the night tide.
Sitting alone, the Avalokiteśvara, the parrot, and the pure water jar have no place to stay; Sudhana and the Dragon Girl do not follow. Vast and silent, sitting alone, one is as free as space.
I am indeed at this very moment when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted;
when the Dharma came from the West, it vanished into the marketplace. Crossing water, one again encounters a sheep; pointing directly is but a minor expedient—excising flesh only to treat a wound.
In response to Emperor Wu of Liang’s “The vast void has no sages,” he added more moxa cones upon the scars of his previous burns.
To Xuguang, he said, “You have obtained my marrow”; yet behind the funeral carriage, he hung his medicinal pouch high. Everyone says that Mount Xionger was unable to bury him;
who knew that this old fellow could not forget his native ties? Fortunately, there were later generations to compete for his reputation and ensure that the family’s disgrace was not made public.
The treasury of the True Dharma Eye has been extinguished; let the mountains be high and the waters long.
In the midst of the lion’s den, within the Hall of Standing in the Snow—even a Buddha does not attach himself to it—so why do you?
I do not value your nine years of facing the wall, nor do I value your ten thousand miles from the West; I only value your straightforward mind and straightforward speech. Do not...

Accordant with the sentiments of the Emperor, his vision was lofty and his spirit was high; he did not lose the essence of a patriarchal master. He sat and cut off the tongues of all people under heaven.
With one flower and five petals, the fragrant breeze arose.
The Master of the Cloth Bag (with one leg tucked in) drags his staff horizontally;
the cloth sack leans askew. When he descends in a future birth, everyone will say it is you. At the crossroads, he waits for a person;
his outstretched foot has always been within his tucked-in foot.
Hanshan (Holding a broom while looking at a scroll):
The more you sweep, the more there is to sweep; you must let it go. Unfurling and rolling up by yourself, look closely at the teachings. Your entire being is this teacherless wisdom;
it is not like those who forget their brooms while reciting the *Bimbara Sūtra*.
Shide (Carrying the vegetable basket to gather scraps):
Gathering them as they appear, using them as they appear. Within, it is empty, yet truly not empty. It is originally the inexhaustible treasury of the Wish-Fulfilling King;
toward people, he speaks only of the vegetable scrap basket.
Hanshan and Shide once shared a single axle with Fenggan, sleeping on their pillows beside tigers; they also faced Zhaozhou as he practiced the "ox-fight.
To call them Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra is to knit one’s eyebrows in dismay beneath the monk’s hood.
Where the morning sun breaks through, the teaching is perfected; the work is accomplished in a single moment. As the red sun rises three poles high, I shall open a single thread for you.
Facing the moon...
One must realize the final word; its strokes are most distinct. Do not, because of the moon in the sky, lose both your eyes.

With ghosts supporting him as he crosses the sea, the Arhat’s shoulders and back brush against the single reed raft. One who contemplates the ocean finds it difficult to regard it as mere water. When the Dragon Kings compete in wealth, I compete with them.
The poor man, without spending a single coin, was able to command ghosts.

Zengyou painted the face of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) with an eagle’s nest upon it; though the manifestations were a thousandfold, no painting could match them. The masters of recent times have favored Yan’s style.
As for form, it is like Emperor Liang’s summons of Gu Kaizhi;

Chan Master Ying’an employs the mechanism of seizing food from the tiger’s mouth, acting at will with the five rebellious acts, and using the hand that rubs an itch on a snake’s head to provoke and strike.
In all directions, before the surging peaks of the sea, the clash of arms has ceased; atop the Golden Wheel Peak, monsters and spirits remain hidden.
Gazing upon the Gate of Amṛta in Abhirati, the two powers do not descend; transmitting the orthodox Dharma lineage of Yangqi, its prosperity shall flourish for five generations.
Rain-soaked peach blossoms in the spring wind are blown forth as the fragrance of the udumbara flower, pervading the entire world.
Master Gaofeng has golden eyes and a face of cast iron; his three-foot bamboo whisk is like a flash of lightning. He sits and cuts off Gaofeng, standing at the Gate of Death.
Everyone says he has no expedient means. Yet there is an expedient means: a thousand hearings are not equal to one seeing.
This old fellow, Master Zhongfeng, has no precedent. He champions the Dharma-gate of Great Illusion and extinguishes ready-made koans.

He allows not even a hair’s breadth of conjecture regarding the meaning of the Patriarchs or the meaning of the Teachings. Whether dwelling among mountains or by waters, he does not permit anyone to approach his influence; thus he remains utterly detached.
When he spoke his words and delivered his discourses, they resounded like the thunderclaps of a bright day. Abiding in the station that has no station, he was uniquely honored;
dragons and elephants from all quarters ran to him.

Having encountered the sagely Son of Heaven, he was titled National Preceptor Puying (Universally Responding), leading all people across the land to offer incense and make offerings wherever they went.
On the first day of the first month, Master Duanya’s single stroke shattered the vast celestial net; his final move overturned the moon-bearing boat.
The mountains and rivers of the great earth melted away like snow, while at the summit of Mount Tianmu in the Western Land, the waves surged to the heavens.
Tiantai Master Zhizhe (In Response to the Request for Unimpeded Discourse):

Yao had the eyebrows and Shun the eyes; Yu had the back and Tang the shoulders. He spoke of the inherent nature within the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses—where water is waves and waves are water.

He manifested the permanence of phenomena within the single mind and the three contemplations—where the fist becomes the palm and the palm becomes the fist, demonstrating that sages and worthies are one and the same.
As for the body of its essence, it is not hindered by description; the unimpeded eloquence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs may likewise proclaim it.
Yet, were one to speak of personally witnessing that single assembly on Vulture Peak as solemnly remaining undispersed, I would have no words with which to praise it.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Rulin Tianru,
Compiled by His Junior Disciple Shanyu.
Poems.
The Lazy Cloud’s Nest is truly extraordinary! O Cloud, your transformations are unfathomable and your vast expanse cannot be bound. In stillness you seem indolent; in motion you are not indolent.
This movement and stillness seem as if governed by a divine spirit. I observe you, the reclining cloud, amidst the three thousand nine hundred fathoms.
Beholding Tianmu, the eastern and western regions of Zhejiang appear as one vast expanse of white like the sea, its boundaries and origins indiscernible.

Furthermore, observing the drifting clouds atop the forty-eight thousand *zhang* high Mount Tiantai, they rise with a momentum that seems to roll up the ocean; they surge like ten thousand horses racing in competition.
Gathering and dispersing across mountain peaks and riverbanks, wandering immortals and soaring phoenixes present a myriad of wonders and marvels. At that moment—
When unrolled, it moves; though heaven and earth serve as its dwelling, the space remains narrow. Yet when it is rolled up and stored away, even Li Lou cannot discern a single hair or thread.
The young master Xiyang has constructed a "Cloud Nest" (*Yunwo*), inscribing the two characters "Languan" (Lazy Clouds) upon its lintel.

With eyes that look down upon the lakes and seas, he reclines amidst hills and ravines; practicing idleness, he intends to make an appointment with the clouds. I visited the host of Lazy Clouds and observed his state of indolence.
Cloud Poem: I do not know whether Xi-yang is the Lazy Cloud, or whether the Lazy Cloud is Xi-yang.
I only perceive the autumn sun piercing through the windows and doors, casting a shimmering radiance across the four walls. Once again I address him: "O Xi, O Cloud!

The Perfected Man does not cling to outward traces, yet he is able to move in harmony with all things. When wind and thunder roar through the hundred valleys, and dragons dance upon the great lake, he too shall—"
Riding upon its momentum to respond to the needs of the time—whether rolling up or unfolding, moving or still—I respond with a mind free of intention.
Whether it be indolence or the absence thereof, what do I know? *Bilu* (Reed-Oboe) Introductory Melody.
Xi-yang’s Lan-yun-wo (Lazy Cloud Nest) is about half a li from my meditation chamber. We frequently visit one another, and he plays the pi-li (oboe) as an offering.
Furthermore, he requested something from me; thus, I have composed this long song to present to him.
Xi-yang blew the pi-li for me, awakening my ten years of dreams and memories. Under the moonlight at Qiantang, atop Fenghuang Mountain, I once heard San-zhai blow his iron flute.
When he first played a single melody, the river wind arose; its lingering echoes entered the trees with autumnal lamentation.
When he played a second melody, the river tides were startled; sorrowful clouds suddenly lowered as the frosty moon turned black. Those among us who listened...
Six or seven people—half of them travelers from the rivers and lakes who have not yet returned home. Those who were joyful sang wildly as they walked around the trees;
those who were sorrowful hung their heads, their tears soaking their knees. At that time, I snatched away Suān-zhāi’s flute and, folding my robes, sat together upon the stone at the foot of a pine.
Casting aside both joy and sorrow, all myriad thoughts dissolved. I realized that sound has no inherent nature and hearing leaves no trace. "Xī-yīng, do not blow your pí-lì flute for now. Pí...

The flute has been called "the sorrowful reed" since ancient times; its sounds of grief and joy fill the vastness of heaven and earth. Human sentiment is moved by it across all ages, past and present.
Even this mountain monk relies on his stubborn pair of ears to request that you, Xiying, pour forth your innermost thoughts. When sound and hearing strike one another, deluded emotions arise;

when hearing is exhausted and sound vanishes, emotion is naturally released. Do not say that hearing is extinguished when there is no sound; when the mechanism moves, the pipes resound. There is no... [end of fragment].

The intervals between sounds—do not say that sound is absent when it has ceased. Coming and going are clearly manifest as both clamor and stillness. As for the subtlety of the one who blows, I know it not;
as for the awakening of the one who hears, you cannot fathom it. You return to your quiet sitting in the Lazy Cloud Nest;
with a mind empty, there is naturally its own true news.
Regarding Bu-zhi’s plum blossoms, everyone says that Bu-zhi painted them. In his depiction of thousands upon thousands of plum trees in the imperial gardens, he scatters heaps of jade-white snow;

their celestial fragrance and national splendor manifest the richness of their inherent nature, unlike those sparse branches and cold buds withered by the miasmic fogs and mirages of the barbarian lands.
Rained down upon, it crumbled into ruin. Once painted, it was offered to the abode of the immortals; those who sought it found gold as cheap as soil.
Where did the old mountain man Zhongqian obtain these two trunks? They illuminate the woods and ravines, and those who see them call out to one another in amazement.
One is like the solitary tree at Shanxiang in the waters of Mount Luofu, with countless branches and countless blossoms. The other is like the ten-foot-tall tree of Chengdu.

The recumbent dragon lies coiled; its body is hidden by heavy clouds while its tail-tip is revealed. Its jade-like scales shimmer brightly from beneath the water, where mandarin ducks on the surface carry fallen blossoms.
Above them fly a pair of white egrets, appearing as if they were a snowy slope under a clear night sky.
At times, the Mountain Hermit sits amidst the plum trees, shaking his fly-whisk. The cold sunlight’s clear radiance strikes the window and walls;
suddenly, a celestial being appears to come for the Dharma, while fresh plum blossoms fall in profusion across the grove.

Only then do I realize that Lü Buzhi was able to capture the true likeness of the plum, and the plum flower, in turn, transmitted the spirit of the Hermit. Yet the Hermit is even more ethereally pure than the plum flower—his gaze pierces through all.
"Corals and Moons.

Regarding "Sudō’s Bamboo," everyone says that Sudō painted bamboo. His "Bamboo of the Hanlin Academy" consists of thousands and tens of thousands of stalks, their *langgan* joints unbound. [The bamboo of] Wei...
The "Guanyu" River emerges from a vast and boundless breast; it is not like those who treat every inch of land as gold, forbidding even a speck of moss to grow green before their steps.
This vigorous brush in his later years is truly pitiable—though there may be one or two in the world that are not true transmissions, where did the mountain elder Zhongqian obtain these four scrolls?
Their excellence surpasses that of Yuke, such that I dare not boast of being ahead by a horse-length. As for the rain, it is accompanied by mist.

Misty and empty, the lush greenery seems as if it could drip; it is like beholding the mountain colors from across West Lake. The snow forms heaps of salt and piles of jade, its weight like a collapsing mountain;
though its stiff neck briefly lowers, its waist remains unbent. The wind blows, causing the phoenix-tail branches to sway; one can almost hear their rustling sound by one’s ear.
In the clear weather, they are sparse and pure as if washed clean, standing tall and upright, piercing the clouds and the sky.
At times, the Mountain Hermit sits amidst the bamboos, observing the young and old shoots as they grow; their formation is not a matter of haste.

As the offspring stand in a circle, offering pure joy, every movement—bending, looking up or down, turning, or circling—is exactly like them. Only then do I realize that Dongpo was able to create this "Portrait of the Gentleman" (Cijun tu);
this Gentleman is indeed the peer of the Hermit. I see that within the grove there is the vitality of my Way, appearing all at once before my eyes.
How could one do without this?
Presented to Mr. Xuegu Wei of Songjiang, who was carrying ink into the capital.
For generations his family has practiced the Confucian profession, while he himself has been exceptionally skilled in the manufacture of ink. People say that Xuegu has mastered [the craft].
His transmission was especially refined. I once sought to verify his ink and found it to be truly as people say—unerring.
Therefore, I have composed this short song to praise him, for I believe he must have attained great mastery in the art of ink-making.

I have heard that ink made by Li Chao is not easily obtained; when the Son of Heaven of the Jianlong era gathered it in heaps like hills and mounds, the monasteries of Bianjing used it for lacquer, and once the storehouses were swept clean, it was difficult to recover again.
I have also heard that the ink of Pan Gu was like jade scepters and ceremonial vessels;
the palace ladies of Penglai played with it without ceasing. Yet when a great wind swept the earth into the desert sands, over the long years the objects transformed and vanished.

He was able to preserve the tradition; as a scholar of antiquity, he mastered the ancient methods. Beyond Pan Yue and Li Daoyuan, there was no one his equal. He taught his students within crimson curtains, while his own lofty library remained closed.
Seated in his smoke-filled chamber, he wore a dark robe and fur cloak. Under the cool moon of a deep night, the glue for his ink cakes ripened.

When the emerald cakes were infused with musk, dragon-patterns floated upon them. Upon the "horse-liver" stone, they exhaled clouds and mist; a single drop falling onto paper seemed to flow with light. [The Emperor summoned him to] the Jade Hall.
The masters who wield the brush rely on you for immortality;
those waiting at the Golden Gate for their tribute rely on you as well to enjoy a grand journey. The people of this world know how to appreciate beauty but not its value;
there will surely come one who knows how to provide a fitting recompense. If the Creator indeed provides such recompense, who would then envy the "Mysterious Fragrance"?—the Pine of the Governor.
Zihou. Sent by Venerable Yuewei as he returns to his hometown, these two letters—one to mourn my Master and one to visit my mother.
The bell tolls at South Mountain; the sun rises over West Lake. The traveler calls out to the boatman, urging him to write; the letter is completed, filling the page.
Like a crow smeared with soot approaching the sun; weeping for my teacher, both eyes have grown dry. A single movement of the heart is difficult to sustain for even a moment.
My soul follows the road in dreams; will you be able to come in the fifth or sixth month?

The sea breeze blows through the clouds as the heavens and the ocean turn half crimson; beyond the shore, a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks emerge. The tide-head reaches all the way to the city of Fuyang;
in but a moment, it carries me up to the Yantan rapids. Once the time has passed, do not seek out Chen the Straw Sandal-maker;
I am but a traveler from the Three Wu regions who has yet to return home.

My old home is to the north of West Village; leaning against the gate, my white hair grows day and night. My former estate is to the west of West Village; beneath the high hall in the night rain lies my ancestral spirit.
When you come to seek me, do not be in too great a hurry; a single word from the ends of the earth is truly difficult to obtain. When you come again, do not be in too great a hurry;
a single word from the ends of the earth is truly difficult to obtain.
Presented to the Venerable Daolin Xun:
A Horned Hawk. Its gaze reaches beyond the heavens; its wingspan and talons are not for mere satiation. When a fine steed shakes its mane, there is no wilderness too vast for it to traverse.
Yet, how can one expect constant rest while tethered in the inner stable? The heart and gall of a man of spirit fill the heavens.

The earth causes the body and the worldly path to rise and fall; how much more so when one departs from the world to pursue lofty aspirations? How could the weeds and brambles suffice for boasting of soaring flight?
I pity that the ancient Way is filled with thorns, and that at year’s end, foxes and hares scramble and leap about.

This year, by the banks of the Gu River, I came to know you; I admire your noble spirit, which rises like a soaring falcon. I pray that you do not become like me, who have learned to walk only to stumble.

I pray that you do not be like me; employing my own clumsiness, I am content with the six repositories. Deeply dwelling in a thatched hut, there are no horses for the Master to inquire about the plum blossoms.

With wooden leaves covering my knees, I still have Lan Zan who knows Nanyang. Beyond the nine peaks, the heavens are vast and boundless; the cold plum is about to flower, yet spring remains within the frost.
When inspiration strikes, I shake out my sleeves and bid farewell to the hills and valleys; casting a wide gaze across the four seas, they are all my hometown.
I have a song of untethered liberation; like striking a clay jar, it lacks the notes of Gong and Shang. Upon the banks of the Wu Song River, I sing for you:
with a single surge, the tide rages, rolling up the snow-white waves as the heavenly winds grow wild.
Watching the Lock at Wusong Jiang:

The waters of the Wusong River rush as swiftly as arrows. Having once seen them in paintings, I now recognize them face-to-face. The hundred streams respond to their mandate, vying with one another to hasten forward;
they pour eastward toward the Sea Gate as if rushing to battle. The ocean waves rise in fury, driving the tide-heads back, and thus the waters of Wusong are repelled.
The tide flows backward; twice a day the river and the tide clash. For ten thousand ages they remain unresolved, like sworn enemies.

The river water is clear, while the tidal water is turbid; the river water is not as foul as the tidal water. The wicked tide pushes out the islands from the sea, piling them up upon the river’s surface to form hills.
The officials fear the calamity of the waters and find it difficult to dredge; thus, four floodgates were constructed across the river at once. When the tide comes...
The lower sluice gate opens when the tide is level; within the gate, the tide cannot flow back and forth. When the surging waves have subsided, they sweep along the bottom;
at the gate, the river's waves appear once more in fury. Above the gate, ten thousand eddies divide; below the gate, ten thousand galloping waves rush on.

Ten thousand thunders roar and ten thousand drums resound; stones roll and sand flies amidst a chaos of spears and armor. The Yellow River breaks through the roots of Mount Hua; mighty waterfalls split open the Jade Green Gorges.
People say the nature of water is perilous and fierce, yet they do not realize that water and human emotion are the same.
The surging tides and turbulent waves are angry and resentful—not because of the river's ebb and flow, but because of the square inch of the heart. The dangers of water may still be...
Avoiding the dangers of men is ultimately difficult to know; men vie with one another incessantly, day and night. Even the waters vie, yet they still have their tides and periods of calm.
[This was written] as a gift to Master Louban-yun; Master Lou named his dwelling "Half-Cloud. People say the room and the clouds are divided equally. I know that Master Lou is not as [wise] as...
This "room" is merely a metaphor for the half-cloud. The room of the half-cloud is like the great void; I and the myriad things dwell together therein.
The half-cloud is the thing, and the half-cloud is the self; as the thing-self-half-cloud, there is nothing that is not possible. This is because of the stillness of the self.
Responding to the movements of phenomena, I grasp their essential substance; when things are fully provided for my use, I am then wandering together with the True Sovereign (Zhenzai).

I do not pursue worldly trends as transient vanities. Try going to observe the song-platforms and dance-pavilions; they are no different from the Mysterious Garden (Xuānpǔ) or the Azure Isles (Cāngzhōu).
If one were to abandon this and seek to enter the "Half-Cloud" chamber, Half-Cloud would simply shake his head in disapproval.

South of the city, atop the tower, the flowers on the treetops sway in the breeze under a clear sky. Beneath the trees south of the city, fishing boats glide along. Beyond the stream, several bamboo-roofed houses serve wine;
at the low fences, the path turns as people pass to and fro. The immortal mountains and stone caves lie before one’s eyes; the reflection of the pagoda’s pole falls upon the azure waters.
Waves brighten; we wait for the crossing, yet the day has grown late. Sitting here, I watch the blue smoke rise from the plains.
Three Poems on Seeing Gan Maoshu Depart for the Capital:
Do not envy the heavenly steed’s colt, for even it once drew a salt cart with its sweat-drenched blood. Do not mock the fish in the parched ruts; the sea... [is vast].

Instead, you dwell with the *jiao* and dragons; the rise and fall of a man depends on the great destiny of the age. Why must it necessarily be like the melon patch at the East Gate or the thatched cottage at Nanyang?
To the east of your family’s Taibai Mountain, painted beams shroud in misty spring rain.

You traveled up the Huai and Fei rivers and across the Five Ridges, where the Ghost Gate and Bronze Pillars brought sorrow as your journey reached its end. Returning to the six or seven prefectures of Jiangnan, leaning upon your staff...
His sword lies fallen among the ranks of eminent men; he spent his youth reading books on the banks of the Wen River. Having built a thatched cottage by the Gan Water, he has known many autumn winds.

His father’s bones are not yet buried, and his mother grows old; clad in simple cloth, covered in dust, he is like any other traveler. Ah, the times! Oh, the times! Could it be that you, my son, shall never find your destiny?
You are also skilled in the scripts of the Yellow River and Luo River; with a single stroke, you know the fullness and emptiness of the myriad phenomena.

You are also skilled at long-form songs; your power surpasses Li He and outshines Su Dongpo. At dawn, you swallow the qi of the rosy clouds and gulp down the *hangji*; at night, you sit beneath the Big Dipper and gaze upon the Milky Way.

A thousand pieces of gold fall into one’s hands, yet one plays with pebbles; ten thousand words issue from the mouth, yet they turn into spring ripples. A single lifetime of intoxication lasts for three days;

the immortal disciples and the lineage of the seed doubt that he was once known to them. How many times in dreams did he encounter Zhonglian and Gongjin racing side by side, their iron steeds following the imperial procession?
The chessboard of Lanke and the ink of Lü Dongbin—when these masters of art meet, they are both struck with awe. Forest upon forest.
Alas! Will you truly never employ me?
It is not that I do not wish to see you off on your journey; it is that I cherish your brush and inkstone, which have occupied my entire life. It is not that I do not wish for you to remain;

a man at forty should be in the prime of his career. At this flourishing time, the world shares a single system of writing and measurement, and the robes of office fill the markets of the ten thousand nations.
I pray you gallop your horse at the head of Mount Yan; with a single word that moves the world, you shall be enfeoffed as a marquis. The wind-blown leaves whistle; the river waves flow on and on.
A man of honor travels ten thousand li, and even further; drinking a hundred doubs at once, he empties his parting sorrows.
Go! Go! Are you not indeed a man of honor?
Two Poems Written While Wandering on the Terrace of the Three Prime Ministers, Shown to My Friends Gan and Yang.
This terrace was where Yao Chong, Niu Sengru, and Liu Hang studied.
I ascend the Terrace of the Three Prime Ministers and gaze south toward the twin peaks of Xunfeng. Looking down upon the world below, it is as if I am soaring through the void. The Founding Elder...
The trees stand a hundred *zhang* tall; on the precipitous cliffs, one calls out all day against the whirling winds. Gan Lang climbs for fruit like a monkey hanging from a branch;
Yangzi rests his head upon a stone amidst flying springs. With hanging vines far from the ground, I sit securely; baring my shoulders and barefoot, I let out a long cry as if riding a dragon.
Alas! Those ancients can never be found again; how many autumns have the earth-mosses grown upon the terrace? The former self does not wait for the latter self.
How could white clouds know the guest in his moss-robe? How might Yan Hui of recent times come here to paint me upon this rock amidst the startling winds and thunder?

I have heard that at the place where Master Chu once studied, he severed the roots of the clouds with his own hands to plant jade trees; there, the golden fish and the five-horse carriage followed him as he flew.

Smoke. The morning markets have changed many times, yet the trees remain as they were. Is it not the case today that some watch long candlestands while vomiting blood, while others spend their gold ascending to the high roads?
Before one has even stabilized their station, gray hairs have already grown. Who would believe that that which possesses feeling cannot endure for long?
For you, I shall plait the jade flowers; I shall sing long songs around the tree as the white sun slants. For you, I shall inscribe upon the jade leaves, staining them amidst the wilderness.
The ruins and old scenes of the past—may you hear this and have your mind’s eye opened. Once youth has departed, it never returns.
I present this song to the Go-player Gao Xianqing:
"I shall sing for Xianqing; Xianqing departs, and what can I do? The mountains of Shang cannot summon him back, nor can the Elephant..."
Mountains cannot be cast; in this age, one such as you is likewise difficult to encounter. There is no need for discussions of killing or saving, nor of military encirclements.
I observe the divine mechanism through your countenance and expression. An autumn hawk loses its rabbit as the brush and weeds stir; paths are cut off by night snows and travelers are few.

The cinnabar returns to the golden cauldron where dragon and tiger meet; across the sea kingdom, a lone sail breaks through the waves back home. At the Grand Beginning, a single blackness stirs within the depths.
Ten thousand transformations clash in white, surging up from the void; when has there ever been a single path without birth and death?
Among the bustling spectators, few understand this. I have Lords Liu and Gan—mad and yet magnificent. Before the game even begins, their talent and spirit are already lofty.

Once they unfurl their strategic mastery, they test the hands of national masters; when they overturn the chessboard, what remains of it? They have come from the West to visit the ancient Kunlun heights, plucking...
The sword dances through the night, summoning the azure dragon; ascending the White Crane Peak, he inquires of Mount Wangwu. With boundless freedom, he sings the long melody of the purple fungi.
Alas, Master Xianqing! When shall I hear such a song? Together we shall laugh at how many broken pieces remain in this world.
I send these verses to see off Mr. Liang Shouchuan as he departs for his post as Medical Instructor in Nankang.
