Have you not seen that before one’s eyes, there are no people entirely free from chronic ailments? Nor have you not seen that in the Apricot Grove, the seeds sown in the rain sprout anew year after year?
How could it compare to the Marquis of Liang, who briefly tested his hand at healing the state? Lightly he held his official warrant and traveled through the springtime.

On and on he went eastward toward the Lu Jiang road; the starry marshes, the winds and mists, and the trees of Pengli Lake. At the Twin Pools he gazed upon the waterfall as the Nine Rivers brightened;

at Mount Wulao he heard the temple bells as the chaotic mountains grew dark. I pity the people and all things, their wounds and sores running deep; perhaps nurturing life was not beyond his heart’s intent. Yuan Yang.
Supporting what is withered and decaying, even a single blade of grass is sufficient to repay a thousand pieces of gold. Do not decline the seal and ribbon, for they are not against your will;

yet at Tiger Creek, you shall not be permitted to indulge in the drunkenness of Master Tao. We shall soon see you gathering medicinal herbs upon Mount Penglai, trailing your long robes through the azure peaks of Mount Yan.
Parting at Zhenzhou for Yue Xi-yun: Along the banks of the Long River, wind and sand drift everywhere.
From the roots of the sand, green reed sprouts are blown forth. As I travel, I see you off; as you travel, you see me off.
Our laughing conversation remains before our eyes, yet our hearts are worlds apart. The three realms are like a dream-house; the four elements are like bubbles and flowers. Coming from the East...
Heading west, I ask for the way home; I know not where my true home may lie.

Wishing to part yet unable to part, we hold one another close once more. The thoughts of parting have already followed the cold clouds as they fly. Once the flying clouds have gone, they cannot be recovered;

through a thousand villages and ten thousand hamlets, the slanting glow of the sun shines bright. Turning my head, I gaze upon the mountains of Wu; every eye meets with their lush, lingering green. It is also like this—
Seeing me off, you bid me farewell; standing there until the mists and smoke have vanished, I cannot bear to return.
Year after year I have crossed the snow at the summit of the western peak; for eternal nights before the green lamp, I sat in meditation. Discussing birth and death, my thoughts flowed like water;
even iron or stone could not compare to the firmness of my liver and entrails. Human affairs undergo change and decline; dispersal and gathering ultimately follow conditions. Mountains and rivers...
One may abandon friends and part from others, yet at the first moment of thought, one should not lightly cast each other aside.
A diet of mugwort and coarse rice is the sustenance of mountain men; high reputation and bodily glory are not true blessings.

When literary compositions fill the world and gold fills the bed, karmic burdens deepen and the mind grows increasingly worldly. A single breath is as fragile as a thread—how could it possibly endure forever? (The skull)
There is only the karmic connection of a handful of earth; do not recklessly pursue this wretched life.
Heaven and Earth are but a temporary lodging for travelers; one’s heels cannot be forged from pure steel.

I shall take the yellow *jiǎng* sprouts from Tiānmù Mountain and plant them deep within the ravines of my native mountains. Upon moss-covered rocks I shall sleep by day amidst the clouds; at night, by the pine hearth, I shall roast yams. In years to come...
There are still those who have not yet forgotten their bond; let us seek one another and attempt to cite verses from our shared practice.
As I see off Zhizhao back to Guhong, the clouds above Qujiang drift away.
Chaos of peaks reflects the emerald lake’s light; the autumn colors of the Six Bridges are now clearly visible.
Very well. This man refuses to linger or turn back again. A hundred years and ten thousand affairs pass like mist and rain. Yet the single thought of one’s native village can never be extinguished.
Singing aloud, he returns; I see him off as he goes. When will the dream of the waters of Chu ever come true?
At the Double River Island above Luanjiang Town, the great ship unmoors from the headland of the desolate isle. Raising sails that veil the sky, the drums are struck to set sail;
white waves roll like snow as the wind whistles through the air. My old mountain home, long forgotten, suddenly comes into view—like a spirited steed galloping across the heavens in a flash.
Such was my longing for home in the past, yet today, as I see you off, my heart is filled with lingering sorrow.
Shaking off the clusters of *fúhuā* flowers from Tianmu, I stroke my iron spine, cold as frost. My noble spirit is vast enough to encompass lakes and seas;

my thoughts of returning flow forth like a rushing torrent. Beneath the shade of camphor trees, amidst the halls and pavilions by the Qujiang, I listen to the bells and the rain as the lamp’s light fades.
At this moment, there must be a place where the heart truly meets; let us pour out our sentiments upon this traveler’s road.

The Lion King has departed, beyond recall; autumn fills the crags and valleys as the mountain winds wail. Even the dragon-pools and elephant-thickets abound with scholars, yet they gaze on in silence as the ancestral lineages collapse.
Who can join me in sweeping the thatched hut beneath the pines? There, yellow jing and yellow du roots grow thick before the door.
When the moon rises over the frosty woods, the scent of taro rises; point the way and stir the cold ashes of the hearth.
Worldly conditions are as sweet as drinking fine wine; one drinks them without realizing they have become intoxicating and heavy. Once this worn-out sack is exchanged, it is no longer "I.
How much leisure time do we truly possess? A man of honor bears an iron-like heart and gallbladder; amidst ten thousand changes, he refuses to forget his original resolve.
Parting at the ends of the earth, we offer one another gifts; a single bitter word is worth a thousand pieces of gold.

Entering Xiandong Mountain, the mountain air is so profound it is as if one hears distant thunder. The mountain pheasants call out repeatedly, flying alongside me. The wind through the pines washes the clamor of the marketplace from my ears;

the dew upon the pines sprinkles my green moss-clad robes. Throughout my life, my habitual tendencies have favored deep appreciation for the secluded; thus, I find my heart in harmony with the scenery and the things of this world.
Lingeringly. Who can sing of the purple mushrooms? I shall sing of the gathered mugwort. Summoning the azure phoenixes from beyond the clouds to return.

In the painting of the evening ferry at Songling, the setting sun lingers; the year draws to a close and the river is empty. Upon the level sands stand ancient trees, whistling in the desolate north wind.
The eminent man drags his meditation staff and beckons his small boat; he composes a "Return" poem for the old palace of green mountains and azure clouds.
Both painter and observer alike call it "The Evening Ferry at Songling. I alone think of the ten-thousand-li peaks of Chu, so steep and yet so majestic:
at first they are like surging waves seen from Lake Li, revealing the Five Elders behind the cloud-screens of Mount Lu; then again, they are like a cavern...
Gazing from the south bank of the courtyard at the clusters of peaks on the foothills of Daolin, I sigh: Alas!
Do I have no old palace of green mountains and azure clouds? I sing my vast song and return—whom shall I share it with?
On the River Boat in Shanghai:
An Occasional Account The Wu River passes through the lock, urging the twin oars; we hasten with the ebbing tide down to the Huangpu.

We expect to arrive at Shangyang City before noon, yet I fear the tide will reach us near midday. The night tide has already receded, leaving high marks upon the banks, as the wind sweeps the flower-like spray upward.
The brine of the snow; at the ferry-head, people scrambling for passage are like chickens. Traveling by water and traveling through mud is truly arduous.

On the western bank, waves crash as they reach deep into the village; on the eastern bank, surging sands form groves and gardens. The residents upon the banks have no fixed dwellings; it is quite strange that the tides have no constant place.
At fifty years of age, I traveled to Shangyang; now returning this year at fifty-five, is it not so?
A jade-white, beautiful youth; with a single bow in the past, he became a legend for all eternity. Yet there was also one who, like a soaring hawk, presided over ten thousand *shi* of wealth;

when his power vanished in a single morning, not an inch of land remained. Alas! Human life is an illusory transformation like drifting clouds; the shifting of hills and valleys is nothing worth counting.
While traveling to Zhanggong Cave in Yixing, the entrance descends directly from the mountain summit. Holding a torch, one enters crosswise;
after traveling a short distance, a sliver of light appears, and by following that light out, one arrives at the level ground at the foot of the mountain.
Why must Penglai and Cangzhou be far out at sea? Why must the Peach Blossom Spring and Wuyi be deep within the mountains? Zhanggong—
The Immortal’s Ancient Cave is a realm that exists within the human world yet is not of this world. From the crown of the head, a ladder ascends into the void, descending for several thousand feet;
one feels as if they have rashly breached the Dragon Pass of Death. In the shadowed cliffs, stone marrow remains unknown from what age, frozen into jade-like mounds and crags.
*Yao-zhi* fungi and *qiong-sun* shoots break through the earth, vying with one another in their rugged beauty. Above, they are like the interlacing nets of Indra, like precious banners.
The pearl-canopy is as cold as ice and snow; below, it is like the furious battle of whales and turtles, where silver waves surge and the tide-teeth overturn.

Staggering ghostly beings line the way with ten thousand monsters; mud fields and medicinal furnaces show the mottled patterns of lead-ash. A mountain boy holding a torch points urgently, yet my search for the obscure and exploration of the profound only makes my mind grow more stubborn.
When the path ends, a slight glimmer of light finally breaks through; suddenly, I transcend the primordial chaos and return to the source.
In this dusty world, the crags call and the valleys respond as the cold whistling wind arises; phoenix flutes and jade pendants chime with a *shanshan* sound.

I contemplate that since the self has no birth, there is no intention to transform it into an immortal bone; nor is there any need for the practice of nourishing life—what use are the nine-fold elixirs?

Having realized that there is no dharma apart from the mind, I ascend these heights merely to follow my inspiration upon meeting the occasion. How can one weary of existence escape the net of the world and find even a moment’s rest?

Meditation and contemplation circulate in turn. Furthermore, how could one possibly sweep away eighty thousand kalpas? The Immortal of Liberation and the Buddha enter birth and enter death according to my leisure.
Three Poems Presented to a Friend.

The net of worldly dust brings much suffering and entanglement; a brief moment of leisure is like being freed from a tether. Why is it that while your tracks lie beyond the mundane world, you still gallop hither and thither?
Our gatherings for discourse are always hurried; once we have departed, there is much more to reflect upon. Before one’s eyes, the true Master is lost; what is there to be sought outside of oneself?

The hundred bones are like servants and horses; their momentum joins, and they follow one another for a while. Yet when the movement of the vital breath suddenly shifts and passes away, once they are scattered, there is no time for reunion.
The coming day cannot be waited for; the passing day cannot be pursued. One must preserve the conditions of stillness for oneself, for worldly affairs are truly boundless.
Gone waters do not flow back; yellowed leaves do not flourish again. All things have their end; what can be accomplished in this ephemeral life?
Once stained by the conditions of craving, the intellect’s calculations run rampant. Who knows that yesterday’s affairs, in the blink of an eye, have undergone many changes?

The Sage displayed the *qīqì* (tilting vessel): when it is slightly full, it immediately tilts back. If one does not cherish the present moment, when the time has passed, one will only grieve in vain.
The trees atop the wall rustle; the grasses beneath the wall wither away. How long has it been since they were lush and flourishing? Yet already we see them withered and decayed.
Human life has no fixed root; one's station in the world is a mixture of the beautiful and the ugly. Since the moment of birth, ten thousand thoughts have been in daily turmoil.

As the process of transformation silently wears them away, one’s appearance and hairline do not realize they are aging. How is it that within these hundred years, moments of true joy are so seldom found?
Behold those of antiquity: whose inner aspirations were ever fully realized?

Ascending West Forest, I am so weighed down by melancholy that I can no longer remain; I have spontaneously thought to clear my distant gaze. As I, the Master, ascend West Forest, I rest against the tall bamboos on the precipitous cliffs.
Blossoms bloom amidst the thickets upon the cliffs; birds fly about, chasing one another. Below the cliffs, a clear stream flows; its shimmering light reflects upon the noble trees.
In the fourth month, wind and rain are frequent; the vast plains turn green all at once. With a long啸 (shout of joy), the white sun sinks low; mist and clouds rise from the empty valley.
Looking down upon the myriad transformations of the world, what worth is there in this weary life?
Sitting by night, I hear the crickets;

a mountain man sits beneath the shade of trees. As the branches shift, the moon is now at its zenith. The city market is still noisy at night, with the sounds of pipes and songs mingling with the clatter of mortars and pestles.
The cold cricket possesses what kind of feeling? Its "jiji" chirping is like a conversation. The preceding sound is somewhat sorrowful; the succeeding sound grows increasingly piteous and bitter.
You do not understand the human heart, and people should not heed your words. Each of the myriad species has its own private concerns; how could their sorrows and joys follow the same course?

Within the vast and boundless primordial transformation, all are moved by the same wind and spirit. How much better it would be to awaken to one’s true nature and find joy in life and death as they come.
At the Secluded and Remote Pavilion of Yunlin on Mount Mao, a guest from Huayang seems to have returned once more.
Newly beholding the opening of the Yunlin Guest House, the cold sun lingers over half the crags, where pines and cranes dwell.

Rising up, a pungent wind sweeps through ten thousand ravines as the rain-dragons turn back; dew flows upon the zither-stand, nourishing the jade-like grasses, while the elixir cauldron sends forth springtime onto the jade plum blossoms.
Those who dwell here know not its purity and distance; from this world, Penglai lies but a few inches away.

In the same rhyme, I bid farewell to the Magistrate of Guqian as he resigns his seal and returns home swiftly—what is his intent? I, the mountain man, shall long remember our former visits. Your literary prowess reveals a subtle touch of Chan insight;
your official records are no more than your scrolls of verse. Amidst the flower-rain, listen to the orioles as spring fills the wine; amidst the willow-wind, stand your horse beneath the moon.
Waves ripple; all matters that delight the heart and bring joy are but the fruits of one’s meritorious deeds, left for the old man by the stream and the maiden by the stream to sing.
I, [Name], a magistrate of ten thousand households, have escaped peril at sea;

thus I harmonize these verses to console him. Before my words are even spoken, his countenance has already changed. In former days, maritime transport endured many hardships; the shadows of row upon row of ships fell into the dragon’s spittle.
In this cave, my soul flies as I sleep alone upon a pillow amidst the ghostly bones of the mountains. The dragon roars in alarm at the sword drawn from its scabbard;
the tiger was fortunate to survive when the family jewel was passed down. Though gold may accumulate higher than a bushel, it cannot purchase a single day’s leisure of retiring from office.
At Mount Jing, Seeing Off Master Xiang on His Return to Wumen:
Wumen has long been the state I cherish in my thoughts. North of the city and south of the city, half are places of my former travels. Buddhist towers mark the boundaries of groves and wild temples;
Traveler’s sails fly around the market towns and river pavilions. Seeing you off, I suddenly feel my heartstrings stir; Grown old as I am, I find it hard to forget these footsteps.
Repaying his debts, he gazes upon the tangerines and oranges of the seventy-two peaks; he purchases a boat to renew his appointment for the autumn of Lake Tai.
As he departs, Vinaya Master Wuzhe returns to Min;

though he employs every means, he cannot restrain his longing to go home. His karmic ties remain unexhausted in their joy: he listens to the bell amidst the rain on *láng* leaves, and rests his head against the breeze of *lì* flowers.
Long accustomed to the Min dialect, my friendships have deepened through the customs of Chu. With a single sail, tomorrow I shall be far away; the clouds part, leaving the sea and sky vast and empty.

Ascending again the Tower of the Autumn Moon, my ailing strength revives with the fresh rain. Climbing the tower to gaze at the setting sun, the riverbanks shift as the market town recedes; the islets join the mulberry groves stretching long.

In the village at dusk, smoke hastens the onset of twilight; from the shadows of the water, clouds bring a sense of coolness. My feelings as a traveler have become seasoned; wherever I am, I find the ability to forget myself.
Four Poems Sent to the Monk Yuxiao of Hometown: The sea rain blows the flowers into piles of snow;
at that moment, it knocked upon my bamboo gate and opened it. I pity myself in this land of waters—three thousand [miles] away.
A village monk also came from the countryside to ask the way:
Wind-blown sand and whirling leaves ruffle my traveler’s robe; Today, by the riverbank, I see you off on your return. Looking west toward your native land, where can it be found?
The heavens of Chu stretch vast and empty, as a lone cloud drifts by.

Village dreams and homesickness have long since grown distant for me; for ten years I have not received a letter from my native land. Those with whom I gathered as a child are like figures in a dream;
now that I am old, I know not whether they still exist.
When the villagers asked me when I would return, I told them: "I have entered the mountains once again.
With a single meditation cushion and half a room, I dwell amidst the nine peaks upon the banks of the Wu Song River."
Four Poems on Ascending the Tianshi Altar at Maoshan The celestial market leans against the azure void;
the mountains and waters of the two capitals appear in hazy obscurity.
Ten days of wind and frost upon my eastern journey—everything lies within a single stroke of cold mist.
White clouds are cut into snow upon the jade altar; The cold morning sun steams open the flowers in the jade cavern. Viewed from north and south of the mountains, it is even more beautiful;
Every cluster of rising smoke belongs to a realm of immortals.
A grove of pines and yet another palace; opening the gates, one gazes at Maofeng Peak from every side.
Wandering with a mind in a daze along the path of Mount Lu, I return for a meal as the monks share the upper and lower bells.

When Master Guo strikes the boat-railing in the clear night, ten thousand sounds blend with the autumn zither and the moon over the pond. Who, through a thousand years, has transmitted the "Numinous Phoenix" melody?
The feathered youth chants it as a *buxu* hymn.
One Peak Beyond the Clouds Hermitage, in Response to the Rhymes on the Four Scenic Views:

A green rainbow divides the two halves of the mountain bridge; beneath the bridge, spring thunder rolls over the surging waves. The old monk, having returned from meditation, opens the door to look out:
across the stream, the wild cherry blossoms have fully opened.
In the bamboo hut, the fragrance of tea fills the misty ravine; deep within the green cypress trees, flowing springs resound. Who can speak of the Dharma present before one?
As the setting sun and gentle breeze stir, a single tree is filled with cicadas.
The waters of Heiraku speak of the fragrance of rice blossoms; Half-unfastening my moss-clothed robe, I enjoy the evening cool. Scenery and objects both pure, autumn is truly fine;
Beyond the chaotic mountains, the clouds part for another slanting sun.
A patched robe covers my head as the embers glow red; in the cold of the snow, I listen with sorrow to the bell from above. Opening the door, I am suddenly startled to see the mountains become a sea;
ten thousand layers of silver waves reveal but a single peak.
On Three Successive Days at Lake Village Hermitage Daily the waters of Xiataang are shrouded in mist;
A stone bridge and tall willows face my thatched gate. The frost wind stirs the tree leaves like falling rain;
Suddenly, I see a single sail approaching from the distant village.
Bamboo roots and barking dogs lie west across the creek; The geese on the lake cry out as leaves fall from the trees. Only upon listening closely do I realize the sound of two oars;
A single lamp floats on the water as a night boat returns home.
Ditches were opened and embankments built to protect the low-lying fields; sitting there, I listened as the neighbor recounted last year’s events:
he had sold his plow and hoe to buy a fishing net, and now his children paddle their boat right up to the edge of my bed.
Seeking the Immortal’s Cave, I travel by boat to the mouth of the Great River:
Where can one find the secluded abode of the immortals? The setting sun flickers as chaotic clouds deepen. The Great River cuts across, merging with the green mountains;
Along the single path, wind-swept sails enter the forest.
A Gift for My Younger Brother Renyuan upon His Departure for the Capital (With Preface) When I first left my home, my younger brother Renyuan was only seventeen years old; now he is nearly forty.

His beard and whiskers stand out like spears, and his speech reveals a far-reaching ambition. Having completed his term of service as an instructor in Xiangnan, he is now setting out upon the wind [to the capital].
While traveling to the capital, he moored his boat in Yangzhou and took a detour to visit Jingshan during the plum rains. There, they shared a meditation couch by lamplight for several nights.
Upon his departure, [the author] presented four verses as a gift to record the sentiments of parting and to urge him to return soon.
Curled whiskers, an iron-like countenance, and a headband of coarse hemp; his courage is bold and his speech overawes others.
Not having seen him for twenty-three years, I suspect that this youth is my former self.
Rain falls upon the peaks, misty ridges where emerald hues seem to flow; Heaven has unveiled a painted scroll atop ten thousand mountain heads.
From the balustrade of Lingxiao Pavilion, my lingering thoughts remain for later years to recount this old journey.
White Cloud Peak lies on the edge of the setting sun; I gaze after the clouds of Wu as they enter the land of Chu.
When you reach Mount Yan, turn your head back once more—three thousand li away, yet another three thousand.
The brocade robe reflects the flowers, brightening the Phoenix Pond; the jade pendants shimmer, casting light upon the Azure Palace.
Wealth and honor intoxicate one as if in a dream, yet the compassionate mother leaning at her gate keeps her eyes ever wide awake.
Traveling at dawn along the Wu Song River, the north wind blows against my face as the snow falls thickly. Crossing the frozen river is like passing through a forest of thorns.
Yet I recall, beneath my thatched hut with head covered, the single warmth of the earthen stove was worth a thousand pieces of gold.
The waters turn around the sandy shoals once more at another bend; a solitary pagoda rises to greet the boat from the misty peaks.
A single current of the Great River stretches across as the wind arises, and on both banks, sails fly upward and downward in competition.
Sixteen Poems on the Scenery of Shizilin (Lion Forest) Birds sing and flowers bloom from house to house, east and west; Cypress smoke rises blue, and taro fires glow red.
People say I dwell within the city; I suspect my body is amidst ten thousand mountains.
Ten thousand green jade-like bamboos surround the meditation hall; their tips and joints stand dense as young shoots grow tall.
Rising and sitting, he carries his seven-foot rattan cane, weaving through the forest in a continuous stream as if on inspection rounds.

Light flickers upon the plain walls, doubling the clarity of my sight; Through the curtains, wind and trees play amidst the fresh clearing. At the roots of the trees, frogs beat their drums as the last rain falls;
Vaguely, it is like the sound of the Nan Shan Water Music.

Pointing to six or seven monks within the Cypress Pavilion, he said: "In the state of sitting-forgetfulness, suddenly a strange fragrance arises; pushing open the window, the sunlight is warm as fire;
the *campaka* flowers bloom like a canopy of snow."
The Chancellor comes to seek the Shaolin lineage; officials crowd the gate until it is impassable.
Scattered into the deep bamboo of Fengting Pavilion, they sit together on stone beds as flying rainbows swirl around them. (The pavilion is named Qifeng; the bridge is named Xiaofeihong.
Beneath the eaves, the setting sun dries cold robes; a single bowl of fragrant soup contains wild ferns grown fat. Spring rains and spring mists, two or three...
My son, returning from planting pines on the plains west of the river, I saw crows and magpies contending for their nests as if they were enraged soldiers.
They shrieked in fury and fought to the death, scattering in wild disorder. Piteous indeed are the broken *sāla* trees;
with fallen blossoms covering the ground, there is no path to walk upon.
The practitioner carries water on his shoulder to irrigate the garden vegetables; returning by boat with his alms bowl, he has a surplus of grain.
Satiated from their meal, the monastics have nothing else to do but circle the pond to share food with the wandering fish.
In the Cloud-Resting Chamber, cold, the demon of sleep awakens; the sound of the final watch strikes again and again, urging on the fifth watch. One dream is like a lifetime passed;
when the sun rises in the east, that shall be my next life.
To the west, the neighbor’s mother cries out like a crane without ceasing. I know the crane’s intent: it grieves for its master. If you raise a crane until it is grown, you may ride it away;
yet Yangzhou may not necessarily surpass Suzhou.

The kitchen boy recites the Lotus Sūtra deep into the night; the moon passes over the western wall as the shadows of the cypresses slant. When the recitation ends, the sound of the pulley suddenly stirs;
he draws water from the spring to test his tea brewed before the rains.
The Zen gate beneath the forest opens all day long; it lets people come to view the "Sleeping Dragon" plum. Do not disdain the bustle at the gateway, O mountain servant;
it is not that I am fond of idleness, but that others do not come.
Slanting plum branches press against the stone balustrade; The flowers seem to bow their heads as they gaze at their reflections. In broad daylight, clouds darken the sky as if snow were to fall;
Across half the pond, the stars and constellations press upon one with a chilling cold.
The snow is three feet deep, closing the wattle doors; at year’s end, I have no mind to engage in idle entanglements. Before the Hall of Standing in the Snow, people cannot see me;
Mount Xiuyun resembles a white-haired monk.
A guest came seeking a song of admonition; having composed it, I withdrew my thoughts to enter *dhyāna*.
The tea-boy urged me down from the tower, where new guests had arrived in even greater numbers below.
In speech or silence, without a mind, the Way flourishes of itself. Who before one's eyes can manifest our school? Long and short are the ivory and bamboo;
strange and marvelous is Lion Peak.

the Elder Zhao-tang Ji, passed away on the twenty-first day of the third month in the Dingchou year of the Zhizhen era (1297) in Wumen.
Regarding Zhi Nengren’s Hermitage: his righteous conduct moved people so deeply that their grief could not be contained;

they gave vent to it through poems and prose, which were scattered throughout the forests and valleys of the Three Wu regions. Tiantai Zhujū Kexī, the Hall Master, compiled these works and titled the collection *Yìgǎn* (Moved by Righteousness).
Upon passing through Songjiang, he requested of me: "The poems and prose do not yet reveal the circumstances of his life and career."
Regarding the details of this transmission: you, Master, and Zhao Tang both studied under Tianmu; I trust you will provide a detailed account so that readers may have something upon which to rely.
I said: "Zhao Tang is a descendant of a renowned clan from Gaochang.

Among his kinsmen and fellow villagers who left their native land to settle in the capital cities of the Great Court, all have attained high office. Their customs still honor Buddhism and they are fond of—"

He was generous in giving and skilled at providing support and advancement so that others might prosper. Indeed, having lived far from his native land, he regarded even distant countrymen as kin when he saw them;
thus, those among their families who became śramaṇas often received bountiful offerings or attained great fame and status.
Yet, Zhao Tang took none of this; he delighted only in the Way. Among all the great figures of both the Exoteric and Esoteric schools, he was truly one of substance.

These were men of such caliber that he served them all, exhausting their teachings without ever wearying of his resolve. During the Yan-you era, he traveled south to Mount Tianmu to seek the direct pointing (zhizhi) of the Chan school from my late teacher, Master Huanzhu.
He advanced daily in his realization until the Master looked upon him with deep affection and could not bear to let him depart.
Clad in grass garments and wearing sandals of *phusa* grass, he sustained himself on the bitterness of pine and gall for many years. Only when my late teacher passed away did he finally return north.
The various high officials were drawn to his Way and vied with one another to recruit him. Nevertheless, he remained cautious and maintained his own integrity;

he would not converse with those who did not sincerely seek the Way, nor would he associate with those who were not the right people. When he did associate with others, he invariably fulfilled his obligations to the utmost.
He once presented the thirty-fascicle *Huazhu guanglu* (Extensive Record of Abiding in Illusion) for imperial inspection.
The Emperor read this and was greatly pleased. He granted him entry into the Imperial Library and posthumously conferred upon his late master the title National Teacher Puying (Universal Response).
Having thus successfully completed his mission through many hardships and travels, he returned to Tianmu Mountain, vowing to remain there until old age to guard the National Teacher’s stupa.
When he fell ill, those living with him urged him to leave the mountain to seek medical treatment; consequently, he passed away at Wumen. This is what I have personally known.

This concludes it. Other matters are not detailed here. Nevertheless, by collecting and examining these materials, one is sufficiently able to perceive the long-standing reserves of Zhao Tang, the profound sincerity of their mutual friendship, and the high regard for righteousness held by Zhujū.
Whatever is sufficient to be praised by others, transmitted through the ages, and to inspire one's contemporaries—all of it is contained herein.
Why, then, must there be further elaboration?
This is the preface to the eulogy for the bronze Buddha.
In the summer of the Jia-shen year of the Zhizheng era, the Bodhisattva Jù of Zhà’ān held a great assembly at Qiantáng.
For forty-eight days, monastics and laypeople performed Buddhist rites on Gēshí Mountain to celebrate the completion of the bronze statues of Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
This was also done to propagate his transformation so that it might become increasingly vast and far-reaching. To trace the origin of the creation of these images: approximately...
He converted forty-eight people, each giving one copper coin and reciting the Buddha’s name one thousand times as their standard practice.

In this manner, each of these forty-eight people further converted forty-eight others. Through this successive conversion, they accumulated four million eight hundred thousand coins, which were melted down to cast a Buddha image.
The Buddha was one zhang and six chi in height, with two Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) of equal stature, their features perfectly proportioned.
It was excellent, detailed, and complete. Subsequently, he ascended by scaling the mountains to establish a great hall for its enshrinement;
thus, the present assembly came to be. Thereupon, eulogies and praises from scholars of the four quarters converged, citing three points worthy of commendation.

First, although there are tens of thousands of Buddhist sites in Qiāntáng, large and small, numbering in the millions, they have never possessed a bronze image. Second, the method of soliciting donations...

To take but little and transform it so extensively is different from the ordinary; this is the second point. To unite all virtues into a single assembly, universally encompassing the capacities of both the high and the low;
this is the third point. Having recorded these verses into a scroll and awaiting my preface, I may perhaps have something further to say beyond these three points.
When the image was not yet completed, the whole Buddha was but copper; once it was fully completed, the whole copper was the Buddha.
It is said that "Buddha" and "bronze" are two names for one essence. This is because the Buddha does not exist as a Buddha in himself, but arises from conditions (*pratyaya*).
By extrapolating this principle of dependent origination, one realizes that among the myriad things of the world, every single thing is the Buddha. Furthermore, there is another teaching:
whenever a person gives rise to a single thought or offers a single coin, the entire body of the bronze image is already present therein.
He responds in accordance with one’s recollection. If this is so for a single thought-moment, it is likewise so for many thought-moments.
Thus, the Buddhas who manifest in response to such thoughts—how could they possibly be limited to four million eight hundred thousand? Furthermore, there is another point to be made:
as the minds of many people reciting the Buddha’s name are transmitted and spread from one to another, reaching from this life through future lives to infinity, then the Buddhas...
Responding accordingly in this manner is likewise inexhaustible. Just as the breadth of horizontal response is thus, so too is the depth of vertical response.

How could its measure or number ever be conceivable? This arises from the study of the inherent nature (shōgu) taught by Shōan Zōshō, which enables one to realize that every person shall awaken to the truth that "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha."
This teaching proceeds from layer upon layer to infinity and from mutual interpenetration without obstruction.

Whether as principle or as phenomenon, throughout the entire Dharma-realm, there is not a single thing that is not the Buddha. Thus, when a single faculty is activated or a single image is formed, it is able to bring about such vast and far-reaching transformation.
Since I perceive the transformation of Zhaoyingzhao’an to be thus, I have composed this preface for his volume of eulogies.
Thus it is.

Dao-lin says: When a superior person travels abroad, if there are those among the scholars who possess the vessel for receiving the Way, they must not fail to travel to the great quarters. Once their travels are complete, they shall broaden what they have heard.

To pursue the Way—once the Way is accomplished—it is further sufficient to bring about a fine reputation and a high station. By extending one's own realization to share it with the multitude, this has been the norm throughout antiquity and the present.
Otherwise, one will sink to the heels of others and be swept along in the dust of the common and base.

Having no means by which to hear the Way oneself, how can one guarantee that what one possesses—the vessel of the mind—will not be ruined or lost? From this, we know that wandering [as a seeker] does no harm to a scholar.

Furthermore, there are those who have long been devoted to travel, yet ultimately fall into heterodox studies; they concern themselves only with oral tradition and superficial learning, cultivating an air of arrogance while overlooking their own inner deficiencies.

Often, they amass great wealth to establish their reputations or curry favor with the powerful to secure positions. In the end, they bring ruin upon themselves in a state of frantic disorder, only to become objects of ridicule for their fellow villagers.
This is not the fault of travel; rather, it is because the resolve to seek the Way was not firm. It is due to this lack of firm resolve...
They bitterly lament the injustice of their failure to reach success; consequently, they do not prioritize the Way, but instead prioritize fame and rank.
Thus, those in high positions who wield the power of promotion and demotion are neither able to alleviate what people deem urgent, nor are they able to prioritize what is truly urgent.

Therefore, it is inevitable that they fall into the corruption of following contemporary fashions. How could this corruption be a product of the present alone? It has existed since antiquity; only those whose will is resolute can remain steadfast.
One knows that fame and rank are not what is urgent, yet one attains what is truly urgent. When one attains what is urgent, that which is not urgent follows of its own accord.
Should one’s Way conflict with the times and one is unfortunate enough to fail to achieve success, one then takes one’s own failure as a means to succeed alongside the ancients;
one acts as a model for all things. What does it matter whether one possesses fame and rank or not? Therefore, a scholar is not merely a vessel.
This is already proof of his capacity; one must surely firm up one’s resolve so that there may be a means to verify that this journey does not fail me.
The monk Huating Xun, whose courtesy name is Daolin, possesses vast capacity and abundant talent. His appearance is imposing, such that he is fit to realize the Way and achieve success.
He was about to set out on a journey, but planted his staff and did not depart, as if harboring some doubt regarding my words. Thus—

He spoke exhaustively to inform him, saying: "I have observed that those currently in office who promote the enlightened and select the public-spirited all act with urgency to find worthy men to succeed to their Way.
Who would dare encounter you with unrighteousness? Rather, it depends on what you yourself consider urgent."

Preface for Sending Attendant Cai Home to Bury His Master Our clan follows the study of world-transcending enlightenment. To do so, one must distance oneself from parents to follow a teacher and receive instruction.

The teacher plants and nurtures the student, striving to cultivate their completion as a trust for the continuation and transmission of the lineage; such profound kindness and deep affection are regarded as equal to those of one's own parents.
There was no lack of such instances. Yet his disciples would sometimes depart abruptly; they traveled across thousands of miles to visit great masters, never considering it a distance.

They left their youth and returned with hair already white from old age, never considering it a long time. They viewed their formal studies as a mere lodging-house and regarded their teachers as ordinary people;
even when aged, ill, or on the verge of death, they had no leisure to look back. From the perspective of the mundane world, this was so.

To turn one's back on the fundamental and sever the meaning is indeed extreme. Yet, the mind of this person considers that he has not begun by turning his back or severing [the tradition], for he clearly aspires to the Way of the Separate Transmission (biezhuan).
If he were truly without shame before the Way, he would be sufficient to perfect himself and others, joining in the fragrance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
then, whether called "Master" or "Parent," he would bestow benefit upon an infinite age. Compared to merely guarding one another within the village lanes—
Is there not a vast difference between nourishing the aged and serving as their attendants? Therefore, the intention of those who act as teachers is also this:
"Our disciples, though dwelling beyond the mundane world, must follow renowned masters and befriend upright men.

Although what we have learned and attained may not yet suffice to emulate the footsteps of our predecessors, is it not sufficient to cultivate talent and flourish in virtue so as to manifest a fragrant reputation for the sake of our elders?"
Are you not the light of the family? We have looked forward to you day after day throughout the year. We have supported our failing strength and endured death in the hope that we might see you.
Even if we should die without seeing you—unfortunately not beholding you—those who look toward you will not be willing to die along with us.
Thus, those who are your disciples, if they cannot take their teacher’s heart as their own heart, merely wander and dwell together in a dull and aimless manner.
We have followed one another’s habits down to the present, yet there is nothing worthy of praise in our way; is this not a failure of mutual responsibility?
The attendant Cai has been traveling to various monasteries for many years; now that he is returning to bury his master, he seeks my words.
My own master died and was buried long ago, yet I have not been as able to return as Cai has been. Therefore, I record what I cannot bear to say, alongside what I cannot bear not to say.
I have taken this as a gift for you.
This preface to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is written in blood;
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* of my own mind. Outside of one's own mind, there is no *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to be found.
The temporal teachings throughout the lifetime of Kāśyapa [the Buddha] are like sowing a hundred kinds of grain, yet the harvest lies in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This is because it awakens sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, culminating only after they receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood. There are various differences in these accounts of the predictions.
There are both the fundamental source and the traces. The traces serve to reveal the ultimate reality by disclosing the provisional for the sake of the śrāvakas;
the fundamental source serves to reveal the distant by disclosing the near for the sake of the great assembly.

It is like reducing all worlds to fine dust, taking each particle of dust as an eon, and calculating the lifespan since his attainment of Buddhahood through those eons until the end of time, yet its duration remains inexhaustible. Within this interval, he has preached.
How could those who receive the prediction of attaining the Dharma be counted? Although their distance may seem so great, it still does not transcend the realm of numerical quantity.
To investigate these measures of birth and Buddhahood, awakening and delusion, near and far, and beginning and end:
they reside within one's own mind and are merely the manifestations and influences of a single thought-moment responding to conditions. Therefore, a single thought-moment...
When expanded, even the mountains and seas of ink and the hairs of a single needle cannot suffice to record even a small fraction of it.
When contracted into a single thought-moment, even the pores of a single needle’s eye contain it with room to spare.

This is what is meant by that which cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination, and which is so profound, firm, and remote that no one can reach it—the essential meaning lies herein. How could a person of humble and mediocre capacity be fit to speak of this? It is permissible.
The abbot Tingju received his training at Xianqing Chan Monastery on Mount Panlong in Yuanzhou. Early on, he carried his satchel to travel throughout the four quarters.
In the eighth year of the Zhi-shun era (1353), the monastery was ravaged by fire; its master, Chan Master Yunfeng Zhi, exerted great effort to restore it, and now seven years have passed.
While residing in Wumen, Tingju obtained the letter concerning his formal ordination, whereupon he pricked his finger and wrote this in blood.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* consists of seven fascicles. He further prostrated himself before each single character of this sutra, assisting his master in offering prayers to the Buddha for the swift restoration of the temple and for the long endurance of the Dharma.
His application of mind was indeed diligent. Once the transcription was complete, he intended to present it and return home.
He held it up for me to see. I bowed my head in prostration, offered words of praise, and said to him: "Does not the Sūtra say?

'If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one hears this sūtra and is able to write it oneself, or teaches others to write it, this is equivalent to having already built monasteries, constructed various halls, gardens, bathing pools, walking paths, and meditation caves, with all manner of delightful requisites filling them. Furthermore, it says:"
When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa, consumed by a great conflagration, my land remains peaceful and secure,
ever filled with devas and humans. Viewed from this perspective, within a single pore, a single strand of blood, or the arrangement of a single dot or stroke,
one can exercise the power of transformative skillful means, erect banners and stūpas, and manifest the fundamental radiance of all Buddhas, even unto the jewels.
This is the ultimate destination. It is the bestowal of the crest-jewel by the Wheel-Turning King; it is the assembly on Vulture Peak that has not yet dispersed.
Whether gods or humans, they all offer palaces, thrones, flowers, incense, banners, and canopies as acts of worship—all of which reside herein.
If you truly understand this, then my own teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* from within my own mind shall likewise find its verification in this.
Preface to the Poetic Scroll on the Bronze Pagoda of the Money King:
Extraordinary, precious, strange, and ancient objects are invariably held in high esteem by people. Yet, there are differences in the reasons for this esteem.

Some value them for pleasure and amusement; some for being heirlooms from their ancestors; and others to adopt them as a method for spiritual cultivation. By observing what they hold in esteem, one may discern their character.
Thus, one may know whether a person is worthy or unworthy, good or evil. Master Chunye of Heyang is a descendant of the Qian family of Wuyue.
He possesses a hall called Cishou, which he uses to enshrine a bronze pagoda constructed by his ancestor, King Zhongyi.

Morning and evening, he kneels and bows in praise and prayer, seeking blessings to ensure the longevity of his mother. This year, his mother is eighty-four years old and remains in good health. Great!
Scholars have composed poems and prose to praise this work. I have written a preface to explain its origins, saying:

In the past, King Aśoka of the Western Regions once constructed eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas to enshrine the relics of Śākyamuni Buddha, dispersing them throughout the four directions so that devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits might rely upon them to cultivate merit.
Of those located within the Eastern Lands, there are five; now, at Chang [Mount Tiantai] in Siming...
This is precisely what Ning did; thus, Zhongyi was able to follow his example. Measuring about one chi in height, their form and number were identical to those [of the original].
He distributed them among his kinsmen and monasteries—examples of which include those currently at Cishou Hall.
That King Aśoka, despite his sage wisdom, was able to treat his treasures as no more than mere pagodas, was because he knew how to extend his goodness to others.
It is a supreme treasure. If Zhongyi had gathered the copper, he would have discerned that it was better suited for being fashioned into basins, pillars, camels, or platforms rather than a stupa;

thus, he captured the spirit of Aśoka. As for Chunye, he honored the legacy of his predecessors and did not succumb to the vice of mere playthings, yet remained earnestly devoted to what is virtuous, thereby moving [the hearts of others].
My friends and associates—these are those who have gathered the heart of Zhongyi. Now, a stupa is constructed because of śarīra;
yet how could śarīra be an external thing? Our Buddha extended his goodness to manifest the ultimate proof of great perfection.
As for this proof of great perfection, how could the Buddha have kept it to himself? It is something that every person is capable of achieving and inherently possesses.
I wish that Chunya might contemplate the *śarīra* through the stūpa, and through the *śarīra*, contemplate what is inherently possessed within himself.
May he advance in its cultivation and expand its fulfillment to verify the ultimate state of great perfection—this is yet another aspect of sublime education that has not been fully realized.
Chunya is broad in learning and quick in talent; he is a gentleman-scholar (*junzi ru*) who does not emulate the Confucians’ exclusion of Buddhism.
Furthermore, I have served him; thus, I venture to present this discourse on cultivation to bring his preface to completion.
The Preface by Zhanbixuan:
Longxi Dingguang Temple is located forty *li* south of the city of Yuzhang. It was the former residence of my friend Yue Xi-yun.
The monastery has a pond. Upon the pond, ten thousand bamboos stand like jade pillars. His master, the Great Master Gudao, built a pavilion by the pond; it was exceedingly pure.

Xiyun obtained the large calligraphy of Yu Gong, the Imperial Preceptor of the Quizhang Academy, which read "Zhanbi" (Azure Green) to serve as its plaque. Various renowned scholars also composed poems in their imagination to celebrate it.
Intending to take it back with him, he met me again in Wu. I said to him: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]

He said: "Do you understand the discourse on 'deep blue' (*zhanbi*)? When water is still and clear, it is called 'deep' (*zhan*); when water and bamboo reflect one another, it is called 'blue' (*bi*).
Blue does not harm its depth; though present, it is as if non-existent. Depth does not obstruct its blueness; though non-existent, it is as if existent."
If, unfortunately, the wind stirs and waves arise, and turbid waters mingle within, then the deep azure vanishes. My mind is likewise.

When all sensory dusts subside, one should contemplate that which is limpid and clear—this is "deep" (zhan). To possess all dharmas within its nature, like a mani jewel reflecting colors as they come, is "azure" (bi).
One who dwells in this pavilion opens the window and leans against the railing; when the mind meets with the environment through these conditions, it becomes both deep and azure.

"It resides in me, not in that [external world]. Yet, one must first attain profound realization and dwell in peace before knowing that while that [world] depends on conditions, what resides in oneself depends on nothing.
Truly being without dependence, even if the winds of external circumstances fan upon one and the waves of emotion rage and toss, my deep azure clarity remains as it is.
Filling this state, one may circulate through foreign lands and merge into strange realms.

In all things, there is nothing that is not profoundly blue. Previously, when you and I together visited Tianmu Mountain, we spoke most intimately of what is called "that which resides within oneself.
Yet, as time passed, my dwelling therein remained uneasy. Seventeen years have gone by since our parting, and I feared that this profound blue had drifted further from you.
Now, fortunately, you know how to return. Having returned and sought it, you have found it; this provides a means to verify my [words].
Thus it was said.
Regarding the "Postscript to the Record of the Renaming of Qianxi":
Master Hui of Jianlin changed the name of his monastery from Qianbu to Qianxi; I have indeed obtained this record of that renaming.

This is the theory [of the former master]. Now, the area of this temple is no less than a thousand paces in breadth; yet it was named for those thousand paces. Thus, the name did not correspond to the reality, so he changed it to "Creek" (Kik).
But is the creek actually a thousand paces? If the creek is not a thousand paces, then the reality again does not correspond to its name.
Now, "not corresponding" is one and the same in both cases. However, when the name does not correspond, one changes it; when the reality does not correspond, one does not change it.
"Is he at peace? I further observe that while his walking by the stream is free of illness, his illness lies in the 'thousand.
Since he finds the 'one' step base for its scarcity, and the stream feels ashamed of the 'thousand' for its abundance, he must surely exchange the thousand for the one before he can find peace.
If the 'one' step could not have been exchanged in the past but awaits exchange now, then the 'thousand' of the stream will likewise not be exchanged now, and it must necessarily—"
It is easier to wait for it later. Between waiting for that future ease and perfecting it now in your hands—which is better?
Yet, you have already labored extensively over the *Xici* with its myriad words and the grand scrolls of the various gentlemen of the Jade Hall.
Why then do you not weary of my tedious words as I request another thousand hexagrams? Moreover, these are a thousand hexagrams.
The meaning of this has never been spoken of by the gentlemen; only I have spoken of it. My words are not yet sufficient for verification.
I request that you, sir, resolve this through the principles of ascending Yin and descending Yang.
Preface to the Names of the Five Hundred Venerable Ones:
At the beginning, the World-Honored One used the three vehicles to guide sentient beings; the Śrāvaka vehicle is one of them.

The Śrāvakas perceive suffering, sever the origin [of suffering], cultivate the path, and realize cessation. There are distinctions between the four fruits and the four stages of approach, yet they take transcendence from the triple world as their ultimate goal.
This is realization. Although it is said that one has "exited" the three realms, in reality, one does not leave them.

It is simply because the delusions of views and thoughts have been severed and the fetters of existence have been emptied, such that one no longer undergoes birth according to the delusions and fetters of the three realms; therefore, it is called "exiting the three realms.
Though one has exited the three realms and though what is realized is ultimate, one still does not yet know how to seek the Buddha-way to deliver sentient beings. Compared [to this],...
Since many who follow the Mahāyāna still fall into the partiality of the Hīnayāna, the World-Honored One again used reprimands and rebukes to cause them to turn their minds.

When the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* revealed the provisional to manifest the real, he said, "That which you practice is the path of the bodhisattva," and "By the sound of the Buddha-way, let all hear it.
Only then did they receive their predictions of enlightenment; only then did they accord with the Tathāgata’s original intention. Now, as for what is called the five...

Regarding the hundred venerable ones who manifested their presence or disappeared at the Stone Bridge (Shiqiao) Fangguang Temple, it is suspected that they were all among those who had received predictions of enlightenment.
The Venerable Qing of Yunyin Monastery in Wumen once visited the scenic sites of Tiantai’s Stone Bridge;

he subsequently compiled five hundred names into a scroll for his monastery so that they might be used for recitation and ritual offerings. He requested a preface for the beginning of this scroll. As I have the misfortune of practicing Chan meditation, I have complied with his request.

Regarding the teachings, there is no fixed direction; those who roughly distinguish between the Small and the Great do so with the intention that those who study the Buddha-dharma should proceed directly toward the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna) rather than following the tracks of the partial and limited.

However, the World-Honored One first used inducement, then employed refutation, and finally revealed the truth; such was the sequence of his transformation of beings. Now, as for me making this statement, it is [in accordance] with the World-Honored One’s...
Whether to reject or to embrace depends on the appropriate response to the occasion; let the practitioner choose for themselves.
Regarding the Preface by the person who sent it, Master Dezang, everyone knows how to study, yet no one knows how to seek the Way through study. If study does not reach the Way, it is not true study.
There is the worldly path, and there is the supramundane path. Within the supramundane path, there are further distinctions:
the small and the great, the shallow and the deep, the provisional and the ultimate. If one does not reach the pinnacle of finality, it is not what I call the Way.
Therefore, those who study do not suffer from an inability to reach that pinnacle; they simply suffer from their own lack of resolve. Once their resolve is attained—

Furthermore, there is the distress of not finding a teacher; or having found one, failing to reach the destination before parting ways midway, whereby one must inevitably turn elsewhere to seek another;
and having sought another, failing to reach him, one turns again and again to seek yet others.
For this reason, the ancients had no fixed teachers and no settled direction, never ceasing until they reached the Way. Now, consider those who are once more in distress...
To confine oneself to a single corner and limit one's learning to what has been attained by a single master—can this truly be called seeking the Way?
The Abbot De of Lingfeng Temple in Qingjiang is dignified, refined, and possesses great ambition; at an early age, he followed Master Guyun Gao to master both Buddhist and secular learning.
His peers esteemed and submitted to him. In the year Jiazi of the Taiding era, I was about to return to Tianmu from Jiyun;
passing through Qingjiang, I took my leave of Guyun and first came to know him. After Guyun passed away, De traveled eastward and attended upon Elder Zhutian at Dantu Lake.
Not long after, his grandfather moved to Lengquan and also passed away. De then visited the great elders of Jinling and served as the librarian at Mount Zhong;
what he acquired through these associations increased daily and was by no means small. Scholar Bosheng and Master Yu once saw him and marveled at his talent.
Formerly, Guyun had given him the name Wuxin (My Mind), but Master Yu remarked that "My Mind" seemed to violate the taboo name of Zhu Tian.
He then inscribed "Daolin" in large characters to replace it. This autumn, he came to Zhejiang to visit me amidst the ten thousand bamboos at Wanzhu.
From our first meeting until now, fourteen years have passed. When I examine his learning, it is no longer that of the man of former times;
yet he still feels a pressing anxiety regarding what he has not yet attained, lamenting the loss of his teachers and friends, and grieving for the withering of the monastic community.
I asked him about his travels and where he had been. He said, "You may truly be called one who seeks the Way well. Now your style name is Daolin (Forest of the Way).
Since you take the Way as a forest, what place could you go that would not be a thicket or grove? By using 'forest' as a metaphor for the Way, what aspect of the Way is not complete within you?
Return and seek it; you will find more than enough teachers."
Preface to the Combined Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra is the life-force of wisdom for all Buddhas, the path to realization for all sentient beings, and the grand mainstay of the net of the teachings.

This is the essential gateway of the Chan school. Since the World-Honored One attained enlightenment, his teachings established throughout the five periods have been nothing other than for the sake of the one great cause and condition.
To seek that which universally encompasses the capacities of sentient beings, directly points to the essence of mind, and proclaims the nature of true ultimate reality—this is it.

It establishes the definitive, true, and perfect penetration, enabling people to master external objects so that they may, like the Tathāgata, transcend the stage of no-more-learning with a mere snap of the fingers;

nothing surpasses the *Śūraṅgama*. To explain its name, it signifies that all phenomena are ultimately firm and solid—what is called "penetrating to the very source of dharmas, unmoving and indestructible.
Furthermore, the secret cause of the Tathāgatas and the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas all derive their beginning from this.

This is it; one returns to the ultimate by means of this alone. Examining what is expounded therein: it discusses the perfect principle to clarify true nature and opens up the perfect practice to demonstrate true cultivation.
As for that nature, both essence and function are simultaneously manifested; as for that cultivation, cause and fruit are unified in a single accord.

"Examining the beginning and tracing back to the end" is a teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). This is truly because various practitioners turn their backs on the truth and head toward delusion, failing to achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.

Some cherish the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and consider a small attainment sufficient; others fail to eliminate the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and allow their learning to become a source of fault.
Thus, with Ānanda’s extensive learning and perverse attachments serving as conditions, the Great Teaching was brought forth, and the World-Honored One—

He addressed them, saying: "The continuous cycle of birth and death for all sentient beings arises entirely from their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature.
By employing various false thoughts, and because these thoughts are not true, there is this wheeling through saṃsāra. He further said:
"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices and serves as the single gateway for the Tathāgatas of the ten directions."

To transcend the Path of Sublime Adornment—this is surely the fundamental principle for the practice of the Way. From this, one breaks through the攀緣 (pān-yuan, objective attachments) of the seven locations and distinguishes the two kinds of roots.
Through seeing, the mind is revealed; through the mind, seeing is revealed. Although mind and seeing reveal each other, the primary revelation resides in the mind.
It is like the metaphor of a blind man gazing into darkness to illustrate that seeing is not the eye, or as when one bends one's fingers and flicks a light.
Verifying that it is immovable, one observes that the river does not change; comparing it to the hanging hand, one sees there is nothing omitted.

Discerning through the "eight returns" and selecting among various objects, one finds neither expansion nor contraction, neither right nor wrong. This causes one to realize that the pure, perfect true mind is falsely manifested as form, emptiness, hearing, and seeing.
Having realized that these are false manifestations, one may still harbor doubts regarding their confusion and intermixture; therefore, the "natural cause" is further refuted.

By showing that what is perceived as seeing is not actually seeing, and by combining the distinct karmic activities of various individuals to point out that seeing arises from delusion, he uses one person as an example for many people, and one country as an example for all countries, thereby revealing in general that the physical world, the sense organs, and the body are all equally illusory.
Moving from the shallow to the deep, and from the narrow to the broad, although he employs manifold methods to reveal their falsity, that which is revealed is ultimately only the True. Thus...
Furthermore, the aggregates (*skandhas*), bases (*āyatanas*), realms (*dhātus*), and extensively the seven great elements are brought together and integrated into the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

This causes one to realize that things and self share the same root and that right and wrong are of one substance; that delusion has no inherent nature, and that its entire body is precisely this [Tathāgatagarbha].

All phenomena of the ten realms, both the environment and the sentient beings therein, are merely manifestations arising in accordance with karma. Since awakening is itself the truth, yet one still remains deluded regarding these karmic manifestations, therefore [the text] further...

In response to the question regarding mountains, rivers, and the great earth, [the text] profoundly investigates the causes of their arising. It is likened to empty space, which does not obstruct the manifestation of all phenomena;

it reveals that the true, wondrous, awakened clarity and brightness universally illumine the Dharma-realm, wherein the one and the many respond to one another and the small and the large contain one another.
This is both essence and function, neither mundane nor transcendent. When one reaches the state of departing from "is" and "is-not," and being neither "is" nor "is-not," then it is the *ālaya*-mind.
The wondrous nature does not involve names or words. Furthermore, the analogy of a madman running while looking into a mirror is cited to show that delusion has no cause.

This concludes the reprimand of mere erudition and the exhortation to cultivate the outflow-free (anāsrava) state. Generally speaking, all of this pertains to the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*).

Although understanding may be perfect, it cannot be realized without practice. Therefore, the two definitive meanings are further clarified: first, examining the ground and generating the aspiration for enlightenment to subdue and sever ignorance, which serves as the cultivation.
The essentials for practicing this are as follows: Next, one must examine the root of the afflictions and discern which faculty is most perfect, as this serves as the basis for initiating practice.

Thereupon, one determines the relative superiority and inferiority of the six faculties and causes them to enter deeply through a single gateway. By striking a bell, one tests the permanence [of hearing]; by tying a cloth, one demonstrates the formation of knots.
The Dharma-gates realized by the twenty-five sages are presented, and it is decreed that the faculty of hearing be selected as the expedient means for beginners. Furthermore, one is taught...
The rules for collecting the mind and establishing the *maṇḍala* lead to hearing the fourfold grave precepts and the *uṣṇīṣa-raśmi-dhāraṇī*.
Generally speaking, these are all practices of perfect cultivation. Even through the three stages of progressive advancement, one achieves the fifty-five positions of the true path to Bodhi.

Although this discusses the positions of realization, it does not exhaustively detail the causal practices; furthermore, the karmic habits of the precepts involve the emotional perceptions of the seven realms of existence.
Guarding meditative concentration against the demonic deceptions of the five aggregates is nothing other than the practice of the gate of non-action.
Only when one aims for the perfection of Bodhi and returns to the state of non-attainment can it be called the ultimate, firm realization.
Thus, based on the principle of ultimate firmness, one establishes the practice of ultimate firmness; by cultivating the practice of ultimate firmness, one realizes [the fruit].

The principle of ultimate solidity is, for the most part, the purport of the *Śūraṅgama* teachings. Thus we know that among the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle, the *Śūraṅgama* is designated as the definitive (nītārtha) exposition;
there is nothing superior to this. The commentator on the sūtra takes the principle and practice together as the orthodox core (*zhengzong*), and divides the rest of the text into five sections:
first, the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*); second, the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); third, the Realization of the Fruit (*phalaprāpti*); fourth, the Conclusion of the Sūtra; and fifth...
Aiding the Path: This refers to practicing the Path after seeing it, and realizing the fruit after practicing the Path; such is indeed the standard sequence.

However, when examining the cultivation and realization of those of superior faculties, there are instances such as "attaining the Dharma-body without passing through the kalpas" following the revelation of the nature of the storehouse consciousness, or "the doubts being eliminated and the mind awakening to the true reality" prior to entering the jeweled hall.

Moreover, how could it be limited to the ordinary? How great is this Teaching! For those who wish to give rise to the truth, return to the source, clarify the mind, and perceive their nature, they should devote themselves to this with all their heart.
Yet there is no teaching in this scripture that is not included, and no capacity for understanding that is not encompassed.

Sometimes the words are partial while the meaning is complete; sometimes the names are identical while the substance differs. Those of dull and inferior faculties may fail to comprehend these points; let the propagators of the scripture reflect upon them.
To facilitate understanding, I have accordingly provided an explanation. From the Tang through the Song dynasties, there were some ten or more commentators.
Initially, I consulted the exegeses of Master Changshui Xuan, Master Gushan Yuan, and Master Wenling Huan;
I further examined the compendium of Master Wuxing Yue, and additionally obtained the works of Masters Zizhong Yuan, Zhenji Jie, Zhulin Min, and Xingfu Kuo.

In their underlying intent, there is nothing that does not share a great harmony; it is only because their perspectives may each follow a particular strength that they cannot help but differ slightly.

This causes practitioners to weep at the fork in the road, unable to distinguish the true guide. Thus, the peril of failing to reach the goal lies not with those [teachers], but with this [situation].
Now, I have synthesized the essential commentaries of various schools to open up the main path. Those points that do not accord with the public consensus...

I have edited this work. Those passages that differ yet are mutually compatible have been preserved together; those that challenge and clarify one another have been selected after careful examination of their core evidence.
Where there were occasional omissions, obscurities, or contradictions, I have appended my own interpretations as supplementary notes.

Since these diverse streams are now united and flow into the same ocean, it is called the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Commentary). Alas! The Way is fundamentally wordless, yet it is not revealed without words.

The Buddha spoke because he could not help it. If his words failed to reach others and the Way remained unilluminated, then the words of the various masters would likewise have no choice but to express themselves.
Since words are numerous and divergent, they drift further from the Way; thus, how could those who synthesize and interpret them allow themselves to remain silent?
Once the interpretations have been synthesized, it is hoped that readers will, by means of these syntheses, [attain understanding].
To know the words of others is to know the words of the Buddha by means of those words of others. Once the words of the Buddha are known, that which is ultimate and firm is attained.
To speak of practice, principle, teaching, Chan, the realization of the Way, or the life of wisdom—all are but superfluous words;
how much more so the so-called "understanding" and "realization"? Written on the day of the Buddha’s Enlightenment in the second year of the Zhizheng era, the Renwu year. Narrated.
In Shizi Lin (Lion Grove) within the city of Gusu,
Shi’an delivered this discourse.
The attendant Zhizhe of Songling was given the name "Stone Hut" (Shi'an). He requested a discourse from me. I asked him in surprise, "Dasu’s 'Wooden Hut' was a hut carved from wood;
Shitou’s 'Grass Hut' was a hut woven from grass. What do you mean by your 'Stone Hut'?
Is it that you sit amidst rows of stubborn stones like Sengzhong’s lecture platform? Or is it that you pile ten thousand stones to form a circular wall?"

Is it like stone pavilions, stone halls, and stone porches? Is it that one carves and opens up a stone mountain to create rafters, eaves, pillars, walls, doors, windows, beds, seats, and utensils—all of stone?
Is it because one prizes its hardness and stubbornness, thinking it will not decay as easily as grass or wood?
If so, then to attack the hard and strike the stubborn, their completion would not be more difficult than [building with] grass.
"Is it made of wood? Or is it a chamber moved by supernatural power, like the stone cell where Kāśyapa entered meditative absorption?
Or is it a grotto fashioned by heaven and earth, like the rock dwelling where Gaganagañja sat in quietude? Zhixu laughed and replied:

How could Shigan (Stone Hermitage) be like this? I practice the teachings and contemplations of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Now, my "Shigan" is an alternative designation for the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The hermitage being stone is the Dharma-realm of principle (*li-fajie*); the stone being the hermitage is the Dharma-realm of phenomena (*shi-fajie*). Stone is the hermitage;

the hermitage is stone—this is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wuai fajie*). According to whatever objects exist, there is not a single thing that is not the Stone Hermitage.

This is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of all phenomena. Once the principle of the Dharma-realm is manifest, the meanings of the general and the particular, difference and identity, and formation and disintegration are preserved therein.
One who realizes this meaning points to a single speck of dust or a single grain of sand as a stone hermitage;
it is not narrow. He expands the void of the ten directions into a stone hermitage; it is not broad. He dwells in solitude, separated from the multitude; it is not one. The three periods of time...
From the Tathāgata and the boundless bodhisattvas down to the seers, ghosts, and animals, they dwell amidst one another in dense profusion;
yet this multiplicity does not constitute a plurality. This oneness and multiplicity are mutually fused, and its breadth and narrowness are sovereign and free.

This is neither something that can be brought about by the power of artificial spiritual feats, nor is it something that can be known by Kāśyapa or Śāriputra. It is a matter with which Shitou and Daguī may be discussed as peers.
Ah! Having heard this, I was both startled and delighted. I have therefore penned these responses as an exposition for Shí Ān.
As for the "Exposition on Sincerity" (Chéng Ān Shuō), sincerity is the ultimate limit of faith. When faith reaches the state of sincerity, the Great Foundation finds its establishment, and the Way...

It can indeed be accomplished. Sincerity (*cheng*) is the ultimate of the truly real, the ultimate of purity, and the ultimate of constancy. Because it is the pinnacle of reality, it is free from delusion;

because it is the pinnacle of purity, it is free from admixture; because it is the pinnacle of constancy, it is unceasing. That which is free from delusion is sincerity as it exists within the ontological essence (*li-ti*);
that which is free from admixture is sincerity manifested in phenomenal appearances (*shi-xiang*); and that which is unceasing is sincerity in its responsive function.
This is the wondrous function. Because of the sincerity of its fundamental principle, everything from the vastness of heaven and earth down to the minute of dust and hair is established through it.
Because of the sincerity of its phenomenal manifestations, the myriad phenomena within the void of the dharma-realm are arrayed in dense profusion, interacting without obstruction.
Because of the sincerity of its wondrous function, illusions come and go, beginning and ending, arising and ceasing.
Extinction and transformation manifest inexhaustibly. Thus, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, embodied this sincerity and attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions take this sincerity as the foundation for the six perfections and myriad practices.

As for the worldly dharmas—cultivation, rectification, regulation, and governance—they likewise take sincerity of intention as their fundamental basis. Reaching this point, the significance of sincerity is vast indeed. Now...
If one takes sincerity as the hermitage, then even the subtle dust motes of the oceans of lands—whether sages or ordinary beings—are all within a single gate from which they emerge and dwell.

If one takes the hermitage as sincerity, then such acts as tilling the soil, cutting the thatch, hauling wood, drawing water, raising a fist, or pointing a finger are all the natural functioning of the Way of one's own original nature.
Thus, the title "Sincerity Hermitage" (Cheng-an) is surely not something easily attained.
I trust that you, Venerable Shangren, will exert yourself in this endeavor.
Yunhai says:
I once leaned against the railing with the Elder Huanzhu at Liyu Pavilion on Lion Rock. At that time, the summer heat was intense.
The air was clear and serene; the morning sun shone like the moon. Looking down, the clouds lay spread out, a single expanse of azure as vast as the sea.
