Peaks near and far emerged above the clouds, appearing like fallen caps, like floating sandals, or like empty boats setting their rudders free amidst silver waves.

We sighed together in wonder, saying, "How extraordinary is this ocean of clouds! Before long, they rolled up from the earth and rose upward like ten thousand cavalry charging forward, then transformed once more.
They appeared as wondrous peaks, as jade trees, and as soaring dragons and dancing phoenixes; yet before long, not even a hair’s breadth of them could be found.

A guest stepped forward and said, "Now, observing this illusion of the cloud-sea, I have finally realized that the multiplicity of all things and the vastness of heaven and earth are but a single cloud-sea. The old man said, "You know that the illusion is an illusion, but..."
One does not yet know the illusion that is non-illusion; one knows the illusion that is non-illusion, yet does not yet know that which constitutes its non-illusory nature.
Now, that which gathers to become the sea is cloud; that which transforms into manifold things is also cloud.
What is it that constitutes this "cloud"? The guest was at a loss for a reply. He withdrew and composed a chapter on "Cloud and Sea," which I have often sung.
I harmonized with it; it was the pinnacle of the profound realization attained at that time. Alas! Times have changed and circumstances have diverged;
the Elder has passed away, and I and my guests have scattered to the four quarters. How few are those who can understand the sentiments stirred within my heart!
There was a śramaṇa from Gaochang named Yunhai, who encountered me at Wutai and sought a word to authenticate his name. Moved by compassion, I granted him this.
Yet he raised his voice to address him, saying: "The western peak rises in staggering ten-thousand-fathom heights; with a single leap of its golden-haired lion, the rocky caverns are emptied.
Heaven is desolate and the world has grown old, yet no trace remains; through a thousand cliffs and ten-thousand ravines, the autumn wind sighs in sorrow.

Previously you wandered aimlessly east and west, your straw sandals worn through, yet there was no news. Now that the year draws to a close and the rivers are empty, the roads are cold; foxes and hares run wild across the land."
Filled with thorns—who could ascend for me once more those ten-thousand-fathom crags? Together at the roots of pines, we sweep away the moss upon the stones.
At the hearth where yams are roasted, there is the smoke of frost-leaves; in the boiling common cauldron, there is the snow-eyed spring.
Summoning sea-clouds from the four fields, I recite the ancient verses of the Cloud-Sea. The sea becomes cloud and retreats into my chamber; the cloud becomes...
The sea covers the mountains and rivers everywhere; the man of the Way cares not for sun or rain.
He sits watching the clouds and seas transform and rise, undaunted that the Buddha-dharma may crumble away in three thousand years.

"An 'abrupt cliff' (duan ya) refers to that which is said to split the void; it is called a 'cliff' because it stands upright for ten thousand fathoms. Flying birds dare not cross it, and returning clouds cannot settle upon it.
Those who behold it are struck with awe, and those who hear of it feel sorrow in their hearts. This is where the Great Spirit (Juli) raised his hand and cleft the Great..."
This refers to cases such as Huairang’s “A koṭi of shouts” that opened the stone cliff. What is called "severance" (duan) is the non-arising of a single thought;

what is called a "precipice" (ya) is standing out in solitary existence. Sweeping away views and understandings to directly reveal the root source, it passes through a single thread like the "tiger-trap" mechanism;
it cuts through all doubts like a hair-cutting sword. A difference of even a hair’s breadth leaves heaven and earth worlds apart. This is Linji.
This is precisely the occasion for Deshan’s staff and shout. "Ceasing study and non-action" is called the severance; "having no path to climb" is called the precipice.
To shatter the dead-lock barrier and penetrate the all-encompassing net is like a lion cub who knows how to turn itself around by its own power.
Without employing the occasions of staff or shout, and without falling into the tracks of language, one leaves Deshan and Linji with no way to catch up. Vast!
The spiritual Kūṭi is beyond the reach of the gaze; this, moreover, is the wondrous function of the Elder Tiānmù Duànyá.
The Elder once raised the meaning of Duànyá to challenge me, and I was about to employ this very principle to resolve it. When my words reached this point—
The old man rose abruptly and withdrew, saying, "You slander me! You revile me! Please stop and do not speak. Thereupon, he ceased.
Qingyin said, "In the past, a guest passed by me and said: 'How defiled is the sticky glue of worldly dust, and how turbulent is the clamor of the human realm!'"
"Is it already time? I intend to distance myself from worldly entanglements and withdraw from my social circle in order to seek a life of pure seclusion.
Would this be acceptable? I then asked him, "What do you mean by 'pure seclusion'? He replied, "Sleeping alone on a solitary peak, dwelling deep within a thatched cottage;

a single boat upon the misty waves, ten thousand pines as one's cloud-roofed house—is this not the pure seclusion of the ancients? I said, "Alas! You are merely clinging to their outward traces. As for what I..."

Those who have heard of this differ from it; let me attempt to discuss it. There is the pure seclusion of true emptiness (*tathatā*), there is the pure seclusion of illusory existence, and there is the pure seclusion of absolute transcendence.
As for true emptiness: it does not oppose the various sensory objects (*dharmas*) nor does it take them as companions;
in the pure realm of suchness, all is obliterated and never again exists. As for illusory existence: it is like reflections in a mirror.
The reflection of the moon in water appearing in a mirror is not disturbed by external conditions; it is pure. Yet, if one seeks that reflection within the mirror, the reflection cannot be grasped;
it is hidden. The same is true for the moon in water. Although these two states are without attachment, they still depend upon something else.
That which transcends dependence is empty yet not empty, not empty yet empty, existent yet not existent, and not existent yet existent.
There is purity; it is hidden within this very midst. If you understand this, then even flowing with the current and merging with the turbid is not inherently impure;
even standing solemnly before ten thousand people is not inherently a lack of seclusion. This purity and this seclusion do not even adhere to the extremes of emptiness or existence.
"How much more so its traces! The guest said, "How profound! O Qingyin, I have received your instruction. He thanked him and withdrew.
Now, the Chan master Haishan Zhi has requested a text from me concerning Qingyin. I have long since ceased my interest in writing;
therefore, I shall relate to him the words I once spoke to that guest.
Gaoquan said:
"I was traveling with Xun Dao-lin to visit Cold Spring. On the way, we passed by Jade Spring and watched the fish. Suddenly, mountain rain arrived, so we entered Lingfeng Temple.
There, the monk Mishi, whose courtesy name was Gaoquan, invited us to sit in the depths of the Yunshen (Cloud-Deep) hermitage and asked for paper."
Gaoquan said, "I have discussed this with him, saying: 'A spring on a mountain is already a marvel; one that rises high upon the mountain is even more marvelous;
and one that, being high, can flow forth to benefit the world and nourish all things is a complete marvel.
Yet while springs on mountains are many, those that possess this complete marvel are always few. Cold Springs and Jade Springs are not without their wonders.'"
It is unfortunate that it is not high. It enters West Lake to carry songs and dances;
it pools in square ponds for fish to swim. Is this sufficient to exhaust its utility? As for Gulian Spring at Mount Kuanglu, it is indeed high;
yet Lu Ji said it was suitable for tea. As for Nangquan Spring emerging from Langya, it is indeed high; yet Ou-yang Xiu said—
"It is fit for wine; its flying cascade falls straight down three thousand feet. This describes the topography of Gaoquan by Li Zhexian.
"How could the mountain brooks and gullies ever detain it? This indicates the direction of Gaoquan’s course by the Tang patriarch.
These two [streams]—one emptying into the river and one reaching the sea—are both insufficient to fully manifest their wondrousness. Such is the Dharma of our lineage, the Lotus Sūtra.
There are those who say that one who digs at the source to seek water relies upon a high spring as a metaphor for the method of seeking the Way, yet no such actual spring exists.
Now, among these several [analogies], what do you take from this "high spring"? Mi replied, "That which I desire lies in digging at the source.
Thereupon, Daolin joyfully said to me, "The entirety of its excellence lies herein. Please [accept it]."
I wrote this and left it for him.
Regarding "Juetong" (Ceasing to Listen):
I heard from a fellow villager that the record of these writings uses "Juetong" as a distinct title. In the autumn of the Gengchen year, we met at Mount Jing; he requested [this].
This is for the purpose of attachment to words. I said: "The true essence of the teaching in this land resides in the purity of hearing.
Can hearing be severed? Sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; because they follow sounds, they transmigrate. Can hearing not be kept from being severed?

For the Sage uses words to manifest the Principle, so that those who hear may contemplate and cultivate it. To merely accumulate what one hears without applying oneself to contemplation and cultivation is in vain."

Thus, to be deluded regarding the fundamental and to follow after sounds is a fault no small matter; herein lies the principle of "severing the hearing. This principle of severing the hearing has both shallow and deep dimensions.
The shallow pertains to cultivation (*xiū*), while the deep pertains to the nature (*xìng*). Cultivation involves effort (*yònggōng*), whereas the nature is effortless.
As for turning back the hearing to escape sound, forgetting words to enter the principle: when a single faculty returns to its source, the six functions cease and restore themselves.

This is what is meant by "severing the hearing through cultivation"; it is not like Danxia covering his ears as a precept against sound, nor like Baizhang being deafened by a shout—such is the severing of hearing.
Once the faculties and their objects have dissolved, emptiness and awareness become perfectly pure; every land and every particle of dust is my wondrous nature.
Yet, throughout the dust-motes and the lands, there is not a single sound that does not arise from the movement of nature. There is no one who can hear, and no object that is heard.
This is the hearing of my own nature, inherently and naturally severed from [external objects].

How could it be like the "insentient" severance of hearing—wherein the iron ox fears not the lion’s roar and the stone woman is not startled by thunder? Nevertheless, I have further heard this: long ago, the Great Tree Kinnara...
When King Nala played a single strain of song, it shook the great trichiliocosm; even Mount Sumeru surged and submerged because of it.
If so, can even insentient things hear? If insentient things can hear, by what means would they cease to do so?
This is not something I dare to speak presumptuously; one must surely add a word of one’s own.
Yingshan says that mountains resemble humans.
Their temperaments, appearances, and physical forms vary in ten thousand ways: some are grotesque, some are extraordinary; some are jagged, irregular, concave, convex, bulbous, or emaciated.
Each is thus according to what it has been endowed with. Speaking in terms of appearance, there are places where no plants or trees grow.
A mountain devoid of trees is called a "child-mountain" (tóngshān). One that is overgrown and desolate from birth is called a "waste-mountain" (huángshān).

One where fine timber and exotic flora flourish luxuriantly, and where springs are secluded and rocks are wondrous, is called "refined" (xiù) or "flourishing" (huá). When it is both flourishing and refined, the world may sometimes call it an "excellent mountain" (yīngshān).
That which the excellent mountain receives from Heaven must necessarily be profound in substance and abundant in its vital energy; only then can such qualities be brought forth.
Furthermore, while mountains resemble humans, there are also aspects in which they cannot be compared. Humans possess the power of cultivated learning and the merit of self-preservation;
when they fill their inner being with virtue and morality, what manifests externally is a serene countenance and a radiant aura that extends from face to back.
Moreover, their literary works and exemplary conduct become increasingly prominent day by day. This is how one is able to manifest one's own brilliance. If, however, one does not reflect upon this...
When one brings about the destruction and injury of what has been bestowed upon them, such states as "waste" and "barrenness" ensue.
These are all matters of humanity and heaven; how could they be the business of mountains? Upon hearing this discourse, the Venerable Xiū of Yīngxīng bowed twice and requested, saying:

"I am named Yīngshān (Heroic Mountain). There is a lesson in this name. I would be grateful for your grace in instructing me so that I may use it for self-reproach. Therefore, I have written this for him.
Regarding the discourse on "Non-thought," Master Sian of Yunju questioned me on the meaning of the term "non-thought. I replied that there are three aspects of non-thought:

when a thunderclap shakes the earth and the mountains tremble, the ears of the clay ox do not cover them; when a white blade flashes in the air and ghosts and gods weep, the wooden man... [remains unmoved].
The horse’s pupils do not flicker; this is the state of insentient oblivion where thought ceases.

To let go with both hands atop a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, to pour oil into a bronze sandalwood gong—seizing the essential ford where the wind is high and the current swift, one sweeps away all traces of practice until the path is cut off and the gate hangs empty.
"This is non-thought that severs the攀緣 (pān-yuan, object-dependent clinging) of this sitting. When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are simultaneously stilled;

the past and future limits are severed, and the sentiment of birth-and-death is forgotten. This is the non-thought of the emptiness of the mind. Regarding these three [types of non-thought], where will you, my son, abide?
He replied, "It is not so. Within a single moment of my thought, I fully contain the Dharma-realm; it is not merely the emptiness of the mind. All things..."
Interacting with and responding to all capacities simultaneously is not a matter of cutting off all activity. A wooden horse dances upon the three terraces;
a clay ox fights its way into the sea. This is not a state of dull insensibility. It is like the reflection of the moon falling into rivers and seas, making no distinction between shallow and deep.
It is like a lotus flower emerging from mud and water, adhering to neither defilement nor purity. Thus, it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; it acts without acting. Because of this—
"Is it possible to be without thought? I then held up my fist to show him, and then opened my hand to show him again. He was at a loss for words;
with a single laugh, he departed.
— Recorded by Chùnguk.
The Way in man is like spring in a valley. Yet, there have been those in the world who debate the story of Zou Yan blowing his pitch-pipe so that spring returned to the cold valley.
Some say it was moved by the resonance of the human heart; others say it was merely a coincidence of celestial timing. Heaven and man—no one can distinguish between them.
Furthermore, when discussing how even a square inch of soil contains the nature of spring, they say: "The valley is my own body; spring is my own function."
Furthermore, when discussing how the Yang energy emerges and there is no hard ground, it is said that "Spring is the essence (tǐ) and the valley is the function (yòng).
Yet, even between essence and function, they cannot be distinguished. I once had a verse that says: "The Yang harmony with feet travels everywhere across the earth."
In the empty mountains, a gentle warm breeze arises; one knows not who within can hear it. One call is made, and there is a response to each call.
A commentator further says: "This is the valley of spring (*chun-gok*), wherein the many and the single are identical, and the small and the large are mutually contained.
If such a valley of spring exists within every grain of sand, every stone, every blade of grass, and every tree, then the grasses, trees, sands, and stones are all one valley of spring."
It is thus. When it fills a single nation, that nation becomes a spring valley. When it extends universally to every atom of a buddha-field, those atomic fields become a single spring valley.
Their mutual identity and mutual containment are such that they can no longer be distinguished.
The Venerable Karmadāna He of Wulin is named Chonggu (Spring Valley). I have thus broadly illustrated this for him; may he discern it.
Regarding this, Wenjiang (Textual River) says that eastward down from Luling there is a river called Wenjiang. It is deep and wide, broad and level; for forty li it flows without any bends.
It narrows. Its upper reaches consist of the two rivers, Zhang and Gong, which emerge from the Eighteen Rapids and converge with the waters of the various prefectures of Yongxin and Tàihé.
Fierce and raging, they clash and surge with a force that cannot be resisted. It is only upon reaching this point that the waves begin to resolve;

the ripples flow and drift, neither hurried nor slow, possessing an air of self-satisfaction. This is what is called the "Patterned River" (Wénjiāng). Thus it has been handed down by the elders of old.

Regarding the geomantic features of this site, a prophecy states: "The Wen River is deep and elegant; surely there shall arise in this world teachers of morality and virtue, and men of loyalty and integrity.
I have examined the period from the Tang through the Song dynasties, and among the patriarchs of the Chan school was Qingyuan Xingsi;
among scholars was the Duke Wenzhong of Ouyang; and at the end of the Song, there was Wen Tianxiang. Over several centuries, such figures were few indeed.
Why do the prophecies of Heshenxiu not come true more often? Nevertheless, the nature of virtue, wisdom, loyalty, and goodness is rooted in humanity;
who does not possess it? Extraordinary monks and eminent scholars have appeared in every age. What I mentioned previously was merely to cite those who were preeminent and renowned in their eras.
The Abbot Yuzang of Daochang Mountain on Mount Hu was born in the same year as I in Lushan.
He overstepped the bounds of propriety by styling himself "Wenjiang" (Literary River). During this autumn when the groves and shrubs were falling into decay, we met unexpectedly in a foreign land;
thus, he again invoked the prophecy of Wenjiang to encourage me.
Regarding the person from Dongzhou who styled himself Dongzhou, he was a native of the coastal regions. I once questioned him, saying: "Surrounding Mount Sumeru are four great continents;
the eastern one is called Pūrvavideha, and the southern one is called Jambudvīpa. Now, as for this continent of Jambudvīpa, its east and west..."
Its breadth is calculated at two hundred and eighty thousand *li*. Among these, there are countless small islands scattered and separated by vast distances.
Thus, that island situated to the east where the country is named Zhendan (China) is the eastern sub-continent of Jambudvīpa.
"Do you currently reside on this [island] and take it as your designation? He replied, "No. Thereupon, he questioned him further: "As for the accumulated waters..."
This refers to the ocean. Within the ocean, that which can be inhabited is called an island (*dvīpa*).

At a time when the mountain-like waves and billows surge and overflow, such that they inundate everything, an island enables those crossing to find a place of refuge and those dwelling there to find peace. Thus, the contribution of the island to the ocean is great indeed.
To use the human mind as an analogy: its objective realm is like the wind and consciousness is like the waves, which together fan and stir one another, pounding [the mind] like a mortar.
The emotions of collision and violent impulse drift and surge; the conditions of drowning and submersion are perilous and urgent. The nature of this anxiety and suffering cannot be fully described.
There must be one who provides skillful rescue to save them, enabling them to find their proper place. Only then will those in anxiety rejoice and those in suffering find joy.
The calamities of peril, hardship, and distress will have no way to reach you. Now, the teaching of our Buddha and our Patriarchs has come from the West to the East;
by providing relief according to where people find peace, is its benevolence not indeed great?
Thus, your name is not a sea of accumulated water, but the sea of your own mind. Your title is not the "Victorious Body" (Śrīkāya).
"Danzhi’s Eastern Island is the Eastern Island of one's own mind. Your resolve must first contemplate saving yourself, and only thereafter contemplate saving others.
Is it by this principle that you name yourself 'Eastern Island'? Haizhi replied, 'Yes. I admire his resolve;
therefore, I record these words to present to him, so that he shall not forget that which he alone holds fast to."
Record of Huìqǐng Chán Monastery in Wú Commandery:
Approximately five li west of the city of Gūsū, pine forests and willow-lined streams reflect one another like a painting; there stands a multi-storied pavilion and a spacious hall.
Rising above the treetops and vying for height with the Western Mountains is Huiqing Chan Temple.

Although the temple does not rank among the ancient sites, its reputation for spiritual transformation resounds far and wide, drawing both monastics and laypeople there like a bustling marketplace; this is due to the influence of Chan Master Puan.
Initially, Puan spread his transformative teachings at Nanyuan Mountain in Yuan, where his monastic center flourished to become the foremost in the world before his passing.

Although it has long been renowned throughout the world as possessing spiritual efficacy, officials and commoners alike pray to it during droughts, floods, epidemics, and calamities, as well as for matters concerning ritual prohibitions and the construction of buildings;
its responses are as swift as an echo.

The Great Yuan Emperor posthumously honored him as Chan Master Dade Huiping. Yearly offerings of incense and silk, along with the alms of the common people, were presented in such abundance that there was not a single inch of land left for his own sustenance.
His followers always numbered several thousand, and his transformative influence had almost entirely spread throughout the regions of the Yangtze, Xiang, Huai, and Han rivers;
yet it alone had not reached Wu. Was its arrival dependent upon the timing? Or must it wait for the right person before it can proceed? Yan...
In the spring of the Jiǎyín year, the śramaṇa Zōngcōng of Wúxiá in Nánkāng came to Wúmén to seek the Way.
Reciting the lines of Hanshān regarding the night bell, the river maples, and the fisherman’s lamp, he was moved with deep compassion within his heart.

He then devised a plan to construct a hermitage to welcome traveling monks and, to honor the Chan Master, led the local layman Jīn Guóbǎo to take the initiative in providing funds to acquire the land and oversee its completion.

Every day, his door was filled with visitors who brought shoes for him; he would daily carry his alms bowl to provide them with food. Along the Changhe River, the road to the Changguan Pass was plagued by mud and mire, causing great hardship for the local people.
Zong raised funds from the public to pave it with bricks and build bridges over it, restoring all dilapidated structures.

Indeed, there was no beneficial deed for others that he did not undertake, and whenever he acted, he invariably invoked the spiritual protection of Puan. Among those traveling on rivers and seas, many received mysterious responses and were delivered safely from wind and waves.
When [the Master] arrived, they prostrated themselves, regarding Puan as their second birth. Consequently, donors gathered in great numbers.

They subsequently constructed the Amitābha Pavilion to enshrine the Buddha, as well as a pavilion for the images of the five hundred arhats; this later became the Universal Radiance Hall (*Puguangming Dian*), where the image of Puan was enshrined.
Behind the hall was built the Great Adornment Pavilion (*Dazhuangyan Ge*), which contained the images of Vairocana Buddha and the fifty-three worthies.

Its lower section was opened to serve as a hall for expounding the Dharma. While the construction and repairs were still in full swing, Cong passed away on the first day of the seventh month of the gengwu year of the Shizhun era.
His disciple Fazhi succeeded to his will, remaining diligent day and night; thus, the regulations and scale of the institution grew increasingly expansive.
In the second year of the Yuantong era, he...
By imperial decree of the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi), the current name plaque was bestowed. As the temple was not yet fully established, the assembly all vowed to contribute their labor.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu Fahui constructed the triple gate, and Daxin built the Avalokiteśvara Hall. Yang Shanqing, a man from Shu, fashioned the outer gate;
they piled stones along the riverbank to connect it with the main thoroughfare. And Master Cao Zhezhi, the Governor of Songjiang Prefecture, constructed the wheel.
In the palace of the Treasury, King Seonnyang (Prince Sunjong) donated five thousand strings of silver to assist in the construction of a hall for the monks' residence.

Subsequently, the bell tower, the Gandha-kuṭi kitchen, the *jñāpaka* grove, the storehouse, the refectory, the two corridors, and the abbot’s quarters were all completed in succession through the collective efforts of the community.
Furthermore, a pagoda courtyard was established on Lotus Peak to the south of the temple, with the plaque inscribed: "The Return."
Truly. Within the central hall were three pagodas, sharing a single chamber but having separate burial crypts, so that both monastics and laypeople could enshrine their remains therein.

At this point, the structural integrity of the temple was fully realized. Zhi petitioned me, saying: "The final instructions of our late master were to receive all who look up to him for guidance and to ordain disciples according to their merit.
However, those who succeed to the seat are chosen by the consensus of the assembly and do not advance based on seniority. As for Fazhi, he is not [of such standing]."
My talent is insufficient to carry on this legacy; it is only by the grace of Master Puan that it has been brought to completion.

Fearing that future generations might obscure its fundamental source, I pray that you will compose a record for me. I replied: "The World-Honored One entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana to Mahākāśyapa.
It was transmitted twenty-eight times to Bodhidharma, and another ten transmissions later reached Linji. Linji [transmitted it] thirteen..."
It is traditionally said that he was Puan. Puan refined his disciples through the steep mechanisms and great functions of Linji;
without traversing the gradual stages, they reached the profound inner sanctum of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—this was the very foundation of his transformation of beings.

As for his ability to quell calamities, rescue those in distress, and respond to prayers through conditioned, functional efficacy, these were merely secondary matters. Now, Huiqing possesses his dwelling; he possesses...

It is many indeed. You must attend to the Great Root to lead and instruct, so that every person may give rise to the truth and return to the source, collectively awakening to the *pú-ān* (universal canopy) of their own self-nature.
Only then, by establishing transformations according to circumstances, shall each manifest the *pú-ān* of their own self-nature. Thus, above, you will prolong the Sage’s person;
below, you will bring blessings to the common people. In this way, the lineage of the school will flourish in future times, the banner of the Dharma will remain firm, and the sound of transformation—
How great this is! Could it be merely like this?
Regarding the Record of the Tea-Field Donation for the Shanhui Hermitage:
our Buddha attained the fulfillment of Bodhi because he did not abandon a single dharma, and because there was not a single dharma [to be abandoned].
This is not the practice of saving others. Therefore, among all those who study the Buddha-dharma, whenever they see a single deed sufficient to save others, they must courageously perform it.

Yet, deeds vary in their magnitude, and there are differences in the urgency with which one saves others. Building bridges and boats, establishing monasteries and pagodas, or sacrificing one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain—these deeds are indeed great.
However, there are also instances where a single ladle of hot water or a single sip of tea brings someone back to life.
For those on the road, the merit may even double; this is because it provides relief in times of urgency.

Along the riverbank west of the Changguan Gate in Wu Commandery lies a thoroughfare where those carrying loads on their backs or heads, those driving horses with reins, and those pulling boats with cables crowd together like swarming ants, their arms crossing and feet interlocking at the busy intersection.

Every year during the summer and autumn, the heat is extreme; the dust of the road flies like flames and the waves of the river boil and splash. People suffer from parching thirst and physical exhaustion.
There were those who perished from exhaustion, exposure, or heatstroke while resting there.

In the year Wushen of the Great [Yuan] Dynasty, the śramaṇa Huizhi of Shanhui Hermitage requested a person of influence to construct a pavilion outside the hermitage and dig a well beneath it. Each year he would solicit tea and medicinal herbs;
when the time came, he would draw clear water, boil fragrant decoctions, and personally distribute them as alms. Consequently, those who benefited from his kindness were beyond counting. (Yanyou)
Jianchi passed away, and Shenda succeeded him. Twenty years have now elapsed. Suddenly, he said to his disciples:

"In seeking [offerings] grain by grain and begging for a mere fraction, I did not dare to spare my own toil. Should those who succeed me find such labor tedious and abandon this practice, what will become of it?"
Thereupon, those moved by these words joyfully led one another to donate several fields. They further deliberated, saying:

"The fields shall be registered under the monastery, while the rice shall be stored separately, so that public and private interests do not become confused. Each year, we shall tally the surplus accumulation to prepare for droughts and floods."
In this way, there will be a constant source of resources; even if a thousand years pass, there is no need for concern. I have entrusted this record to you. I replied: "Alas!
It is easy to save oneself, but difficult to save others. For one who saves others, it is easy to apply what remains from one's own efforts, but difficult to seek it from others."
To seek out others in order to assist them may be easy for a brief moment, but it is difficult to sustain over the long term.
Now, although providing tea and soup to others is a most minor matter, [you] have spent your entire life visiting and seeking them out; your resolve has not diminished despite these trivialities.

Since you are already able to maintain the precept against becoming weary until the end, you further strive diligently to plan for the distant future. Were it not for one who possesses the insight and vision of the Buddha, how could you be so tireless?
If one does not repay the labor of others with a corresponding gift, it burdens oneself; will it not further burden one’s descendants for infinite generations?
Those who come after should know that the practice of aiding others must be undertaken, and they should know that in the Way of Perfect Enlightenment, not a single dharma may be abandoned.
May those who read this surely be moved by it and exert themselves therein; therefore, I do not decline to compose this record.
Record of the Stūpa for the Relics of the Universal Respondent National Preceptor (Puying Guoshi).
In the autumn of the Guihai year of the Zhizhi era, my late teacher, Master Zhongfeng, entered nirvana at Shiziyan on Western Mount Tianmu.
His disciples erected a stūpa to the west of the cliff and interred his entire body therein. The second year of the Tianli era... Quanzhang... [text fragment].
The Palace Academician Yu Ji, by imperial decree, composed this stele inscription. He named the stupa Fayun (Dharma Cloud).
In the year Jiaxu of the Yuantong era, the present Emperor bestowed upon him the title National Preceptor Puying and granted his recorded sayings for inclusion in the Buddhist canon.
The Imperial Supervisor of Arts and Literature, Jie Xisi, was commanded to compose the preface.

The details of his spiritual practice, his eloquence, his lineage of dharma transmission and its succession, his life of renunciation and transformation, and the weight of the imperial gifts bestowed upon him over successive reigns are all clearly presented in this inscription and preface.
In the winter of that year, a separate stupa was erected at Yunju Chan Hermitage on Qibao Mountain in Hangzhou to enshrine his remaining hair-relics.
The stupa itself was made into a shrine, where a rock-carved portrait of him was installed for veneration.

The śramaṇa Zhuyue, who resided at the hermitage, planned to record its origins upon a stone. He visited me and said: "Initially, the National Teacher did not wish to remain in secular life; his parents were concerned..."
In the neighborhood lived Yang Miaoxi, a former palace lady from the old Song dynasty who had become a *nüguan* (female Daoist priest) following the teachings of Laozi.

Recognizing that the Master was no ordinary vessel, she persuaded his parents to allow him to leave the household life. When he shaved his head, she further assisted by providing the monastic certificate (*sengdie*) and robes;
she then took a small portion of the hair that had been shorn, stored it in an incense casket, and enshrined it in a pure chamber. After several days...
In his later years, śarīra relics began to grow from his hair; over time, they increased in number until more than fifty had accumulated, shimmering with five colors.

Those who beheld them were struck with wonder and amazement. From that point on, Yang changed his studies to study Buddhism. Upon reaching old age, he entrusted the relics to Yunju (Yunju Temple), for he clearly had a specific intention in doing so.
Furthermore, regarding the founding of Yunju, it was achieved through the transformative power of the National Teacher, which [Yang] had not yet attained.
In response, I wish to record these auspicious omens through the legacy of the Yang family, to inform the descendants of the hermitage. I say:
the National Teacher succeeded to the lineage of Linji when it was on the verge of extinction and proclaimed its Way with great vigor, universally responding to the capacities of all beings.

From the coasts of the sea within and without, its influence spread like a galloping wind or a crashing thunderclap, reaching from our own followers to those of other teachings, and extending upward to kings, dukes, and gentlemen.
From the street children below to the wives at the hearth, all were imbued with this transformation and led one another to ascend to the realm of the sages and worthies.
Such was the universality and greatness of its response. As for Yang’s obtaining a śarīra through the impulse of faithful aspiration, this is merely a minor instance of a hidden response;
how could it be worth recording? The intention behind observing the moon is to allow future generations to behold it.
A minor verification was used to awaken his great potential; thus, it could not but be recorded.
Regarding the record of the deeds of Master Lingyun Tierniu:
his name was Chiding, and his style name was Tierniu. He was born into the Wang family of Baxi in Taizhou, Jixian. Therefore—
He was the ninth-generation descendant of Zhi, the former Minister of the Ministry of Revenue during the Song dynasty. From childhood, he abstained from meat and lived with austere purity;
he was firm in his resolve and possessed aspirations beyond the mundane world, yet worldly conditions thwarted him. In the year Gengwu of the Xianchun era, at the age of thirty-one, he passed away.

He visited Master Ken’an Qin of Xifeng Temple in Yongxin to have his hair shaved and heard the essential teaching of the separate transmission (*biezhuan*), whereby his emotional entanglements were completely released.
He subsequently relied upon Master Xueyan of Yangshan, serving in the fodder shed and practicing the *dhūta* (ascetic) observances. When Xueyan addressed the assembly, he said:
"Brothers, when you practice your work, if for seven days and nights your single thought is uninterrupted and your eyes do not meet [with distraction]..."

"Blblink! There is no place for entry. I will chop off this old monk’s head to make a ladle for scooping excrement! The Master silently grasped the meaning of these words and applied himself with vigorous diligence.
Yunyan ordered him to serve as the attendant for the purification of the assembly. When the assembly suffered from dysentery, he devoted himself entirely to their service.
Before long, the Master himself fell ill. As his condition grew critical and physicians declared it incurable, he took a wash-tub, went to a secluded spot, and sat upright upon it.
He strictly prohibited himself from all medicinal gruels, porridges, and drinks. For seven days, he maintained right mindfulness alone, his eyes not closing for a wink.
At midnight on the seventh night, he suddenly perceived that the mountains, rivers, great earth, grasses, trees, and forests throughout the world were like a bright moon under a snowy sky;
his own person stood majestic and vast, such that heaven and earth could not contain it. After a long while, as if hearing the sound of wood being struck, he was startled.

He awoke; sweat poured from his entire body and his illness was cured. He leaped for joy, unable to stop celebrating his own good fortune. This was indeed on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month in the year of Guiyou.
At dawn, he went to the abbot’s quarters and recounted the incident to Master Yan. Master Yan presented him with a *gong'an* (public case) to test him, and his responses were unhindered.
Master Yan then showed him a verse, which said: "What is this bright and lucid awareness? In the blink of an eye, it has already been missed."
The tally-stick by the latrine emitted a brilliant light. [He realized: "All along, this has been nothing other than myself. In the Wuyin year of the Yuan dynasty (1318), he was ordained as a monk.
The master bestowed upon him his robe and spoke this verse: "This markless field-of-merit robe, I now bestow upon you. After you have awakened to and clarified the ground of the mind,"

Like a dragon exhaling sweet rain, from that time on he followed the great assembly back to the hall. For another six years, his side did not even touch the mat. One day, he heard the Master ascend the hall and raise the question: "When a deceased monk has died and been cremated, where does he go? He offered this in his stead: [He remained silent. The Master said, "If you had answered, 'He goes to the place of no coming,' I would have approved. The Master then asked him, "Why do you not speak? He replied, "I am afraid of being wrong. The Master said, "If you had spoken, I would have given you a staff. He then asked the Master, "What about you, World-Honored One? Where do you go? The Master said, "I go to the place of no going. He then asked, "Where is the place of no going? The Master said, "It is right here before your eyes. He then asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Recently, I shared with the Elder Beyond Things (Wu-wai Chang-lao) the company of the Master Who Severs the Limits (Jue-ji Wu), knocking at the gate of his chamber. Amidst a cold brazier and a night lamp, we brewed tea and listened to the snow. He said: "Master..."

Of the old friends before our eyes, eight or nine out of ten have perished. Worldly habits shift daily, tending more and more toward the low. Only you, Master, sit firmly at Mount Jingxi, illuminating all phenomena;
compared to those who drift with the waves and follow the current, how vast is the difference! I, in my humble state, entrust myself to this hidden seclusion.
I have spent twelve years at the head of Lehe Beach; as the marshlands are vast and boundless, it was impossible for me to submit even a single formal report.
This summer, I happened to go out and stopped by a path. In the ninth month, I met with Layman Wu-ai, who inquired after my well-being, yet the details were not fully conveyed.

Because my boat waited for a favorable wind for several days without setting sail, I filled the sheets to their full capacity to provide a reply. Suddenly, a great wind arose; the boatmen beat drums and sang out, and in a single day we traveled several hundred li.
This was no less than the ancient metaphor of a fine steed galloping through the heavens. From then on, whether sailing against or with the current, it has been so. However—
There was not a single day that we did not hoist our sails. Within a few days, we had already passed Little Solitary Mountain (Xiaogu) and the Hai-men Pass.
Anchoring for the night outside the pass, I said to myself with joy: "The treacherous dangers of the Long River have now fallen behind me; the face of Mount Lu shall be visible at dawn.
My only regret was that Ziming’s boat was heading for Wuchang and would not reach Lake Kou (Hukou). I was just about to—
I boarded a boat bound for Jiangzhou. Heaven granted me a favorable opportunity; just then, a large vessel from Luling was moored alongside.
I joyfully moved my luggage to join them and said to myself with delight, "The news of reaching home lies in this. With the shimmering water and cool moonlight, I could not sleep.
I then thought that you must surely be worrying about me, unaware of my joy, while I, on the contrary, am filled with anxiety.
Your sorrow is without cause. If you understand my question regarding the son’s clear return date, then you may say that his return shall precede mine.

Thus, I have lit the lamp and written this letter, detailing the itinerary and entrusting it to report on his safety. I trust that the *Lengyanhui jie* (Commentary on the Shurangama Assembly) has already been set for carving into blocks;
I hope you will strive day and night without slackening to hasten its completion. As for the disciple’s transcription, let it be like the polishing of the Dao-lin Temple stone.
Examine this. One should keep in mind that hundreds of thousands of copies have issued from this single text; one must surely exhaust the powers of hand and eye to achieve such refinement and skill.

Regarding the forty-eight-day Great Assembly of the Bodhisattva Jù in Qiāntáng, it has already been agreed that the Dharma talk will be concluded and dispersed during the first ten days of the fifth month.
This appointment must certainly not be violated. As for my plan to turn back toward my native land—my...
I have also deliberated upon this thoroughly. On this occasion, your return by boat will surely proceed via the small stream at Changshan to reach Qiantang;

it will be both secure and favorable. Once this letter arrives, the doubts regarding the "sinking of the weight into the well" and the anxieties concerning "turning one's face away from this life" can all be resolved with a single laugh.

In response: In the second month of the Gengchen year, I parted from the Retired Scholar Xia of Jingshen at the residence of Lord Qianzhai of Lingfu. I thought that we would see one another before long;
alas, how such lack of autonomy in one’s movements can be! This year, I traveled eight thousand li to the Western River to visit my mother, and upon returning...
It has been a long time since you graced our monastery with your presence. The profound sense of longing and separation regarding life and death is beyond words.

I have not hesitated to offer my humble incense as a token of consolation, fearing it might be late compared to others. However, due to the heat of the journey, my humble body contracted a cold, from which I have suffered for two months.

Therefore, at the end of the seventh month, I first dispatched a disciple to convey these sentiments on my behalf; I hope that once my physical strength has somewhat recovered, I shall personally pay my respects.
Tian Ci: I have now received your letter and learned that the funeral rites have been solemnized and you have received the command to carry firewood and cover the mound.
What further excuse could I possibly offer? However, to proceed only after you have summoned me would only increase my sense of shame.
In response to the layman Miaokong (Prince Tulu):
When I established a thatched hut at Shizilin, you visited me repeatedly; the grasses, trees, bamboo, and rocks have gained a hundredfold in spirit and luster.

I, a disciple of little talent, am indebted for your gift of refining me like jade. Furthermore, the two marquises Shi and Hao have taken charge of providing external protection. The seventh month of autumn.
I have received the official document from the Xingyuan Court forwarded by Yuecheng. In August, I also received the *Verses of Master Fu* that you published;

through this, I see your heart to circulate the Dharma. Since you, as a layperson, harbor the vows of a Bodhisattva within while manifesting the body of a civil official without, you frequently possess the strategic resolve to tower over the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
With such a faculty and such power, you shall surely reach the state of Buddhahood.

How could even the ground where the Patriarchs have not reached be difficult to attain? It is simply because your skillful application has not yet been profound and the burdens of worldly emotion have not yet been forgotten.
Now, having examined your recent appointment, you hold the reins of the administrative code and inspire both superiors and subordinates.
While this is indeed an act consistent with what you, O Layman, habitually practice, the people of the region south of the Zhejiang River have long looked up toward you with expectant hope.
Now, fortunately, their hopes have been comforted; there is none who does not place their hands upon their foreheads in private celebration.
However, the intention of this mountain monk is otherwise. I hope that from this day forward, you, Layman, will not forget your mindfulness of the Great Dharma.

At every moment, when you have not yet fully understood or thoroughly penetrated it, you must vigilantly reflect and exert yourself in its cultivation. Suddenly, when the time arrives and conditions ripen, your public affairs—

Once you have thoroughly understood both worldly affairs and the Buddha-dharma, you shall then grasp the fundamental principles of our Way and vigorously inspire the multitudes within the three realms.
This is what will cause the patriarchal lineage and the scholars of the world to turn their gaze toward you in unison and offer their congratulations.
As the distance is great and the weather cold, I am unable to pay my respects in person; during intervals from official duties, I shall cultivate myself through the Way.
I have long been anxious,
for two years now we have not seen one another. Recently, I heard that you sit high upon the pinnacle of the throne, surveying the various provinces with the gaze of a tiger.
When one is solemn and reverent, the command is carried out without being issued.

Beyond the lifelong sustenance of a single almsbowl beneath the forest trees, and within the peaceful seclusion of settled dwelling where external disturbances do not reach, all are illuminated and reflected by his residual radiance. How could I dare forget this for even a single day?

I have often reflected that while there are indeed noble sons of high station who reside in prominent positions and faithfully admire the Buddha-dharma, how many can be found—like this lay practitioner—who refuse to settle for mere trifles and instead desire to personally reach the ground of great rest and ultimate repose?
It is likely because he has long possessed a karmic affinity with the Prajñāpāramitā; therefore, his worldly...

The world is luminously clear; one does not remain in self-obscuration. Moreover, I have heard it said that the ground of great rest and great repose does not lie on the shores of desolate wilderness or silent solitude.
It resides precisely within the midst of the blazing activity of fame, achievement, and worldly affairs. Thus it is said:
amidst the bustle of a hundred tasks and the turmoil of myriad conditions, there is, at every turn, a path for emergence. If one can, within these conditions and affairs...
Amidst the turmoil, one who can apply the eye and manifest the body in the midst of blazing activity is like refined gold of a hundred smeltings—unbreakable even when struck or cast down.
Having attained its total essence and great function, its adaptive responses are inexhaustible.

Compared to those who cling to desolate seclusion and are confined by mere fragments of knowledge, the difference between them is as vast as heaven and earth. As the ancients said: "Illusory conditions are..."
The true mark is that afflictions are themselves bodhi; its subtlety lies in this single turning. It is right here and now.

If one does not encounter gnarled roots and knotted joints, how can one distinguish a sharp tool? If it were not for the toil of worldly karma and consciousness, how could the wondrous function of the Buddhas and Patriarchs be revealed?
For example, in the past, when the Duke Qingxian of Zhao retired from his meal in the official hall and leaned against his desk, he suddenly attained realization.
They attained what belongs to their own house. Chancellor Zhang, while at Mount Doushuai, pushed and prodded [his teacher] night after night until he could not sleep;
thus, he shattered his lifelong mass of doubts. Vice-Chancellor Fan, upon being called by name by Elder Yuan Tong, recognized his own true face in the mere instant of one call and one response.
Such was often the case with our predecessors. Amidst the mundane conditions of worldly life...

One must accomplish the great matter within one's duties. Why wait until one has retired from office and left public service to dwell in seclusion by the waterside or beneath the trees before one may engage in the study of the Way?

Now, observing the loftiness of your aspirations, the profundity of your capacity, and the breadth of your insight, how could you differ from or be distinct from the predecessors of old? I venture to hope that you will attend to your public affairs.
From this point forward, one must use the eyes of a sober man to see through the drunken dream; with renewed vigor and energy, one must spur oneself forward to advance.
To act on behalf of the Buddhas and Patriarchs by providing them relief—this is the highest hope of the world.
Furthermore, during the seventh and eighth months, I clearly heard that while he sat alone in the Zhongshutang Hall, his transformative voice shook everything to the right of the Great River.
Not long after, I again heard that he led ten thousand cavalry southward on campaign, sweeping clean the lairs of the rebels. My ancestor said: "He exerted great courage and valor as if..."
One person facing ten thousand enemies: holding the precious sword of the Vajra King, one completely slays and completely brings to life, achieving Great Peace while seated.
These are all matters one has long been accustomed to hearing. Now, fortunately, having tested and put them into practice, their spiritual efficacy has already been witnessed.
In the future, as described in the Lotus Sūtra, one shall employ the army of sages and saints to battle the various demons of the five aggregates, destroying them.

To cast one’s net across the three realms and achieve great merit—such that one may receive the precious jewel from within the topknot of a Wheel-Turning King—is not difficult for those who abide in the station of a lay practitioner (*gṛhapati*).
Having received your letter, I hereby offer this reply. As I have no means of meeting you in person, my thoughts run toward you beyond measure.
Let us set aside this talk for now; tell me, where are the demons of the five aggregates right now? If you say...
He is a demon; he himself is not a Buddha. If one says he is a Buddha, then one becomes a demon oneself.
Precisely when Buddha and demon stand in opposition and person and environment intersect, who ultimately is the self?
Furthermore, if both person and environment are stripped away and both Buddha and demon are forgotten, where does the self remain? Investigate!

I accompanied the Abbot Yuzang of Shouye Monastery on his previous journey, during which he caused great disturbance among the various quarters from top to bottom. Upon our parting, each of us offered gifts as a token of our lingering affection, leaving nothing undone.
Reflecting on this, I think that from my departure in the Jiazi year to my return in the Jia Shen year, barely twenty years have passed.
In the span of a year, the kinsmen within this mountain have almost entirely vanished from memory; those who remain meet as if they were meeting for the first time in another life.
The world flows and changes so rapidly that one cannot even blink; in twenty years, when we meet again, what will it be like? Alas!

The winds of karma and the fires of karma scorch us day and night; ten here and five there are all of the same measure—half a catty and eight taels. Only the man of refined talent does not lose his way.
Those who possess their own spiritual awakening should reflect deeply upon this. Four months after our parting, on the eighteenth day of the fourth month, I arrived at Guxu.
My attendant followed me to Shizilin Monastery, where we settled for a time. Suddenly, Xueting from Longshan arrived, stirring my longing for my hometown; it was impossible to remain longer.
As he was returning home, I felt there was no way to provide him with the support of a Dharma-kinsman. It happened that the commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* had just been published.
I have briefly left behind one copy for the public to peruse and examine. This sutra points directly to the human mind and fully expounds the essential meaning of Chan;
therefore, practitioners of Chan regard it as a formal contract. Twenty years ago, I received the entrustment of my late teacher, Master Huan, and dared not disobey his command.
It was only in recent years that I finally completed this work. Students must read it carefully. Read!
One must reflect deeply upon this; having reflected, one must practice it with vigor.
To read and reflect without acting is merely black ink upon white paper.
He replied, "In the past, the Venerable Master Zhuyuan of Daochang Temple loudly proclaimed the Way of the Elder Yuanjian.

Tracing his lineage back to the Patriarch Zhengxu on the summit of Wujie Peak, he was truly a 'Dragon Gate' of this age. Although many have emerged from his school, it is only the Master who, due to illness..."
With your lofty character and ever-advancing talent, it is certain that this ancestral estate and its green felt mat will not remain with others for long.
I am unworthy to be linked by kinship to you, yet I am as parched and ruined as one who has failed; held back by old age and indolence, I dare not presumptuously seek to attach myself to you.

For this reason, I have not dared to lightly undertake the formalities of offering congratulations or sending inquiries. Recently, I have built a small hut near Wucheng to provide for my old age and illness.

Day by day, I associate with bamboo and stones, laughing and strolling; I have not realized that the poison of seeking stillness while fleeing noise has become increasingly deep the more I indulge in it.
Now that the Abbot Yin has come from the lectern, I am honored that the two teachings have been further augmented by his presence.

I am filled with shame and trepidation. Because you have requested this second audience, I have set forth my humble sincerity as follows. I only pray that, as the Great Dharma rests upon your shoulders, you will not grow weary of receiving visitors.
In reply to the Venerable Master Yunfeng of Panlong.
In the first year of the Taiding era, I returned from Zhejiang. I once visited Jiyun Pass, but before long I departed again for Zha’e Longfeng.
There, the Wansong Peak rises majestically, appearing and disappearing amidst the Milky Way; yet with my feet blistered and exhausted, it was something I could behold from afar but never reach.
I have only now come to believe that [this path] ascends thirty-six turns into the heavens; how could it possibly be reached by ordinary steps?

I look up with reverence to our Venerable Teacher, who has inherited the tradition of the ancient Buddhas and whose transformative influence has permeated both China and foreign lands for twenty or thirty years.

Talented and eminent men from all quarters have all desired to sit beneath your chair. As for the sweeping away of the ashes of the kalpa and the dispersing of the demonic fortresses, soaring pavilions and surging halls manifest before us...
In the mere blink of an eye, the inconceivable power of liberation and spiritual efficacy has likely surpassed even the excellence of such extraordinary realms.

Yet, I alone have been burdened by the debt of failing to pay my respects, harboring a persistent sense of regret within my breast. Recently, for several years, I have had the opportunity to associate with your worthy disciple Ketim in the Wu and Kuai regions.
During our informal discussions on an equal footing, we occasionally touched upon certain aspects of our family precepts, which deeply inspired me.
I have continued on. Subsequently, I again encountered Master Wu-xiao, as if two scholars seeking one another at the edge of a desolate marsh.
Although I had not yet met you, sir, I did know your sons; thus, my former obstructions have gradually diminished day by day.

When Master Xiao returned from Shuangjing, he brought with him the instructions you had granted me and two bolts of white ramie cloth. A sense of both shame and gratitude welled up within me all at once, yet I do not know from whence it arose.
At this time when the Great Dharma is on the verge of extinction, it is still fortunate that the Elder Master holds the fundamental principles of our school;

students daily look forward to his tireless guidance. Furthermore, I have heard those who mock the story of the Ancient Master of Tan returning his staff—this, however, is the internal mechanism of a father and son, where letting go and holding fast are each applied as appropriate; it is not something others can emulate.
I am well aware of this. Taking advantage of his return, I venture to offer these few words. Looking westward against the wind, I cannot help but feel profound trepidation.
In response to Elder Xinghai of Jiangling:
In the past, during my stay at Ketang Monastery, we once discussed how you, Xinghai, were able to trace and transmit the lineage of Nanquan’s Way, spreading it far and wide.
In Jingnan, those who wished to offer alms arrived spontaneously without waiting for a call; there was no labor required, yet all works were accomplished.

I regret that my lingering stay in the Three Wu regions prevented me from seeing him even once. I have often said that the Elder Puan was an ancient Buddha appearing in this world, who, at the point where the realization of the fundamental nature causes all emotions to vanish and the knowing mind merges with the essence, revealed the traces of his awakening. He is a distant successor to the orthodox lineage of Linji. Recently...

Thus, he took Muan as his father and Foyan as his patriarch. Inheriting the legacy of his ancestors, he transformed sentient beings through a manner that was broad-minded, peaceful, compassionate, and patient. He enabled his students to be like those sailing a boat amidst calm winds and tranquil waves—avoiding all perilous turbulence and reaching the further shore while remaining seated. This was the great application of his skillful means (*upāya*). As for his relief of disasters, his succor of those in distress, and his responding to prayers according to conditions: [The text continues with the following: ...he would not fail to act. Whether it was the case of the monk from Mount Tiantai who had been struck by lightning, or the layman of Mount Lu who suffered from a chronic illness, or the official of the Southern Circuit who was plagued by demonic possession, or the commoner of the Eastern Market who was afflicted by a malignant spirit—he would invariably manifest a response. Furthermore, when the people of the capital were suffering from a drought, he manifested a great rain; when the people of the countryside were suffering from a flood, he manifested a great wind. He could cause a single drop of water to become a vast ocean, and he could cause a single blade of grass to become a towering mountain. Such were the wondrous transformations of his spiritual power. His disciples numbered over three thousand, and his fame spread throughout the world. Thus, he was truly a great master who upheld the Dharma-eye treasury and acted as a true successor to the Buddhas and Patriarchs. He passed away on the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the second year of the Shaoxing era at the age of seventy-one. His remains were enshrined in the pagoda at the West Pagoda Monastery on Mount Jingshan. The Emperor bestowed upon him the posthumous title "Great Master Wanshan.
