These are all merely secondary matters. While those within the realm who have received his bounty are certainly many, those who truly understand the secret of his "lowering of the hand" are few indeed.
I have also often wondered whether the one who spreads the Great Transformation kept its transmission secret and did not strive for rapid exposition.

I believe that I, Xinghai, must diligently propagate this great capacity, so that students may lose their emotional attachments and, in the state where body and essence merge, personally behold the Old Master.
To behold the countenances of these people is a profound blessing for this Dharma-gate.

Since our parting at the assembly in Gusu during the Xinsi year with the Elder Xiyun, we have lingered together at the traveler’s lodgings, yet our mutual intentions remained unfulfilled. In the Jiashen year, I returned.
While on an inspection tour of Luling, I passed through Hongdu on my way. I inquired about your whereabouts but could not obtain detailed information;

furthermore, because we were traveling as fellow passengers, our movements were constrained and I was unable to identify you or meet with you. Recently, I heard that you have been preaching the Dharma at Dongshan, and your excellent reputation has spread far and wide.
Yet, from thousands of miles away, this first letter of congratulation arrives so belatedly—without cause, it is indeed too late. You, sir, are... [text ends]
You have applied yourself with vigorous diligence to your studies. Heaven does not fail those of talent;

it has allowed you to fulfill your aspirations and put your learning to the test at a time for transcending the world that is neither too early nor too late. Even those who dwell in mountain caves and remote valleys, secluding themselves from the world, would rejoice a hundredfold at this.
Twenty-three years have passed since we parted by the Luan River, during which I have forgotten the five verses I composed then. Only—
Even the final two lines are occasionally uttered by me inadvertently; I do not know whether you, sir, are perhaps able to unravel and expound them.
Whether the monastery is large or small, and whether the assembly is numerous or few, one must take up the ancient Way with all one's strength, leading by example and guiding others.
Advancement or withdrawal, honor or lowliness—leave these entirely to one’s destined lot. Be careful not to follow the tracks of your contemporaries who are plagued by the anxiety of gain and loss.
As long as I am old and not yet dead, how could there be no day for us to meet again, so that I might pour out all that I wish to say?
Elder Zhenxiang of Fengcheng sent a letter while residing at that monastery; I have already replied to it yesterday, sending it back with a monk from Xingan. It happened that we met by chance.
I trouble you once more to convey my greetings.

It has been several days since I last followed the venerable Master Tánfāng of Lóngxiáng to reminisce at the abbot’s quarters of Zhōngshān, where we received your compassionate instructions; now four or five intercalary months have already passed. Recently, I have learned that you have taken up [residence]...
He ascended the path to Zhongshan and brought the Jingwu Valley back to Longhe; furthermore, he uprooted the two Eme peaks and placed them between the Five Crests.
Going and coming, not a single thread of effort was expended from his wrists—these are all extraordinary accounts from antiquity.

For several years now, I have moved my thatched cottage into Central Wu, lingering among the grasses and trees at their base, while the Great Square (the Dharma realm) has carried out its promotions and demotions.
Matters such as these did not reach my ears or eyes; therefore, when the carriage and attendants came and went through the Wu Gate, none of us were able to run to offer a formal send-off or welcome.
This was not out of any intention to be disrespectful, but simply because we had no prior notice. May your lofty insight and vast magnanimity forgive this.

One must certainly regard this with illumination and compassion. Some may say that the magnificent splendor of Longhe (Dragon River) is no different from the celestial reward realm of the Sūtravana Heaven.
In the past, Master Xiaoyin exerted all his efforts to establish it; now, Master Tan has reached its lofty heights and dwells therein securely.

In time, by incorporating the outer precincts into the inner precincts, he will hasten the descent of the Buddha who is to succeed him, and his own person shall hand over the charge to his successor. Is this not so?
What a waste of effort! Hehe. It is my regret that I have no means to meet you in person. As I face the wind, I can do nothing but direct my heart toward you with boundless longing.
Your reply was received;

at the beginning of summer, when I was staying before Qifeng Pavilion, I repeatedly had the honor of knocking at your door. Observing your cultivated bamboos, I have always admired how your strategic brilliance and administrative skill are combined. I shall soon—
He is a man of true talent. At a time when his meritorious fame was at its zenith, he was able to seek out the carefree recluses beneath the forest trees;
none but one whose worldly tastes are淡泊 (dàn bó—tranquil and simple) could speak of such a thing. When his banners departed from Wu and Min, the rats in the caves were thrown into turmoil.

I mean that you must surely lead your troops southward. That you have remained amidst the mountains and waters of Tiantai since receiving your letter—how can you not yet abandon the pleasure of reclining upon moss and dwelling among the green depths?
Heaven has produced heroes; you should consider emerging for the sake of the times.
As for our lofty discourse beyond the mundane world, it will not be too late for us to meet again in the future.
I replied that it had been over a month since I parted from Dole Temür, the Director of the Grand Treasury (Taifu Jian), at Wulongmei.
A man from Jingkou arrived again with a handwritten note, stating that he would cross the Yangtze River northward to return home this very day.
I look back upon him from afar, imagining that divine beings protect him so that his carriage travels in safety and health as he returns for an audience.
Pure radiance and joyful celebration converge; what joy could equal the happiness of arriving home? I have only one uncertainty:

as for the matter of "original entry," are you able to remain focused upon it in every thought-moment? Is there correspondence in every thought-moment? Are you able to bring forth that joy of self-congratulation and self-celebration?
For you, sir, dwell in the nobility of a prince and possess a spirit of heroic brilliance and keen discernment.
To be able to humble oneself and follow others in order to investigate this matter to its depths—how could this be anything other than the result of having planted the roots of virtue in past lives?
However, the essence of this matter lies in diligent practice. To know it but not practice, or to practice it but not diligently, makes it impossible to reach the final destination.

Among the officials and scholars of recent times who study the Buddha-dharma, there are many who, relying on their cleverness, engage in intellectual dissection and grasp it through their ordinary consciousness.
To grasp but a fragmentary understanding and consider it sufficient is, little do you realize, precisely the root of delusion and confusion.
Only you, sir, possess extraordinary talent and far-reaching aspirations; you shall never fall into such traps.
Therefore, what I hope for in you is that you will personally verify and personally awaken, arriving at the House of the Dharma King to walk hand-in-hand with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

One practices until one has extended grace to all beings and then ceases. How could one possibly associate with those of shallow roots and inferior capacity who follow the current to grasp at empty appearances?
Now, as General Feng departs for the capital to take his leave of me, I have composed this response to urge him toward diligent practice.
In response to Secretary Zhan:
On the morning of the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month, after finishing the gruel, I stood at Zhuofeng Peak seeing off the Tiantai monk Tai as he departed.
Just as I was on Feihong Bridge, disrobing to sit in meditation, I suddenly heard a cry—how could I simply sweep the fallen leaves from the courtyard and the pond? Suddenly, he called out!
I received news that several branches of osmanthus were blooming amidst the dew. Thereupon, I moved my earthen drum and sat encircling the tree.
I called the mountain boy Xiao Yan to draw water from the well with its ice-cold pitcher and brew *yuhua* (well-flower) tea using the head-tea leaves of Yu Zide from Wuning Yishan to enjoy.
Taking the fragrance of the incense as a condition, I entered deeply into the state of non-attachment, non-obstruction, and sovereign play in leisure.
Before he had fully mastered samādhi, a fellow villager named Dihui Lin came to knock at the gate. Two or three of his disciples said, "This is a state of ultimate, carefree joy;
do not let that fellow know of it," and so they dispersed. [The Master] then invited him inside. That very day, he respectfully paid his respects.
Later, the monk Daozhan delivered a message, sending a fan from Qiu Zhongrong and presenting a sheet of white paper to request [a poem].
Dharma Words: I have neither words nor Dharma; there is only a measure of impoverished joy that cannot be borne as a gift for you.
In reply to Master Mingjie of Yuantang in Bianjing:
Amidst howling frost winds and fallen leaves filling the roads, Master Zhu of Xuancheng suddenly arrived. Having received his letter, I learned of his circumstances since our last meeting.
I am still residing on the left bank of the Yangtze River. I had planned to borrow a seat at the Huangjiao Monastery next year to open a dharma assembly and bestow the precepts.

However, I have been mistakenly invited by you to deliver a public discourse for the assembly to elucidate the Way of Direct Pointing. Furthermore, it is said that the various officials of the Censorate, who are presiding over this gathering, all hope that I will come forth, shaking my monk’s staff;
they have already drafted an official letter to request my presence, and thus I cannot decline this journey.
I have long reflected that ascending the dharma-platform to receive full ordination is the path traversed by all schools—whether sudden or gradual, Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna.

It is a pity that the ordination platforms have been abandoned for so long that students have nothing to rely upon. If this tradition were to be put into practice once more, those in the age of the Dharma’s decline would surely receive great benefit.

However, regarding the command to deliver a general discourse (*pūsē*), I, in my humble state, dare not presume to participate. To investigate the essence of our own school, it is fundamentally based on...

The single transmission of the mind-seal is intended for those of the highest faculties. To speak of "direct pointing" is already a deviation; how could there be any room for further verbal explanation?
Later, as the capacities of disciples were not uniform, the masters, in their compassionate outreach, were compelled to employ skillful means through indirect methods.

This is like Huangbo’s severe blows or Linji’s shouts; when Linji saw a monk, he would immediately shout. These instances of the "blow and the shout" are not... [the mechanism of]... [intended for all].
That which is encompassed by the Tripiṭaka cannot be fathomed by ordinary consciousness;
yet the three thousand codes of dignified conduct, the eighty thousand subtle practices, and even the teachings of the five periods are all contained within the blows and shouts.

Such is their swift and essential nature, yet none were able to receive and uphold them. Thereupon, in order to accommodate the capacities of those who came, the discourse on "requesting instruction" began. Subsequently—
That he conformed so perfectly to their needs and further offered this great request for instruction, yet titled it a "General Teaching" (fusetsu), was he not constrained by necessity?

Nevertheless, such a general teaching is not something that any genuine master dares to deliver; it is only spoken by one who is truly a master when the disciples possess the necessary capacity. If they lack that capacity, he does not speak.
There is its underlying principle: one does not speak unless there is an intense state of faith, joy, and mental agitation.
Only when one is at the extreme of thirst and hunger will one be given drink and food; thus, the listener gains the benefit of realization, and the speaker avoids the fault of speaking in vain.
Otherwise, to establish a facade at one's gate for the sake of ostentation and to attract the gaze of others is something the Master would not permit.

As for me, I know myself that there is no Dharma to be preached, nor am I a teacher of the Dharma. To "boil yellow vegetables in an earthenware pot" and to sit cross-legged watching the white clouds—these are my way.
That you were twice humbled by my humble reception upon your recent visits, and that my cold and retreating household style was witnessed by you in person, is well known.
How could this be a teaching intended for those traveling from afar to gather before a vast assembly? Moreover, I have heard that "to conceive a thought is to transgress the precepts.
Master Yuetang used this to instruct his disciples, commanding them to see through to the very source at the very moment of such conception.
This is precisely what constitutes direct pointing. Furthermore, I have heard that the Guangjiao Monastery was once the Zen grove of Huangbo; although it is now...
It is easier to lecture on Chan than to practice it. My forehead remains as it was before. Those who come may ascend the hall and enter the room; there, the Way exists through direct encounter.

There is nowhere that does not embody the essence of Chan—so why wait for a general discourse to seek it elsewhere? I hope you will appreciate this sentiment and spare me the trouble of further commands.
If, however, this is not possible, I would instead trouble you to pass my request to the masters of the Great Vehicle; please allow me to gaze from afar without moving a single step.
Jieguang: This is truly one who has received his master’s grace.
In response to the questions posed by Vice Commissioner Zhongwen during his illness:
On the day he was departing for the north, leaving me behind, the officials stood in rows like a forest; his countenance was serene as the springtime, yet you alone appeared somewhat obscured.

I, Se, privately considered that for one who has left home and severed worldly attachments, such a reaction was not to be wondered at. On the following morning, I received word that he had boarded his boat, but suddenly fell ill;
consequently, he moored and remained outside the pass. After staying there for three days, his illness did not abate, and thus he was unable to proceed.

I privately suspected that since his journey was obstructed, the force of his illness would surely increase. I then reasoned to myself: "Zhongwen is a man of profound understanding; he halts when the ground is uneven and flows when the way is open."
You have always been skilled in managing affairs; how much more so now that you have devoted yourself to the Way in recent years?
Now that father and son, brothers, who were separated, are reunited, and various excellent physicians vie to offer their sincere services to bring about a cure, it will surely be healed before long.

Yet, who would have expected that the illness would linger until reaching such a state? This is truly lamentable. Your talent and virtue are pure and refined; those who hold positions of high office and authority under your guidance number over ten.
He was fully capable of his duties; thus, both loyalty and filial piety were perfected, and he was praised by both the court and the common people.

Among the populace, regardless of rank, age, or status, all who were graced by his benevolence and moved by his influence did not wish for him to leave office for even a single day. When they heard that he was ill, they lamented that they could not offer their own bodies as a substitute.
Such was the depth of the gratitude and longing he inspired in those he governed. Yet, while his meritorious achievements were just beginning to flourish, he suddenly withdrew in hesitation.
He withdrew in order to investigate the teachings of our school’s distinct transmission.
He would often say to others, "In spirit and in dreams, there is not a single day that I am not beneath the Lion Grove.

Now that his illness has become critical, he has again taken the essential words of my former exhortations and encouragements, writing them out and posting them upon the windows, walls, beams, pillars, desks, couches, and screens, so that—
Whether sitting, standing, reclining, rising, bowing, or looking up, he was always within the range of [the Master’s] sight.

Aside from the two pages who attended him morning and evening with medicine and gruel, all other visitors, favorites, and distractions were strictly excluded. This clearly demonstrates that his arrangements were methodical and his self-discipline powerful;
how could such a person be compared to those of ordinary caliber? Last night, your honorable father, the Chancellor, came and repeatedly entreated me, saying that you—
He wished to invite me for a meeting. Since I have long not emerged from the mountains, and knowing that even in illness one tires of clamor and distraction, I thought:
"What benefit would there be in a hasty meeting? I then entrusted my intention to the Chancellor, saying: "Not meeting is most intimate."

This morning, I again received your instructions. You raised several points regarding my inquiries, through which I have been able to thoroughly perceive the depths of your realization and thereby find the means to express what I ought to tell you.

Question: Within the various scriptural teachings, some speak of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), some speak of existence, and some speak of neither emptiness nor existence. Which of these is the definitive meaning? Answer:

You should know that our Buddha always teaches the Dharma by relying upon the two truths (*satyadvaya*). His teaching of the Dharma adapts to the capacities of sentient beings; he does not adhere to a single path of skillful means (*upāya*).
If sentient beings are deluded by names and signs (*nāma-nimitta*) and become attached to existence, he speaks of emptiness.

To refute this, if there are those who do not cling to existence but instead cling to emptiness, one speaks of existence to overcome that clinging. Clinging to either emptiness or existence is certainly not the true Dharma; neither "neither existence nor emptiness" constitutes the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). As for directly revealing the wondrous, perfect, and circular essence of the single mind, it should be clarified through four principles. There is. It is neither empty nor existent; it is precisely that which is both empty and existent. As for emptiness, there is no movement, no change, and not even a single dharma established.
As for existence, it manifests all dharmas according to conditions, appearing vividly and distinctly. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is not all dharmas; it is precisely all dharmas.
Departing from 'is' and departing from 'is not,' it is both 'is' and 'is not. That "it is not all dharmas" refers to emptiness.
"Thus, all phenomena are existence. Regarding the phrase "that which is apart from is that which is identical," this corresponds to the third and fourth meanings [of the fourfold negation].
By correlating them with the three truths of the Middle Way—the ultimate, the conventional, and the middle truth—the ultimate truth is emptiness; the conventional truth is existence;

and the middle truth is neither ultimate nor conventional, yet it is both ultimate and conventional. This is the same as that which is "doubly apart from" emptiness and existence, while being "doubly identical to" emptiness and existence.
Furthermore, one should know that "separation" and "identity" are non-dual, and the "one" and the "four" mutually interpenetrate. To cite the one, the four meanings are fully present;
to speak of the four, their substance is but one. This is the principle of the nature inherently possessed by every person. If one were to investigate and examine this:
while the former two meanings involve the opposition of emptiness and existence and still pertain to names and concepts, the latter two meanings...
It cannot be subjected to discrimination and it cannot be approached or settled upon. Because it cannot be subjected to discrimination, the path of language is cut off.
Because it cannot be approached or settled upon, the sphere of mental activity ceases. When the sphere of mental activity ceases, it is inconceivable;
when the path of language is cut off, it is beyond discussion. This is precisely the One True Dharma-realm, the Tathāgatagarbha mind, which is inconceivable.
This is the subtle essence [of the Dharma]. Those who awaken to and realize such a subtle principle are sages; those who are deluded and turn their backs upon it are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
For those who are sages, their virtuous attributes are perfectly integrated, and their responsive transformations are unimpeded.

For those who are ordinary beings, the functioning of their cognitive-emotional consciousness prevails, and their inversions are endless. Thereupon, the sage takes pity on them, intending to open their awakening so as to transform them.
That delusion is resolved by relying on the principle of the inherently present nature to initiate the methods of cultivation, which is termed "Teaching.

This causes one to establish contemplative practice based upon those methods of cultivation; when contemplative practice is perfected, one realizes according to the principle, realizing nothing other than the essence of the inherently present principle.

Although the methods of cultivation are many, let us discuss them by way of the three contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way. The contemplation of emptiness contemplates the True.

The Contemplation of Reality (*satya*) consists of the Contemplation of the Conventional (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through the gate of the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the Contemplation of the Middle (*madhyama-satya*) through the gate of the middle way. Now, this Contemplation of the Middle possesses two aspects:

the dual negation of emptiness and the provisional, and the dual illumination of emptiness and the provisional. Negation and illumination are mutually necessary; these constitute the three contemplations within a single mind.

When the wisdom of contemplation and the principle of reality are unified, such that wisdom and principle are of one essence, this is called the teaching of the non-duality of nature and cultivation—the perfect and subtle doctrine. Originally, as for the separate transmission...
Although study is said to be "outside the teachings" (*jiaowai*), it has never actually been outside the principles of the teachings; it is merely that its function and direction differ slightly.
As in the past, when a monk asked a Chan Master: "Is the Way to be sought with a mind that possesses [discrimination]?
He replied, "No. "Is it to be sought with a mind devoid of [discrimination]? He replied, "No. "Is it to be sought with a mind that both possesses and lacks [discrimination]?"...
"Can one seek the acceptable? He replied, "No. "Can one seek the acceptable with a mind that is neither existent nor non-existent? He replied, "No.

Thus, when one tastes the underlying meaning beyond these four answers, they perfectly accord with the four meanings of the nature-principle (*xingli*) and the four meanings of the teachings (*jiaofa*).
However, Chan practitioners transcend names and phrases and dissolve all phenomenal characteristics; they do not enter the pathways of conceptual meaning.
To directly cut through to the root source, one must strive to cause consciousness to cease and emotions to vanish, so that the deluded mind is suddenly realized.
Thus, there is the teaching of "transcending in a single leap to enter directly into the stage of the Tathāgata. Is this not indeed the perfectly wondrous Dharma?

From this point downward, whatever is called "emptiness" or "existence" is all merely the preaching of the Dharma according to circumstances. Therefore, the essential point of the transmission outside the teachings lies in forgetting intellectual understanding and severing discursive thought.

Transcending emotional views, free from subject and object, one alone wields the single transmission; this is true inquiry and genuine realization. It is absolutely forbidden to cling to branches and leaves, thereby obstructing the gateway to self-awakening.
If one does not act thus, then even if one were to extensively employ texts on the principles of nature to fuel one's discursive arguments, it would be of no avail.
To speak of fine food will never cure hunger; not only does it fail to alleviate hunger, it even serves to further intensify the blazing fire of hunger within.
Within the very soles of my friend Zhongwen’s feet lies a single, living path that reaches to the heavens;
he need only stride straight forward, with no further necessity to inquire as to what constitutes the ultimate meaning.

A question was asked: "Among those who study Chan, there are some who attain sudden enlightenment upon hearing it once, while others practice for a long time and cultivate for a long duration yet fail to achieve realization.
Is there a difference in difficulty between the Dharma they hear and the Dharma they investigate?

Furthermore, it is said that 'when the season arrives, the principle manifests of itself. If this is so, then one need not exert oneself in investigation and study, but may simply wait for the time when awakening occurs naturally."
"Indeed, so it is. I have previously heard the teaching of the Middle Way: 'Whether ordinary person or sage, all are equal without high or low;
it depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements, where realization is attained as easily as turning over one's palm. Observing the metaphor of turning over the palm, realization seems easy;

yet when discussing these mental defilements, they are not extinguished except through cultivation. As for this single word 'extinction,' it is easy [to speak of] in a single kṣaṇa, but difficult [to achieve]."
Throughout successive kalpas, one should know that the Dharma itself possesses neither difficulty nor ease; it is the person who determines whether it is difficult or easy. Why is this so?

It is because of the varying degrees of thickness in one's defilements, the varying degrees of diligence or negligence in cultivation, and the varying degrees of suddenness or gradualism in the extinction of impurities.

Therefore, there is difficulty or ease in awakening and realization, and consequently, differences in the timing of these realizations—whether they are slow or swift, distant or near. This is what is meant by the saying: "When the time arrives, the principle is revealed."

This means that when one’s practice of the threefold cultivation has reached completion, the time arrives for the defilements of the mind to be extinguished, and the principle of awakening and realization manifests of itself.
It does not mean that there is a time for self-awakening without practicing or cultivating.
To illustrate this with the analogy of a farmer: there is the time of sowing, the time of ripening, and the time of harvest. From sowing to ripening, and from ripening to...
As for "liberation," it is the time when one's cultivation reaches its harvest. Can one hope for ripeness without having planted, or hope for liberation without having ripened?

People see only the ease of sudden enlightenment upon hearing [the Dharma], yet they do not realize that prior to such realization, their practice and merit were never without difficulty. People merely fear it...

It is difficult to practice for a long time and cultivate for a long duration; yet one does not realize that this is precisely the time when the stains of the mind are being scrubbed away and one's efforts are not in vain.
The Confucian classics also say: "First there is hardship, and then there is attainment.

If one does not apply oneself to what is difficult while recklessly hoping for what is easy, then that which is easy will ultimately remain unattainable, and that which is difficult will only seem more difficult. This is just like...
Is it not difficult for one who is indolent toward farming to abandon the sowing of seeds yet vainly hope for a bountiful harvest?

I hope that you will not inquire into the thickness or thinness of the defilements staining your mind, nor calculate the slowness or swiftness of the timing of your awakening and realization. Rather, apply yourself with diligence and progress in the place where you practice;
whether in times of distress or in moments of haste, remain steadfast therein. First, cultivate a heart that is patient with toil and hardship, and find sweetness in it.
If one maintains what is difficult and does not seek swift efficacy, then the ease of sudden awakening will arrive unexpectedly and reach one all at once.
Thus it is said: "Were it not for the strength of galloping through the sweat of battle, how could one fully achieve merit that covers the age?"
He came to inquire: "Illness is the excellent medicine for sentient beings; I have already recognized the internal illness within myself.

I know that my provisions for the journey ahead are meager, and I have deeply realized this with vigorous self-reflection. Yet, how can it be that the four elements manifest such agony and a hundred anxieties?"
Although one may say that they maintain right mindfulness and apply vigorous introspection at all times, if they lose even slightly their vigilance, they will be disturbed by it.
What strategy can be employed to dispel this? I have examined what you call "recognizing the illness," and it seems you merely recognize its delusion and inversion as an internal ailment.
As for what you call "deeply understanding," it seems you merely know its role as a resource for the path.
It is simply that provisions have not yet been fully supplied. While this knowledge and this consciousness are indeed excellent, alas, the mark of self (*ātman*) has not yet been eliminated.

As long as the mark of self is not eliminated, the root of the disease remains unextracted; how then can there be any means of dispelling the states of suffering and grief associated with the four great elements?
You should know that the self is fundamentally not-self, and birth is fundamentally without birth. The body belongs to the impure; the body is like a magical illusion. As for what is impure:
As the sutra says: "This body is not sandalwood, nor is it a lotus; it is nurtured by filth and excrement, emerging solely from the urinary tract.
From birth until death, whether internally or externally, it is entirely impure.

At the moment of its initial birth, one should not conceive the thought that it is a single entity destined for certain death; yet at the time of its death, it is merely this single entity that dies—it was never anything else."

As for this body of mine: while alive, it is merely a leaking bag of excrement, meeting with nothing but burdensome entanglements; when dead, it is like a decayed piece of wood—what does it truly have to do with me?
As for illusory transformations, as the sutra says: "One falsely identifies the four elements as the characteristics of one's own body."
The shadows conditioned by the six sense-objects are the manifestations of one’s own mind, comparable to a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky;
though the sky is actually devoid of flowers, the sick person falsely clings to them. One who can contemplate in this manner finds that all internal and external ailments are empty.

This is what is called the Dharma of Peace and Leisure. As the Patriarch said: "This old monk has his own Dharma of Peace and Leisure; even when the eight sufferings burn together, it remains entirely unaffected."

It is an obstacle. The eight sufferings are birth, old age, sickness, death, separation from what one loves, meeting with what one hates, not obtaining what one seeks, and the intense suffering of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Sickness is merely one of these eight sufferings. If one is not hindered by the intense torment of these eight sufferings, it may be said that one has deeply attained the dharma of profound peace and leisure.
However, as long as the dharma still remains outside of suffering and the state of dualistic opposition has not been forgotten, one must further...
To turn the pivot before one’s eyes and reveal the true mechanism beyond the ordinary, one observes that the realm of the eight sufferings is entirely the Dharma of tranquility;
only then may medicine and illness both be forgotten, as one personally arrives at the state of liberation where all is free and unimpeded.
A question was asked. Guifeng said: "When distracted, one follows the sway of emotions; at the moment of death, one is dragged away by karma.

When awakening does not depend on emotion, one can transform karma at the moment of death. Since ancient times, those who have attained thorough realization certainly know where the point of transition lies clearly.

Nevertheless, when it comes to the occasion of sitting to pass away or dying while standing, could there not be a method for such a disposition? As for someone like me, my approach to the Way has been late, and my emotions...
If karma has not yet been emptied, and if one lacks both awakening and the capacity for decisive action, what can one rely upon at the moment of death?
I have heard that matters concerning the shores of birth and death are not to be settled at the final hour. As the ancient masters said:
"If you do not strike through thoroughly beforehand, when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, you will surely find yourself flustered and at a loss. Therefore, the ancients all...

Zhaozhou asked, "What about after it has passed? Xuansha replied, "A ditch across level ground. Later, he indeed passed away without illness after six cycles [of breath].
Such freedom of coming and going is unfathomable; how could this be something merely arranged at the moment of death?
Indeed! Now that your illness has reached this point and you have nothing else to rely upon, I ask that you set aside all domestic affairs, both great and small, with total detachment;
and furthermore, relinquish your own life and body with complete surrender. Let it be as it may—whether you become a Buddha or an ancestral patriarch.
It is possible that you will fall forever into the evil realms. Leave all gain and loss, right and wrong, to them and do not concern yourself with them.
Instead, rely solely upon this fundamental koan, allowing not even a hair’s breadth of leakage. Live together with it in life and die together with it in death.
Suddenly, let go at the precipice, passing beyond the end to be revived again; then, it will not hinder you from turning a single pivot for your sake.

The fame of your loyalty and heroism has moved the world, yet for a thousand years it has remained silent. Now we see that your father’s transformative power and singular ingenuity accord perfectly with our Dharma.

Such-and-such a person is a magnificent scion of the military nobility; his formidable presence embodies his father’s spirit. His writings fill entire houses, and his trees brush the clouds—how could a son of a house worth a thousand pieces of gold not be capable of literary excellence?
His tally-sticks fill his bedchamber, and his seals are as large as bushels—what need is there to speak further of a lord whose wealth amounts to ten thousand *shi*?
Alas! At the prime of one’s years, when intent upon learning, one must now face this great matter of seeing off the deceased.

When the auspicious tomb is revealed to the bright sun, the entire commandery shares in this heart-wrenching sorrow. As the white curtains follow the crimson banners, people from the four quarters come to observe the propriety of the rites;
only after these words have been inscribed does the procession finally set forth. Yet the jade fungi, the lapis lazuli herbs, and the city of lotuses are not yet the place of ultimate rest. Gold...

This is the memorial text for the offering to the Heavenly Eye, the Venerable Monk Huanzhu.

The great tree of Yīngliáng in Jīběi has withered toward decay after enduring through many generations; yet, upon reaching old age and snow, it flourished once more. This flourishing passed through three transmissions until it reached our Master.
Our Master wielded the Great Function, responding to changes as circumstances required. His transformative reputation spread in all eight directions, like the roll of thunder and the rush of wind.

Reflecting on what I have produced, it shares the same root yet branches into different forms. Having abandoned my home and forgotten the world, five years have passed since then. Mount Tianmu is towering, lofty, and perilous;
its rocks are withered, its pines are ancient, and mists rise like steaming incense. I have often thought to myself: "As for the solitary cloud and the wild crane, where in heaven would they not fly?
As for clear water and white rice, where is there not to be found? Why, then, do I not abandon this place to go elsewhere? Thus, I have returned once more.

While dwelling in desolation and cold, he found joy within himself; the Master immediately revealed the undulating terrain as level ground. He used a fleeting glance to serve as a staff or a shout, and laughter and jesting as needles and awls.
The point where he aids others is known only by those who know it for themselves—it is like medicine that turns back an attack, or like a chess move that changes the entire game.
It subdues fierce troops without battle and raises one on the brink of death from a single thread. Last year, in the year of Renxu...

Many scholars have come to take refuge with me, setting me apart from the crowd. The multitude is both startled and suspicious, handing me a three-footed black viper and threatening me with whips and lashes as if I were a dragon or an elephant.
Yet I still rely on the protection of those who shelter the weak wings of a fledgling; it is like attempting to test the prowess of a lion that has turned back to leap.
The Master has suddenly abandoned me; upon whom shall I rely? I can only endure death to carry out his command, vowing to act in secret and bestow [his teachings] in private.
Yet, how can I refuse those of noble status and power who press their words upon me?

With pen and ink, I stir my voice and tongue to voice the lamentations of the many scholars, expressing their grief as they describe the beauty and ugliness of the vast void and the ebb and flow of the great ocean. Who truly knows the Master? Who truly knows me?
Who is this person? If I do not shoulder the task of diligent practice to repay [my debt], then even if my eyes wither and my intestines break, what benefit would it bring?

This memorial for my father was written on the seventh day of the seventh month in the second year of the Zhishun era by the renunciant son, [Name], residing in Huating. I have received this from my younger brother, Zhongxing.
Letter. I learned that my late father, [Name], passed away on the fifth day of the fourth month of this year at the ancestral home in Luling, Jiangxi.
Six days later, on the thirteenth day of the seventh month, I was finally able to go to my place of residence, assemble the monks, perform Buddhist rites, and set up an altar to offer sacrifices.
I set forth my circumstances to announce them clearly, saying: "The offenses of this unworthy son are threefold; these are from my life."

I do not wish to speak, yet at present I cannot refrain from speaking. First, to abandon one’s worldly estate early on, without awaiting the command of one's parents, and to become a monk by altering one's physical appearance—this is the first [transgression].
Second, having already entered the monastic order, to then wander far away, causing anxiety to one’s parents’ hearts—this is the second.
Having wandered so far, one is unable to reach one’s father at the proper time; and when hearing of his death, furthermore—
To be able to crawl back home to bury [the deceased]—this is the third [point]. Alas! I, the unworthy one, have once read the books of the world and am somewhat familiar with its prevailing opinions;
how could I truly bear to act in such a way? It is simply because I admire the Dharma that transcends the world, which brings great benefit to my parents;
therefore, I have followed what is of greater significance, forgetting what the world calls filial piety. My father has passed away; how can I endure this separation? I only—
I constantly urge you to practice my Dharma so as to fulfill my heart’s intent. Father, if you possess spiritual awareness, you will not be dead though your body has perished.

If you truly partake in the benefits of my Dharma, then know that this unworthy son’s failure to serve you is not true unfiliality. Thus, I draw a cup of water and express my feelings through these words;
though ten thousand *li* may seem as close as a span, may your spirit behold this with clarity.
When the Head Seat Jiupeng Shou was nearing the end of his life, he spoke this verse: "Seventy-two years, here and there, Eating the rice of the ten directions, Studying the Chan of Bodhidharma.
This morning, with one leap, I turn over; I laugh until bystanders are split asunder."
The Beak is half-portioned.
My Way of the True Lineage of Tianmu is certainly not something that can be fully explained by words and letters. It lies in being able to cast off life and death at the moment of encounter;
thus, one uses language to verify the true transmission. It is like the final phrase of my Nine Peaks: [the text ends here].
My son, this is sufficient to stir the future and illuminate the past. Now I summon the myriad phenomena to listen together;
for your sake, I shall provide annotations and proclaim it once more. For seventy-two years, the barefoot Persian has been casting his divination coins—this side, that side.
Carrying the sun and moon on a staff, he pierces through the golden ring; eating the food of the ten directions, let the teachings of old rot away.

Studying the Zen of Bodhidharma, the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is but the drool of a wild fox. This morning, with one leap, he turns over and goes; from his wrist, he tears apart the mother-born trousers.
He laughs until half the mouth of the bystander is split open. If you are a fellow practitioner, it is not so. Why is that?
Not so! O Blue Heaven, O Blue Heaven!
Sacrifice at Songjiang!

The Way of the Bodhisattva is such that those whose paths differ do not consult one another; yet those whose hearts know each other seek one another out from a thousand li away. You first met me here.

Lion Rock is a chamber where many scholars have gathered for joint study. I have long recognized your sincerity, gravity, and unassuming nature; you are truly an excellent companion in aiding the Way.
Now that the lion’s roar has fallen silent, the cliffs and valleys are startled by autumn. May these many scholars disperse to all quarters like phoenixes and qilin.
I feel ashamed that the iron net is so difficult to retrieve. You, Master, wielded your adze amidst the reeds and rushes of Huating;

I have heard you call out for the "sons of Bodhisattvas" as you followed the fragrant traces of Nanyue Jin-niu. The Way of the Patriarchs declines daily, while worldly habits grow ever more superficial.
Sighing over the dispersal of my fellow practitioners, I long to board a raft and wander the seas. Now that you have sent a formal letter to summon those in hiding, I too—

Seizing the moment, I plucked the lingering strains of the boatman’s oar-song; I took up residence in a snail-shell hut to accommodate my knees and modeled my posture after the "elephant-bone" bow to lower my head.
We gazed at one another with eyes that seemed to scrape away their own lids, and exchanged our very hearts and livers as our recompense.

Is it not that there are ancestral mountains where one may cherish the memory of one's homeland? Is it not that there are great lands where one may build a retirement retreat? Why, then, linger until this point?

Moved by your disregard for age and your profound sense of righteousness, I have come to cherish our friendship with deep intimacy. You have gathered a multitude of talents to establish this vast monastery;

spirits and deities transport the materials while you search through ravines and woods. Exhausted by the constant running of errands—responding to the east and replying to the west—you toil incessantly day and night, forgetting rest.
Others feared that your accumulated labor would lead to illness, yet I, in turn, cherished your selfless devotion.
His bodily benefits for the masses were vast and his transformative influence all-pervasive. Suddenly, a demonic illness arose; no divine remedy could be applied.

His eyes could not lift their gaze, and his breath could not be restrained. Yet he still directed his official duties and exhorted his subordinates to assemble. Some feared that, facing such a crisis, he might lose his composure;
I, however, verified all the more that the Master’s integrity was long-established, remaining free from anxiety even at the brink of death as his body grew frail.
Birth and death have passed through countless ages; the Dharma-body is revealed amidst the myriad phenomena, while the ocean of awakening dissolves into a single bubble.
Others may lament over this eternal parting for all eternity, but I alone see that your countenance is present before me.
With the tracks of coming and going severed, I shall wipe away your tears and restrain your sobbing throat. I shall sing my *Chu-suo* dirge and offer my cup of tea. Thus shall I act for you.
You have exhausted your sincerity in the rites of the world. Do not say that my sword has departed while you mark the boat.

To offer sacrifice to the worthy and virtuous is like being in the same sea; though we are in different lands, I regard you as my own limbs—this is the principle of fellow practitioners. Alas, my brother!
His talent was sufficient to provide for practical utility; his conditions were sufficient to unfold transformation; and his resolve was sufficient to shoulder the Great Dharma.

Formerly, when Master Huan sat at Mount Tianmu, the mechanisms of transformation radiated outward in a flurry of manifold activities. You, brother, undertook the labor while the assembly relied upon you to find ease.

Upon the Master’s passing into stillness and his enshrinement in a stupa, there was a hall for offerings and land for sustenance; the elder brother assumed responsibility for these, and the community relied upon them for peace.
In this, the elder brother’s talent and conditions were sufficient to fulfill his allotted duty.

As for such matters as withdrawing to Mount Chishi to practice alone and in solitude, or staying at Bianwu to nurture his ailment while refining his cultivation in secret—this elder brother’s resolve was such that he would advance further and further, never ceasing.
As for myself, why must it end in this way? That azure Heaven surely intends to grant all things to man.
Having already bestowed such excellent talent upon him and provided him with so many favorable conditions, why does it alone withhold his longevity to thwart his aspirations? Alas!
All things are like falling leaves; a hundred years are but a collapsing wave. You, brother, do not wait for me; what shall I do?
I see you off, brother, to the mountain’s edge. The days of departure are few, but the days to come are many. Your resolve, brother, cannot be worn away.
Nine peaks pierce the heavens, their green summits towering high.
Duanya Weng’s Memorial for Master Huanzhu (on behalf of another):
Our late teacher’s gate stood as steep as a thousand-fathom cliff; only I and my elder brother dared to violate its severity, planting our feet at the dead-lock barrier.

Turning back from the edge of the white blade, you wondrously accorded with the profound identity. From that time when you called out and your brother responded, we have been rushing about between east and west.
I hold the authority of transformation, while you maintain the correct command. For twenty or thirty years, our family’s reputation has finally begun to flourish;

how can you now abandon it and cast it aside? Can you alone ride upon transformation to return to ultimate extinction? Since the ancestral style has grown cold and the patriarchal lamp is about to go out, I pray that you, my elder brother, will—
Having departed, you have returned once more; for the sake of the Dharma and the Way, you assist in upholding the teachings during this final age.
Do not weary of sentient beings who are difficult to save, but remain steadfastly seated and do not arise from the great *nāga*-samādhi.
The Monks of Fusang Country Offer Sacrifices (on Behalf of) My Family:
Gazing toward Fusang from the East Sea, the waters and heavens stretch out boundlessly. Only the Master’s transformative teachings are without limit;
throughout distant lands and foreign realms, all look up to his radiance. Therefore, I long to behold that true lamp even once.
Facing ten thousand acres of whale-tossed waves, I entrusted my life to the wind-swept sails. Granted by Heaven the gift of immortality, I was able to pay homage at the lion throne.

I was moistened by the drizzling rain of the Dharma and stilled the delusional frenzy of outward wandering. Yet, amidst the treacherous obstacles of worldly affairs, I relied upon the Master as a soldier relies on his standard.
How could the fortune of the Dharma not flourish? Why then did the Dharma King not grant us his lingering presence, leaving us far behind?
A person has a body yet finds no place of rest; why not perish before the Master? With words as firm as arrows and incense smoke, tears flow profusely.
Thus one laments the desolation of the journey; thus one wails the凄凉 (qīliáng—sombre and forlorn) state of the village shrine.
On the evening before the late Master’s enshrinement, he led his assembly of Dharma relatives in singing this chapter once more for the second funeral offering.
For thirty years, the lion’s string had vibrated with rarefied sound throughout the great trichiliocosm; yet one night, its lingering resonance turned into wailing.
Heaven and earth, the grasses and trees, all shared in the same sorrow. From the desolate autumn sky, yellow leaves fell; from the mountain springs, a rustling sound arose.
Sobbing: My grief is such that there is nothing to be done. Cold monkeys cry out as the moon falls from a thousand peaks.
The mountains are vast and green, the waters are deep and wide. Your majestic countenance—how could it ever be hidden? This bitter heart and stinging tears cannot be endured;
gazing at the water, gazing at the mountains, my bowels are broken. Master, do not dwell on Tiantai or Mount Wuyue; Master, do not linger in Yāma or Tuṣita. Vast and boundless...
The winds and waves of the ocean of suffering are fierce; sentient beings, day and night, harbor the wish for a compassionate boat.
In the region west of the Great River, Mount Shouzu is renowned as a sanctuary of the Dharma, and between Mount Kuang and the Fan Water, the most eminent talents flourish even more abundantly.
For several decades, the great masters of old have passed away like drifting smoke or falling rain. Those who come after them have no model to emulate;

These very deliberations of good and evil, these delusive thoughts and attachments, are what is called "impurity. What are delusive thoughts?
They are when, in your daily lives, you lack an internal sovereign and instead allow your empty, false, and floating minds to run wild, wandering in random fancies.

This is what is meant by "perception" (saṃjñā). One may perceive the causes and conditions of the five desires; one may perceive the enjoyments of oneself or others; one may contemplate the good or contemplate the evil;

Because these mental states arise and cease in manifold confusion—like dust, like sand, like smoke, and like mist—they defile your body, speech, and mind-organ layer upon layer. Seek [to understand this].
Purity cannot be attained for even a single moment. Thus it is said: "The mind and thoughts are like a monkey;

Because these deluded thoughts do not pause for a moment, the body, speech, and mind are impure. Because the body, speech, and mind are impure, one falsely creates all manner of evil karma.

Because they falsely create various evil karmas, they consequently transmigrate through the various evil realms. Because they transmigrate through the various evil realms, birth and death are like a revolving wheel.
Tracing the current back to its source, it is entirely due to a single thought of delusive imagination that arises.
Therefore, within our school, we value cutting off the source and its point of origin in one decisive stroke;
thus, naturally, the seas become calm and the rivers clear. It was as in the assembly at Huangmei in the past, when the Venerable Ming followed the robe and bowl to the summit of Dayu Ridge.
At the very moment he could not lift them, his wild mind was subdued. Old Lu then said to him: "Do not think of good."
Do not think of evil. At such a time as this, what is the original face of Elder Ming? Under these words, Ming attained sudden enlightenment;
he immediately saw that the ten directions are pure, with neither Buddha nor sentient beings, and no body, speech, or mind.

What further need is there to seek nirvana or birth-and-death? Only then did he gain self-confidence, realizing that whether one transcends the world or does not transcend it, it is all merely a fabrication.
Regarding names: fundamentally, there is no Buddha in nirvana, nor is there a nirvana-Buddha.

Not even an instant can allow for the slightest pause; not even a breath can allow for self-composure. When the metaphor reaches this point, is it not indeed a matter of profound urgency?

First: To become a Buddha and yet remain with remainder, remaining unchanged from beginning to end—such a true great man! How many people nowadays can remain unchanged from beginning to end?

If we examine the causes and conditions for this retreat from the Way, it is because each has their own attachments that lead to it. What are these attachments? There are three kinds of attachments.
First, regardless of whether one is a monk or a layperson, male or female, everyone is burdened by the constraints of their own body and speech.
Next, those with kinsmen are burdened by their kinsmen; those with the "household fire" are burdened by that household fire. These three kinds of burdens slaughter the people of the world.
All people throughout the world encounter these three burdens, busying themselves for an entire lifetime and remaining in turmoil.
One has suffered for a lifetime; one has spent a lifetime in vain; one has passed a lifetime in emptiness.
How much more so, because these three kinds of burdens give rise to immeasurable greed, anger, and delusion, and one commits immeasurable great and small evil karmas?

Due to the retribution of these karmas, one falls into the ocean of suffering within the three miserable realms and eight difficult conditions, transmigrating through birth and death and undergoing immeasurable [suffering].
They suffer affliction and fail to attain liberation. Though they encounter immeasurable suffering and distress, they remain perpetually unawakened from beginning to end.
This lack of awakening is due to a lack of realization. What is this lack of realization? It is not realizing that one’s own body, family, and household are not one's own.
Now, when I tell you that the body is not yours, you still do not believe it.
I, this mountain monk, shall simply explain it for you from the beginning. When you first entered your mother’s womb to take conception, there was nothing but a single *vijñāna* (consciousness).
Where was there ever a body? This body is merely a lump of inert flesh formed by the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood; it originally possesses no sentience and has no awareness.
One does not know itching; one does not know cold or heat; one does not know hunger or satiety;
one does not know suffering or joy. This is because your single *vijñāna*-spirit is attached within this lump of stubborn flesh.
From this point on, you know itching, you know cold and heat, you know hunger and satiety, and you know suffering and joy. Once you have emerged from the womb, you simply recognize it as such.
You cling to it, calling it "my body. When I tell you that the body is not yours, you resolutely refuse to believe.
For this reason, the Buddhas and Patriarchs take pity on you and, with bitter words, tell you again: "This is not your body; it is a stinking leather bag formed from semen and blood.
It does not belong to your management, nor can it be arranged by you. Even birth, old age, sickness, and death are not under your control."
This is the case. How do we know this is so? For instance, from the moment you first entered the womb, you underwent a transformation every seven days while dwelling therein, growing stage by stage.

What are called the five viscera and six bowels, the hundred bones and nine apertures, the four limbs and six sense organs, the tendons, bones, skin, and flesh—these gradually took shape until your emergence from the womb; all of these were impelled by the winds of karma.
Driven by the power of karma, you are unaware and unconscious of it; when has it ever been arranged by you?
Once born, you are nurtured until you reach thirty or forty years of age; then your hair turns white, your teeth waver, your face becomes yellowed, and your flesh grows emaciated.
You change gradually and grow old gradually. When the signs of aging appear, illness follows; once illness arrives, death comes. It is just like this.
Each of these transformations and decays does not depend on you; originally, you did not wish for things to be thus, yet how could you possibly control them?

Consider how, from birth until death, you have bestowed upon this stinking skin-bag so much affection and loyalty—preserving it in every way, cherishing it in every way, and providing for its medical treatment and arrangements in every way—and yet it...
To forget kindness and betray righteousness is enough to incur the hatred of others; how much more so when there are further grounds for such hatred?
Consider, for instance, the months of intense summer heat: suppose a robust and strong man suddenly meets with a fatal illness at the hour of dusk and dies.

Even one’s most intimate relatives and loved ones are not permitted to linger.
Viewed from this perspective, he who was still a robust man last evening becomes today, upon waking, but a handful of ashes.
Ashes. You know that his single conscious spirit has gone elsewhere; such a sudden transformation was not under your control.
Since it was your body, it ought to have been under your management. Since it was not under your management, how could you falsely claim it as your own?
You have merely suffered the consequences of this delusion, causing you to retreat from the Way and bringing misfortune upon your kin as well.
Indeed. Both you and I drag this stinking skin-bag; both are without freedom; neither can control the other.
When impermanence arrives, neither can substitute for the other. During our ordinary lives, we are entangled by a certain kind of affection, calling one another kin;
yet once the light of the eyes is closed, we no longer recognize one another. How can you be so deluded?
You recognize others as your kin, yet you are burdened by them and retreat from the resolve for the Way. It is the same with the "household fire" of your own home.

While your eyesight is clear and your feet are agile, you engage in scheming and management, guarding your possessions with stinginess, thinking that you will enjoy their benefits for hundreds of thousands of years.
Who would have known that when the vital breath does not return, not even a single hair’s breadth can be taken along? How can you delusively claim this as yours?
Your family is on fire. Because you have been burdened by others, you have retreated from the resolve for the Way and suffered much hardship. Who is it that causes this?
Now that everyone here has heard these words, you should immediately turn the light back upon yourselves to break through [this delusion]. Awaken yourselves with great urgency.
Regarding these three kinds of burdens, do not recognize them, do not cling to them, and do not crave them. Settle into your proper lot.
Let time pass naturally; you must then turn your mind back toward the matter of birth and death, exerting yourself with fierce vigor and diligence to reach a clear understanding.

Having cut his hair and altered his appearance, he retreated into the depths of the Snowy Mountains.

The boundless Flower Treasury Ocean worlds are his *saṃbhogakṣetra*. Inferring the cause from the fruit, because of this...

Had he remained in the royal palace, greedily clinging to the things before his eyes and unable to renounce them, how could he have obtained such sublime and magnificent rewards? This matter is [known to] everyone.

This is a matter within everyone's reach; if one exerts oneself, one can accomplish it without lacking even a single hair’s breadth. Those who fear falling into emptiness should reflect deeply upon this.

The root source. To attain a state of liberation, self-mastery, and stability for one’s person and livelihood—this is the purpose behind your request for a general discourse.

Father Xianggong has attained profound awakening to his own mind and entered the realm of the sages and worthies;

This is because they do not realize that while the physical death has occurred, there remains that which does not die. It is the luminous and numinous clarity of Chancellor Xianggong that is capable [of hearing].

When examined through ultimate principle, birth is fundamentally non-arising, and death is likewise not dying. Birth and death, coming and going, originally possess no self-nature, nor do they possess any substantial reality;
they are merely illusory appearances manifested through the following of karma. Therefore, the Way of the Teachings says: "Because..."
Through the conjunction of conditions, there is illusory birth; through the separation of causes and conditions, there is what is illusorily called extinction. To examine the origin of this birth:
it arises from the meeting of the three conditions—the father, the mother, and the self—termed their "conjunction," which generates an attraction based on shared karma (*karmasabhāga*).
Thereupon, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of earth, water, fire, and wind combine, and thus a body comes to be. At that moment, its clarity...
The brilliance of the numinous, capable of both discerning and awakening, resides within this interval. Since there is the physical form, there are the six sense organs.
Examining it from the perspective of that body: externally there are hair, fur, nails, and teeth; internally there are liver, gallbladder, intestines, and stomach.

These thirty-six components, internal, external, and intermediate, originally possess neither seeing nor hearing, nor do they possess cognition or awareness. It is because of my six sense organs and...

Those six sense-objects exist as mutual counterparts. Consequently, through the conjunction of the eye and form, there is the false perception of seeing; through the conjunction of the ear and sound, there is the false perception of hearing;

through the conjunction of the body and touch, there is the false perception of sensation; and through the conjunction of the mind and mental phenomena, there is the false perception of cognition. This seeing, hearing...
That which is experienced through smelling and perceiving is called the six consciousnesses; yet they originally possess no self-nature.
Rather, they arise as false existences within the sense organs and their objects due to the manifestation of that which is luminous and discerning.

From this, there arise various forms of discrimination, various recollections and thoughts, various defiled attachments, and various conditions of grasping; internally, they thus undergo transformations according to emotional states.

It migrates. Outwardly, it wanders through successive realms; inwardly, emotional consciousnesses interact and resonate, giving rise to one another. Thus, various kinds of false delusions arise, and various kinds of false karmas are created.

Consequently, the infinite retributions of birth and death—the cycles of suffering and pleasure, rising and sinking—within the twenty-five states of existence across the three realms, proceed from this without end. As for this illusory body composed of the four elements, it is...
Thought after thought, things pass away: from youth to old age, from old age to illness, and from illness to death. Death is merely the dispersal of the four great elements.
As for that which is luminous and numinous, how could it ever die? An ancient Buddha said: "The body receives birth from within the formless;

There is no abiding. Therefore, as soon as a man of resolve hears these words, he is able, within the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses, to illuminate and shatter the false conjunction of birth and death.

He realizes that circumstances, objects, afflictions, and karma are like illusions, like dreams, like shadows, like echoes, and like magical transformations. Once he can thus illuminate and shatter them, he will no longer follow after them.

Fundamentally, one must wait until a single thought does not arise, so that the boundaries of past and future are severed; only then can one be permitted to recognize the scenery of the original ground and behold one’s original face.

Once one has beheld the original faces of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one immediately beholds the original faces of all sentient beings.
The eyes are neither one with nor two from oneself; they are without distinction and without difference. Together, they are not mixed; separated, they are not divided.

Having reached this state, if you still harbor doubts and have not yet forgotten the "sage's vision," then that sage's vision remains unextinguished and you have not attained the ultimate. You must further strike [this point].
Leaping over the upper barrier and treading where the Buddhas and Patriarchs have not gone—this is the ultimate ground of non-doubt.
Once you reach this ultimate ground of non-doubt, they cannot cause you to be born; they cannot cause you to die;

It is attained. To go against it is impossible. There is no Buddha, no Patriarch, and no sentient beings;
there is neither ordinary nor holy, neither pure nor defiled, neither true nor conventional. All is non-existent.
This is called the great sovereignty of the single suchness of all phenomena, which is unmoving and unchanging. Although its essence does not change, its function follows conditions. For example:
The essence of empty space is not comprised of manifold characteristics, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those various characteristics.

Thus, through non-alteration while following conditions, it can become Buddhas, patriarchs, and all sentient beings—both animate and inanimate—and even become birth-and-death, nirvana, the ordinary, the sage, the pure, and the defiled.
Although it blazes with the activity of conditioned existence, its entire substance is quiescent.
Extinction. This is called the great sovereignty of dependent origination—birthless, unattached, and unimpeded.
Only upon reaching this point can one truly believe in the Way of the Patriarchs; that Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his servants is hardly an overstatement.

Listen, all you virtuous practitioners of dhyāna. The precepts are the vanguard of the six pāramitās, the foundation of the myriad practices, the root of the Buddhas’ attainment of the Way, and the method for the manifest conduct of Bodhisattvas.

Although the Buddha has taught immeasurable Dharma-gates and hundreds of thousands of wondrous meanings, when one examines their ultimate aim, they are none other than precept, concentration, and wisdom.
Therefore it is said: "To restrain the mind is the precept; from the precept arises concentration; from concentration issues forth..."
Wisdom. These are what are called the three trainings in the outflows-free (anāsrava). Among these three trainings, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the foremost and most essential matter.

However, my Bodhisattva Great Precepts were not first proclaimed by the present Buddha; rather, they are the fundamental precepts of all Buddhas of the past, transmitted and recited from one Buddha to the next.
This is because when the Buddhas were formerly in the stage of a Bodhisattva, they practiced these precepts.

Upon reaching the full stage of Buddhahood, at the very moment of attaining enlightenment, [the Buddha] immediately recites these precepts so that all Bodhisattvas may know what to cultivate and study.

Therefore, as soon as the World-Honored One Vairocana sat upon the lotus pedestal, he immediately recited the Bodhisattva precepts and transmitted them to the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis. The hundreds of thousands...

Eunuchs, male and female libertines, slaves, the eight classes of spirits and deities, *vajra* deities, animals, and even those who are transformed beings—provided they understand the Dharma Master’s words, all may receive the precepts; they are all called the foremost pure ones.
From the great Bodhisattvas above down to the foul, base, and lowly below, the holy and the mundane, the great and the small, are all gathered together in a single net.
This may be called a vast and expansive Dharma-gate. Some might say that among the ten grave precepts of a Bodhisattva, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are presented first.

For example, there are the Eight Precepts of the Fast (Aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) received by the ignorant laity, and the Upāsaka-precepts received by those who have recently entered the Buddha-dharma. As for those who have left the household life...

The ten śrāmaṇera precepts received by beginners and the precepts of the *Piṭaka* and other collections received by śrāvakas and arhats all take killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying as their fundamental roots.
Since the precepts they receive are identical, on what basis can one distinguish between "small" and "great"? It is simply that the precepts have no inherent size;
rather, smallness and greatness reside in the capacity of the practitioner. This is because [the distinction] arises from the way one generates the resolve and establishes oneself.
Because their vows differ, there consequently arise the distinctions between the various vehicles, both Great and Small.

For instance, when a Bodhisattva resolves to attain enlightenment and receives the precepts, they take the three clusters of pure conduct (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) as their fundamental principle and the fruit of Buddhahood as their goal. As for these three clusters: the first is the cluster of the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).
One generates the vast mind and vows to sever all evil; this is the second, the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas.
One generates the vast mind and vows to cultivate all goodness; this is the third, the precept of benefiting sentient beings. One generates the vast mind and vows to deliver all living beings.
Therefore, the ten grave precepts and others that one receives are not merely for the cessation of evil, but are dedicated to the cultivation of goodness. Whatever is severed...
Whether practicing evil or cultivating goodness, one must always prioritize the salvation of sentient beings as the primary task.

Regarding the Four Great Vows that one makes, even though one’s own afflictions have not yet been severed, the Dharma gates have not yet been studied, and the Buddha-way has not yet been perfected, one must nonetheless take the salvation of sentient beings as the foremost vow.
Therefore, a sutra says: "To seek first to save others before one has attained salvation oneself is the aspiration of a Bodhisattva. Thus it is called the "arousing of the mind" (bodhicitta).
This mind is that which, at all times and in all places, practices compassion toward all sentient beings;
it feels pity for all sentient beings, loves and cherishes all sentient beings, respects and honors all sentient beings, rescues and protects all sentient beings,
exhorts and inspires all sentient beings, guides all sentient beings, teaches and transforms all sentient beings, and gathers them in.

They take upon themselves all sentient beings, even unto the accomplishment of their deliverance; they desire nothing less than to lead them to the unsurpassed enlightenment before they themselves cease.
The resolve they have generated is not only vast, but furthermore, they have made a solemn vow for an eternity, swearing:
"From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the reaches of the future, in every lifetime I shall constantly practice as a Bodhisattva."
This is the Way. Because it is able to give rise to such a far-reaching and vast mind, it is called the Bodhisattva-mind.
To initiate practice based on this mind is termed Bodhisattva-conduct. To maintain the precepts by means of this mind constitutes the supreme Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-precepts.
How much more so when the myriad practices are fully encompassed within the three aggregates of the precepts, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The gateway of causes is fully present within a single thought-moment. Now, regarding that which takes the three aggregates as its principle, there are both the aspect of principle and the aspect of phenomena.
As for phenomena, one restrains the three karmas so that evil ceases and goodness is practiced; as for principle, one governs the single mind so that delusion perishes and wisdom is established.

When evil ceases and wholesome conduct is practiced, the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) can be shattered. When delusion perishes and wisdom is established, the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is forever abandoned.
When the obstruction of karma is shattered, merit is perfected; when the obstruction of afflictions is abandoned, wisdom is fulfilled. This is the ultimate purport:

to abandon the two obstructions and achieve the two adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*). To discuss this in detail: by means of the three categories of the fundamental [teachings], one increases the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) and achieves...

Regarding the stages of the three worthies and ten sages, it ultimately brings about the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood—the unimpeded realization of the three virtues and three bodies. As for these three virtues and three bodies:
first, through the observance of discipline (*śīla*) and the elimination of faults, the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is manifested as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

second, through the gathering and cultivation of myriad virtues, the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is perfected as the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); and third, through the benefiting of sentient beings, the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*) is perfected as the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This is the teaching.

Within it, it is said: "A bodhisattva who first cultivates the Mahāyāna practices and the Bodhisattva precepts, although not yet having attained Buddhahood, first obtains five kinds of merit and eight kinds of excellence. The benefits thereof are inconceivable.
